17. Low-level CUDA and C++ optimizations

Training and inference speed often come from CUDA kernels (custom or library), kernel fusion, efficient matmuls, and memory layout. PyTorch uses cuDNN/cuBLAS under the hood; you can add custom ops or drop to C/CUDA (e.g. llm.c) for full control.

Concepts and techniques

  • Matmul and cuBLAS/cuBLASLt – Most FLOPs are in matrix multiplies. cuBLASLt offers flexible matmul + fused bias/activation (e.g. matmul + bias + GELU in one pass). TF32 on Ampere+ gives near-FP32 precision with higher throughput.
  • Kernel fusion – Combine several small kernels (e.g. softmax + mask + scale, or linear + GELU) into one to reduce global memory traffic and launch overhead. Flash Attention fuses attention score → softmax → × value and uses tiling to cut memory.
  • CUDA graphs – Record a sequence of kernel launches and replay them with one CPU call. Cuts launch latency and improves GPU utilization; useful for fixed-shape training steps or inference.
  • Custom CUDA kernels – Loop unrolling, coalesced memory access, warp-level primitives, and shared memory for hand-tuned ops (e.g. backward bias, softmax). Target high % of peak compute or memory bandwidth.
  • Memory optimization – Activation checkpointing (recompute activations in backward to save memory); pinned host memory and async copies for data loading; avoiding unnecessary syncs.
  • C++ / CUDA extensions in PyTorch – torch.utils.cpp_extension or load_inline to compile and load custom kernels; JIT or AOT.

Where these show up (PyTorch vs raw C/CUDA)

# PyTorch: use fused/custom kernels via libraries or torch.compile
# Flash Attention (fused attention kernel) - often via optional dependency
# pip install flash-attn; then in model use flash_attn_func or equivalent
from flash_attn import flash_attn_func
# q,k,v: (B, T, n_heads, head_dim); output replaces attn @ v with one fused kernel
out = flash_attn_func(q, k, v, causal=True)

# Activation checkpointing: trade compute for memory (recompute in backward)
from torch.utils.checkpoint import checkpoint
def forward(self, x):
    x = self.attn(checkpoint(self.ln1, x))  # ln1 recomputed in backward
    x = x + self.mlp(checkpoint(self.ln2, x))
    return x

# TF32 matmuls on Ampere+ (PyTorch)
torch.backends.cuda.matmul.allow_tf32 = True
torch.backends.cudnn.allow_tf32 = True
// Raw C/CUDA (llm.c style): custom kernel for matmul + bias backward
// Fused: one kernel does bias gradient from output gradient (no separate pass)
__global__ void matmul_backward_bias_kernel(const float* dout, float* dbias, int M, int N) {
    // Coalesced reads, warp reductions, minimal casts for 7–8% speedup
    int row = blockIdx.x * blockDim.x + threadIdx.x;
    if (row < N) {
        float sum = 0.0f;
        for (int i = threadIdx.x; i < M; i += blockDim.x)
            sum += dout[i * N + row];
        dbias[row] = sum;
    }
}
// cuBLASLt: matmul + fused bias + GELU in one call (llm.c PR ~2x perf)

Where to see it

  • llm.c – Pure C/CUDA training: dev/cuda kernels, cuBLASLt, TF32, CUDA graphs, kernel fusion (~2×), matmul_backward_bias_kernel (7–8% speedup), fused classifier, streams. A100 perf analysis.
  • nanoGPT – Optional Flash Attention; relies on PyTorch/cuDNN for matmuls and fused ops.
  • nanochat – Uses Flash Attention 3 and modern kernels where available.
  • PyTorch custom ops – C++/CUDA extension tutorial; torch.utils.cpp_extension.load_inline for JIT-compiled kernels.

18. Vision, audio, multimodal & other models

PyTorch syntax commonly used for vision (CNNs, ViT), audio, multimodal (vision+language, etc.), and basic/advanced ML (MLPs, RNNs, embeddings). The Karpathy repos in this tutorial focus on LLMs; the building blocks below appear in torchvision, torchaudio, and multimodal codebases.

Vision: convolutions, pooling, BatchNorm, pretrained

Core layers

  • Conv2d(in_c, out_c, kernel_size, stride, padding) – 2D convolution over images. Input shape (B, C, H, W); output (B, out_c, H', W'). kernel_size=3, padding=1 keeps spatial size when stride=1.
  • MaxPool2d(kernel_size, stride) – Downsamples by taking max in each window. Often kernel_size=2, stride=2 → half H and W.
  • BatchNorm2d(num_features) – Normalizes each channel across the batch (zero mean, unit var); stabilizes training. Use model.eval() at inference so it uses running stats.
  • AdaptiveAvgPool2d(output_size) – Pools to a fixed size (e.g. (1, 1)) so you can flatten to a vector regardless of input resolution.
import torch.nn as nn

# Simple CNN: conv -> relu -> pool -> flatten -> linear
class SmallCNN(nn.Module):
    def __init__(self):
        super().__init__()
        self.conv1 = nn.Conv2d(3, 32, 3, padding=1)   # (B,3,H,W) -> (B,32,H,W)
        self.pool = nn.MaxPool2d(2, 2)               # -> (B,32,H/2,W/2)
        self.conv2 = nn.Conv2d(32, 64, 3, padding=1)
        self.bn = nn.BatchNorm2d(64)
        self.adapt = nn.AdaptiveAvgPool2d((1, 1))   # -> (B,64,1,1)
        self.fc = nn.Linear(64, num_classes)

    def forward(self, x):
        x = self.pool(nn.functional.relu(self.conv1(x)))
        x = self.adapt(nn.functional.relu(self.bn(self.conv2(x))))
        return self.fc(x.flatten(1))

Transforms & torchvision

from torchvision import transforms
from torchvision.models import resnet18, ResNet18_Weights

# Image preprocessing: resize, normalize to ImageNet stats
transform = transforms.Compose([
    transforms.Resize((224, 224)),
    transforms.ToTensor(),
    transforms.Normalize(mean=[0.485, 0.456, 0.406], std=[0.229, 0.224, 0.225]),
])
img_tensor = transform(pil_image)  # (3, 224, 224)

# Pretrained ResNet: replace classifier head for your num_classes
model = resnet18(weights=ResNet18_Weights.IMAGENET1K_V1)
model.fc = nn.Linear(model.fc.in_features, num_classes)

Audio: 1D conv, spectrograms, torchaudio

  • Conv1d – Convolution over time (or frequency). Input (B, C, T); used for raw waveform or spectrogram frames.
  • Spectrograms – Short-time Fourier transform (STFT) turns waveform into (time, freq) representation; often then mel filterbank → mel spectrogram. Models often take mel specs as input.
import torchaudio
import torchaudio.transforms as T

# Waveform (B, 1, samples) -> mel spectrogram (B, n_mels, time)
mel_spec = T.MelSpectrogram(sample_rate=16000, n_fft=400, hop_length=160, n_mels=80)
mel = mel_spec(waveform)  # (B, 80, T)

# Or load audio and resample
waveform, sr = torchaudio.load("clip.wav")
waveform = T.Resample(sr, 16000)(waveform)

Multimodal: two encoders, projection, fusion

Combine vision and text (or audio and text): encode each modality, project to a shared dimension, then fuse (concat, add, or cross-attention).

# Minimal vision–language: image encoder -> vector; text encoder -> vector; fuse
class VisionLanguageEncoder(nn.Module):
    def __init__(self, vision_dim=512, text_dim=768, hidden_dim=256):
        super().__init__()
        self.vision_encoder = resnet18(weights=...)
        self.vision_encoder.fc = nn.Linear(512, hidden_dim)
        self.text_proj = nn.Linear(text_dim, hidden_dim)  # e.g. from transformer last hidden

    def forward(self, image, text_embeds):
        img_feat = self.vision_encoder(image)           # (B, hidden_dim)
        text_feat = self.text_proj(text_embeds)         # (B, T, hidden_dim) or (B, hidden_dim)
        # Fusion: concat and classify, or cosine similarity for retrieval
        return img_feat, text_feat

# Cross-attention: query from one modality, key/value from the other
# q = text_proj(text_hidden); k, v = vision_proj(vision_patches); attn_out = attention(q, k, v)

Basic ML: Sequential, Dropout, activations, losses

  • nn.Sequential – Stacks layers; forward is apply each in order. Good for simple feedforward stacks.
  • nn.Dropout(p) – Randomly zeros elements with probability p (during train); scaled by 1/(1-p) so expectation unchanged. Disabled in eval().
  • Activations – F.relu, F.gelu, F.silu (Swish), F.sigmoid (0–1), F.softmax(dim=-1) for probabilities.
  • Losses – F.mse_loss(pred, target) regression; F.binary_cross_entropy_with_logits(pred, target) binary classification (pred = logits, no sigmoid); F.cross_entropy multi-class (see glossary).
mlp = nn.Sequential(
    nn.Linear(784, 256),
    nn.ReLU(),
    nn.Dropout(0.2),
    nn.Linear(256, 10),
)
loss = F.mse_loss(pred, target)   # regression
loss = F.binary_cross_entropy_with_logits(logits, target.float())  # binary

Embeddings & RNNs

  • nn.Embedding(num_embeddings, embedding_dim) – Lookup table: integer indices → vectors. Input shape (B, T) of long indices; output (B, T, embedding_dim). Used for token/word IDs.
  • nn.LSTM / nn.GRU – Recurrent layers. Input (T, B, C) or (B, T, C) with batch_first=True; output hidden state and optionally cell (LSTM). Good for sequential data before transformers dominated.
embed = nn.Embedding(vocab_size, 256)
lstm = nn.LSTM(256, 128, batch_first=True, bidirectional=False)
x = embed(token_ids)    # (B, T, 256)
out, (h_n, c_n) = lstm(x)  # out: (B, T, 128), h_n: (1, B, 128)

LayerNorm, residual, ViT-style patches

  • nn.LayerNorm(normalized_shape) – Normalizes over last dimension(s). For (B, T, C) use LayerNorm(C). Often used in transformer blocks (pre-norm).
  • Residual – x = x + sublayer(x) or x = x + sublayer(norm(x)). Helps gradient flow in deep nets.
  • ViT (Vision Transformer) – Split image into patches; flatten each patch to a vector; add position embeddings; feed to standard transformer. nn.Conv2d(in_c, embed_dim, kernel_size=patch_size, stride=patch_size) can create patch embeddings.
# Patch embedding for ViT: (B, 3, 224, 224) -> (B, num_patches, embed_dim)
patch_embed = nn.Conv2d(3, 768, kernel_size=16, stride=16)  # 224/16 = 14 -> 196 patches
x = patch_embed(img).flatten(2).transpose(1, 2)  # (B, 196, 768)
x = x + pos_embedding
# Then transformer blocks (attention + MLP with LayerNorm and residual)

Where to look (outside Karpathy repos)

  • Vision – torchvision models (ResNet, ViT, etc.); transforms.
  • Audio – torchaudio (transforms, models, datasets).
  • Multimodal – Hugging Face transformers (CLIP, LLaVA, etc.); OpenCLIP.

19. Model approaches: modeling and evaluating different problems

Different problems need different outputs, losses, and evaluation metrics. This section maps problem types to modeling choices and how to evaluate them.

Problem Model output Loss Evaluation
Multi-class classification (one label per example) Logits (B, C) or logits per token (B, T, C) F.cross_entropy(logits, targets) Accuracy, top-k accuracy; precision/recall/F1 per class; confusion matrix; ROC-AUC (if binary or one-vs-rest).
Multi-label classification (multiple labels per example) Logits (B, C); each position is independent binary F.binary_cross_entropy_with_logits(logits, targets.float()) with targets (B, C) in {0,1}. Subset accuracy; macro/micro F1; precision@k; average precision per label.
Regression Continuous (B, out_dim) F.mse_loss(pred, target) or F.l1_loss (MAE); Huber for robustness. MSE, RMSE, MAE; R²; MAPE if scale matters.
Sequence / language modeling (next-token prediction) Logits (B, T, V); predict next token at each position F.cross_entropy(logits.view(-1,V), labels.view(-1), ignore_index=pad_id) Perplexity (exp(mean CE)); bits per byte; downstream: accuracy on benchmarks (MMLU, GSM8K, etc.), human eval.
Retrieval / embedding similarity Embeddings (B, D); similarity = dot product or cosine Contrastive: InfoNCE / cross-entropy over batch (positive pair, negatives = rest of batch); triplet loss. Recall@k, MRR, NDCG; accuracy when retrieval is used for classification (e.g. k-NN).
Ranking / learning to rank Score per item (B, n_items) or per (query, doc) pair Pairwise: BCE on (score_i − score_j) vs label; listwise: ListNet, LambdaRank; pointwise: MSE/CE on relevance. NDCG, MAP, MRR; precision/recall at k.
Reinforcement learning (policy learning) Logits over actions or log prob of chosen action; value head optional Policy gradient: −log_prob * advantage; PPO: clipped objective + KL; DPO: preference loss (no reward model). Average return, success rate; for LLM RL: reward model score, preference win rate, downstream task accuracy.
Segmentation (pixel-wise label) Logits (B, C, H, W) per pixel class F.cross_entropy over spatial dims (reshape to (B*H*W, C) and labels (B*H*W)); or dice / focal for imbalance. mIoU (mean intersection over union), pixel accuracy, Dice; per-class IoU.
Object detection Boxes (bbox) + class logits per proposal or per anchor Classification (CE) + box regression (L1/smooth L1); matching (e.g. Hungarian) for set prediction (DETR). mAP (mean average precision) at IoU thresholds; COCO AP@.5, AP@.5:.95.

Choosing the right setup

  • Single label from fixed set → Multi-class: linear (or MLP) head with num_classes outputs, cross_entropy, accuracy.
  • Multiple non-exclusive labels → Multi-label: same head but BCE per class; macro F1 if classes are imbalanced.
  • Predict a number → Regression: linear head, MSE or MAE; eval with RMSE and R².
  • Generate text / sequence → Next-token CE; eval with perplexity and task-specific benchmarks.
  • Match or retrieve → Embeddings + contrastive loss; eval with Recall@k and NDCG.
  • Order matters (search, recommendation) → Ranking loss (pairwise or listwise); NDCG/MAP.
  • Agent / policy → RL loss (PPO, DPO, etc.); eval with return or downstream success.

PyTorch snippets for evaluation

# Accuracy (multi-class)
pred = logits.argmax(dim=-1)
acc = (pred == targets).float().mean().item()

# Precision / recall / F1 (binary or per-class)
from sklearn.metrics import precision_recall_fscore_support, confusion_matrix
p, r, f1, _ = precision_recall_fscore_support(y_true, y_pred, average="macro")

# Regression: RMSE, R²
rmse = torch.sqrt(F.mse_loss(pred, target)).item()
# R² = 1 - SS_res / SS_tot

# Retrieval: recall@k (for each query, is the true item in top k?)
# sim = embeddings @ embeddings.T; for each row, argsort desc; check if gt in top k

# Perplexity (language)
mean_ce = total_loss / total_tokens
perplexity = math.exp(mean_ce)

Summary

Match the output shape and loss to the problem (classification → CE; regression → MSE; multi-label → BCE; sequence → CE with ignore_index). Then choose metrics that reflect your goal (accuracy, F1, NDCG, perplexity, mAP, etc.) and compute them on a held-out set or benchmark.

Quick reference – repo → PyTorch features

Repo PyTorch features

Hugging Face Transformers – Architecture Study Guide

This guide compares model architectures as implemented under src/transformers/models/ in the Hugging Face Transformers library. It anchors on the original Vaswani et al. Transformer, then explains what was removed, changed, or added in landmark families and why. Code blocks are simplified teaching sketches (structure faithful to typical HF code; class names and line numbers may differ by release).

Note: Newer Transformers versions may split logic into modular_*.py files. Always check both modeling_*.py and modular_*.py for your installed version.
Table of contents
  1. Baseline: original Transformer blocks
    1. Building-block code (LN, FFN, MHA, causal, cross)
    2. Call graph (how §1.1 stacks)
  2. Three common forks in practice
  3. Taxonomy tables + pattern code
  4. Curated architecture comparisons
  5. How to read any model in the repo
  6. Worked examples (stitched code paths)
  7. References

1. Baseline: original Transformer (Vaswani et al.)

The paper defines an encoder stack and a decoder stack. Each encoder layer has multi-head self-attention (bidirectional over the source), then a position-wise FFN, with residuals and layer normalization (exact norm placement varies by implementation; the paper uses post-LN). Each decoder layer adds masked self-attention (causal) and cross-attention to encoder outputs. Positions use sinusoidal encodings added to embeddings.

Encoder layer (calls §1.1; post-norm like original paper)

def encoder_layer(x, pad_mask, n_heads, ln1_g, ln1_b, ln2_g, ln2_b, attn, ff):
    # x: (batch, seq, dim); pad_mask: optional additive mask for padding (see §1.1)
    h = multi_head_self_attention(x, attn, n_heads, attn_mask=pad_mask)
    x = layer_norm(x + h, ln1_g, ln1_b)
    h = feed_forward(x, ff)
    return layer_norm(x + h, ln2_g, ln2_b)

Decoder layer (same primitives + causal self-attn + cross-attn)

def decoder_layer(x, encoder_out, causal, enc_key_pad_mask, n_heads,
                  ln1_g, ln1_b, ln2_g, ln2_b, ln3_g, ln3_b, self_attn, cross_attn, ff):
    # causal: (1,1,T_dec,T_dec) from causal_mask(); enc_key_pad_mask: mask encoder keys (pads)
    h = masked_multi_head_self_attention(x, self_attn, n_heads, causal, extra_mask=None)
    x = layer_norm(x + h, ln1_g, ln1_b)
    h = multi_head_cross_attention(x, encoder_out, cross_attn, n_heads, attn_mask=enc_key_pad_mask)
    x = layer_norm(x + h, ln2_g, ln2_b)
    h = feed_forward(x, ff)
    return layer_norm(x + h, ln3_g, ln3_b)

1.1 Building-block implementations (stacked references)

These snippets are minimal PyTorch-style sketches. Order matches dependency: layer_norm and feed_forward are independent; attention builds on a shared _scaled_dot_product_attention; multi_head_self_attention is used by the encoder; masked_multi_head_self_attention wraps it with a causal mask; multi_head_cross_attention reuses the same MHA core with Q from the decoder and K,V from encoder memory.

(1) layer_norm — normalize over hidden dim (post-norm residual path)

import math
import torch
import torch.nn.functional as F

def layer_norm(x, gamma, beta, eps=1e-5):
    """x: (batch, seq, dim). gamma, beta: (dim,) — learnable scale & shift."""
    mean = x.mean(dim=-1, keepdim=True)
    var = x.var(dim=-1, unbiased=False, keepdim=True)
    x_hat = (x - mean) / torch.sqrt(var + eps)
    return gamma * x_hat + beta

(2) feed_forward — two linear layers with nonlinearity (position-wise)

def feed_forward(x, ff):
    """ff holds weights/bias for W1: dim→ff_dim and W2: ff_dim→dim."""
    h = F.linear(x, ff.w1, ff.b1)
    h = F.gelu(h)  # paper used ReLU; BERT/GPT often GELU
    return F.linear(h, ff.w2, ff.b2)

(3) Shared core — split heads, merge heads, scaled dot-product

def _split_heads(t, n_heads):
    """(B, T, D) → (B, n_heads, T, d_head) where D = n_heads * d_head"""
    B, T, D = t.shape
    d_head = D // n_heads
    t = t.view(B, T, n_heads, d_head).transpose(1, 2)
    return t

def _merge_heads(t):
    """(B, n_heads, T, d_head) → (B, T, D)"""
    B, H, T, dh = t.shape
    return t.transpose(1, 2).contiguous().view(B, T, H * dh)

def _scaled_dot_product_attention(q, k, v, attn_mask=None):
    """q,k,v: (B, n_heads, T_q or T_k, d_head). attn_mask: broadcastable, additive (0 or -inf)."""
    d_head = q.size(-1)
    scores = torch.matmul(q, k.transpose(-2, -1)) / math.sqrt(d_head)
    if attn_mask is not None:
        scores = scores + attn_mask
    weights = F.softmax(scores, dim=-1)
    return torch.matmul(weights, v)

(4) multi_head_self_attention — Q, K, V all from x (encoder / bidirectional)

def multi_head_self_attention(x, attn, n_heads, attn_mask=None):
    """attn: packed Q/K/V output projections + output projection W_o."""
    B, T, D = x.shape
    q = F.linear(x, attn.w_q, attn.b_q)
    k = F.linear(x, attn.w_k, attn.b_k)
    v = F.linear(x, attn.w_v, attn.b_v)
    q, k, v = _split_heads(q, n_heads), _split_heads(k, n_heads), _split_heads(v, n_heads)
    # Optional padding mask as (B,1,1,T) large negative at pad positions
    ctx = _scaled_dot_product_attention(q, k, v, attn_mask=attn_mask)
    ctx = _merge_heads(ctx)
    return F.linear(ctx, attn.w_o, attn.b_o)

(5) masked_multi_head_self_attention — same as (4) + causal mask

def causal_mask(T, device, dtype):
    """Additive mask: allowed=0, disallowed=-inf (upper triangle). Shape (1,1,T,T)."""
    m = torch.triu(torch.full((T, T), float("-inf"), device=device, dtype=dtype), diagonal=1)
    return m.view(1, 1, T, T)

def masked_multi_head_self_attention(x, attn, n_heads, causal_only_mask, extra_mask=None):
    """Decoder self-attn: causal_only_mask from causal_mask(T,...); add padding via extra_mask."""
    mask = causal_only_mask
    if extra_mask is not None:
        mask = mask + extra_mask  # combine padding + causal
    return multi_head_self_attention(x, attn, n_heads, attn_mask=mask)

(6) multi_head_cross_attention — Q from decoder state, K,V from encoder memory

def multi_head_cross_attention(x, memory, attn, n_heads, attn_mask=None):
    """x: (B, T_dec, D); memory: (B, T_enc, D). attn_mask often masks pad keys (enc padding)."""
    q = F.linear(x, attn.w_q, attn.b_q)
    k = F.linear(memory, attn.w_k, attn.b_k)
    v = F.linear(memory, attn.w_v, attn.b_v)
    q, k, v = _split_heads(q, n_heads), _split_heads(k, n_heads), _split_heads(v, n_heads)
    ctx = _scaled_dot_product_attention(q, k, v, attn_mask=attn_mask)
    ctx = _merge_heads(ctx)
    return F.linear(ctx, attn.w_o, attn.b_o)

1.2 Call graph (how the pieces stack)

Encoder layer (top of §1) = multi_head_self_attention → residual → layer_norm → feed_forward → residual → layer_norm. Decoder layer = masked_multi_head_self_attention (wraps multi_head_self_attention + causal mask) → layer_norm → multi_head_cross_attention (same _scaled_dot_product_attention core, different Q/K/V sources) → layer_norm → feed_forward → layer_norm.

# Dependency summary (all defined in §1.1):
# layer_norm ─────────────────────────────┐
# feed_forward ──────────────────────────┤ used by encoder & decoder layers
# multi_head_self_attention ──────────────┤
#    ↑ called by masked_multi_head_self_attention
# multi_head_cross_attention ─────────────┘ (shares _scaled_dot_product_attention with self-attn)

Hugging Face does not expose one single class as “the baseline” for all models. Instead, each folder under models/ implements a paper’s variant. Use §1.1–1.2 as the mental diff target when reading HF models/.

2. Three common forks in practice

ForkTypical useHF exemplar folders
Encoder-onlyUnderstanding, classification, embeddingsbert, roberta, deberta_v2
Decoder-onlyCausal LM, chat, completiongpt2, llama, mistral, opt
Encoder–decoderSeq2seq: translation, summarization, ASRt5, bart, pegasus, whisper

What “forking” removes (sketch)

# Encoder-only: keep encoder_stack; no decoder, no cross_attn
def forward(input_ids):
    x = embed(input_ids) + position_embed
    for layer in encoder_layers:
        x = encoder_layer(x)
    return pool_or_sequence_output(x)

# Decoder-only: keep decoder blocks with causal self-attn only (no cross_attn)
def forward(input_ids):
    x = embed(input_ids) + position_embed
    for layer in decoder_layers:
        x = decoder_layer_causal_only(x, causal_mask)
    return lm_head(x)

# Encoder-decoder: both stacks; decoder has cross_attn to encoder hidden states
def forward(encoder_ids, decoder_ids):
    enc = run_encoder(encoder_ids)
    dec = run_decoder(decoder_ids, encoder_hidden_states=enc)
    return lm_head(dec)

3. Taxonomy tables + pattern code

3.1 Backbone topology

TopologyPurposeExamples
Encoder-onlyBidirectional context for NLUbert, roberta, deberta_v2
Decoder-onlyAutoregressive generationgpt2, llama, opt
Encoder–decoderConditional generationt5, bart, whisper
Dual encodersAlign modalities / contrastive trainingclip
Vision encoder + (optional) textImages as token sequencesvit, swin

3.2 Positions & length

PatternPurposeExamples
Learned absolute embeddingsSimple; fixed max lengthbert, gpt2
Sinusoidal (fixed)Original paper; extrapolation limitedConceptual baseline
RoPE (rotary)Relative structure in Q/K; common in LLMsllama, mistral
Relative bias / position bucketLength generalization in enc-dect5
Local + global / sparseLong documents without full O(n²) everywherelongformer, big_bird

RoPE idea (applied to Q and K after projection)

# Simplified: rotate pairs of dimensions of q, k by position-dependent angles
def apply_rotary_pos_emb(q, k, cos, sin):
    # q, k: (batch, heads, seq, head_dim)
    # cos, sin: broadcastable to q, k
    q_embed = (q * cos) + (rotate_half(q) * sin)
    k_embed = (k * cos) + (rotate_half(k) * sin)
    return q_embed, k_embed

3.3 Normalization & MLP

PatternPurposeExamples
Post-LN (norm after residual)Original Transformer styleSome older stacks
Pre-LN (norm before sublayer)Often more stable deep traininggpt2, llama, many modern models
RMSNormFaster than LayerNorm; no mean centeringllama, mistral
GELU MLPSmooth activation; BERT/GPT-era defaultbert, gpt2
SwiGLU MLPTwo gated linear paths; strong empirical perfllama, mistral

SwiGLU MLP (compare to single-gate FFN)

class SwiGLU(nn.Module):
    def __init__(self, dim, hidden_dim):
        super().__init__()
        self.gate_proj = nn.Linear(dim, hidden_dim, bias=False)
        self.up_proj = nn.Linear(dim, hidden_dim, bias=False)
        self.down_proj = nn.Linear(hidden_dim, dim, bias=False)

    def forward(self, x):
        return self.down_proj(F.silu(self.gate_proj(x)) * self.up_proj(x))

3.4 Attention variants

VariantPurposeExamples
Multi-head attention (MHA)Full rank per headbert, gpt2
Grouped-query attention (GQA)Fewer K/V heads; less KV cache memoryllama (many checkpoints), mistral
Sliding / local windowLong sequences with bounded attentionmistral (windowed layers)
Cross-attentionDecoder conditions on encodert5, bart, whisper

GQA: same Q heads, repeat/slice K,V heads

# Conceptual: num_heads=32, num_key_value_heads=8
# After projecting K,V with 8 heads, expand/repeat to 32 for attention broadcast
def repeat_kv(hidden_states, n_rep):
    if n_rep == 1:
        return hidden_states
    batch, num_kv_heads, slen, head_dim = hidden_states.shape
    hidden_states = hidden_states[:, :, None, :, :].expand(batch, num_kv_heads, n_rep, slen, head_dim)
    return hidden_states.reshape(batch, num_kv_heads * n_rep, slen, head_dim)

4. Curated architecture comparisons

Each block: HF module path, vs parent, removed / changed / added, purpose, plus inline code.

BERT (models/bert/)

Vs full Transformer: encoder-only.

  • Removed: entire decoder; cross-attention; autoregressive head (replaced by MLM/NSP training heads in original BERT).
  • Changed: self-attention is bidirectional (no causal mask on encoder).
  • Added: [CLS], [SEP]; token type / segment embeddings; learned position embeddings.
  • Purpose: Deep contextual representations for NLU; sentence-pair tasks via types.
# Embedding sum typical of BERT-style models
def embed_bert(input_ids, token_type_ids):
    tok = word_embeddings(input_ids)
    pos = position_embeddings(position_ids)  # learned table
    seg = token_type_embeddings(token_type_ids)
    return layer_norm(tok + pos + seg)

# No causal mask in self-attention for standard BERT encoder
# attn_scores visible to full sequence (plus padding mask only)

RoBERTa (models/roberta/)

Vs BERT: same encoder architecture family; training recipe differs.

  • Removed: NSP objective (next sentence prediction) in the RoBERTa recipe.
  • Changed: dynamic masking, larger batches, byte-level BPE—mostly training, not a new layer type.
  • Purpose: Better NLU with simpler objectives and more data/compute.
# Modeling stack mirrors BERT-like encoder; difference is not a new op:
# RoBERTaForMaskedLM(...) still uses RobertaEmbeddings + RobertaLayer x L
# Key idea: only MLM (and sometimes sequence-level tasks), no NSP loss in RoBERTa pretraining

GPT-2 (models/gpt2/)

Vs full Transformer: decoder-only.

  • Removed: encoder; cross-attention.
  • Changed: causal self-attention; pre-LayerNorm stack in GPT-2.
  • Added: learned position embeddings; single LM head tied or untied to embeddings.
  • Purpose: Unconditional and conditional text generation via left-to-right modeling.
def causal_attention_mask(seq_len, device):
    # prevent attending to future positions
    mask = torch.full((seq_len, seq_len), float("-inf"), device=device)
    mask = torch.triu(mask, diagonal=1)
    return mask  # added to logits before softmax

def gpt2_block(x, attn, mlp, ln_1, ln_2):
    x = x + attn(ln_1(x))   # pre-norm
    x = x + mlp(ln_2(x))
    return x

T5 (models/t5/)

Vs vanilla Transformer: still encoder–decoder, but relative position biases inside attention and text-to-text framing.

  • Changed: position info often via learned bias per head and relative bucket (not additive sinusoidal on embeddings only).
  • Added: task prefixes as text (“translate: …”)—data/API convention; architecture is seq2seq.
  • Purpose: Unified supervised objective across many NLP tasks.
# Conceptual: attention logits get a bias from relative position bucket
scores = (q @ k.transpose(-1, -2)) / math.sqrt(d)
scores = scores + compute_bias(relative_position_bucket)  # shape broadcast to scores
probs = softmax(scores, dim=-1)

BART (models/bart/)

Vs T5: also encoder–decoder; BART uses Transformer-style absolute sinusoidal or learned configs depending on variant; denoising pretraining (corrupt document, reconstruct).

  • Changed: Encoder is often bidirectional; decoder is autoregressive with cross-attn—classic seq2seq Transformer pattern.
  • Purpose: Strong seq2seq for summarization, dialogue, etc., with denoising objective.
def bart_forward(encoder_ids, decoder_ids, encoder_padding_mask):
    enc = encoder(input_ids=encoder_ids, attention_mask=encoder_padding_mask)
    dec = decoder(
        input_ids=decoder_ids,
        encoder_hidden_states=enc.last_hidden_state,
        encoder_attention_mask=encoder_padding_mask,
    )
    return dec.last_hidden_state

DistilBERT (models/distilbert/)

Vs BERT: shallower (fewer layers), knowledge distillation from a teacher BERT.

  • Removed: token type embeddings in DistilBERT (single sentence); pooler for NSP not used same way.
  • Changed: ~half the layers; smaller/faster inference.
  • Purpose: Speed and size with minimal accuracy drop.
# Fewer Transformer layers; same per-layer pattern as BERT-like encoder
# Student forward matches teacher logits/hidden states during distillation (training)
for i in range(config.num_hidden_layers):  # e.g. 6 vs 12
    hidden_states = transformer_layer(hidden_states, attn_mask)

OPT (models/opt/)

Vs GPT-2: decoder-only LM; similar pre-norm and learned positions; scales to larger models.

  • Changed: architecture details (layer norm epsilon, init, bias flags) per OPT config.
  • Purpose: Open reproduction of large decoder LMs.
# OPTDecoderLayer: self-attn + FFN, residual, LayerNorm before each sublayer
def opt_decoder_layer(hidden_states, attention_mask, layer):
    residual = hidden_states
    hidden_states = layer.self_attn_layer_norm(hidden_states)
    hidden_states, _ = layer.self_attn(hidden_states, attention_mask=attention_mask)
    hidden_states = residual + hidden_states
    residual = hidden_states
    hidden_states = layer.final_layer_norm(hidden_states)
    hidden_states = layer.fc1(hidden_states)
    hidden_states = activation_fn(hidden_states)
    hidden_states = layer.fc2(hidden_states)
    return residual + hidden_states

DeBERTa / DeBERTa-v2 (models/deberta, deberta_v2)

Vs BERT: encoder-only but disentangled attention (separate content vs relative position) and enhanced mask decoder in v2.

  • Added: relative position as separate keys; content-to-relative interaction.
  • Changed: v2 uses convolution or bucketed structures in some components (see config); stronger on long contexts and GLUE-style tasks.
  • Purpose: Richer pairwise modeling than standard dot-product + absolute positions only.
# Conceptual disentangled idea: two streams for c (content) and r (relative)
# Attention scores combine interactions between content and relative position embeddings
scores = (
    (q_c @ k_c.transpose(-1, -2))
    + (q_c @ k_r.transpose(-1, -2))
    + (q_r @ k_c.transpose(-1, -2))
    + (q_r @ k_r.transpose(-1, -2))
) / math.sqrt(d)

ViT (models/vit/)

Vs NLP Transformer: images → patch tokens; encoder stack; CLS or pooling for classification.

  • Removed: decoder (for classification ViT); no text tokenizer.
  • Added: Patch embedding (Conv2d with stride = patch size); optional [CLS] token.
  • Purpose: Apply Transformer to vision without hand-crafted CNN stem (still patch projection).
def patchify(images, patch_size, proj):  # images: (B, 3, H, W)
    # Conv2d(in_ch, dim, kernel=patch_size, stride=patch_size) -> (B, dim, H', W')
    x = proj(images)
    x = x.flatten(2).transpose(1, 2)  # (B, num_patches, dim)
    return x

def vit_encoder(x, cls_token, pos_embed, layers):
    x = torch.cat([cls_token.expand(x.size(0), -1, -1), x], dim=1)
    x = x + pos_embed
    for layer in layers:
        x = layer(x)
    return x

Swin (models/swin/)

Vs ViT: hierarchical feature maps + shifted window self-attention.

  • Added: attention inside local windows; cyclic shift across blocks for cross-window connections.
  • Changed: patch merging stages reduce resolution → CNN-like pyramid.
  • Purpose: Linear-ish complexity in image size vs global ViT attention cost.
def window_partition(x, window_size):
    # x: (B, H, W, C) -> windows
    B, H, W, C = x.shape
    x = x.view(B, H // window_size, window_size, W // window_size, window_size, C)
    windows = x.permute(0, 1, 3, 2, 4, 5).contiguous().view(-1, window_size, window_size, C)
    return windows

# Alternate blocks shift windows to allow information flow between windows

CLIP (models/clip/)

Vs single-stack LM: two encoders (image + text) and contrastive alignment in embedding space.

  • Removed: autoregressive decoder for the core CLIP model (generation is not the pretrained objective).
  • Added: dual towers; logit scale temperature; cosine similarity / contrastive loss training.
  • Purpose: Zero-shot classification and multimodal retrieval via shared embedding geometry.
def clip_logits(image_embeds, text_embeds, logit_scale):
    # L2-normalize
    image_embeds = image_embeds / image_embeds.norm(dim=-1, keepdim=True)
    text_embeds = text_embeds / text_embeds.norm(dim=-1, keepdim=True)
    logits = (image_embeds @ text_embeds.T) * logit_scale.exp()
    return logits  # (batch_img, batch_txt) similarity matrix

BLIP-2 (models/blip_2/)

Vs CLIP: adds a Q-Former (lightweight transformer) between frozen image encoder and frozen LLM.

  • Added: learnable query tokens attending to image features; projection into LLM hidden size.
  • Purpose: Cheap adaptation of powerful frozen models for VQA / captioning without full finetune of huge backbones.
def qformer_forward(query_tokens, encoder_hidden_states, cross_attn_layers):
    # query_tokens: learned embeddings (B, num_queries, D)
    x = query_tokens
    for layer in cross_attn_layers:
        x = layer.self_attn(x)
        x = layer.cross_attn(x, context=encoder_hidden_states)  # attend to image tokens
        x = layer.mlp(x)
    return x  # compressed visual tokens -> feed LLM as soft prompts

LLaMA (models/llama/)

Vs GPT-2: decoder-only but RMSNorm, RoPE, SwiGLU, typically no bias in linear layers; often GQA in larger variants.

  • Changed: norm type; position handling; MLP shape.
  • Purpose: Efficient, high-quality open-weights LLM inference and finetuning ecosystem.
class LlamaDecoderLayer(nn.Module):
    def forward(self, hidden_states, attention_mask, position_ids, past_key_value):
        residual = hidden_states
        hidden_states = self.input_layernorm(hidden_states)
        hidden_states, present_kv = self.self_attn(
            hidden_states=hidden_states,
            attention_mask=attention_mask,
            position_ids=position_ids,
            past_key_value=past_key_value,
        )
        hidden_states = residual + hidden_states
        residual = hidden_states
        hidden_states = self.post_attention_layernorm(hidden_states)
        hidden_states = self.mlp(hidden_states)
        return residual + hidden_states, present_kv

Mistral (models/mistral/)

Vs LLaMA: same broad decoder + RoPE + RMSNorm + SwiGLU family; adds sliding-window attention on many layers.

  • Added / changed: local attention window (global layers optional in some configs).
  • Purpose: Long context efficiency with strong quality per parameter.
def sliding_window_mask(seq_len, window, device):
    # True = allow attend; causal + only last `window` positions
    mask = torch.ones(seq_len, seq_len, device=device, dtype=torch.bool).tril()
    for i in range(seq_len):
        mask[i, : max(0, i - window + 1)] = False
    return mask

Mixtral (MoE) (models/mixtral/)

Vs dense LLaMA-like decoder: FFN replaced by sparse mixture-of-experts.

  • Added: router logits per token; top-k expert selection; per-expert feed-forward.
  • Purpose: Increase parameter count (capacity) while activating only a subset per token (compute).
def moe_ffn(x, gate, experts, top_k=2):
    # x: (batch*seq, dim)
    router_logits = gate(x)  # (batch*seq, num_experts)
    weights, selected = torch.topk(router_logits, k=top_k, dim=-1)
    weights = torch.softmax(weights, dim=-1)
    out = torch.zeros_like(x)
    for i, expert in enumerate(experts):
        mask = (selected == i).any(dim=-1)
        if mask.any():
            out[mask] += expert(x[mask])  # simplified; real code uses batched routing
    return out

Longformer (models/longformer/)

Vs BERT: encoder with local window + global tokens (e.g. [CLS]) attending everywhere.

  • Changed: attention pattern is sparse (not full n×n for all tokens).
  • Purpose: Long documents with manageable memory.
# Pattern: diagonal band (local) + special global indices attend to all / attended by all
# Implementation uses custom CUDA/CPU kernels in HF for efficiency
def longformer_pattern(seq_len, window, global_indices):
    allowed = torch.zeros(seq_len, seq_len, dtype=torch.bool)
    for i in range(seq_len):
        lo, hi = max(0, i - window // 2), min(seq_len, i + window // 2 + 1)
        allowed[i, lo:hi] = True
    for g in global_indices:
        allowed[g, :] = True
        allowed[:, g] = True
    return allowed

BigBird (models/big_bird/)

Vs BERT: random + window + global sparse attention pattern (theoretical approximator of full attention).

  • Added: random attention edges; blockwise structure.
  • Purpose: Long sequence encoder with scalability.
# Three-part pattern per query block (conceptual):
# - attend to nearby tokens (window)
# - attend to a few random keys (approximation)
# - global tokens (e.g. first few) attend bidirectionally to all
# HF implements this with block-sparse attention kernels, not a dense n x n matrix.
def bigbird_attention_allowed(i, j, window, random_partners, global_idx):
    if j in global_idx or i in global_idx:
        return True
    if abs(i - j) <= window:
        return True
    return j in random_partners[i]

Whisper (models/whisper/)

Vs text-only: audio encoder (Conv front-end) + decoder for token prediction.

  • Added: mel-spectrogram → Conv layers before Transformer encoder.
  • Purpose: End-to-end speech recognition / translation to text.
def whisper_forward(mel, decoder_input_ids):
    x = conv_stem(mel)  # (B, n_mels, time) -> (B, C, T')
    x = x.permute(0, 2, 1)  # (B, T', C)
    enc = encoder(x)
    dec = decoder(input_ids=decoder_input_ids, encoder_hidden_states=enc)
    return dec

Wav2Vec2 (models/wav2vec2/)

Vs Whisper: self-supervised speech pretraining; encoder-focused; CTC or finetune heads.

  • Added: multi-layer CNN feature encoder; contrastive / masked prediction pretraining objectives.
  • Purpose: Learn speech representations with limited labeled audio.
def wav2vec2_features(raw_waveform, feature_extractor):
    # CNN downsamples time; outputs (B, T', hidden)
    x = feature_extractor(raw_waveform)
    x = transformer_encoder(x)  # contextualization
    return x  # + projection head for contrastive loss in pretraining

5. How to read any model in the repo

  1. Open configuration_<arch>.py. Fields like hidden_size, num_hidden_layers, num_attention_heads, intermediate_size, num_key_value_heads, max_position_embeddings, rope_theta, sliding_window, num_local_experts tell you what differs between checkpoints.
  2. Open modeling_<arch>.py (or modular_<arch>.py). Find: Embeddings, Attention, MLP/FeedForward, DecoderLayer/EncoderLayer, and the task head (LMHead, ForSequenceClassification, etc.).
  3. Use editor search for: causal, past_key_values, rotary, rope, alibi, cross_attn, encoder_attn, relative_position, router, expert.

6. Worked examples (stitched code paths)

Each example: files, symbols to search, inline stitched path.

6.1 BERT vs GPT-2 (bidirectional encoder vs causal decoder)

Files: modeling_bert.py, modeling_gpt2.py. Search: BertSelfAttention, GPT2Attention, causal.

# BERT: no causal mask on encoder self-attention (padding mask only)
def bert_self_attention_scores(query, key, attention_mask):
    scores = (query @ key.transpose(-1, -2)) / math.sqrt(d_head)
    if attention_mask is not None:
        scores = scores + attention_mask  # large negative for pad
    return softmax(scores, dim=-1)

# GPT-2: causal mask so position i cannot attend to j > i
def gpt2_attn_scores(query, key, causal_mask):
    scores = (query @ key.transpose(-1, -2)) / math.sqrt(d_head)
    scores = scores + causal_mask  # -inf above diagonal
    return softmax(scores, dim=-1)

6.2 T5 (encoder–decoder + relative bias)

Files: modeling_t5.py. Search: T5Attention, compute_bias, encoder, decoder.

def t5_layer_step(decoder_hidden, encoder_hidden, self_attn, enc_dec_attn, ln_1, ln_2, ln_3):
    y = decoder_hidden
    y = y + self_attn(ln_1(y), is_decoder=True, causal_mask=True)
    y = y + enc_dec_attn(ln_2(y), context=encoder_hidden)
    y = y + ff(ln_3(y))
    return y

6.3 LLaMA (RMSNorm + RoPE + SwiGLU)

Files: modeling_llama.py. Search: LlamaRMSNorm, apply_rotary_pos_emb, LlamaMLP.

class LlamaRMSNorm(nn.Module):
    def __init__(self, hidden_size, eps=1e-6):
        super().__init__()
        self.weight = nn.Parameter(torch.ones(hidden_size))
        self.variance_epsilon = eps

    def forward(self, hidden_states):
        input_dtype = hidden_states.dtype
        hidden_states = hidden_states.to(torch.float32)
        variance = hidden_states.pow(2).mean(-1, keepdim=True)
        hidden_states = hidden_states * torch.rsqrt(variance + self.variance_epsilon)
        return self.weight * hidden_states.to(input_dtype)

# RoPE on q,k then SwiGLU in MLP — see sections 3.2 and 3.3

6.4 ViT (patches + encoder + head)

Files: modeling_vit.py. Search: ViTPatchEmbeddings, ViTEncoder, classifier.

def vit_forward(pixel_values, vit):
    x = vit.embeddings(pixel_values)  # patchify + cls + pos
    x = vit.encoder(x).last_hidden_state
    cls = x[:, 0]
    logits = vit.classifier(cls)  # or pooler path depending on config
    return logits

6.5 Mixtral MoE (router + experts)

Files: modeling_mixtral.py. Search: MixtralSparseMoeBlock, gate, experts.

class MixtralSparseMoeBlock(nn.Module):
    def __init__(self, config):
        super().__init__()
        self.gate = nn.Linear(config.hidden_size, config.num_local_experts, bias=False)
        self.experts = nn.ModuleList([MixtralBLockSparseTop2MLP(config) for _ in range(config.num_local_experts)])

    def forward(self, hidden_states):
        b, s, d = hidden_states.shape
        x = hidden_states.reshape(-1, d)
        router_logits = self.gate(x)
        routing_weights, expert_indices = torch.topk(
            F.softmax(router_logits, dim=-1), k=2, dim=-1
        )
        # For each expert, run forward on tokens assigned to it; scatter-add weighted outputs.
        # HF uses batched GEMMs; see MixtralSparseMoeBlock in modeling_mixtral.py.
        y = torch.zeros_like(x)
        return y.reshape(b, s, d)

Disclaimer: Symbol names and file splits change across Transformers releases; use this guide for architecture, then confirm against your installed version.

References

  • src/transformers/models (model implementations)

lessons.html:
1 · The Bricks

Compute — the Workers

Virtual Machines

AWS EC2 · Google Compute Engine · Azure VMs

The standard 2×4 rectangular brick: sturdy and fully customizable, but heavy. You own everything from the operating system up.

A hypervisor slices one physical server into isolated guests, each running its own kernel and operating system. You pick the CPU, memory, disk and image, and you are responsible for patching, configuring and scaling what runs inside.

Reach for it when

  • The software needs a full OS, a custom kernel module, GPUs, or licensed software tied to a machine.
  • You run long-lived, steady workloads where reserved or committed-use pricing beats paying per request.
  • You host your own databases, message brokers or Kubernetes worker nodes.

Trade-offs

  • Boots in tens of seconds to minutes, so scaling reacts slowly to sudden spikes.
  • You patch the OS, rotate credentials and fight configuration drift between machines.
  • You pay for idle capacity unless an autoscaling group shrinks the fleet.

How it breaks

  • The physical host fails and takes the VM with it. Spread instances across availability zones behind a load balancer.
  • Hand-patched 'pet' servers drift apart until one behaves differently in production. Build immutable images (Packer, AMIs) and replace instead of repair.
  • Noisy neighbours on shared hardware cause unpredictable latency.

Remember

  • Classic trio: machine image + autoscaling group + load balancer with health checks.
  • Treat servers as cattle, not pets.

Read more

  • Xen and the Art of Virtualization (SOSP 2003) — The paravirtualization paper behind early EC2
  • AWS Nitro System — How modern EC2 offloads virtualization to dedicated hardware
  • Static stability using Availability Zones — Amazon Builders' Library

Containers

Docker · containerd · OCI images

Uniformly sized modular bricks that stack perfectly on any baseplate, because each brick carries its own dependencies inside.

A container is an ordinary process isolated with Linux namespaces and limited with cgroups. It shares the host kernel, so it starts in about a second and packs densely. The image bundles the app with its libraries, so the same artifact runs on a laptop, in CI and in production.

Reach for it when

  • You deploy stateless web services and microservices.
  • You want 'works on my machine' to mean 'works everywhere', with the same image in development, CI and production.
  • You want to pack many small services onto fewer machines.

Trade-offs

  • Isolation is weaker than a VM because every container shares one kernel.
  • One container is easy; hundreds need an orchestrator for placement, networking, secrets and rollouts.
  • State must live outside the container, in a database, cache or volume.

How it breaks

  • The container restarts and its local disk is gone. Never keep the only copy of data inside it.
  • It is OOM-killed when it exceeds its memory limit, often in a restart loop.
  • Bloated images slow down every deploy and scale-out.

Remember

  • Twelve-Factor rules: stateless processes, configuration in environment variables, logs to stdout.
  • Container = process + namespaces + cgroups + an image filesystem.

Read more

  • Docker overview
  • The Twelve-Factor App: Processes — Why services should be stateless and share nothing
  • The Twelve-Factor App — The whole checklist for container-friendly services

Container Orchestration

Kubernetes · Amazon ECS · Nomad

The baseplate plus a robot that reads the instructions. You declare what the finished model should look like, and it keeps rebuilding it whenever a piece falls off.

You declare the desired state: which images, how many replicas, how much CPU and memory. Controllers keep reconciling reality toward it. They restart crashed pods, reschedule them off failed nodes, roll out new versions gradually, give services stable DNS names, and autoscale on metrics.

Reach for it when

  • You run many services that need rolling deploys, service discovery and autoscaling.
  • You want to use machines efficiently by bin-packing many workloads onto shared nodes.
  • You need one deployment model across clouds or on-premises.

Trade-offs

  • Operating it is a job in itself: networking, upgrades, RBAC and YAML sprawl.
  • For one or two services, a managed platform or serverless is usually cheaper and simpler.

How it breaks

  • A misconfigured liveness probe restarts healthy pods, which can cascade across the service.
  • Missing resource requests and limits cause noisy neighbours and surprise evictions.
  • A control-plane outage leaves running pods serving (static stability) but blocks deploys and scaling.

Read more

  • Borg, Omega, and Kubernetes (ACM Queue) — Lessons from a decade of container management at Google
  • Large-scale cluster management at Google with Borg (EuroSys 2015)
  • Kubernetes overview

Serverless Functions

AWS Lambda · Cloudflare Workers · Google Cloud Run functions

Tiny micro-bricks that appear the instant two pieces need connecting, then disappear. You never store or maintain them.

You upload a function and choose what triggers it: an HTTP request, a queue message, an object landing in S3, or a schedule. The platform runs one instance per concurrent event, scales to zero when idle, and bills per millisecond. Lambda isolates each function in a Firecracker microVM; Cloudflare Workers use V8 isolates, which start in under a millisecond at the edge.

Reach for it when

  • Traffic is spiky or rare, so paying for idle servers is wasteful.
  • You need glue between managed services, such as 'image uploaded to S3, so resize it'.
  • Event handlers, webhooks, scheduled jobs and edge logic (redirects, auth checks, A/B tests).

Trade-offs

  • Cold starts: the first request to a new instance can take from about 100 ms to several seconds, depending on runtime and package size.
  • Hard limits: Lambda runs at most 15 minutes and has memory, payload and concurrency caps.
  • Functions are stateless, harder to debug locally, and tie you to the vendor.
  • At steady high load, per-request billing can cost more than containers.

How it breaks

  • A traffic spike launches thousands of instances that exhaust the database's connections. Put a queue or a connection proxy (such as RDS Proxy) in between.
  • Asynchronous invocations are retried, so side effects can run twice. Make handlers idempotent.
  • Account concurrency limits throttle unrelated functions that share them.

Read more

  • Firecracker: Lightweight Virtualization for Serverless Applications (NSDI 2020) — How AWS Lambda isolates functions
  • Cloud Computing without Containers — Cloudflare on V8 isolates
  • Serverless Computing: One Step Forward, Two Steps Back — A sharp critique from Berkeley (CIDR 2019)
  • Cloud Programming Simplified: A Berkeley View on Serverless Computing

Storage & Databases — the Memory

Relational Databases

PostgreSQL · MySQL · Amazon Aurora

The rigid LEGO grid: every piece must click into clean rows and columns, and nothing that doesn't fit is allowed on the board.

Data lives in tables with a fixed schema. You query it with SQL, joining tables as needed. Indexes (usually B-trees) keep lookups fast, and constraints such as foreign keys and uniqueness protect integrity. ACID transactions (atomicity, consistency, isolation, durability) make a group of writes all-or-nothing, even with many concurrent users.

Reach for it when

  • Money, orders, inventory and bookings: anything where a half-applied change is a bug.
  • You need ad-hoc queries, reports and joins across entities.
  • The shape of the data is known and relationships matter. This is the default choice until proven otherwise.

Trade-offs

  • Writes scale vertically until you add sharding (Vitess, Citus) or move to distributed SQL (Spanner, CockroachDB).
  • Schema migrations on big tables need care: online migrations, backfills and dual writes.
  • Read replicas scale reads but serve slightly stale data (replication lag).

How it breaks

  • A burst of clients exhausts connections. Use a pooler such as PgBouncer and cap the size of the app's pool.
  • Hot rows, such as one inventory counter in a flash sale, serialize on locks.
  • A missing index turns a 1 ms lookup into a full table scan that drags down everything else.
  • Reading your own write from a lagging replica shows the user old data.

NoSQL & Document Databases

DynamoDB · MongoDB · Cassandra · Bigtable

Flexible Bionicle pieces that morph into whatever shape you're storing, as long as you decide in advance how you'll pick them up.

There are four families: key-value (DynamoDB, Redis), document (MongoDB), wide-column (Cassandra, Bigtable) and graph (Neo4j). Most scale horizontally by hashing a partition key across many nodes and allow flexible, schema-on-read records. You model the data around your access patterns, not around entities, and usually denormalize.

Reach for it when

  • The scale is huge but access is simple and known: get by key, or a range inside one partition.
  • Write throughput is very high: messages, events, IoT readings, activity logs.
  • Records carry flexible, evolving attributes, such as product catalogs, user profiles, carts and sessions.

Trade-offs

  • Joins and ad-hoc queries are weak or missing. Adding a new access pattern can mean a new index or a copy of the data.
  • Many are eventually consistent by default, and multi-item transactions are limited.
  • The partition key is the most important design decision and hard to change later.

How it breaks

  • A hot partition, such as a celebrity's key or everything written under today's date, throttles while other nodes sit idle.
  • Full-table scans are slow and expensive.
  • Schema-on-read drift: old records in shapes the code no longer expects.

Object Storage

Amazon S3 · Google Cloud Storage · Azure Blob Storage

Huge storage bins where you dump media, raw text and massive static assets. Each bin has a label, and you fetch things by label.

A flat namespace of buckets and keys, each pointing to an immutable blob plus metadata, accessed over HTTP. Capacity is effectively unlimited and cheap, and S3 is designed for 11 nines of durability. It is not a filesystem: you replace whole objects rather than editing them in place.

Reach for it when

  • Images, video, audio, documents, backups, logs, ML datasets, a data lake.
  • Static website assets served through a CDN.
  • Any large blob: put the bytes in object storage and keep only the key and metadata in your database.

Trade-offs

  • Each request takes tens of milliseconds, far slower than local disk or a cache.
  • You cannot edit part of an object; you rewrite it. Listing huge buckets is slow.
  • There are request-rate limits per key prefix, so spread hot keys across prefixes.

How it breaks

  • A misconfigured public bucket leaks data. Block public access by default.
  • Routing uploads through your servers wastes bandwidth and CPU. Hand clients presigned URLs so they upload directly.
  • Event notifications are at-least-once, so the same upload may trigger processing twice. Consumers must be idempotent.

Remember

  • S3 has provided strong read-after-write consistency since December 2020.
  • Lifecycle rules move old objects to cheaper tiers such as Glacier automatically.

Wide-Column Stores: Cassandra

Apache Cassandra · ScyllaDB · Google Bigtable · HBase

A huge rack of labelled drawers spread over many tables. Every table can take new pieces at any moment, and each drawer keeps its pieces sorted.

A masterless, Dynamo-style cluster with a Bigtable-style data model. Rows are placed on a consistent-hash ring by partition key and replicated to N nodes (typically 3, across racks or zones). Any node can coordinate a request, and the consistency level is chosen per query (ONE, QUORUM, LOCAL_QUORUM, ALL). Writes go to a commit log and memtable and are flushed to immutable SSTables that are compacted later (an LSM tree), so writes are very fast. Inside a partition, rows are sorted by clustering columns, which makes 'latest N items for X' queries cheap.

Reach for it when

  • Write-heavy, always-on workloads: messages, events, time series, activity feeds, IoT, audit logs.
  • Multi-datacenter active-active with local-quorum latency.
  • Access patterns are known up front: design one table per query.

Data modeling rules

  • Primary key = (partition key, clustering columns…). The partition key spreads load; clustering columns sort rows inside it.
  • Bound partition size (roughly under 100 MB) by adding a time bucket to the key, for example (channel_id, day).
  • Denormalize: write the same data into several query-shaped tables. There are no joins.

Trade-offs

  • No joins, limited secondary indexes, and ad-hoc queries are expensive.
  • Lightweight transactions (Paxos-based compare-and-set) exist but are slow. Use them sparingly.
  • Repairs, compaction tuning, JVM garbage collection pauses (Cassandra) and tombstones take real operational care.

How it breaks

  • Hot or oversized partitions (a mega-channel or celebrity key) overload a few replicas.
  • Tombstone buildup from heavy deletes makes reads scan dead data and time out.
  • Skipped anti-entropy repair leaves replicas silently diverged, and deleted data can reappear.

Similar blocks

  • ScyllaDB: Cassandra-compatible, rewritten in C++ with a shard-per-core design. Discord moved to it from Cassandra.
  • Google Bigtable and HBase: range-partitioned wide-column stores with a single master for metadata. Row-key design is the whole game.
  • Amazon DynamoDB: a managed service with similar partition and sort-key modeling.

Distributed SQL (NewSQL)

Google Spanner · CockroachDB · YugabyteDB · Amazon Aurora

The rigid LEGO grid, but built from many baseplates snapped together, and it still feels like one board.

Relational databases that keep SQL and ACID transactions but scale out horizontally. Data is split into ranges or tablets, each replicated with Raft or Paxos, and transactions that span ranges use a distributed commit protocol. Spanner uses TrueTime for external consistency; CockroachDB and YugabyteDB use hybrid logical clocks. Aurora takes a different route: one writer, with a shared, replicated storage layer that scales reads and durability.

Reach for it when

  • You've outgrown a single Postgres or MySQL primary but still need transactions and SQL.
  • Multi-region deployments with strong consistency and automatic failover.
  • You want to avoid hand-rolled application-level sharding.

Trade-offs

  • Every write pays for consensus. Cross-region transactions add tens to hundreds of milliseconds.
  • Hot ranges (sequential primary keys) still bottleneck. Use hashed or UUID keys.
  • Costs more and has more moving parts than a single-node database.

Search Engines

Elasticsearch · OpenSearch · Apache Solr · Lucene

The index at the back of the instruction booklet: look up a word and it tells you every page it appears on.

Search engines build an inverted index (term → list of documents), plus BM25 relevance scoring, analyzers for tokenizing and stemming, facets and aggregations, and increasingly vector search too. An index is split into shards with replicas across nodes. It is fed from the source-of-truth database, usually asynchronously through change data capture or events, and is almost never the system of record.

Reach for it when

  • Full-text product and catalog search, typeahead, log search and analytics, faceted filtering.

Trade-offs

  • Near-real-time rather than instant: refresh intervals of about 1 s. Reindexing after a mapping change is costly.
  • The index drifts from the database if the update pipeline drops events. Plan full rebuilds.

How it breaks

  • Too many small shards overload the cluster state. Deep pagination and heavy aggregations exhaust memory.
  • Split-brain from bad quorum settings on older versions.

Vector Databases

pgvector · Milvus · Vertex AI Vector Search · FAISS · Pinecone

A bin sorted by shape-similarity instead of by label: hold up a piece and it hands you the ones that look most like it.

Vector databases store embeddings (dense vectors from a model) and answer 'k nearest neighbours' queries with approximate nearest neighbour (ANN) indexes. HNSW is a graph index: fast with high recall, but memory-hungry. IVF plus product quantization clusters and compresses vectors, so it is cheaper at billion scale. Metadata filters and hybrid search (combined with BM25) narrow the results. They are the retrieval brick behind RAG, semantic search, recommendations and deduplication.

Reach for it when

  • Retrieval-augmented generation (RAG) for LLM apps, semantic or product search, similar-item recommendations.
  • Start with pgvector if you already run Postgres. Move to a dedicated engine for more than about 100 million vectors or very high QPS.

Trade-offs

  • Recall vs latency vs memory is tuned through index parameters (HNSW M and efSearch, IVF nlist and nprobe).
  • Re-embedding the whole corpus when the embedding model changes is a batch job to plan for.

Coordination Services

ZooKeeper · etcd · Consul · Google Chubby

The small, trusted referee's notebook that every builder checks to find out who's in charge and which instructions are current.

Coordination services are small, strongly consistent (consensus-replicated) key-value stores for coordination, not bulk data. They provide leader election, distributed locks and leases, service discovery, configuration, and cluster membership through watches and ephemeral keys. etcd stores all Kubernetes state. ZooKeeper historically coordinated Kafka, HBase and Hadoop; Kafka has replaced it with its own KRaft quorum.

Use it well

  • Keep data tiny (KBs to MBs), and keep writes infrequent.
  • A lock needs a fencing token (a monotonic number checked by the resource). Otherwise a paused client can act on an expired lease.

How it breaks

  • Losing quorum (for example 2 of 3 nodes) blocks all writes and leader changes. Run 3 or 5 nodes across zones.
  • Abusing it as a general database causes slow disks, huge snapshots and election storms.

Google Cloud Storage Buckets

GCS · gs:// · the data lake and model store on GCP

Google's version of the giant storage bins, with a choice of how close to the front door each bin sits (and what it costs to open).

GCS is Google Cloud's object store. Objects live in buckets under a flat namespace with '/' only as a naming convention. Location types are region, dual-region and multi-region. Storage classes are Standard, Nearline (30-day minimum), Coldline (90-day) and Archive (365-day), with Autoclass available to tier automatically. It offers strong global consistency for object reads, writes and listing, IAM with uniform bucket-level access, signed URLs, object versioning, lifecycle rules, and Pub/Sub notifications. It is the default landing zone for data lakes, Spark and Dataproc jobs, BigQuery external tables, training data and model artifacts.

Reach for it when

  • Raw and curated data-lake zones (Parquet or Iceberg files), batch pipeline inputs and outputs.
  • ML datasets, checkpoints and model weights. Mount with Cloud Storage FUSE, or stream with parallel readers.
  • Media and static assets behind Cloud CDN. Backups and logs with lifecycle rules to cheaper classes.

Design tips

  • Co-locate buckets with compute (same region) to avoid egress cost and latency.
  • Ramp request rates gradually. Very high QPS on sequential names (timestamps) can hot-spot, so prefer random or hashed prefixes.
  • Use Pub/Sub notifications or Eventarc to trigger pipelines when objects land. Delivery is at-least-once, so make consumers idempotent.
  • Many small files hurt Spark and BigQuery. Compact them into files of about 128 MB to 1 GB.

How it breaks

  • Early deletion fees and retrieval costs on cold classes surprise batch jobs that reread old data.
  • A publicly readable bucket through a mistaken IAM binding. Enforce public access prevention.
  • Loading model weights from GCS on every pod start slows GPU autoscaling. Cache or pre-stage the weights.

Networking & Routing — the Connectors

DNS & Global Traffic Routing

Amazon Route 53 · Cloudflare DNS · Google Cloud DNS

The address printed on the box lid. Before anyone can touch your model, they have to find which table it's sitting on.

DNS turns names into IP addresses through a hierarchy of cached lookups, and each record has a TTL. Managed DNS can also route: by latency or geography to the nearest region, by weight for canaries and blue/green deploys, and by failover when health checks fail.

Reach for it when

  • This is always the first hop: every request starts with a lookup.
  • Multi-region active-active or active-passive failover.
  • Weighted shifts of traffic between old and new stacks.

Trade-offs

  • Caching makes changes slow to propagate. They take at least the TTL to spread, and some clients ignore TTLs.
  • Short TTLs mean faster failover but more lookups and more dependence on the DNS provider.

How it breaks

  • An outage at the DNS provider makes healthy services unreachable, as in the 2016 Dyn attack.
  • A long TTL on a record pointing at a dead region keeps sending users there.

Load Balancers

AWS ALB/NLB · NGINX · HAProxy · Envoy

The traffic manager that splits an incoming stream of LEGO pegs evenly across many identical worker bricks, and stops feeding any brick that has cracked.

A load balancer spreads requests across a pool of healthy targets. Layer 4 balancers route raw TCP or UDP connections and are fast and simple. Layer 7 balancers understand HTTP: they route by path or header, terminate TLS, and retry. Common algorithms are round-robin, least-connections and consistent hashing (for stickiness). Health checks eject failing targets.

Reach for it when

  • You scale any stateless tier horizontally, whether web servers, APIs or workers behind RPC.
  • You want TLS termination in one place, zero-downtime deploys, and blue/green or canary releases.

Trade-offs

  • The balancer itself must be highly available: use a managed service, or a redundant pair with a floating IP or anycast.
  • Sticky sessions undermine even distribution and make scaling in painful. Prefer stateless servers.

How it breaks

  • A health check that is too shallow keeps a server in rotation that returns 200 while its database is gone.
  • A health check that is too deep (it checks the database) means one database blip ejects every target and causes a total outage.
  • Long-lived connections (WebSockets, gRPC) stay pinned to old servers, so newly added servers get no load.

API Gateway

Amazon API Gateway · Kong · Apigee · Envoy Gateway

The single front-door stud every piece must pass through. It checks your ticket, limits how fast you can push, and routes you to the right sub-assembly.

A single entry point in front of many backend services. It handles cross-cutting concerns in one place: authentication and authorization, rate limits and quotas, routing by path or version, request and response transformation, protocol translation (REST to gRPC), and metrics and tracing. A Backend-for-Frontend (BFF) is a gateway tailored to one client, such as mobile.

Reach for it when

  • Mobile and web clients talk to many microservices, and you don't want each client to know about each service.
  • You expose public APIs that need keys, quotas and usage plans.
  • You want auth, throttling and observability configured once rather than in every service.

Trade-offs

  • It adds a network hop and a component that must scale and stay highly available.
  • Business logic tends to creep in. Keep the gateway thin.

How it breaks

  • One bad routing or auth config change takes every API down at once. Roll out config gradually.
  • Without per-client limits, one noisy client starves everyone else.

Content Delivery Network

Amazon CloudFront · Cloudflare · Akamai · Fastly

Small caching outposts built on every block of the city, so kids grab pieces from the corner shop instead of walking to the main warehouse.

A CDN is a global network of edge servers (points of presence, or PoPs) that cache content close to users. It cuts latency and offloads your origin. It serves static assets, video segments and downloads, can cache some dynamic responses, terminates TLS near the user, and absorbs DDoS attacks. Edge compute such as Workers or Lambda@Edge runs logic there.

Reach for it when

  • Images, JS/CSS, fonts, video (HLS/DASH segments), software downloads.
  • You have a global audience, or you need DDoS protection and a web application firewall at the edge.

Trade-offs

  • Invalidation is hard. Prefer versioned, content-hashed filenames (app.3f9a.js) with long TTLs.
  • Personalized or rapidly changing responses cache poorly.

How it breaks

  • A global purge or a cold cache sends every miss to the origin at once. Add an origin shield or tiered cache.
  • Caching private responses (a missing Cache-Control: private) leaks one user's data to another.
  • Stale assets after a deploy break the page if HTML and JS versions mismatch.

Service Mesh: Istio

Istio · Envoy · Linkerd · ambient mode

A clip-on connector attached to every brick, so every connection between bricks is locked, counted and steerable without redesigning the bricks themselves.

A service mesh moves service-to-service networking out of application code into a proxy layer. In sidecar mode an Envoy proxy runs next to every pod; in ambient mode per-node ztunnel proxies handle L4 and optional waypoint proxies handle L7. The control plane (istiod) pushes configuration to the proxies. You get mutual TLS and workload identity, fine-grained traffic management (weighted canaries, header routing, retries, timeouts, circuit breaking, fault injection, mirroring), authorization policy, and uniform metrics and traces.

Reach for it when

  • Many microservices on Kubernetes need zero-trust mTLS and consistent retries, timeouts and telemetry.
  • Progressive delivery: shift 1% → 10% → 100% of traffic to a new version, or mirror production traffic to a shadow model.
  • Chaos drills: inject delays and aborts with a VirtualService, no code changes needed.

Key resources

  • Gateway (ingress and egress), VirtualService (routing rules), DestinationRule (subsets, load balancing, outlier detection), PeerAuthentication and AuthorizationPolicy (mTLS and access).

Trade-offs

  • Sidecars add memory and CPU per pod and extra latency per hop, which ambient mode reduces.
  • Mesh-level retries stacked on client retries multiply load. Own retries in one layer.
  • A bad mesh config push can break traffic cluster-wide. Canary your control-plane changes.

Torbit: Walmart's Edge Platform

Edge proxy · L7 routing · edge caching and security

Walmart's own front gate and sorting station at the edge of the city. Every visitor passes through it before reaching any building, and it decides which building they go to.

Torbit began as a web-performance startup (real-user monitoring and dynamic front-end optimization) that Walmart Labs acquired in 2013. The team went on to build Walmart's in-house edge infrastructure: proxies, load balancers, edge security and real-user monitoring. Walmart engineers use Torbit for edge traffic control such as path-based routing between legacy and new services. Conceptually it plays the role of a CDN or edge proxy plus L7 load balancer in front of the origin: TLS termination, caching, request routing and rewriting, bot and WAF protection, and gradual traffic shifting.

Where it sits

  • Client → DNS → Torbit edge (TLS, cache, security, routing) → regional load balancers or ingress (Istio gateway) → services.
  • The public equivalent is Cloudflare, Akamai or Fastly, combined with an Envoy or NGINX edge tier.

Use it for

  • Path-based migration: route /api/cart/* to the new microservice at 10%, then increase, with instant rollback at the edge.
  • Shielding origins from flash-sale spikes with caching, rate limits and request collapsing.

How it breaks

  • An edge misconfiguration affects everything behind it. Stage and canary routing changes.
  • Caching personalized responses leaks data. Split what is cacheable from what is personalized.

Integration & Communication — the Glue

Message Queues

Amazon SQS · RabbitMQ · Google Cloud Tasks

A buffer tray between two builders. When one passes pieces faster than the next can snap them in, the pieces wait safely in the tray instead of falling on the floor.

Producers put messages on a durable queue and consumers pull them, process them, and then acknowledge (delete) them. Each message goes to one consumer (point-to-point). The queue decouples the producer from the consumer's speed and availability, levels out bursts, and makes retries easy. Most queues deliver at least once, so a message can arrive more than once.

Reach for it when

  • Background jobs: emails, video encoding, report generation, order fulfilment.
  • Load leveling: absorb a 10× spike and drain it at the rate the database can handle.
  • Spreading work across a pool of workers that you scale on queue depth.

Trade-offs

  • Processing becomes asynchronous: the user sees 'processing…' and the result arrives later.
  • Ordering is not guaranteed unless you use FIFO queues or message groups, which limit throughput.
  • At-least-once delivery means duplicates, so handlers must be idempotent.

How it breaks

  • A poison message fails forever and blocks or wastes workers. Move it to a dead-letter queue (DLQ) after N attempts.
  • If the visibility timeout is shorter than processing time, the message reappears and is processed twice.
  • If consumers are permanently slower than producers, the backlog grows without bound. Queues absorb bursts; they don't fix sustained overload.

Event Streams

Apache Kafka · Amazon Kinesis · Redpanda · Google Pub/Sub

A central conveyor belt that constantly carries every change past every station. Each station takes what it needs, and the belt remembers what went by so a station can rewind.

A stream is an append-only log, split into partitions and replicated across brokers. Consumers track their own offsets, so many independent consumer groups can read the same events at their own pace. Retention lets you replay history. Order is guaranteed within a partition, and all events with the same key land in the same partition.

Reach for it when

  • Fan-out: one event (OrderPlaced, DriverMoved) feeds many services such as billing, analytics, search and notifications.
  • Change data capture from a database, real-time analytics, activity and telemetry pipelines.
  • Event sourcing, or rebuilding a read model by replaying history.

Trade-offs

  • Clusters, partitions and schemas are heavy to operate.
  • Order holds only within a partition, and consumer parallelism is capped at the partition count.
  • Exactly-once processing needs idempotent producers plus transactions or idempotent sinks.

How it breaks

  • Consumer lag grows until data ages out of retention before a slow consumer reads it.
  • A skewed key (one busy city, one mega-customer) creates a hot partition.
  • Rebalancing storms pause every consumer in the group while partitions are reassigned.

Queue vs stream

  • Queue: a message is consumed once, then deleted. Good for work distribution.
  • Stream: an event is retained, read by many, and can be replayed. Good for broadcasting facts.

Caches

Redis · Memcached · Valkey · in-process caches

An ultra-fast shelf at arm's reach for the pieces you grab most, so you don't open the heavy bottom drawer (the database) every time.

A cache is an in-memory key-value store that answers in under a millisecond. The common patterns are cache-aside (the app reads the cache, and on a miss loads from the database and fills the cache), read-through, write-through and write-behind. Entries expire by TTL and are evicted by LRU or LFU. Redis adds data structures such as sorted sets for leaderboards, geo indexes, counters, streams and pub/sub.

Reach for it when

  • Reads far outnumber writes and the same hot data is read over and over.
  • Sessions, rate-limit counters, leaderboards, feature flags, computed or aggregated results.
  • Fast geo lookups, such as nearby drivers, with Redis GEO.

Trade-offs

  • Staleness: you choose how wrong the data is allowed to be, and for how long.
  • Invalidation adds complexity, and memory costs more than disk.
  • It is another system that can fail or disagree with the source of truth.

How it breaks

  • Stampede (thundering herd): a hot key expires and thousands of requests hit the database at once. Fix with request coalescing, locks or leases, or early refresh.
  • A cold cache after a restart or failover sends the full read load to the database.
  • Treating the cache as the source of truth loses data on eviction or restart.

Remember

  • Main memory ≈ 100 ns, SSD read ≈ 100 µs, a same-datacenter round trip ≈ 0.5 ms.
  • Track the hit ratio. Going from a 90% to a 99% hit rate cuts database load 10×.
