Apache Kafka Deep Dive

Brokers · topics · partitions · consumer groups · KRaft

The master conveyor belt, split into parallel lanes (partitions). Each lane keeps its pieces in order, and every station bookmarks how far down each lane it has read.

A topic is split into partitions. Each partition is an ordered, append-only log stored on a leader broker and replicated to followers; the in-sync replica set is the ISR. Producers choose the partition by key hash, and batch and compress records. Consumers in a group split the partitions between them (one partition to at most one consumer in the group) and commit offsets. Retention is by time or size, or by compaction to the latest value per key. KRaft (a Raft metadata quorum) has replaced ZooKeeper. Kafka Connect moves data in and out; Kafka Streams and Flink process it.

Durability knobs

  • Producer acks=all, enable.idempotence=true, and topic min.insync.replicas=2 with replication factor 3 means no loss if one broker dies.
  • Transactions plus read_committed consumers give exactly-once read-process-write within Kafka.

Sizing and scaling

  • Partitions cap consumer parallelism. Choose for peak throughput per consumer, with headroom, because adding partitions later reshuffles key-to-partition mapping.
  • Key by the entity whose events must stay ordered (order_id, driver_id), and watch for skew.

How it breaks

  • Consumer rebalances: a slow handler exceeds max.poll.interval.ms, the consumer is kicked out, partitions move, lag spikes. Decouple polling from processing.
  • Under-replicated partitions and unclean leader election lead to data loss. Keep unclean.leader.election.enable=false.
  • Poison messages block a partition. Route them to a dead-letter topic after N retries.

At Walmart

  • Walmart describes 25,000+ Kafka consumers processing trillions of messages a day. Its Messaging Proxy Service decouples consumption from processing to avoid rebalance-driven lag.

Read more

  • Apache Kafka documentation — Design, replication, delivery semantics
  • KIP-500: Replace ZooKeeper with a Self-Managed Metadata Quorum — KRaft
  • Reliably Processing Trillions of Kafka Messages Per Day — Walmart Global Tech
  • Apache Kafka for Item Setup — Walmart Global Tech
  • The Log: What every software engineer should know about real-time data's unifying abstraction — Jay Kreps
  • Exactly-once Semantics Are Possible: Here's How Kafka Does It — Confluent

Distributed Cache

Redis Cluster · Memcached pools · Netflix EVCache · client-side sharding

Many arm's-reach shelves spread down a long table, with a rule that tells every builder which shelf a given piece lives on, and spare shelves that hold copies.

When one cache node isn't enough memory or throughput, keys are partitioned across many nodes. Redis Cluster uses 16,384 hash slots assigned to primaries with replicas; Memcached uses client-side consistent hashing, often through a proxy such as mcrouter or twemproxy. Replicas and zone-aware copies add availability, and cross-region replication (for example through Kafka, as in Netflix EVCache) keeps global caches warm. A near cache (in-process L1) in front of the distributed L2 absorbs the hottest keys.

Design choices

  • Sharding: Redis Cluster hash slots or consistent hashing, so adding a node moves only about 1/N of keys.
  • Replication: a replica per shard for failover, and copies in each zone so reads stay local.
  • Consistency: invalidate on write (preferably driven by change data capture), TTL as a safety net, versioned keys for immutable data.

How it breaks

  • Hot keys: one shard melts while the rest idle. Replicate hot keys, add an L1 near cache, or split the key.
  • Node loss or resharding means a cold slice and a database spike. Warm the cache gradually and coalesce requests.
  • Big values or keys (multi-MB) cause latency spikes and network saturation.
  • Multi-key operations fail across slots in Redis Cluster. Use hash tags {user42}:… to co-locate keys.

Read more

  • Redis cluster specification — Hash slots, failover, redirection
  • A large scale analysis of hundreds of in-memory cache clusters at Twitter (OSDI 2020)
  • Caching for a Global Netflix — EVCache cross-region replication through Kafka
  • How we rebuilt the Walmart Autocomplete Backend — Walmart: Memcached-backed index, daily writer, geo-replicated readers
  • Scaling Memcache at Facebook
  • twemproxy — Sharding proxy for Memcached and Redis

Observability — the Inspectors

Metrics & Alerting: Prometheus

Prometheus · Grafana · Alertmanager · Thanos / Mimir

Gauges clipped onto every brick, read every few seconds and written into a logbook, with an alarm bell when a needle crosses the red line.

Prometheus pulls (scrapes) metrics over HTTP from /metrics endpoints every 15–60 s and stores them as time series identified by a metric name and labels, in a compressed time-series database. The metric types are counters, gauges, histograms and summaries. You query with PromQL, for example rate(http_requests_total[5m]) and histogram_quantile(0.99, …). Alertmanager deduplicates and routes alerts. Grafana draws dashboards. Thanos, Cortex or Mimir add long-term, global, highly available storage.

What to measure

  • RED for services: request Rate, Errors, Duration (as histograms, for p50/p95/p99).
  • USE for resources: Utilization, Saturation, Errors (CPU, memory, disk, GPU, queue depth).
  • The four golden signals: latency, traffic, errors, saturation. Alert on SLO burn rate, not on raw CPU.

For LLM serving

  • Time to first token (TTFT), time per output token (TPOT), tokens per second, running and waiting requests, KV-cache usage, GPU utilization (DCGM exporter). vLLM, SGLang and Triton expose Prometheus metrics.

How it breaks

  • Cardinality explosion: putting user_id or request_id in labels creates millions of series and exhausts memory.
  • Averages hide tails. Averaging precomputed quantiles across instances is mathematically wrong; aggregate histograms instead.

Read more

  • Prometheus overview
  • Histograms and summaries
  • Monitoring Distributed Systems (Google SRE book) — The four golden signals
  • Gorilla: A Fast, Scalable, In-Memory Time Series Database (VLDB 2015) — Compression used by Prometheus's TSDB
  • The RED Method: how to instrument your services — Tom Wilkie
  • The USE Method — Brendan Gregg
  • Thanos — Highly available, long-term Prometheus

Distributed Tracing & Logs

OpenTelemetry · Jaeger · Tempo · structured logging

A tracer dye on one peg, so you can watch exactly which bricks it passed through and how long it paused at each.

A trace follows one request across services as a tree of spans (with service, operation, duration and attributes), linked by a trace ID propagated in headers (W3C traceparent). OpenTelemetry is the vendor-neutral standard: SDKs plus a Collector for traces, metrics and logs. Sampling (head-based or tail-based) keeps costs sane. Structured JSON logs that carry the trace ID tie the three signals together.

Use it for

  • Finding which hop inflated the p99, spotting fan-out N+1 calls, and tracing a request through gateway, mesh, model server and database.

Watch out

  • Missing context propagation (async queues, thread pools) breaks traces. Pass the context through Kafka headers.
  • Log volume costs: sample debug logs and never log prompts or PII by default.

Read more

  • OpenTelemetry documentation
  • Dapper, a Large-Scale Distributed Systems Tracing Infrastructure — Google, 2010
  • Jaeger

lessons.title: 2 · Building Rules
lessons.html:
2 · Building Rules

Scaling the Structure

Vertical vs Horizontal Scaling

Scale up vs scale out

Swap a small brick for a giant brick (vertical), or add more identical bricks side by side (horizontal).

Vertical scaling gives one machine more CPU, RAM or disk. It is simple, needs no code changes, and hits a ceiling and a single point of failure. Horizontal scaling adds more machines behind a load balancer or partitioning scheme. It has almost no ceiling and survives a node failure, but requires stateless services or partitioned data.

Rules of thumb

  • Scale the stateless tiers horizontally first; it's cheap and easy.
  • Scale databases vertically as far as is sensible, then add read replicas, then shard.
  • Autoscale on a leading signal (queue depth, concurrency) rather than a lagging one (CPU at 90%).

Watch out

  • Horizontal scale moves the bottleneck downstream. Fifty more app servers can open 5,000 more database connections.

Read more

  • The System Design Primer: Scalability
  • Designs, Lessons and Advice from Building Large Distributed Systems — Jeff Dean, LADIS 2009 keynote

Stateless Services

Share-nothing application tiers

Every worker brick is identical and remembers nothing, so any brick can be swapped, added or thrown away without the model noticing.

A stateless server keeps no user data between requests in its own memory or disk. Sessions, uploads and job state live in shared stores: a database, a cache, object storage or a signed token (such as a JWT). Then the load balancer can send any request to any instance, and instances can be killed or added freely.

Why it matters

  • Enables autoscaling, rolling deploys, spot instances and serverless.
  • Removes the need for sticky sessions, and failover just works.

Where the state goes

  • Session data goes to Redis or a signed cookie or JWT.
  • Uploaded files go to object storage. Work in progress goes to a queue or database.

Read more

  • The Twelve-Factor App: Processes

Replication

Leader-follower · multi-leader · leaderless quorums

Build identical copies of the same model on different tables, so if one table collapses, the others still stand.

Replication keeps copies of the same data on several nodes, for availability, read scaling and locality. In leader-follower replication, one node takes writes and followers replay its log (Postgres, MySQL). In multi-leader replication, several regions accept writes and must resolve conflicts. Leaderless systems (Dynamo, Cassandra) write to W of N replicas and read from R of N; when R + W > N, a read overlaps the latest write.

Key choices

  • Synchronous replication means no data loss on failover but slower writes. Asynchronous means fast writes but possible loss and lag.
  • Automatic failover needs consensus (Raft, Paxos) or a coordinator to avoid split-brain, where two nodes both think they are leader.

How it breaks

  • Replication lag: a user writes, then reads from a follower and doesn't see the change. Fix with read-your-writes routing.
  • An asynchronous leader dies before shipping its last writes, and they are lost after failover.

Read more

  • Designing Data-Intensive Applications, Chapter 5: Replication — Martin Kleppmann
  • In Search of an Understandable Consensus Algorithm (Raft)
  • Dynamo: Amazon's Highly Available Key-value Store — Sloppy quorums and hinted handoff

Sharding (Partitioning)

Split one dataset across many databases

The model is too big for one table, so you split it into sections and give each table one section, using a rule everyone agrees on to know which section lives where.

Sharding splits data by a shard key so each node holds a subset. Range sharding (by date or by A–M) makes range scans easy but creates hot spots. Hash sharding spreads load evenly but loses range locality. Directory or lookup sharding maps keys to shards in a table, which is flexible but adds a lookup. Choose the key so most queries hit exactly one shard.

Choosing a shard key

  • Use what nearly every query filters by: tenant_id, user_id, channel_id.
  • It needs high cardinality and evenly spread traffic. Avoid time or other monotonically increasing keys for hash-less range shards.

Costs

  • Cross-shard joins and transactions become application problems.
  • Resharding is painful. Use many logical shards mapped onto fewer physical nodes so you can move them later.
  • Celebrity keys still create hot shards and need special handling.

Read more

  • Sharding & IDs at Instagram — Logical shards on Postgres, and time-sortable IDs
  • Herding elephants: lessons learned from sharding Postgres at Notion
  • How Figma's databases team lived to tell the scale
  • Vitess documentation — Sharding middleware for MySQL, from YouTube

Consistent Hashing

Stable key placement as nodes come and go

Arrange the tables in a circle. Each piece goes to the next table clockwise, so adding a table only takes pieces from its one neighbour.

Nodes and keys are hashed onto the same ring, and each key belongs to the first node clockwise from it. Adding or removing a node moves only about 1/N of the keys, compared with nearly all of them under hash(key) mod N. Virtual nodes (many points per server) smooth out the load. It is used by Dynamo, Cassandra, CDNs, cache clusters and load balancers (Maglev).

Remember

  • Plain modulo hashing reshuffles almost every key when N changes, which is a cache-miss storm.
  • Replicate by storing each key on the next R distinct nodes around the ring.

Read more

  • Consistent Hashing and Random Trees (Karger et al., STOC 1997) — The original paper, written for web caching
  • Dynamo: Amazon's Highly Available Key-value Store — Section 4.2: partitioning
  • Maglev: A Fast and Reliable Software Network Load Balancer — Maglev hashing

Data & Consistency

CAP & PACELC

What you give up when the network splits, and when it doesn't

Two halves of the model are separated by a gap. Either both halves stop changing until they can talk again (consistency), or each keeps building on its own and you reconcile later (availability).

CAP says that during a network partition (P), a system must choose between consistency (C: every read sees the latest write, or gets an error) and availability (A: every request gets an answer, possibly stale). PACELC adds that Else, when there is no partition, you still trade latency (L) against consistency (C). For example, DynamoDB's default eventual reads favour latency, while Spanner favours consistency.

Use it well

  • Partitions aren't optional, so the real question is how each operation behaves when one happens.
  • Choose per operation, not per system: bank balances need C, like counts can take A.
  • Most real systems are neither pure CP nor pure AP. Describe the exact consistency guarantee instead.

Read more

  • CAP Twelve Years Later: How the 'Rules' Have Changed — Eric Brewer
  • Please stop calling databases CP or AP — Martin Kleppmann
  • Consistency Tradeoffs in Modern Distributed Database System Design (PACELC) — Daniel Abadi, IEEE Computer 2012

Consistency Models

Linearizable · read-your-writes · monotonic · eventual

How quickly does everyone around the table see the brick you just placed: instantly, only you, or eventually?

Consistency models range from strong to weak. Linearizable means the system behaves like a single copy, and every read sees the latest completed write. Sequential and causal consistency preserve order and cause-and-effect. Read-your-writes guarantees you always see your own updates. Monotonic reads guarantee you never go back in time. Eventual consistency only promises that replicas converge when writes stop.

Pick per feature

  • Payments, inventory, unique usernames and leader election need linearizable operations.
  • A profile edit needs read-your-writes: route that user's reads to the leader for a few seconds.
  • Feeds, like counts and analytics can be eventual.

Read more

  • Eventually Consistent: Revisited — Werner Vogels
  • Jepsen: Consistency Models — A clickable map of the hierarchy

Caching Patterns & Invalidation

Cache-aside · write-through · write-behind · TTLs

Decide when the arm's-reach shelf is refilled, and when a piece on it is too old to trust.

Cache-aside (lazy loading) is the default: read the cache, on a miss read the database, then set the cache with a TTL. Write-through updates the cache and the database together. Write-behind writes the cache first and flushes to the database asynchronously, which is fast but can lose data. For invalidation, prefer deleting the key on write over updating it, always set a TTL as a safety net, and use versioned keys for immutable data.

Stampede defences

  • Request coalescing (single-flight): one request fetches while the others wait for its result.
  • Leases or locks per key, as in Facebook's memcache.
  • Refresh popular keys before they expire, and add jitter to TTLs so keys don't expire together.

Gotchas

  • A race between 'delete on write' and a concurrent cache fill can store stale data. Leases or short TTLs contain it.
  • Negative caching (remembering 'not found') prevents repeated misses for missing keys.

Read more

  • Caching challenges and strategies — Amazon Builders' Library
  • Scaling Memcache at Facebook — Section 3.2.1: leases
  • Under the hood: Broadcasting live video to millions — Request coalescing at the edge for Facebook Live

Sagas & the Transactional Outbox

Consistency across services without distributed locks

A multi-builder assembly where each builder finishes their part and passes a note to the next. If a later step fails, each builder takes back their own part in reverse order.

Once data is spread across services, one ACID transaction can't cover it, and two-phase commit is fragile. A saga is a sequence of local transactions, each with a compensating action (for example, refund the payment and release the stock). The transactional outbox fixes the dual-write problem: write the business row and an 'event to publish' row in the same local transaction, and a relay publishes the outbox rows to the queue or stream.

Why the outbox

  • 'Update the database, then publish to Kafka' can crash in between, and you get an order with no event.
  • The outbox plus at-least-once relay plus idempotent consumers gives an effectively-once outcome.

Orchestration vs choreography

  • Orchestration: a central coordinator tells each service what to do. Easier to follow and monitor.
  • Choreography: services react to each other's events. Looser coupling, but harder to see the whole flow.

Read more

  • Pattern: Saga — microservices.io
  • Pattern: Transactional outbox — microservices.io
  • Life Beyond Distributed Transactions: An Apostate's Opinion — Pat Helland, ACM Queue

Unique ID Generation

Auto-increment · UUID · Snowflake IDs

Every brick needs a serial number stamped on it, and thousands of factories must stamp numbers at the same time without ever printing the same one twice.

A single database auto-increment is simple but becomes a bottleneck and a single point of failure. UUIDv4 is random, needs no coordination, and fragments B-tree indexes. Snowflake-style IDs pack a timestamp, a machine ID and a per-millisecond sequence into 64 bits, so they are unique, roughly time-sortable and generated locally. UUIDv7 is a time-ordered UUID standard.

Use it for

  • URL shortener keys (encode the number in base62), tweet and post IDs, order numbers, shard-aware IDs (put the shard ID inside the ID).

Watch out

  • If a clock moves backwards, a Snowflake generator can issue duplicates. Refuse to issue IDs until the clock catches up.
  • Sequential public IDs leak business volume and invite scraping.

Read more

  • Announcing Snowflake — Twitter Engineering, 2010
  • twitter-archive/snowflake — The original implementation and ID layout
  • Sharding & IDs at Instagram — IDs generated inside Postgres

Reliability & Flow Control

Idempotency

Idempotency keys make retries safe

Pressing the same brick onto the same stud twice leaves one brick, not two.

An operation is idempotent if doing it several times has the same effect as doing it once. The client sends a unique Idempotency-Key with each logical request (for example, one checkout attempt). The server stores the key with the result, and a retry with the same key returns the stored result instead of charging again. This is what makes at-least-once delivery and automatic retries safe.

Implementation

  • Enforce uniqueness on (client, key) in the database. Insert the key first; if the insert conflicts, return the saved response.
  • Keep keys for longer than the longest retry window, for example 24 hours.
  • Natural idempotency: PUT and DELETE, 'set status = shipped', upserts keyed by event ID.

Read more

  • Designing robust and predictable APIs with idempotency — Stripe
  • Making retries safe with idempotent APIs — Amazon Builders' Library
  • Stripe API: Idempotent requests

Timeouts, Retries, Backoff & Jitter

Fail fast, retry politely

If a builder doesn't answer, wait a bit before asking again, wait longer each time, and don't let the whole room shout at the same moment.

Every network call needs a timeout; without one, a slow dependency ties up your threads forever. Retry only transient errors, and only idempotent operations. Space retries out with exponential backoff (for example 100 ms, 200 ms, 400 ms…) plus random jitter so clients don't retry in sync. Cap the number of attempts, and use a retry budget so retries can't multiply load during an outage.

How it breaks

  • Retry storms: three layers each retrying three times turns one failure into 27 calls.
  • Retries without jitter synchronize into waves that knock the dependency down again.

Read more

  • Timeouts, retries, and backoff with jitter — Amazon Builders' Library
  • Exponential Backoff And Jitter — Marc Brooker, with simulations
  • Addressing Cascading Failures (Google SRE book)

Circuit Breakers & Bulkheads

Contain failures before they cascade

A breaker switch between sub-assemblies that snaps open when one keeps failing, plus walls between sections so a collapse in one doesn't topple the rest.

A circuit breaker counts failures to a dependency. Past a threshold it opens and fails fast, often returning a fallback. After a cooldown it half-opens and lets a few trial calls through, closing again if they succeed. Bulkheads give each dependency its own thread pool or connection pool, so one slow dependency can't take every thread.

Fallbacks

  • Serve cached or default data, hide the feature (no recommendations row), or queue the request for later.
  • A fallback must be cheaper and more reliable than the thing it replaces.

Read more

  • CircuitBreaker — Martin Fowler
  • Hystrix: How it Works — Netflix's breaker and bulkhead library, now in maintenance mode
  • Addressing Cascading Failures (Google SRE book)

Rate Limiting

Token bucket · leaky bucket · fixed and sliding windows

A turnstile on the front-door stud: each visitor gets a handful of tokens that refill slowly, and no tokens means no entry.

A rate limiter caps how many requests a client (by user, API key or IP) can make. A token bucket allows bursts up to the bucket size and a sustained refill rate. A sliding window gives smoother limits than fixed windows, which allow double bursts at window edges. In a distributed system, keep counters in Redis and update them atomically (INCR with EXPIRE, or a Lua script). Reject with HTTP 429 and a Retry-After header.

Design choices

  • Where: at the gateway, per service, or both.
  • Fail open or fail closed when the limiter's store is down.
  • Layer the limits: per-user limits, global load shedding, and reserved capacity for critical traffic.

Read more

  • Scaling your API with rate limiters — Stripe
  • How we built rate limiting capable of scaling to millions of domains — Cloudflare's sliding-window approximation

Backpressure & Load Shedding

Say 'slow down' or 'no' before you fall over

When the builder's hands are full, they stop accepting pieces, or politely drop the least important ones, instead of letting everything crash to the floor.

Backpressure pushes the signal to slow down back upstream: bounded queues, blocking producers, HTTP 429 or 503. Load shedding deliberately rejects excess or low-priority work so the rest finishes in time. A server at 110% capacity that accepts everything often completes nothing, because every request times out after doing its work.

Techniques

  • Bounded queues and concurrency limits, which can adapt to measured latency.
  • Prioritize: checkout over recommendations, interactive over batch.
  • Drop requests whose client deadline has already passed.

Read more

  • Using load shedding to avoid overload — Amazon Builders' Library
  • Handling Overload (Google SRE book)
  • Queues Don't Fix Overload — Fred Hebert

Delivery Semantics

At-most-once · at-least-once · exactly-once

Will each piece on the conveyor arrive zero or one time, one or more times, or exactly once?

At-most-once means acknowledging before processing: messages can be lost but never duplicated. At-least-once means acknowledging after processing: nothing is lost but duplicates happen, and it is the default for SQS, Kafka consumers and S3 events. Exactly-once delivery isn't possible over an unreliable network in general, but exactly-once effects are: combine at-least-once delivery with idempotent processing or transactional sinks (Kafka transactions, dedupe tables).

Remember

  • Design for at-least-once plus idempotency. It's the pragmatic answer in nearly every interview and production system.

Read more

  • Exactly-once Semantics Are Possible: Here's How Kafka Does It — Confluent
  • Challenges with distributed systems — Amazon Builders' Library: the eight failure points of one request

Numbers & Targets

Latency Numbers & Tail Latency

Know the orders of magnitude

Know how far each drawer is from your hands before you decide where to keep a piece.

Rough orders of magnitude: L1 cache ≈ 1 ns, main memory ≈ 100 ns, SSD random read ≈ 100 µs, a round trip in the same datacenter ≈ 0.5 ms, a disk seek ≈ 10 ms, and a round trip across a continent ≈ 50–150 ms. Tail latency (p99, p999) dominates at scale. If a page fans out to 100 backends, a 1-in-100 slow response slows most page loads.

Tail tolerance

  • Hedged requests: after the p95 time, send a second copy of the request and use whichever answers first.
  • Measure percentiles, not averages. Set timeouts from the p99.

Read more

  • Latency Numbers Every Programmer Should Know — Based on Jeff Dean and Peter Norvig
  • The Tail at Scale — Dean and Barroso, CACM 2013
  • Designs, Lessons and Advice from Building Large Distributed Systems — Jeff Dean, LADIS 2009

Back-of-the-Envelope Estimation

Size it before you draw it

Count how many pieces you need before you pick the baseplate.

Estimate the load for a photo-sharing app with 100 million daily active users, where each user views 50 photos and uploads 0.5 photos per day, and an average photo is 500 KB. Work out the read QPS, write QPS, peak QPS, daily new storage and 5-year storage.

Steps

  1. Seconds per day ≈ 86,400 ≈ 10^5. So 1 million requests a day ≈ 12 per second.
  2. Reads: 100M × 50 = 5 billion per day, so about 58,000 QPS on average.
  3. Writes: 100M × 0.5 = 50 million per day, so about 580 QPS. The read-to-write ratio is 100:1, which says read-heavy: cache and CDN.
  4. Peak ≈ 2–3× average, so plan for about 150,000 read QPS and 1,500 write QPS.
  5. Storage: 50M × 500 KB = 25 TB per day, about 9 PB per year, about 45 PB over 5 years before replication. That means object storage with lifecycle tiers.
  6. Metadata: 50M rows per day × about 1 KB = 50 GB per day, which fits a sharded database or a NoSQL table.

Handy constants

  • 2^10 ≈ a thousand, 2^20 ≈ a million, 2^30 ≈ a billion, 2^40 ≈ a trillion (KB, MB, GB, TB).
  • One modern server handles very roughly 10k–100k simple requests per second. One Postgres primary, very roughly 10k–50k simple writes per second.
  • Round aggressively. The goal is the order of magnitude, not the decimal.

Bricks used

Object Storage, Content Delivery Network, Caches, Sharding (Partitioning)

Read more

  • ByteByteGo: System Design 101
  • Latency Numbers Every Programmer Should Know

Availability, SLOs & Error Budgets

How many nines, and what they cost

Decide how often the model is allowed to have a missing brick, and spend that allowance on shipping new features.

An SLI is a measured indicator, such as the share of requests that succeed in under 300 ms. An SLO is the target for it, such as 99.9% over 30 days. An SLA is a contract with penalties. The error budget is 1 minus the SLO; while budget remains you ship faster, and when it runs out you focus on reliability. Components in series multiply their availabilities (99.9% × 99.9% ≈ 99.8%); redundant components in parallel raise it.

The nines

  • 99% ≈ 3.65 days of downtime a year (7.3 hours a month).
  • 99.9% ≈ 8.8 hours a year (43.8 minutes a month).
  • 99.99% ≈ 52.6 minutes a year (4.4 minutes a month).
  • 99.999% ≈ 5.3 minutes a year. Each extra nine costs roughly 10× more.

Read more

  • Service Level Objectives (Google SRE book)
  • Implementing SLOs (Google SRE workbook)

lessons.title: 3 · Assemblies
lessons.html:
3 · Assemblies

Worked Examples

Uber-like Ride-Hailing

Example A · real-time geospatial matching

A city-sized model where hundreds of thousands of tiny car bricks keep moving, and every few seconds a passenger brick asks, 'which car is closest to me?'

Hundreds of thousands of drivers broadcast their location every few seconds. Passengers request rides and must be matched to a nearby available driver in real time, without two passengers getting the same driver.

Steps

  1. An API Gateway authenticates the driver apps and receives a location ping (driver_id, lat, lng, status) every ~4 seconds.
  2. Pings go straight onto an event stream (Kafka), keyed by geo cell (for example an H3 index) so each region's updates stay ordered. The gateway never writes to a database per ping.
  3. A geospatial compute cluster (containers) consumes the stream and updates an in-memory cache (Redis GEO, or H3 cell → driver sets) with each driver's latest position and a short TTL, so drivers who go silent disappear on their own. Other consumers, such as ETA, surge pricing and analytics, read the same stream independently.
  4. When a passenger requests a ride, a serverless function (or matching service) asks Redis for available drivers within a radius, ranks them by ETA, and claims one atomically (for example SET driver:lock NX with a TTL) to prevent double dispatch.
  5. The match goes into a message queue, and a notifier sends the driver a push notification with retries and a timeout. If the driver declines or doesn't answer, the lock is released and the next candidate is offered.
  6. The confirmed trip is written to a durable database (sharded by city or trip ID) as the system of record for billing and history.

Why these bricks

  • Location is high-volume and short-lived. Keep only the latest position in memory; the stream holds history for replay and analytics.
  • The stream decouples ingestion from consumers, so a slow analytics job never delays matching.
  • Geo cells turn 'nearby' into a handful of key lookups instead of scanning every driver.
  • The queue makes notifications reliable and retryable without blocking the matcher.

Numbers

  • 500,000 active drivers × 1 ping every 4 s ≈ 125,000 writes per second of ingest.
  • Each position ≈ 100 bytes, so all active drivers fit in well under 1 GB of RAM.

Break it

  • A Redis shard dies: its drivers vanish until their next ping (about 4 s) or until the cache is rebuilt from the stream. Is a few seconds of blindness acceptable?
  • Friday night downtown: one geo cell's partition runs hot. Split cells into finer resolution or sub-partitions.
  • Two matchers pick the same driver: without the atomic claim, both riders get a confirmation.
  • The push provider slows down: the queue backlog grows, so set a message TTL and re-match instead of sending stale offers.

Bricks used

API Gateway, Event Streams, Apache Kafka Deep Dive, Containers, Caches, Serverless Functions, Message Queues, NoSQL & Document Databases, Wide-Column Stores: Cassandra, Idempotency

Read more

  • H3: Uber's Hexagonal Hierarchical Spatial Index — Uber Engineering
  • H3 documentation
  • Redis geospatial indexes
  • Introducing Domain-Oriented Microservice Architecture — How Uber reorganized about 2,200 microservices
  • Uber Engineering blog

E-commerce Flash-Sale Checkout

Example B · surviving a purchase surge

Doors open on a toy-store sale. Instead of everyone rushing the one cash register (the database), customers drop numbered tickets in a slot, and a clerk processes them one by one.

During a flash sale, millions of shoppers try to buy at the same moment. Handle the surge without dropping orders, overselling limited stock, or charging anyone twice.

Steps

  1. A CDN serves the product pages and static assets, and an API Gateway applies per-user rate limits (optionally a virtual waiting room) so the origin sees only real checkout attempts.
  2. Load balancers spread millions of concurrent requests across hundreds of stateless checkout containers that autoscale.
  3. Each checkout reserves stock atomically in a fast store (a Redis DECR, or a conditional UPDATE … WHERE stock > 0) and rejects immediately when stock is gone.
  4. Instead of writing the full order to the database under peak load, the container drops an order message (with a client-generated idempotency key) onto a durable message queue.
  5. The user instantly sees 'Your order is processing', and the page polls or receives a push when the order is confirmed.
  6. Isolated order-processing workers pull jobs at a steady pace the database can handle. Each worker writes the order to the relational database in a transaction, calls the payment gateway with the same idempotency key, and acknowledges the message only after both succeed.
  7. Messages that keep failing go to a dead-letter queue for inspection. An outbox table publishes OrderConfirmed events for email, fulfilment and analytics.

Why these bricks

  • The queue turns a spike the database can't survive into a steady flow it can (load leveling).
  • Stateless containers scale out instantly; the database doesn't, so it is protected behind the queue.
  • Idempotency keys make every retry safe, whether from the browser, the queue or the payment call.

Numbers

  • 1 million orders in 10 minutes ≈ 1,700 orders per second on average, with the first seconds at 10× that. Workers might drain 2,000 per second.

Break it

  • A worker crashes after charging but before acknowledging: the message reappears, and the idempotency key stops a second charge.
  • The payment gateway times out: retry with backoff and the same key. Never generate a new key on retry.
  • The queue backlog grows: autoscale workers on queue depth, but cap them at the database's safe concurrency and show an honest ETA.
  • The Redis stock count and the database disagree after a crash: reconcile, and choose reserve-then-confirm with expiring reservations.

Bricks used

Content Delivery Network, API Gateway, Rate Limiting, Load Balancers, Containers, Caches, Message Queues, Relational Databases, Idempotency, Sagas & the Transactional Outbox, Distributed Cache, Service Mesh: Istio, Metrics & Alerting: Prometheus

Read more

  • Designing robust and predictable APIs with idempotency — Stripe
  • Surviving Flashes of High-Write Traffic Using Scriptable Load Balancers — Shopify Engineering
  • A Pods Architecture To Allow Shopify To Scale — Shopify Engineering
  • Pattern: Transactional outbox
  • Avoiding insurmountable queue backlogs — Amazon Builders' Library

Classic Builds

URL Shortener at Scale

Like bit.ly or TinyURL

A giant wall of tiny labelled drawers: each short label opens a drawer holding the long address.

Design a service that turns long URLs into 7-character short links and redirects about 100 million clicks a day with low latency. Reads outnumber writes about 100 to 1.

Steps

  1. Write path: POST /links {longUrl}. Generate a unique ID (a Snowflake ID or a range-allocated counter), encode it in base62 (62^7 ≈ 3.5 trillion codes), and store code → longUrl, owner and expiry in a key-value store.
  2. Read path: GET /{code} goes through the CDN or edge, then a load balancer to stateless services, then a Redis cache, then the key-value store on a miss. Answer with a 301 (cacheable, cheapest) or 302 (every click reaches you, so you can count it).
  3. Publish click events asynchronously to a stream for analytics. Never do it inline on the redirect.
  4. Rate-limit creation per user or IP to stop spam, and check URLs against a malware list.

Trade-offs to discuss

  • Hash of the URL plus a collision check makes duplicate URLs share one code, but costs a read on every write.
  • A counter per range (each server leases blocks of 1,000 IDs) needs no coordination per request.
  • Custom aliases require a uniqueness check, for example a conditional put.

Bricks used

Load Balancers, Containers, Caches, NoSQL & Document Databases, Content Delivery Network, Event Streams, Unique ID Generation, Rate Limiting

Read more

  • The System Design Primer — See the Pastebin/Bit.ly solution
  • Announcing Snowflake

News Feed / Timeline

Like Twitter/X, Instagram or Facebook

Every follower has a personal mailbox tray. Do you drop a copy of each new brick into every tray (push), or does each follower walk around collecting bricks when they look (pull)?

Users follow others and open their home timeline: the newest posts from everyone they follow, loaded in under 200 ms. Some accounts have 100 million followers.

Steps

  1. Post service: store the post in a sharded store (by author) and media in object storage behind a CDN.
  2. Publish PostCreated to a queue or stream.
  3. Fan-out workers look up the author's followers and push the post ID into each follower's timeline list in Redis (fan-out on write), trimmed to the newest ~800 IDs.
  4. For celebrity authors, skip fan-out. At read time, merge their recent posts into the follower's cached timeline (fan-out on read). This hybrid approach is the classic answer.
  5. The timeline read fetches IDs from Redis, hydrates the post bodies from the post cache or store, and ranks them.

Why

  • Reads vastly outnumber writes, so precompute timelines to make reads cheap.
  • Pushing a celebrity's post to 100 million timelines would take far too long and cost too much, hence the hybrid.

Break it

  • The fan-out queue backs up after a viral post: timelines lag. Prioritize active users and skip fan-out to dormant ones.
  • The timeline cache is lost: rebuild on demand from the social graph plus recent posts, and protect the database with request coalescing.

Bricks used

API Gateway, Containers, Message Queues, Caches, NoSQL & Document Databases, Object Storage, Content Delivery Network, Sharding (Partitioning)

Read more

  • Timelines at Scale — Raffi Krikorian, Twitter (QCon 2012)
  • TAO: Facebook's Distributed Data Store for the Social Graph

Real-Time Chat

Like WhatsApp, Slack or Discord

Each person keeps a walkie-talkie line open to a switchboard brick. The switchboard knows who's on which line and relays each message instantly.

One-to-one and group chat with messages delivered in under a second, online presence, message history, and delivery to offline users.

Steps

  1. Clients hold a persistent WebSocket to a fleet of connection-gateway servers behind an L4 load balancer.
  2. A session registry in Redis maps user_id to the gateway that holds their connection, and tracks presence with heartbeats and TTLs.
  3. When a message is sent, the chat service assigns a per-channel sequence number and persists it to a wide-column store partitioned by (channel_id, time bucket).
  4. The message is published to a stream or pub/sub topic. The gateways holding recipients' connections push it down their sockets.
  5. Offline recipients get a push notification through a notification queue, and clients sync missed messages on reconnect using their last seen sequence number.

Break it

  • A gateway server dies: all its clients reconnect at once. Add jittered reconnect backoff, or they stampede the survivors.
  • A huge channel (a server with 1 million members) becomes a hot partition. Use time-bucketed partitions and fan out in tiers.
  • Duplicate sends on flaky mobile networks: a client message ID deduplicates them.

Bricks used

Load Balancers, Containers, Caches, NoSQL & Document Databases, Wide-Column Stores: Cassandra, Event Streams, Message Queues, Sharding (Partitioning)

Read more

  • How Discord Stores Trillions of Messages — Discord Engineering
  • Real-time Messaging — Slack Engineering
  • The WebSocket API (MDN)

Video Streaming

Like Netflix or YouTube

Chop each movie into small numbered bricks at several quality levels, stock copies in every corner shop, and let each viewer's player grab whichever size fits their connection.

Creators upload large video files, and millions of viewers worldwide stream them smoothly on connections ranging from 3G to fibre.

Steps

  1. The client asks the API for a presigned URL and uploads the raw file directly to object storage in multiple parts.
  2. The upload event triggers a transcoding pipeline: a queue of jobs split into chunks that workers encode in parallel into many bitrates and resolutions, packaged as HLS or DASH segments of about 2–6 seconds.
  3. Segments and manifests are written back to object storage, and metadata (title, status, segment locations) goes to a database.
  4. Viewers fetch the manifest and segments from a CDN. The player's adaptive bitrate logic switches quality segment by segment as bandwidth changes.
  5. Views, watch time and quality-of-experience events stream into analytics and recommendations.

Break it

  • A new episode drops and the CDN is cold: pre-position popular titles at the edge before release.
  • A transcode worker dies mid-chunk: the job becomes visible again and is re-encoded. Writes to deterministic output keys make that idempotent.

Bricks used

API Gateway, Object Storage, Message Queues, Containers, Serverless Functions, Content Delivery Network, Relational Databases, Event Streams

Read more

  • Netflix Open Connect — The CDN appliances Netflix places inside ISPs
  • Completing the Netflix Cloud Migration
  • Netflix Tech Blog — Encoding, streaming and resilience posts

Distributed Rate Limiter

Protect an API used by millions of clients

A turnstile at every entrance, all reading the same shared tally board so no one can sneak extra passes by switching doors.

Limit each API key to N requests per minute across a fleet of 200 gateway nodes, adding less than 1–2 ms of latency, and keep the API up even if the limiter's store has trouble.

Steps

  1. Enforce in the API Gateway or a sidecar, before the request reaches business services.
  2. Keep a token bucket per key in Redis, updated atomically with a Lua script that refills based on elapsed time and takes one token.
  3. Shard the Redis keys by API key. Hot keys can keep a small local token cache on each gateway, synced asynchronously.
  4. Reject with 429 Too Many Requests, a Retry-After header, and X-RateLimit-Remaining headers.
  5. Choose deliberately what happens when Redis is unreachable: fail open, with a coarse local limit as a backstop.

Algorithms

  • Token bucket: allows bursts and is simple. Sliding-window counter: smooth and memory-cheap. Fixed window: simplest, but allows double bursts at the edges.

Bricks used

API Gateway, Caches, Rate Limiting, Consistent Hashing

Read more

  • Scaling your API with rate limiters — Stripe
  • How we built rate limiting capable of scaling to millions of domains — Cloudflare

Notification System

Push, SMS and email at scale

A mailroom that sorts every outgoing letter into the right chute (push, SMS or email), throws out duplicates, and keeps retrying any letter the post office bounces.

Many product services need to notify users through push, SMS and email: tens of millions of messages a day, respecting user preferences, never double-sending, and surviving flaky third-party providers.

Steps

  1. Services call a Notification API (or publish events) with user_id, template and data, plus an idempotency key.
  2. The notification service checks user preferences, quiet hours and rate caps, renders the template, and deduplicates on the key.
  3. It enqueues onto a separate queue per channel (push, SMS, email) so a slow SMS provider can't block push.
  4. Channel workers call the providers (APNs/FCM, Twilio, SES) with timeouts, retries with backoff, and circuit breakers per provider, failing over to a secondary provider where possible.
  5. Messages that exhaust their retries go to a dead-letter queue. Delivery status streams into analytics.

Break it

  • The email provider is down for an hour: the email queue grows while push and SMS keep flowing, and the backlog drains when the provider recovers. Set a TTL for time-sensitive messages such as one-time passcodes.
  • A marketing blast of 50 million messages starves transactional ones: use separate priority queues.

Bricks used

API Gateway, Containers, Message Queues, Relational Databases, Caches, Idempotency, Timeouts, Retries, Backoff & Jitter, Circuit Breakers & Bulkheads

Read more

  • Amazon SQS dead-letter queues
  • Timeouts, retries, and backoff with jitter — Amazon Builders' Library
