Mini-MOC: Prefix-Aware Router vs Round Robin

Hands-on: prove why routing matters for LLMs

Run two dispatchers side by side, one random and one who remembers which builder has which pages open, and time them.

Run 2–4 small vLLM replicas (one GPU each, or CPU with a tiny model) and write a simple router in about 100 lines: hash the first N prompt tokens to a replica, with a load cap. Compare it against round robin on a chat workload with shared system prompts and multi-turn sessions.

Steps

  1. Generate a workload: 20 system prompts × 200 users × 5 turns, with each turn appending to the conversation.
  2. Baseline: round robin via nginx or Envoy. Record TTFT p50/p95, the prefix-cache hit rate (vLLM metrics), and throughput.
  3. Your router: consistent hashing on (system prompt plus session ID), falling back to the least-loaded replica when the chosen one's queue exceeds a threshold.
  4. Bonus: try the Gateway API Inference Extension or llm-d's scheduler on kind or minikube and compare it with yours.
  5. Write up the results: the hit-rate and TTFT improvement, and what happens when one replica gets a hot system prompt.

Drill: Bad Model Rollout & Noisy Tenant

Chaos engineering for the model layer, not just the infrastructure

Slip a slightly miswired motor into the line and let one customer hog the dispatcher, then see whether anyone notices before the customers do.

Infrastructure is healthy, but the model is wrong: a new version that is 30% slower, emits malformed JSON 5% of the time, or has a broken chat template. Meanwhile one tenant sends 10× its normal traffic. Do your canaries, evaluations and quotas catch it?

Steps

  1. Hypothesis: the canary at 5% traffic detects the regression within 10 minutes and rolls back automatically, and other tenants' p95 TTFT stays within SLO during the noisy-tenant spike.
  2. Deploy a deliberately degraded model version (a wrong quantization, a missing stop token, or a bad template) as the canary through the Istio or KServe traffic split.
  3. Watch the signals: TPOT and TTFT per version, structured-output parse-failure rate, average output length (runaway generations), user thumbs-down rate, and guardrail triggers.
  4. Simultaneously replay 10× traffic from one tenant key. Per-tenant token limits and fair queuing must contain it.
  5. Record the time to detect and the time to roll back, and which dashboard or alert fired first. Add the missing ones.

The lesson

  • Model regressions return HTTP 200. You need quality and behavior metrics per model version, not just error rates.

ML Builds, Projects & Drills

Online LLM Serving Platform

Serve a 70B chat model to 10,000 concurrent users

The full motor room: front desk, smart dispatcher, racks of motor bricks, and gauges on every wall.

Design an internal platform serving open models (for example, a 70B instruct model plus an 8B) to many product teams with an OpenAI-compatible API, streaming, a p95 TTFT under 1 s, TPOT under 50 ms, per-team quotas, and cost efficiency.

Steps

  1. Clients call the AI gateway (auth, per-team token quotas, model routing, fallbacks, usage metering) behind Torbit or the CDN edge and Istio.
  2. The gateway forwards to a Kubernetes inference gateway (GAIE or llm-d) whose endpoint picker scores vLLM or SGLang replicas on prefix-cache overlap, queue depth and KV utilization.
  3. The 70B model runs in FP8 with TP=2 per replica on H100 or H200 nodes, with continuous batching, chunked prefill and prefix caching. At large scale, split into prefill and decode pools (disaggregation).
  4. Weights come from the MLflow registry into GCS, and are cached on local NVMe or via GCS FUSE for fast cold starts. Images are pre-pulled on GPU node pools.
  5. KEDA or HPA scales on queue depth and KV cache utilization, with minimum warm replicas. The cluster autoscaler adds GPU nodes, and GPU reservations cover the baseline.
  6. Prometheus and DCGM track TTFT, TPOT, goodput, KV usage, GPU utilization and power. OpenTelemetry traces cover gateway → router → engine. Prompts and completions are logged to Kafka and the lake for evaluation.

Capacity napkin

  • 10,000 concurrent streams at about 30 tokens/s each is 300k output tokens/s. If one TP=2 FP8 70B replica sustains about 3k tokens/s at the SLO, you need about 100 replicas (200 GPUs) plus headroom. Measure; don't guess.
  • KV cache: 70B with GQA (80 layers, 8 KV heads, 128 head dim, FP8) is about 160 KB per token, so a 4k context is about 0.65 GB per stream.

Break it

  • Kill a GPU node mid-stream: clients get a retriable error and resume via the gateway retry. The router drains the dead endpoints.
  • A 100k-token prompt flood: chunked prefill or disaggregation protects the TPOT of other users, and gateway limits on max input tokens apply.

Bricks used

Real-Time Recommendations

Feature store + two-stage retrieval and ranking + Triton

Grab a handful of likely pieces from a huge bin fast, then have an expert sort that handful into the perfect order, in under 100 ms.

Personalized product recommendations on the home page for 100M users, with p99 under 100 ms, reacting to clicks within seconds, and retrained daily.

Steps

  1. Clickstream goes to Kafka, then Flink computes real-time features (the last N items viewed, session category affinity) and writes them to the online feature store (Redis, Bigtable or Cassandra).
  2. The nightly Spark batch computes long-term user and item features into the offline store, then materializes them online.
  3. Retrieval: embed the user and run ANN search over item embeddings (vector DB or ScaNN/FAISS) to get about 500 candidates, plus rule-based candidates.
  4. Ranking: fetch features for the user and candidates from the online store, then score them on Triton (dynamic batching, GPU), rerank for diversity and business rules, and return the top 20.
  5. Log served features and outcomes to Kafka and the lake. Daily training with point-in-time joins, registered in MLflow, rolled out as a canary with an A/B test.

Break it

  • The feature store times out: fall back to cached popular items (a degraded but fast default). The circuit breaker opens.

Bricks used

Read more

  • Deep Neural Networks for YouTube Recommendations (RecSys 2016) — Candidate generation plus ranking
  • Meet Michelangelo: Uber's Machine Learning Platform
  • Triton: dynamic batching

Batch LLM Inference Pipeline

Ray Data + vLLM over 100M product descriptions

Run the motor room overnight on a giant pile of jobs: nobody is waiting for any single one, so pack the GPUs completely full.

Every week, generate enriched attributes and embeddings for 100M catalog items with an 8B LLM, maximizing tokens per dollar with no latency SLO, and write the results back to the lakehouse.

Steps

  1. Airflow triggers the job and reads a snapshot of the item table (Iceberg on GCS) with Ray Data, streaming in blocks.
  2. CPU stages build prompts. GPU stages run vLLM engines as Ray actors (one per GPU) with large batches, prefix caching for the shared instruction, and FP8.
  3. Use spot or preemptible GPUs with Ray task retries. Write output per block, idempotently, keyed by item ID.
  4. Write results to an Iceberg table and publish a 'ready' event. The search index and feature store pick up the changes.

Napkin

  • 100M items × about 300 tokens is about 30B tokens. At about 20k tokens/s per GPU for a batch-optimized 8B model, that's about 420 GPU-hours.

Bricks used

Workflow Orchestration, Lakehouse Table Formats, Google Cloud Storage Buckets, Ray, vLLM, Quantization, Batch Pipeline Design Principles

Read more

  • Ray Data: batch inference
  • vLLM offline inference

RAG Shopping Assistant

Retrieval + LLM + guardrails

Before answering, the builder runs to the parts catalog, grabs the relevant pages, and builds the answer from them.

A chat assistant that answers product and policy questions grounded in the catalog and help-center documents, with citations, streaming, and under 2 s to first token.

Steps

  1. An offline pipeline (Airflow, Spark or Ray) chunks documents, embeds them, and indexes them into a vector DB plus a keyword index (hybrid search). CDC keeps prices and stock fresh.
  2. Online: the AI gateway authenticates and applies guardrails, then query rewriting, then hybrid retrieval and a reranker, then a prompt with a stable system prefix (for prefix caching) plus the retrieved context.
  3. The LLM is served on vLLM or SGLang behind the inference gateway. Responses stream via SSE with citations.
  4. Log everything, run offline evaluations (groundedness, answer quality), and collect user feedback in MLflow and the lake.

Break it

  • The vector DB is slow: time out and fall back to keyword search only. The LLM pool is saturated: queue with a clear message, or fall back to a smaller model.

Bricks used

AI Gateway, Vector Databases, Search Engines, Change Data Capture (CDC), vLLM, Prefix Caching & KV-Aware Routing, Distributed Cache, MLflow, Distributed Tracing & Logs

Read more

  • Retrieval-Augmented Generation for Knowledge-Intensive NLP Tasks
  • SGLang documentation

Training-to-Deployment Pipeline

Lakehouse → Spark features → Ray Train → MLflow → canary

The full assembly line from raw pieces to a certified model on the showroom floor, with a rollback lever at every stage.

Automate weekly retraining of a ranking model (or a LoRA fine-tune of an LLM) from fresh data, with evaluation gates, safe rollout and automatic rollback.

Steps

  1. The Airflow or Kubeflow pipeline builds a point-in-time training set from the feature store's offline store (Spark), pinned to an Iceberg snapshot.
  2. Distributed training on GPUs with Ray Train (or PyTorch on KubeRay). Parameters, metrics and artifacts are logged to MLflow.
  3. Evaluation gates: sliced metrics must beat the champion, bias and safety checks pass, and a latency benchmark is run on the serving engine.
  4. Register the version, set the @challenger alias, then shadow it, then canary it (Istio or KServe traffic split) while watching business metrics and SLOs. Promote to @champion or roll back automatically.

Bricks used

Workflow Orchestration, Feature Store, Apache Spark, Lakehouse Table Formats, Ray, MLflow, ML Pipelines & Model Lifecycle, Service Mesh: Istio, Kubernetes Model Serving & GPU Autoscaling, Metrics & Alerting: Prometheus

  • MLflow Model Registry

Mini-MOC: Serve & Benchmark a Model with vLLM

Hands-on: one GPU, one weekend

Build a small working motor yourself and put it on the test bench before designing the whole factory.

Serve a small open model (1–8B) with vLLM, or SGLang if you want to compare, on one GPU (cloud or local). Load-test it and plot how TTFT, TPOT and throughput trade off as concurrency rises.

Steps

  1. Run `vllm serve <model>` with an OpenAI-compatible endpoint. Scrape `/metrics` with Prometheus and graph it in Grafana.
  2. Benchmark at concurrency 1, 8, 32, 128 (vLLM bench serve or a Locust script) with a fixed prompt and output length. Record TTFT, TPOT, tokens/s and KV cache usage.
  3. Toggle one lever at a time: prefix caching (shared system prompt), FP8 quantization, max_num_seqs, and a speculative-decoding drafter. Compare the curves.
  4. Write a one-page capacity model: GPUs needed for X users at a Y ms TTFT SLO.

Bricks used

  • vLLM GitHub — See benchmarks/ for the serving benchmark

Drill: GPU Loss & KV-Cache Exhaustion

Chaos engineering for model serving

Pull a motor brick out while the machine is running, then overload the rest, and watch whether the gauges and dispatcher react in time.

Test that the serving platform degrades gracefully when GPUs disappear or the KV cache fills up, and that you see it coming on dashboards before users do.

Steps

  1. Hypothesis: losing one replica keeps p95 TTFT within SLO, and a traffic spike triggers queueing and scale-up, not errors.
  2. Kill a vLLM pod or cordon a GPU node. The router must stop sending traffic to it within seconds, and in-flight streams must fail cleanly and be retried by the gateway.
  3. Spike traffic with long prompts until KV cache usage reaches 100%. Watch preemptions, queue depth and TTFT. The autoscaler should fire on the queue metric, and the gateway should shed low-priority tenants first.
  4. Check the alerts: KV cache above 90%, TTFT SLO burn rate, and GPU XID or DCGM errors. Record how long GPU scale-up really takes, from node to image to weights to ready.

The lesson

  • GPU capacity is slow to add. Protect it with admission control and keep warm headroom, rather than relying on autoscaling alone.

lessons.title: Foundations & Notation
lessons.html:
Foundations & Notation

The symbols every paper assumes you can read.

Numbers & operations

Three ways to write multiplication

a \times b \;=\; a \cdot b \;=\; ab

“a times b”

All three mean multiply. School books use \times; papers prefer \cdot or simply writing the letters side by side (ab), because \times is kept for sizes such as 3 \times 4 and for the cross product.

Example

3 \cdot 4 = 12, \qquad 2x \text{ means } 2 \cdot x

In AI papers

When a paper writes \mathbf{W}\mathbf{x} with nothing in between, it means “\mathbf{W} multiplied by \mathbf{x}”.

Fraction bar (division)

\frac{a}{b} \;=\; a / b \;=\; a \div b

“a over b”

A fraction bar means divide the top (numerator) by the bottom (denominator). Papers almost never use \div; they write \frac{a}{b} in displayed formulas and a/b inline.

Example

\frac{3}{4} = 0.75

In AI papers

Averages are written with a fraction: \frac{1}{N} in front of a sum means “divide the total by N”.

Power (exponent)

a^{n}

“a to the power n, or a to the n”

Multiply a by itself n times. a^2 is “a squared”, a^3 is “a cubed”.

Example

2^{3} = 2 \cdot 2 \cdot 2 = 8, \qquad 2^{10} = 1024

In AI papers

A 16-bit number can take 2^{16} = 65{,}536 different values; an 8-bit one only 2^{8} = 256.

Square root

\sqrt{x}

“the square root of x”

The number that, multiplied by itself, gives x. It undoes squaring.

Example

\sqrt{64} = 8 \quad\text{because}\quad 8^{2} = 64

In AI papers

Transformer attention divides by \sqrt{d_k}, the square root of the key size, to keep scores from growing too large.

Comparison signs

a < b, \quad a \le b, \quad a > b, \quad a \ge b, \quad a \ne b

“a is less than b; less than or equal to; greater than; greater than or equal to; not equal to”

The open side of < faces the bigger number. A line underneath (\le, \ge) allows equality. Papers write \le and \ge; you may also see \leq and \geq, which are the same symbols.

Example

3 < 5, \qquad 5 \le 5, \qquad 3 \ne 5

In AI papers

Bounds in theory papers are chains of \le: “the error is at most …”.

Approximately equal

\pi \approx 3.14159

“pi is approximately 3.14159”

\approx means “close to but not exactly”. \sim is sometimes used the same way, but in probability it means “is distributed as”.

Example

\frac{1}{3} \approx 0.333

In AI papers

Training in BF16 stores each weight only approximately: \operatorname{bf16}(w) \approx w.

Percent

45\% = \frac{45}{100} = 0.45

“forty-five percent”

“Per cent” means “out of 100”. To turn a fraction into a percent, multiply by 100.

Example

\frac{9}{10} = 90\%

In AI papers

Benchmark scores such as “accuracy 87.3%” are fractions of correct answers, times 100.

Negative numbers and the number line

-3 < -1 < 0 < 2 < 5

“minus three is less than minus one, which is less than zero, which is less than two, which is less than five”

Numbers to the left of zero on the number line are negative. Further left means smaller, so -3 is less than -1.

Example

5 - 8 = -3, \qquad (-2) \times (-3) = 6

In AI papers

Weights and logits can be negative. A negative logit means “less likely than average”.

Ratio

a : b \;=\; \frac{a}{b}

“a to b”

Compares two amounts by division. 3 : 1 means “three for every one”.

Example

80 : 20 = 4 : 1

In AI papers

Datasets are split 80 : 20 into training and test sets; the FFN is usually 4 : 1 wider than the model dimension.

Order of operations

2 + 3 \times 4^{2} = 2 + 3 \times 16 = 2 + 48 = 50

“two plus three times four squared equals fifty”

Brackets first, then powers, then multiply and divide, then add and subtract. Every formula in every paper relies on this order.

Term by term

  • 4^{2} — powers are done first: 16
  • 3 \times 16 — then multiplication: 48
  • 2 + 48 — addition last: 50

In AI papers

In \mathbf{W}\mathbf{x} + \mathbf{b} the multiplication happens before the addition, no brackets needed.

Distributive law

a\,(b + c) = ab + ac

“a times the quantity b plus c equals a b plus a c”

Multiplying a sum is the same as multiplying each part and then adding.

Term by term

  • a\,(b + c) — multiply the whole bracket by a
  • ab + ac — same answer, done piece by piece

In AI papers

The same law holds for matrices, \mathbf{W}(\mathbf{x} + \mathbf{y}) = \mathbf{W}\mathbf{x} + \mathbf{W}\mathbf{y}, which is what makes a layer “linear”.

Area of a rectangle

A = \ell \times w

“area equals length times width”

A rectangle 4 squares long and 3 squares wide contains 4 \times 3 = 12 unit squares.

Term by term

  • \ell — length
  • w — width

In AI papers

A matrix is a rectangle of numbers: a 4096 \times 4096 weight matrix holds 16{,}777{,}216 weights.

Negative exponent

a^{-n} = \frac{1}{a^{n}}

“a to the minus n equals one over a to the n”

A negative power means “one divided by” the positive power. 10^{-3} is one thousandth.

Example

10^{-3} = \frac{1}{1000} = 0.001

In AI papers

Learning rates are written like \eta = 3 \times 10^{-4} (read “three times ten to the minus four”), which code writes as 3e-4.

Coordinates of a point

(x, y)

“the point x comma y”

A point in the plane: go x steps right (left if negative), then y steps up (down if negative). Order matters: (2, 5) \ne (5, 2).

Example

(3, -2): \text{ 3 right, 2 down}

In AI papers

A point with two coordinates is a 2-D vector. Embeddings are the same idea with hundreds or thousands of coordinates.

Percent change

\text{percent change} = \frac{\text{new} - \text{old}}{\text{old}} \times 100\%

“percent change equals new minus old, over old, times one hundred percent”

How much something grew or shrank compared with where it started. A negative answer is a decrease.

Term by term

  • \text{new} - \text{old} — the change
  • \div\,\text{old} — compared with the starting value

In AI papers

If the loss falls from 2.50 to 2.20, it dropped by \frac{2.20 - 2.50}{2.50} = -12\%.

Variables & expressions

Variable

x, \; y, \; n, \; w

“x, y, n, w”

A letter stands for a number that is unknown, or that can change. Algebra is the rules for working with such letters.

Example

3x + 2 = 11 \;\Rightarrow\; x = 3

In AI papers

A network’s weights w are variables: training searches for the values that make the loss small.

Subscript (index)

x_{i}

“x sub i”

A small letter below and to the right picks one item from a list: x_1 is the first, x_2 the second, x_i “the i-th”. It is a label, not a calculation.

Example

\mathbf{x} = (4, 7, 1): \quad x_1 = 4,\; x_2 = 7,\; x_3 = 1

In AI papers

In language models x_t is the token at position t, and w_{ij} is the weight in row i, column j.

Evaluating an expression

f(x) = 3x^{2} - 2x + 1, \qquad f(2) = 3 \cdot 4 - 4 + 1 = 9

“f of x equals three x squared minus two x plus one; f of two equals nine”

Replace every x with the number, then follow the order of operations.

Term by term

  • x = 2 — the input being substituted
  • 3x^{2} = 3 \cdot 4 — powers first, then multiply

In AI papers

A forward pass is exactly this: substitute the input into the network’s formula and compute.

Equation of a line

y = m x + b

“y equals m x plus b”

A straight line: m is the slope (how much y goes up when x goes up by 1) and b is where the line crosses the y-axis.

Term by term

  • m — slope, the weight
  • b — intercept, the bias
  • x — input
  • y — output

In AI papers

A single neuron without its activation is exactly this: output = weight × input + bias. Scaled up it becomes \mathbf{y} = \mathbf{W}\mathbf{x} + \mathbf{b}.

Exponent rules

a^{m} a^{n} = a^{m+n}, \qquad \frac{a^{m}}{a^{n}} = a^{m-n}, \qquad (a^{m})^{n} = a^{mn}

“a to the m times a to the n equals a to the m plus n; a to the m over a to the n equals a to the m minus n; a to the m, all to the n, equals a to the m n”

Multiplying powers of the same base adds the exponents; dividing subtracts them; a power of a power multiplies them.

Term by term

  • a^{m} a^{n} — same base multiplied
  • a^{m+n} — exponents added

In AI papers

Floating-point multiplication adds exponents; softmax uses e^{z_i - m} = e^{z_i}/e^{m} to stay numerically safe.

Implies / if and only if

A \Rightarrow B, \qquad A \iff B

“A implies B; A if and only if B”

\Rightarrow: whenever A is true, B is true. \iff: A and B are always both true or both false.

Example

x = 3 \Rightarrow x^{2} = 9, \qquad x^{2} = 9 \not\Rightarrow x = 3

In AI papers

Optimality conditions: \mathbf{x}^* is a minimum of a convex f \iff \nabla f(\mathbf{x}^*) = \mathbf{0}.

Parenthesised superscript (example index)

x^{(i)}, \quad \mathbf{W}^{(l)}

“x superscript i; W superscript l”

A superscript in parentheses is a label, not a power: x^{(i)} is the i-th training example and \mathbf{W}^{(l)} the weight matrix of layer l. The parentheses are there so you do not read it as x to the i.

Example

\mathcal{D} = \{(\mathbf{x}^{(1)}, y^{(1)}), \ldots, (\mathbf{x}^{(N)}, y^{(N)})\}

In AI papers

Dataset notation in almost every ML paper, following Goodfellow et al., *Deep Learning*.

Is defined as

a := b, \quad a \triangleq b, \quad a \equiv b

“a is defined as b”

:= introduces a new name; it is not a claim to be checked. The colon sits on the side of the new name. \triangleq and \equiv are older ways of writing the same thing (\equiv can also mean “identically equal”).

Example

\bar{x} := \frac{1}{n}\sum_{i=1}^{n} x_i

In AI papers

Papers write things like \mathbf{h}_t := f(\mathbf{h}_{t-1}, \mathbf{x}_t) to name the hidden state.

Proportional to

y \propto x

“y is proportional to x”

y = c\,x for some constant c that is not written, because it does not matter for the argument.

Example

p(\theta \mid \mathcal{D}) \propto p(\mathcal{D} \mid \theta)\, p(\theta)

In AI papers

Bayesian posteriors and softmax probabilities (p_i \propto e^{z_i}) are usually written with \propto.

Functions

Function

f(x)

“f of x”

A rule that takes an input x and gives exactly one output. The brackets mean “apply f to”, not multiply.

Example

f(x) = 2x + 1, \qquad f(3) = 7

In AI papers

A neural network is a function f_{\boldsymbol{\theta}}(\mathbf{x}): input \mathbf{x}, parameters \boldsymbol{\theta}, output a prediction.

Maximum and minimum

\max(a, b), \quad \min(a, b)

“max of a and b; min of a and b”

The larger (or smaller) of the values. With a subscript, \max_{i} x_i is the largest entry of a list.

Example

\max(0, -2) = 0, \qquad \max(0, 5) = 5

In AI papers

ReLU, the most common activation, is \max(0, x).

Composition

(g \circ f)(x) = g(f(x))

“g composed with f of x, or g after f”

Apply f first, then g to the result. Read right to left: the function nearest x runs first.

Example

f(x) = x + 1,\; g(x) = x^{2}: \quad (g \circ f)(2) = 9

In AI papers

A deep network is a composition of layers: f = f_L \circ \cdots \circ f_2 \circ f_1.

Exponential function

e^{x} = \exp(x), \quad e \approx 2.71828

“e to the x, or exp of x”

e is a fixed number, about 2.718. e^{x} is always positive and grows faster and faster. \exp(x) is the same thing, used when the exponent is long.

Example

e^{0} = 1, \qquad e^{1} \approx 2.718, \qquad e^{-1} \approx 0.368

In AI papers

Softmax turns any scores into positive numbers with e^{z_i}.

Logarithm

\log x, \quad \ln x, \quad \log_{2} x

“log of x; natural log of x; log base 2 of x”

The logarithm undoes the power: \log_b x = y means b^{y} = x. In ML papers a plain \log is almost always the natural log (base e, also written \ln). \log_2 counts in bits.

Example

\log_{2} 8 = 3, \qquad \ln e = 1, \qquad \log 1 = 0

In AI papers

Losses are written with logs of probabilities, -\log p, which turns products of probabilities into sums.

Floor, ceiling and rounding

\lfloor x \rfloor, \quad \lceil x \rceil, \quad \lfloor x \rceil

“floor of x; ceiling of x; x rounded to the nearest integer”

Floor rounds down, ceiling rounds up. The mixed bracket \lfloor x \rceil is used in quantization papers for round-to-nearest.

Example

\lfloor 2.7 \rfloor = 2, \quad \lceil 2.1 \rceil = 3, \quad \lfloor 2.5 \rceil = 2 \text{ (ties to even)}

In AI papers

Quantization maps a weight to an integer with \lfloor w / s \rceil.

Logarithm rules

\log(ab) = \log a + \log b, \qquad \log\frac{a}{b} = \log a - \log b, \qquad \log a^{k} = k \log a

“log of a b equals log a plus log b; log of a over b equals log a minus log b; log of a to the k equals k log a”

Logs turn multiplication into addition and division into subtraction.

Term by term

  • \log(ab) — log of a product
  • \log a + \log b — sum of logs

In AI papers

Why every likelihood is maximised in log form: \log \prod_i p(x_i) = \sum_i \log p(x_i). A product of thousands of small probabilities would underflow; a sum of logs does not.

Function signature

f : \mathbb{R}^{n} \to \mathbb{R}^{m}

“f maps R n to R m”

Says what goes in and what comes out: f takes a list of n real numbers and returns a list of m real numbers.

Example

f(\mathbf{x}) = \mathbf{W}\mathbf{x}, \quad \mathbf{W} \in \mathbb{R}^{m \times n}

In AI papers

A linear layer with 768 inputs and 3072 outputs is f : \mathbb{R}^{768} \to \mathbb{R}^{3072}.

Maps to (for one element)

x \mapsto x^{2}

“x maps to x squared”

\to connects sets (domain to codomain); \mapsto (with a bar) connects a single input to its output. It defines a function without naming it.

Example

f : \mathbb{R} \to \mathbb{R}, \quad x \mapsto \max(0, x)

In AI papers

Activation functions are often introduced this way, for example x \mapsto x\,\sigma(x) for SiLU.

Arg max / arg min

\arg\max_{x} f(x), \quad \arg\min_{x} f(x)

“the arg max over x of f of x”

\max gives the largest value; \arg\max gives the input where it happens. It answers “which one?”, not “how big?”.

Example

f = (0.1, 0.7, 0.2): \quad \max_i f_i = 0.7, \quad \arg\max_i f_i = 2

In AI papers

Greedy decoding picks \arg\max_{v} p(v \mid x_{<t}); training picks \boldsymbol{\theta}^* = \arg\min_{\boldsymbol{\theta}} \mathcal{L}(\boldsymbol{\theta}).

Indicator function

\mathbb{I}[\text{condition}], \quad \mathbf{1}[\text{condition}]

“indicator of the condition”

Equals 1 when the condition is true and 0 when it is false. It turns a yes/no question into a number you can add up.

Example

\mathbb{I}[3 > 2] = 1, \qquad \sum_{i} \mathbb{I}[\hat{y}_i = y_i] = \text{number correct}

In AI papers

Accuracy is \frac{1}{N}\sum_{i} \mathbb{I}[\hat{y}_i = y_i]; the ReLU derivative is \mathbb{I}[x > 0].

Sets & logic

Absolute value

|x|

“the absolute value of x”

The distance of x from zero, so it is never negative. It drops the minus sign.

Example

|-3| = 3, \qquad |3| = 3

In AI papers

The L1 loss is |y - \hat{y}|; absmax quantization scales by \max_i |x_i|.

Set

A = \{1, 2, 3\}

“A is the set containing 1, 2 and 3”

Curly braces list a collection of distinct things. Order does not matter and nothing repeats.

Example

\{3, 1, 2\} = \{1, 2, 3\}

In AI papers

A tokenizer’s vocabulary is a set \mathcal{V} of tokens.

Element of

x \in A, \quad x \notin A

“x is in A; x is not in A”

\in (a rounded E, for “element”) says x belongs to A. It is also how papers state types: \mathbf{x} \in \mathbb{R}^{d}.

Example

2 \in \{1, 2, 3\}, \qquad 5 \notin \{1, 2, 3\}

In AI papers

\mathbf{W} \in \mathbb{R}^{d \times k} reads “W is a d by k matrix of real numbers”.

Number sets

\mathbb{N} \subset \mathbb{Z} \subset \mathbb{Q} \subset \mathbb{R}

“the naturals, integers, rationals, reals (blackboard bold N, Z, Q, R)”

\mathbb{N} = counting numbers, \mathbb{Z} = integers (with negatives), \mathbb{Q} = fractions, \mathbb{R} = all real numbers (every point on the number line).

Example

-3 \in \mathbb{Z}, \quad \tfrac{1}{2} \in \mathbb{Q}, \quad \sqrt{2} \in \mathbb{R}

In AI papers

Weights live in \mathbb{R}; token ids are in \{0, 1, \ldots, |\mathcal{V}| - 1\} \subset \mathbb{N}.

Subset

A \subseteq B, \quad A \subset B

“A is a subset of B”

Every element of A is also in B. \subset usually means a proper subset (smaller than B), but some authors use it for \subseteq.

Example

\{1, 2\} \subseteq \{1, 2, 3\}

In AI papers

A minibatch is a subset of the training set: \mathcal{B} \subseteq \mathcal{D}.

Union and intersection

A \cup B, \quad A \cap B

“A union B; A intersect B”

\cup (a cup) collects everything in either set. \cap (a cap) keeps only what is in both.

Example

\{1,2\} \cup \{2,3\} = \{1,2,3\}, \qquad \{1,2\} \cap \{2,3\} = \{2\}

In AI papers

In probability, A \cap B is the event that both happen, A \cup B that at least one does.

Intervals

[a, b], \quad (a, b), \quad [a, b)

“closed interval a b; open interval a b; half-open interval”

All real numbers between a and b. A square bracket includes the end point, a round bracket leaves it out.

Example

[0, 1] \text{ includes } 0 \text{ and } 1; \quad (0, 1) \text{ does not}

In AI papers

Probabilities are in [0, 1]; a sigmoid output is in (0, 1); dropout rate p \in [0, 1).

Size of a set

|A|

“the size of A, or the cardinality of A”

Bars around a set give the number of elements. Around a number, the same bars mean absolute value.

Example

|\{a, b, c\}| = 3

In AI papers

The vocabulary size is |\mathcal{V}|, for example |\mathcal{V}| = 50{,}257 for GPT-2.

Set-builder notation

\{\, x \in \mathbb{R} : x > 0 \,\}

“the set of x in R such that x is greater than 0”

Describes a set by a rule. The colon (or a vertical bar \mid) is read “such that”.

Example

\{\, n \in \mathbb{N} : n \text{ is even} \,\} = \{0, 2, 4, \ldots\}

In AI papers

Top-p sampling keeps the set \{ v : v \text{ is among the most likely tokens whose total probability reaches } p \}.

For all / there exists

\forall x, \quad \exists x

“for all x; there exists an x”

\forall (upside-down A) claims something for every x. \exists (backwards E) claims there is at least one x.

Example

\forall x \in \mathbb{R}: x^{2} \ge 0, \qquad \exists x \in \mathbb{R}: x^{2} = 2

In AI papers

Smoothness assumptions in convergence proofs start “\forall \mathbf{x}, \mathbf{y}: …”.

Cartesian product and R to the n

\mathbb{R}^{n} = \underbrace{\mathbb{R} \times \cdots \times \mathbb{R}}_{n \text{ times}}

“R n is R times R, n times”

A \times B is the set of all pairs (a, b). \mathbb{R}^{n} is all lists of n real numbers, the space vectors live in.

Example

(2, -1, 0.5) \in \mathbb{R}^{3}

In AI papers

An embedding table maps each token to a point in \mathbb{R}^{d}.

Sums, products & indices

Ellipsis (and so on)

x_{1}, x_{2}, \ldots, x_{n}, \qquad x_{1} + x_{2} + \cdots + x_{n}

“x one, x two, and so on up to x n”

Dots mean “continue the pattern”. Low dots (\ldots) go between commas; centred dots (\cdots) go between + or \times signs; \vdots and \ddots fill columns and diagonals of matrices.

Example

1 + 2 + \cdots + 100 = 5050

In AI papers

A sequence of T tokens is written x_1, \ldots, x_T.

Summation (sigma)

\sum_{i=1}^{n} x_{i}

“the sum from i equals 1 to n of x sub i”

Capital sigma means add. The bottom says where the counter i starts, the top where it stops, and the expression on the right is what to add for each i.

Example

\sum_{i=1}^{4} i = 1 + 2 + 3 + 4 = 10

In AI papers

Every weighted sum in a network, \sum_{i} w_i x_i, and every batch loss, \frac{1}{N}\sum_{i} \ell_i.

Product (capital pi)

\prod_{i=1}^{n} x_{i}

“the product from i equals 1 to n of x sub i”

Like \sum, but multiply instead of add.

Example

\prod_{i=1}^{4} i = 1 \cdot 2 \cdot 3 \cdot 4 = 24 = 4!

In AI papers

The probability of a whole sentence is a product of next-token probabilities, \prod_{t} p(x_t \mid x_{<t}).

A neuron’s weighted sum

z = \sum_{i=1}^{n} w_{i} x_{i} + b, \qquad a = \phi(z)

“z equals the sum from i equals 1 to n of w i x i, plus b; a equals phi of z”

Multiply each input by its weight, add them up, add the bias, then pass the total through an activation function \phi.

Term by term

  • x_i — the i-th input
  • w_i — the weight on that input
  • b — bias
  • z — pre-activation (the weighted total)
  • \phi — activation function, e.g. ReLU
  • a — the neuron’s output, its activation

In AI papers

The basic unit of every network. Doing all the neurons of a layer at once is a matrix multiplication.

Sum over a set

\sum_{x \in \mathcal{X}} f(x), \qquad \sum_{i \ne j} a_{ij}

“the sum over x in X of f of x; the sum over i not equal to j”

Instead of start and stop numbers, the subscript can name a set or a condition. Add f(x) for every x that qualifies. A bare \sum_{i} means “over all valid i”.

Example

\sum_{x \in \{1, 2, 5\}} x^{2} = 1 + 4 + 25 = 30

In AI papers

Softmax normalises with \sum_{j \in \mathcal{V}} e^{z_j}, a sum over the whole vocabulary.

Double sum

\sum_{i=1}^{m} \sum_{j=1}^{n} a_{ij}

“the sum over i from 1 to m of the sum over j from 1 to n of a i j”

Add every entry of a table: for each row i, add across all columns j. Sometimes written \sum_{i,j}.

Example

\sum_{i,j} \begin{bmatrix} 1 & 2 \\ 3 & 4 \end{bmatrix}_{ij} = 10

In AI papers

The squared Frobenius norm \|\mathbf{W}\|_F^{2} = \sum_{i,j} W_{ij}^{2} is a double sum; so is a loss over a batch of sequences.

Slices of a sequence

x_{<t}, \quad x_{\le t}, \quad x_{1:T}

“x before t; x up to and including t; x from 1 to T”

x_{<t} is every token before position t (the context). x_{1:T} is the whole sequence. Some papers write x_{i:j} inclusive, like MATLAB, not like Python.

Example

x = (\text{The}, \text{cat}, \text{sat}): \quad x_{<3} = (\text{The}, \text{cat})

In AI papers

Language modeling: predict x_t from x_{<t}.

Greek letters

Alpha, beta, gamma

\alpha, \quad \beta, \quad \gamma

“alpha, beta, gamma”

The first Greek letters, used for constants and hyper-parameters (settings you choose, not weights the model learns).

In AI papers

\alpha is a learning rate or the LoRA scale; \beta_1, \beta_2 are Adam’s decay rates, \beta the KL strength in RLHF and DPO; \gamma, \beta are LayerNorm’s scale and shift; \gamma is the RL discount factor.

Theta, phi, psi

\theta, \; \boldsymbol{\theta}, \quad \phi, \quad \psi

“theta, bold theta, phi, psi”

\boldsymbol{\theta} (bold) usually means “all the model’s parameters”, gathered into one long vector. When there are two models, the second is often \phi (the variant \varphi is the same letter).

In AI papers

p_{\boldsymbol{\theta}}(\mathbf{x}): the model with parameters \boldsymbol{\theta}. In a VAE the encoder is q_{\phi} and the decoder p_{\theta}; in RLHF the policy is \pi_{\theta} and the reward model r_{\phi}.

Mu and sigma

\mu, \quad \sigma, \quad \sigma^{2}

“mu, sigma, sigma squared”

\mu is a mean (average) and \sigma a standard deviation (typical spread); \sigma^2 is the variance. Lower-case \sigma(x) written as a function is the sigmoid.

In AI papers

LayerNorm subtracts \mu and divides by \sqrt{\sigma^2 + \epsilon}. A Gaussian is \mathcal{N}(\mu, \sigma^2).

Eta, lambda, epsilon

\eta, \quad \lambda, \quad \epsilon, \; \varepsilon

“eta, lambda, epsilon”

\eta (looks like an n with a tail) is the learning rate. \lambda is a weighting factor or an eigenvalue. \epsilon is a tiny number or random noise.

In AI papers

Adam divides by \sqrt{\hat{v}_t} + \epsilon with \epsilon = 10^{-8}; weight decay has strength \lambda; diffusion models add noise \boldsymbol{\epsilon} \sim \mathcal{N}(\mathbf{0}, \mathbf{I}).

Pi (three meanings)

\pi \approx 3.14159, \quad \pi_{\theta}(a \mid s), \quad \prod

“pi; pi theta of a given s; capital pi”

Lower-case \pi is the circle constant, or, in reinforcement learning, a policy: the probability of taking action a in state s. Capital \prod is a product.

In AI papers

In RLHF the language model is the policy \pi_{\theta}(y \mid x) and the frozen starting model is \pi_{\text{ref}}.

Sigma, Delta, and the nabla

\Sigma, \; \boldsymbol{\Sigma}, \quad \Delta, \quad \nabla

“capital sigma, bold Sigma, capital delta, nabla (del)”

\sum (large) is a sum, but \boldsymbol{\Sigma} as a matrix is a covariance matrix or the singular values in an SVD. \Delta is “change in”. \nabla (nabla, read “del” or “grad”) is not Greek: it is the gradient.

In AI papers

\Delta\mathbf{W} is a weight update (LoRA learns \Delta\mathbf{W} = \mathbf{B}\mathbf{A}); \nabla_{\boldsymbol{\theta}}\mathcal{L} is the gradient of the loss.

Tau, rho, kappa, delta, xi

\tau, \quad \rho, \quad \kappa, \quad \delta, \quad \xi

“tau, rho, kappa, delta, xi”

\tau: a temperature or a trajectory. \rho: a correlation, a ratio, or the spectral radius. \kappa: a condition number. \delta: a small change or an error signal. \xi: a random variable or noise.

In AI papers

Sampling temperature \tau divides the logits; PPO clips the probability ratio \rho_t = \pi_\theta / \pi_{\text{old}}; backprop passes errors \boldsymbol{\delta}^{(l)}.

Paper conventions

Scalar, vector, matrix, tensor

x, \quad \mathbf{x}, \quad \mathbf{X}, \quad \mathsf{X}

“scalar x, vector bold x, matrix bold capital X, tensor sans-serif X”

The typeface tells you the kind of object: italic lower-case for a single number, bold lower-case for a vector, bold capital for a matrix, sans-serif for higher-order tensors. Many Transformer papers skip the bold and write Q, K, V, so check the paper’s notation section.

Example

x_i \in \mathbb{R}, \quad \mathbf{x} \in \mathbb{R}^{d}, \quad \mathbf{X} \in \mathbb{R}^{n \times d}, \quad \mathsf{X} \in \mathbb{R}^{B \times n \times d}

In AI papers

Follows the notation page of Goodfellow, Bengio & Courville, *Deep Learning* (2016), which most papers copy.

Hat (estimate)

\hat{y}, \quad \hat{\boldsymbol{\theta}}

“y hat; theta hat”

A hat marks an estimate or a prediction, as opposed to the true value. \hat{y} is what the model says; y is the label.

Example

\text{error} = y - \hat{y}

In AI papers

Adam’s bias-corrected moments are \hat{m}_t and \hat{v}_t; the MLE is \hat{\boldsymbol{\theta}}_{\text{MLE}}.

Star (optimal)

\boldsymbol{\theta}^{*}, \quad \mathbf{x}^{*}, \quad f^{*}

“theta star”

A star superscript means the best, or true, value: the minimiser of a loss or the optimal value. (In complex numbers it means the conjugate.)

Example

x^{*} = \arg\min_{x} (x - 3)^{2} = 3, \quad f^{*} = 0

In AI papers

Convergence rates bound f(\mathbf{x}_T) - f^{*}: how far the loss after T steps is from the best possible.

Calligraphic letters

\mathcal{L}, \quad \mathcal{D}, \quad \mathcal{V}, \quad \mathcal{N}, \quad \mathcal{O}

“script L, script D, script V, script N, script O (or big O)”

Curly capitals name special objects rather than numbers: \mathcal{L} a loss (or likelihood), \mathcal{D} a dataset, \mathcal{V} a vocabulary, \mathcal{N} the normal distribution, \mathcal{O} big-O.

In AI papers

“\mathcal{L}_{\text{CE}} on \mathcal{D} over \mathcal{V}” = cross-entropy loss on the dataset over the vocabulary.

Big-O notation

\mathcal{O}(n^{2})

“big O of n squared, or order n squared”

How fast a cost grows as n gets large, ignoring constant factors. Doubling n roughly quadruples an \mathcal{O}(n^{2}) cost.

Example

3n^{2} + 5n + 7 = \mathcal{O}(n^{2})

In AI papers

Self-attention costs \mathcal{O}(n^{2} d) for sequence length n, which is why long context is expensive.

Named operators in upright type

\operatorname{softmax}(\mathbf{z}), \quad \operatorname{LayerNorm}(\mathbf{x}), \quad \operatorname{tr}(\mathbf{A})

“softmax of z; layer norm of x; trace of A”

Multi-letter function names are set upright so they are not misread as products of variables: \operatorname{tr}, not t \cdot r.

In AI papers

Transformer papers define blocks this way: \operatorname{Attention}, \operatorname{FFN}, \operatorname{MultiHead}.

A network as a composition

f_{\boldsymbol{\theta}}(\mathbf{x}) = \left(f^{(L)} \circ f^{(L-1)} \circ \cdots \circ f^{(1)}\right)(\mathbf{x})

“f theta of x equals f L after f L minus 1 after … after f 1, applied to x”

A deep network applies layer 1 first, then layer 2, and so on up to layer L. The layer nearest \mathbf{x} runs first.

Term by term

  • f^{(l)} — layer l, with its own weights \mathbf{W}^{(l)}
  • \circ — composition: feed one output into the next
  • \boldsymbol{\theta} — all layers’ weights together

In AI papers

Backpropagation is the chain rule applied to this composition, from layer L back to layer 1.

Tilde and bar (modified versions)

\tilde{\mathbf{x}}, \quad \bar{\mathbf{x}}, \quad \mathbf{x}^{\prime}

“x tilde; x bar; x prime”

Decorations mark a related but different version of \mathbf{x}. A tilde usually means noisy, perturbed or approximate; a bar means an average (or, in autodiff papers, an adjoint); a prime means a second or updated copy. Always check how the paper defines them.

Example

\tilde{\mathbf{x}} = \mathbf{x} + \boldsymbol{\epsilon}, \qquad \bar{x} = \tfrac{1}{n}\textstyle\sum_i x_i

In AI papers

A denoising autoencoder reconstructs \mathbf{x} from \tilde{\mathbf{x}}; DDPM uses \bar{\alpha}_t = \prod_{s \le t} \alpha_s.

Parameters after a semicolon or in a subscript

p(\mathbf{x}; \boldsymbol{\theta}) \;=\; p_{\boldsymbol{\theta}}(\mathbf{x})

“p of x, parameterised by theta”

What comes after the semicolon (or in the subscript) are fixed parameters, not random variables. Compare p(\mathbf{x} \mid \boldsymbol{\theta}), which treats \boldsymbol{\theta} as a random variable you condition on (the Bayesian view).

In AI papers

f(\mathbf{x}; \boldsymbol{\theta}) and f_{\boldsymbol{\theta}}(\mathbf{x}) both mean “network f with weights \boldsymbol{\theta} applied to \mathbf{x}”.

lessons.title: Linear Algebra
lessons.html:
Linear Algebra

Embeddings, vector spaces, matrix multiplication in Transformer layers, dimensions.

Vectors

Pythagorean theorem

c^{2} = a^{2} + b^{2}

“c squared equals a squared plus b squared”

In a right-angled triangle, the square on the long side equals the sum of the squares on the other two sides.

Term by term

  • a, b — the two short sides, which meet at the right angle
  • c — the long side (hypotenuse)

In AI papers

Extended to d dimensions, this is the length of a vector: \|\mathbf{x}\|_2 = \sqrt{x_1^2 + \cdots + x_d^2}.

Column vector

\mathbf{x} = \begin{bmatrix} x_{1} \\ x_{2} \\ \vdots \\ x_{d} \end{bmatrix} \in \mathbb{R}^{d}

“bold x, a column of x one through x d, is in R d”

A vector is an ordered list of numbers. In papers a vector is a column unless stated otherwise, and d is its dimension (how many numbers it holds). Geometrically it is an arrow, or a point, in d-dimensional space.

Example

\mathbf{x} = \begin{bmatrix} 2 \\ -1 \\ 0.5 \end{bmatrix} \in \mathbb{R}^{3}

In AI papers

Each token is represented as an embedding vector \mathbf{x} \in \mathbb{R}^{d_{\text{model}}} (768 numbers in GPT-2 small, 12,288 in GPT-3).

Row vector and tuple form

\mathbf{x}^{\top} = [x_{1}, x_{2}, \ldots, x_{d}], \qquad \mathbf{x} = (x_{1}, \ldots, x_{d})

“x transpose is the row x one to x d; x is the tuple x one to x d”

Writing a column takes space, so papers write it as a transposed row, [\ldots]^{\top}, or as a tuple in round brackets.

Example

\mathbf{x} = [2, -1, 0.5]^{\top}

In AI papers

Code uses the other convention: PyTorch stores a batch of vectors as the rows of a matrix.

Scalar times vector

c\,\mathbf{x} = \begin{bmatrix} c\,x_{1} \\ \vdots \\ c\,x_{d} \end{bmatrix}

“c times x”

Multiply every entry by the same number. It stretches (or shrinks, or flips) the arrow without turning it.

Example

2 \begin{bmatrix} 1 \\ -3 \end{bmatrix} = \begin{bmatrix} 2 \\ -6 \end{bmatrix}

In AI papers

A gradient step subtracts \eta\,\mathbf{g}: the gradient scaled down by the learning rate.

Adding vectors

\begin{bmatrix} 1 \\ 2 \end{bmatrix} + \begin{bmatrix} 3 \\ -1 \end{bmatrix} = \begin{bmatrix} 1 + 3 \\ 2 - 1 \end{bmatrix} = \begin{bmatrix} 4 \\ 1 \end{bmatrix}

“the vector 1, 2 plus the vector 3, minus 1 equals the vector 4, 1”

Add entry by entry. As arrows: put the second arrow’s tail on the first one’s tip.

Term by term

  • \mathbf{x} + \mathbf{y} — only defined when both have the same dimension

In AI papers

The input to a Transformer is token embedding + position embedding; a residual connection adds a layer’s output back to its input.

Zero, ones and one-hot vectors

\mathbf{0}, \quad \mathbf{1}, \quad \mathbf{e}_{i}

“the zero vector; the ones vector; e sub i, the i-th standard basis vector”

\mathbf{0} is all zeros, \mathbf{1} is all ones, and \mathbf{e}_i has a 1 in position i and 0 elsewhere (“one-hot”).

Example

\mathbf{e}_{2} = [0, 1, 0, 0]^{\top} \in \mathbb{R}^{4}

In AI papers

The label for class y is the one-hot vector \mathbf{e}_{y}; \mathbf{1}^{\top}\mathbf{x} adds up the entries of \mathbf{x}.

Span and linear combination

\operatorname{span}\{\mathbf{v}_{1}, \ldots, \mathbf{v}_{k}\} = \Big\{ \textstyle\sum_{i=1}^{k} c_{i}\mathbf{v}_{i} : c_{i} \in \mathbb{R} \Big\}

“the span of v one to v k is the set of all sums of c i times v i”

A linear combination scales vectors and adds them. The span is everything you can reach that way: a line, a plane, or a higher-dimensional flat subspace.

In AI papers

An attention output is a combination of value vectors, so it lies in the span of the rows of \mathbf{V}.

Dimension and basis

\dim(V) = d

“the dimension of V is d”

A basis is a smallest set of vectors whose span is the whole space. The number of vectors in any basis is the dimension.

Example

\dim(\mathbb{R}^{3}) = 3, \quad \text{basis } \{\mathbf{e}_1, \mathbf{e}_2, \mathbf{e}_3\}

In AI papers

“Hidden size”, “model dimension” and “width” all mean the dimension of the vectors flowing through the network.

Dot products & norms

Dot product (three notations)

\mathbf{x}^{\top}\mathbf{y} \;=\; \langle \mathbf{x}, \mathbf{y} \rangle \;=\; \mathbf{x} \cdot \mathbf{y}

“x transpose y; the inner product of x and y; x dot y”

Multiply matching entries and add them up. The result is a single number that is large when the vectors point the same way.

Example

[1, 2, 3] \cdot [4, 5, 6] = 4 + 10 + 18 = 32

In AI papers

An attention score is the dot product of a query and a key, \mathbf{q}^{\top}\mathbf{k}.

Euclidean (L2) norm

\|\mathbf{x}\|_{2}

“the L2 norm of x, or the length of x”

The length of the arrow: square the entries, add them, take the square root. When the subscript is left off, \|\mathbf{x}\| usually means this norm.

Example

\left\| [3, 4] \right\|_{2} = \sqrt{9 + 16} = 5

In AI papers

Gradient clipping rescales \mathbf{g} when \|\mathbf{g}\|_2 is too large; weight decay penalises \|\boldsymbol{\theta}\|_2^{2}.

Dot product formula

\mathbf{x}^{\top}\mathbf{y} = \sum_{i=1}^{d} x_{i} y_{i} = x_{1}y_{1} + x_{2}y_{2} + \cdots + x_{d}y_{d}

“x transpose y equals the sum over i of x i times y i”

Pair up the entries, multiply each pair, add the results.

Term by term

  • \mathbf{x}^{\top} — a 1 \times d row
  • \mathbf{y} — a d \times 1 column
  • x_i y_i — product of the i-th entries

In AI papers

Every neuron, every attention score and every logit is a dot product.

Length of a vector

\|\mathbf{x}\|_{2} = \sqrt{\mathbf{x}^{\top}\mathbf{x}} = \sqrt{\sum_{i=1}^{d} x_{i}^{2}}

“the L2 norm of x equals the square root of x transpose x, the square root of the sum of x i squared”

Pythagoras in d dimensions: the length is the square root of the vector dotted with itself.

Term by term

  • \mathbf{x}^{\top}\mathbf{x} — sum of squares, also written \|\mathbf{x}\|_2^2

In AI papers

RMSNorm divides by \|\mathbf{x}\|_2/\sqrt{d}, the root-mean-square size of the entries.

L1 and max (L-infinity) norms

\|\mathbf{x}\|_{1} = \sum_{i} |x_{i}|, \qquad \|\mathbf{x}\|_{\infty} = \max_{i} |x_{i}|

“the L1 norm of x; the L infinity norm, or max norm, of x”

Other ways to measure size: L1 adds the absolute values (“taxicab distance”); L-infinity takes the biggest one.

Example

\mathbf{x} = [3, -4]: \quad \|\mathbf{x}\|_{1} = 7, \quad \|\mathbf{x}\|_{\infty} = 4

In AI papers

L1 penalties push weights to exactly zero (sparsity). Absmax quantization scales by \|\mathbf{x}\|_{\infty}.

Orthogonal vectors

\mathbf{x} \perp \mathbf{y} \iff \mathbf{x}^{\top}\mathbf{y} = 0

“x is perpendicular to y if and only if x transpose y is zero”

Vectors at a right angle have dot product zero. Orthonormal vectors are orthogonal and each has length 1.

Example

[1, 0] \perp [0, 5]

In AI papers

In high dimensions random vectors are almost orthogonal, which is why embeddings can store many nearly independent features.

Cosine similarity

\cos\theta = \frac{\mathbf{x}^{\top}\mathbf{y}}{\|\mathbf{x}\|_{2}\,\|\mathbf{y}\|_{2}} \in [-1, 1]

“cosine theta equals x transpose y over the norm of x times the norm of y”

Divide the dot product by both lengths to keep only the angle. 1 means same direction, 0 unrelated (orthogonal), −1 opposite.

Term by term

  • \theta — angle between the vectors
  • \mathbf{x}^{\top}\mathbf{y} — dot product
  • \|\mathbf{x}\|_{2}\,\|\mathbf{y}\|_{2} — product of the lengths

In AI papers

Semantic search and retrieval rank documents by the cosine similarity of their embeddings to the query embedding; CLIP trains on it.

General Lp norm

\|\mathbf{x}\|_{p} = \Big( \sum_{i=1}^{d} |x_{i}|^{p} \Big)^{1/p}

“the L p norm of x is the sum of the absolute values of x i to the p, all to the power one over p”

p = 1 and p = 2 give the L1 and L2 norms; as p \to \infty it becomes the max norm.

In AI papers

Adversarial-robustness papers state attack budgets as \|\boldsymbol{\delta}\|_{\infty} \le \epsilon or \|\boldsymbol{\delta}\|_{2} \le \epsilon.

Frobenius norm

\|\mathbf{A}\|_{F} = \sqrt{\sum_{i,j} A_{ij}^{2}} = \sqrt{\operatorname{tr}(\mathbf{A}^{\top}\mathbf{A})}

“the Frobenius norm of A”

Treat the matrix as one long vector and take its L2 norm.

In AI papers

Weight decay on a matrix is \frac{\lambda}{2}\|\mathbf{W}\|_{F}^{2}; low-rank approximations are judged by the Frobenius error.

Matrices

Matrix and its shape

\mathbf{A} \in \mathbb{R}^{m \times n}

“A is an m by n real matrix”

A table of numbers with m rows and n columns. The shape is always rows first, then columns.

Example

\begin{bmatrix} 1 & 2 & 3 \\ 4 & 5 & 6 \end{bmatrix} \in \mathbb{R}^{2 \times 3}

In AI papers

Each layer’s weights are a matrix: \mathbf{W} \in \mathbb{R}^{d_{\text{out}} \times d_{\text{in}}} in maths, stored as (out, in) in PyTorch.

Matrix entry

A_{ij}, \quad a_{ij}, \quad [\mathbf{A}]_{ij}

“A i j; the entry of A in row i, column j”

The first index is the row, the second the column. For clarity, some papers write A_{i,j} with a comma.

Example

\mathbf{A} = \begin{bmatrix} 1 & 2 \\ 3 & 4 \end{bmatrix}: \quad A_{21} = 3

In AI papers

An attention matrix entry A_{ij} is how much token i attends to token j.

Rows and columns

\mathbf{A}_{i,:}, \quad \mathbf{A}_{:,j}

“row i of A; column j of A”

A colon means “all of this index”, just like NumPy slicing. Some papers write \mathbf{a}_i for a row or column; check which.

In AI papers

Row w of the embedding matrix, \mathbf{E}_{w,:}, is the embedding of token w.

Transpose

\mathbf{A}^{\top}, \quad (\mathbf{A}^{\top})_{ij} = A_{ji}

“A transpose”

Flip the matrix over its diagonal so rows become columns. An m \times n matrix becomes n \times m. Also written \mathbf{A}^{T} or \mathbf{A}^{\prime}.

Example

\begin{bmatrix} 1 & 2 & 3 \\ 4 & 5 & 6 \end{bmatrix}^{\top} = \begin{bmatrix} 1 & 4 \\ 2 & 5 \\ 3 & 6 \end{bmatrix}

In AI papers

In \mathbf{Q}\mathbf{K}^{\top} the transpose lines keys up so each query is dotted with each key.

Identity matrix

\mathbf{I}_{n}

“the n by n identity matrix”

Ones on the diagonal, zeros elsewhere. Multiplying by it changes nothing: \mathbf{I}\mathbf{x} = \mathbf{x}.

Example

\mathbf{I}_{3} = \begin{bmatrix} 1 & 0 & 0 \\ 0 & 1 & 0 \\ 0 & 0 & 1 \end{bmatrix}

In AI papers

Residual connections compute (\mathbf{I} + F)(\mathbf{x}) = \mathbf{x} + F(\mathbf{x}); \mathcal{N}(\mathbf{0}, \mathbf{I}) is standard Gaussian noise.

Inverse matrix

\mathbf{A}^{-1}, \quad \mathbf{A}^{-1}\mathbf{A} = \mathbf{A}\mathbf{A}^{-1} = \mathbf{I}

“A inverse”

The matrix that undoes \mathbf{A}. Only square matrices with non-zero determinant have one.

Example

\begin{bmatrix} 2 & 0 \\ 0 & 4 \end{bmatrix}^{-1} = \begin{bmatrix} 0.5 & 0 \\ 0 & 0.25 \end{bmatrix}

In AI papers

Newton’s method steps by -\mathbf{H}^{-1}\nabla f. Networks avoid explicit inverses because they are costly and numerically unstable.

Diagonal matrix

\operatorname{diag}(\mathbf{v}) = \begin{bmatrix} v_{1} & & \\ & \ddots & \\ & & v_{d} \end{bmatrix}

“diag of v”

A matrix with \mathbf{v} on the diagonal and zeros elsewhere (blank entries mean zero). \operatorname{diag}(\mathbf{v})\,\mathbf{x} = \mathbf{v} \odot \mathbf{x}.

In AI papers

Adam is a diagonal preconditioner: it rescales each coordinate separately, like multiplying by \operatorname{diag}(1/\sqrt{\hat{\mathbf{v}}}).

Determinant

\det(\mathbf{A}), \quad |\mathbf{A}|

“the determinant of A”

A single number giving how much \mathbf{A} scales area or volume. Zero means it squashes space flat and has no inverse.

Example

\det \begin{bmatrix} a & b \\ c & d \end{bmatrix} = ad - bc

In AI papers

Normalising flows need \log|\det \mathbf{J}| to track how a transformation stretches probability density.

Rank

\operatorname{rank}(\mathbf{A}) \le \min(m, n)

“the rank of A is at most the smaller of m and n”

The number of independent directions in the output of \mathbf{A}. The product of a d \times r matrix and an r \times k matrix has rank at most r.

In AI papers

LoRA makes the weight update low-rank: \Delta\mathbf{W} = \mathbf{B}\mathbf{A} with r \ll d.

Much less than

r \ll d

“r is much less than d”

\ll and \gg say one quantity is smaller or larger by a big factor, not just a little.

Example

r = 8 \ll d = 4096

In AI papers

The whole point of a low-rank adapter is r \ll \min(d, k), so it has far fewer parameters than the full matrix.

Trace

\operatorname{tr}(\mathbf{A}) = \sum_{i} A_{ii}

“the trace of A”

The sum of the diagonal. It also equals the sum of the eigenvalues, and \operatorname{tr}(\mathbf{A}\mathbf{B}) = \operatorname{tr}(\mathbf{B}\mathbf{A}).

In AI papers

The Hessian trace, a measure of loss-landscape sharpness, is estimated with random vectors (Hutchinson’s trick).

Matrix multiplication

Matrix times vector

\mathbf{W}\mathbf{x}, \quad \mathbf{W} \in \mathbb{R}^{m \times n}, \; \mathbf{x} \in \mathbb{R}^{n}

“W x”

Each output entry is the dot product of one row of \mathbf{W} with \mathbf{x}. An m \times n matrix turns an n-vector into an m-vector.

Example

\begin{bmatrix} 1 & 2 \\ 3 & 4 \end{bmatrix} \begin{bmatrix} 5 \\ 6 \end{bmatrix} = \begin{bmatrix} 17 \\ 39 \end{bmatrix}

In AI papers

This one operation is most of the compute in a neural network.

Element-wise (Hadamard) product

\mathbf{a} \odot \mathbf{b}

“a Hadamard b, or a element-wise times b”

Multiply entry by entry. Both must have the same shape. In code this is plain `*`, while matrix multiplication is `@`.

Example

[1, 2, 3] \odot [4, 5, 6] = [4, 10, 18]

In AI papers

Gates (LSTM, SwiGLU), dropout masks and LayerNorm’s \boldsymbol{\gamma} \odot \hat{\mathbf{x}} are all Hadamard products.

Outer product

\mathbf{u}\mathbf{v}^{\top} \in \mathbb{R}^{m \times n}

“u v transpose, the outer product of u and v”

A column times a row gives a full matrix, with entry (i, j) equal to u_i v_j. Compare \mathbf{u}^{\top}\mathbf{v}, which is a single number.

Example

\begin{bmatrix} 1 \\ 2 \end{bmatrix} \begin{bmatrix} 3 & 4 \end{bmatrix} = \begin{bmatrix} 3 & 4 \\ 6 & 8 \end{bmatrix}

In AI papers

The gradient of a linear layer for one example is an outer product: \frac{\partial \mathcal{L}}{\partial \mathbf{W}} = \boldsymbol{\delta}\,\mathbf{x}^{\top}.

Matrix multiplication

\mathbf{C} = \mathbf{A}\mathbf{B}, \qquad C_{ij} = \sum_{k=1}^{n} A_{ik} B_{kj}, \qquad \underset{m \times n}{\mathbf{A}}\;\underset{n \times p}{\mathbf{B}} = \underset{m \times p}{\mathbf{C}}

“C equals A B; C i j is the sum over k of A i k times B k j”

Entry (i, j) is row i of \mathbf{A} dotted with column j of \mathbf{B}. The inner sizes must match and cancel: (m \times n)(n \times p) \to m \times p.

Term by term

  • A_{ik} — row i of \mathbf{A}, walking along k
  • B_{kj} — column j of \mathbf{B}, walking down k
  • \sum_{k} — the shared index is summed away

In AI papers

Checking that inner dimensions match is the fastest way to read an unfamiliar layer equation. Order matters: \mathbf{A}\mathbf{B} \ne \mathbf{B}\mathbf{A} in general.

Linear (fully connected) layer

\mathbf{y} = \mathbf{W}\mathbf{x} + \mathbf{b}, \qquad \mathbf{W} \in \mathbb{R}^{d_{\text{out}} \times d_{\text{in}}}, \; \mathbf{b} \in \mathbb{R}^{d_{\text{out}}}

“y equals W x plus b”

Every output is a weighted sum of all inputs plus a bias: a whole layer of neurons in one line.

Term by term

  • \mathbf{x} \in \mathbb{R}^{d_{\text{in}}} — input vector
  • \mathbf{W} — weights; row i belongs to output neuron i
  • \mathbf{b} — biases
  • \mathbf{y} \in \mathbb{R}^{d_{\text{out}}} — output vector

In AI papers

In PyTorch, `nn.Linear` computes \mathbf{Y} = \mathbf{X}\mathbf{W}^{\top} + \mathbf{b} for a batch \mathbf{X} whose rows are examples.

Transpose of a product

(\mathbf{A}\mathbf{B})^{\top} = \mathbf{B}^{\top}\mathbf{A}^{\top}

“the transpose of A B equals B transpose A transpose”

Transposing a product reverses the order. Shapes check it: (m \times n)(n \times p) transposed is (p \times n)(n \times m).

Term by term

  • \mathbf{B}^{\top}\mathbf{A}^{\top} — order is reversed

In AI papers

Explains why the column-vector form \mathbf{W}\mathbf{x} and the row-vector form \mathbf{x}^{\top}\mathbf{W}^{\top} of a layer are the same thing.

Kronecker product

\mathbf{A} \otimes \mathbf{B}

“A Kronecker B”

Replace every entry a_{ij} of \mathbf{A} with the block a_{ij}\mathbf{B}. A 2 \times 2 Kronecker a 3 \times 3 gives a 6 \times 6.

In AI papers

K-FAC and Shampoo approximate the curvature of a layer as a Kronecker product of two small matrices.

Tensors & shapes

Tensor and its shape

\mathsf{X} \in \mathbb{R}^{B \times T \times d}

“X is a B by T by d tensor”

A tensor is a grid of numbers with any number of axes. This one holds B sequences, each of T tokens, each a d-vector.

In AI papers

The activations inside a Transformer have shape (batch, sequence, model dim); with heads split out it becomes (B, h, T, d_head).

Concatenation

[\mathbf{x}; \mathbf{y}], \quad [\mathbf{x} \,\|\, \mathbf{y}], \quad \operatorname{Concat}(\mathbf{x}, \mathbf{y})

“x stacked on y; x concatenated with y”

Join vectors end to end: a 3-vector and a 2-vector make a 5-vector. A semicolon usually stacks vertically, a comma side by side.

Example

[\,[1, 2]; [3]\,] = [1, 2, 3]

In AI papers

Multi-head attention concatenates the h head outputs before the output projection \mathbf{W}^{O}.

Adding a bias to every row

\mathbf{X}\mathbf{W} + \mathbf{b}, \quad \mathbf{X} \in \mathbb{R}^{n \times d}, \; \mathbf{b} \in \mathbb{R}^{k}

“X W plus b”

Strictly you cannot add a vector to a matrix. Papers and code mean “add \mathbf{b} to every row” (broadcasting), which is \mathbf{X}\mathbf{W} + \mathbf{1}\mathbf{b}^{\top}.

In AI papers

Watch for this in batched layer equations: the bias is broadcast across the batch and sequence axes.

Transformer dimension names

d_{\text{model}}, \; d_{k}, \; d_{v}, \; d_{\text{ff}}, \; h, \; n

“d model; d k; d v; d f f; h; n”

Model width; key/query size per head; value size per head; feed-forward hidden size; number of heads; sequence length. Usually d_k = d_v = d_{\text{model}}/h and d_{\text{ff}} = 4\,d_{\text{model}}.

Example

\text{Base Transformer: } d_{\text{model}} = 512, \; h = 8, \; d_k = 64, \; d_{\text{ff}} = 2048

In AI papers

These are the names used by Vaswani et al. (2017) and most later papers.

A layer on a whole batch

\underset{B \times d_{\text{out}}}{\mathbf{Y}} = \underset{B \times d_{\text{in}}}{\mathbf{X}}\;\underset{d_{\text{in}} \times d_{\text{out}}}{\mathbf{W}^{\top}} + \mathbf{1}\mathbf{b}^{\top}

“Y equals X W transpose plus the bias added to every row”

Stack B examples as the rows of \mathbf{X} and one matrix multiplication handles them all. Writing shapes under each symbol is the standard way to check an equation.

Term by term

  • \mathbf{X} — one example per row
  • \mathbf{W}^{\top} — the layer weights, transposed for rows
  • \mathbf{1}\mathbf{b}^{\top} — the bias copied to every row (broadcasting)

In AI papers

GPUs are fast because this batched multiply reuses each weight B times per load.

Index (einsum) notation

Y_{b t j} = \sum_{k} X_{b t k}\, W_{k j} \qquad \Longleftrightarrow \qquad \texttt{einsum("btk,kj->btj", X, W)}

“Y b t j equals the sum over k of X b t k times W k j”

Write the formula for a single entry. Any index that appears on the right but not on the left is summed over. This works for any number of axes.

Term by term

  • b, t — batch and position: carried through unchanged
  • k — shared index: summed away
  • j — new output feature index

In AI papers

Attention scores are S_{bhij} = \sum_{d} Q_{bhid} K_{bhjd}: einsum `"bhid,bhjd->bhij"`.

Eigenvalues & SVD

Eigenvalues

\lambda_{\max}(\mathbf{A}), \quad \lambda_{\min}(\mathbf{A}), \quad \lambda_{i}

“lambda max of A; lambda min of A; lambda i”

The eigenvalues of a square matrix, largest and smallest. For symmetric matrices they are real, and the eigenvectors can be chosen orthogonal.

In AI papers

\lambda_{\max} of the loss Hessian (the sharpness) limits the largest stable learning rate.

Orthogonal matrix

\mathbf{Q}^{\top}\mathbf{Q} = \mathbf{Q}\mathbf{Q}^{\top} = \mathbf{I}

“Q transpose Q equals the identity”

Its columns are orthonormal, so it only rotates or reflects: lengths and angles are preserved, and \mathbf{Q}^{-1} = \mathbf{Q}^{\top}.

In AI papers

RoPE rotates query and key vectors with orthogonal matrices; quantization methods such as QuaRot rotate weights to spread out outliers.

Eigenvector equation

\mathbf{A}\mathbf{v} = \lambda\mathbf{v}, \qquad \mathbf{v} \ne \mathbf{0}

“A v equals lambda v”

An eigenvector is a direction that \mathbf{A} only stretches, without turning it. The eigenvalue \lambda is the stretch factor.

Term by term

  • \mathbf{v} — eigenvector (a special direction)
  • \lambda — eigenvalue (the stretch)

In AI papers

The top Hessian eigenvector is the sharpest direction of the loss; PCA directions are covariance eigenvectors.

Positive (semi-)definite

\mathbf{A} \succeq 0 \iff \mathbf{x}^{\top}\mathbf{A}\mathbf{x} \ge 0 \;\; \forall \mathbf{x}

“A is positive semidefinite”

\succeq 0 is an order for symmetric matrices, not for entries: every eigenvalue is at least 0. \succ 0 (positive definite) means every eigenvalue is strictly positive.

In AI papers

Covariance matrices are PSD; a Hessian \nabla^{2}f \succ 0 at a stationary point means it is a local minimum.

Spectral norm

\|\mathbf{W}\|_{2} = \sigma_{\max}(\mathbf{W}) = \max_{\mathbf{x} \ne \mathbf{0}} \frac{\|\mathbf{W}\mathbf{x}\|_{2}}{\|\mathbf{x}\|_{2}}

“the spectral norm of W equals its largest singular value”

The most that \mathbf{W} can stretch any vector. On a matrix, \|\cdot\|_2 means this, not the Frobenius norm.

In AI papers

Spectral normalisation divides \mathbf{W} by \sigma_{\max} to stabilise GAN training; the Muon optimizer takes steps of fixed spectral norm.

Eigendecomposition of a symmetric matrix

\mathbf{A} = \mathbf{Q}\boldsymbol{\Lambda}\mathbf{Q}^{\top} = \sum_{i=1}^{n} \lambda_{i}\,\mathbf{q}_{i}\mathbf{q}_{i}^{\top}

“A equals Q Lambda Q transpose”

A symmetric matrix is a rotation, then independent scaling along each axis, then the rotation undone.

Term by term

  • \mathbf{Q} — orthogonal; its columns \mathbf{q}_i are the eigenvectors
  • \boldsymbol{\Lambda} = \operatorname{diag}(\lambda_1, \ldots, \lambda_n) — the eigenvalues

In AI papers

Analyses of gradient descent on a quadratic loss rotate into this basis, where each direction evolves on its own.

Singular value decomposition (SVD)

\mathbf{A} = \mathbf{U}\boldsymbol{\Sigma}\mathbf{V}^{\top} = \sum_{i=1}^{r} \sigma_{i}\,\mathbf{u}_{i}\mathbf{v}_{i}^{\top}, \qquad \sigma_{1} \ge \sigma_{2} \ge \cdots \ge \sigma_{r} > 0

“A equals U Sigma V transpose, a sum of sigma i u i v i transpose”

Every matrix, square or not, is a rotation, a scaling along the axes, and another rotation. Keeping only the largest \sigma_i gives the best low-rank approximation (Eckart–Young).

Term by term

  • \mathbf{U} \in \mathbb{R}^{m \times m} — output directions (left singular vectors)
  • \boldsymbol{\Sigma} — singular values on the diagonal
  • \mathbf{V} \in \mathbb{R}^{n \times n} — input directions (right singular vectors)
  • r — rank = number of non-zero singular values

In AI papers

Low-rank compression, the analysis of LoRA updates, spectral norms and the Muon optimizer (which replaces \boldsymbol{\Sigma} by \mathbf{I}) all rest on the SVD.

Transformer layers

Embedding matrix

\mathbf{E} \in \mathbb{R}^{|\mathcal{V}| \times d_{\text{model}}}

“E is a vocabulary-size by d-model matrix”

One row per token in the vocabulary. Looking up a token means reading its row.

In AI papers

Many models reuse \mathbf{E} for the output layer too (“weight tying”): logits = \mathbf{h}\,\mathbf{E}^{\top}.

Embedding lookup

\mathbf{x}_{t} = \mathbf{E}^{\top}\mathbf{e}_{w_{t}} = \mathbf{E}_{w_{t},:}^{\top}

“x t equals E transpose times the one-hot vector for token w t, which is row w t of E”

Multiplying by a one-hot vector just picks out one row. That is why an embedding layer is a table lookup, not a real matrix multiplication.

Term by term

  • w_t — id of the token at position t
  • \mathbf{e}_{w_t} \in \mathbb{R}^{|\mathcal{V}|} — one-hot vector for that id
  • \mathbf{E} — embedding matrix, |\mathcal{V}| \times d_{\text{model}}

In AI papers

The first step of every language model: turn token ids into vectors.

Projection matrices

\mathbf{W}^{Q}, \mathbf{W}^{K} \in \mathbb{R}^{d_{\text{model}} \times d_{k}}, \quad \mathbf{W}^{V} \in \mathbb{R}^{d_{\text{model}} \times d_{v}}, \quad \mathbf{W}^{O} \in \mathbb{R}^{h d_{v} \times d_{\text{model}}}

“W Q, W K, W V and W O”

The superscript letters are names, not powers. They map token vectors to queries, keys and values, and map the heads back to the model width.

In AI papers

With the row-vector convention of Vaswani et al., a projection is written \mathbf{X}\mathbf{W}^{Q} (data on the left).

Queries, keys and values

\mathbf{Q} = \mathbf{X}\mathbf{W}^{Q}, \qquad \mathbf{K} = \mathbf{X}\mathbf{W}^{K}, \qquad \mathbf{V} = \mathbf{X}\mathbf{W}^{V}

“Q equals X W Q; K equals X W K; V equals X W V”

Three linear projections of the same tokens. A query asks “what am I looking for?”, a key says “what do I contain?”, a value is “what I pass on if chosen”.

Term by term

  • \mathbf{X} \in \mathbb{R}^{n \times d_{\text{model}}} — one token per row
  • \mathbf{Q}, \mathbf{K} \in \mathbb{R}^{n \times d_k} — queries and keys
  • \mathbf{V} \in \mathbb{R}^{n \times d_v} — values

In AI papers

In self-attention all three come from the same \mathbf{X}; in cross-attention \mathbf{Q} comes from the decoder and \mathbf{K}, \mathbf{V} from the encoder.

Scaled dot-product attention

\operatorname{Attention}(\mathbf{Q}, \mathbf{K}, \mathbf{V}) = \operatorname{softmax}\!\left( \frac{\mathbf{Q}\mathbf{K}^{\top}}{\sqrt{d_{k}}} + \mathbf{M} \right)\mathbf{V}

“attention of Q, K, V equals softmax of Q K transpose over the square root of d k, plus the mask M, times V”

Score every query against every key, scale, turn each row of scores into weights that add to 1, and take that weighted average of the values.

Term by term

  • \mathbf{Q}\mathbf{K}^{\top} \in \mathbb{R}^{n \times n} — all query–key dot products
  • \sqrt{d_k} — keeps the score variance near 1 so softmax does not saturate
  • \mathbf{M} — mask: 0 where allowed, -\infty for future tokens (causal models)
  • \operatorname{softmax}(\cdot) — applied to each row separately
  • (\cdots)\mathbf{V} — weighted average of value vectors

In AI papers

The core operation of every Transformer. The original paper writes it without \mathbf{M} and describes the mask in the text.

Vaswani et al., “Attention Is All You Need”, 2017

Multi-head attention

\begin{aligned} \operatorname{MultiHead}(\mathbf{Q}, \mathbf{K}, \mathbf{V}) &= \operatorname{Concat}(\text{head}_{1}, \ldots, \text{head}_{h})\,\mathbf{W}^{O} \\ \text{head}_{i} &= \operatorname{Attention}(\mathbf{Q}\mathbf{W}_{i}^{Q}, \mathbf{K}\mathbf{W}_{i}^{K}, \mathbf{V}\mathbf{W}_{i}^{V}) \end{aligned}

“multi-head of Q, K, V equals the concatenation of head 1 to head h, times W O, where head i is attention with its own projections”

Run h smaller attentions in parallel, each with its own projections so it can focus on a different relationship, then join the results and mix them with \mathbf{W}^{O}.

Term by term

  • h — number of heads
  • \mathbf{W}_{i}^{Q} \in \mathbb{R}^{d_{\text{model}} \times d_k} — head i’s query projection (the subscript is the head)
  • \mathbf{W}^{O} \in \mathbb{R}^{h d_v \times d_{\text{model}}} — output projection

In AI papers

Grouped-query attention (GQA) shares each \mathbf{W}^{K}_i, \mathbf{W}^{V}_i across several query heads to shrink the KV cache.

Vaswani et al., 2017

Position-wise feed-forward network

\operatorname{FFN}(\mathbf{x}) = \max(0, \mathbf{x}\mathbf{W}_{1} + \mathbf{b}_{1})\,\mathbf{W}_{2} + \mathbf{b}_{2}

“F F N of x equals max of zero and x W 1 plus b 1, times W 2, plus b 2”

Expand each token vector to a wider hidden layer, apply ReLU, and project back. It acts on every position separately.

Term by term

  • \mathbf{W}_{1} \in \mathbb{R}^{d_{\text{model}} \times d_{\text{ff}}} — up-projection
  • \max(0, \cdot) — ReLU, applied element-wise
  • \mathbf{W}_{2} \in \mathbb{R}^{d_{\text{ff}} \times d_{\text{model}}} — down-projection

In AI papers

Modern LLMs use SwiGLU instead: (\operatorname{SiLU}(\mathbf{x}\mathbf{W}) \odot \mathbf{x}\mathbf{V})\mathbf{W}_{2}. The FFN holds about two-thirds of a Transformer’s parameters.

Vaswani et al., 2017; Shazeer, “GLU Variants Improve Transformer”, 2020

Layer normalisation

\operatorname{LayerNorm}(\mathbf{x}) = \boldsymbol{\gamma} \odot \frac{\mathbf{x} - \mu}{\sqrt{\sigma^{2} + \epsilon}} + \boldsymbol{\beta}, \qquad \mu = \frac{1}{d}\sum_{i} x_{i}, \;\; \sigma^{2} = \frac{1}{d}\sum_{i} (x_{i} - \mu)^{2}

“layer norm of x equals gamma times x minus mu over the square root of sigma squared plus epsilon, plus beta”

Shift and scale each token vector so its entries have mean 0 and variance 1, then apply a learned scale \boldsymbol{\gamma} and shift \boldsymbol{\beta}.

Term by term

  • \mu, \sigma^{2} — mean and variance over the d features of one token
  • \epsilon — small constant (e.g. 10^{-5}) that prevents division by zero
  • \boldsymbol{\gamma}, \boldsymbol{\beta} \in \mathbb{R}^{d} — learned gain and bias

In AI papers

Keeps activations in a stable range. Many LLMs use RMSNorm, which skips the mean subtraction and \boldsymbol{\beta}.

Ba, Kiros & Hinton, “Layer Normalization”, 2016

Pre-norm residual block

\begin{aligned} \mathbf{h} &= \mathbf{x} + \operatorname{MultiHead}(\operatorname{LN}(\mathbf{x})) \\ \mathbf{y} &= \mathbf{h} + \operatorname{FFN}(\operatorname{LN}(\mathbf{h})) \end{aligned}

“h equals x plus multi-head attention of layer-norm of x; y equals h plus the F F N of layer-norm of h”

Each sub-layer reads a normalised copy of the running vector and adds its result back. The running vector \mathbf{x} is called the residual stream.

Term by term

  • \mathbf{x} + (\cdot) — residual (skip) connection: the identity path
  • \operatorname{LN} — LayerNorm or RMSNorm

In AI papers

The residual path lets gradients flow straight to early layers, which is what makes 100-layer models trainable.

He et al., 2016 (ResNet); Xiong et al., “On Layer Normalization in the Transformer Architecture”, 2020

Rotary position embedding (RoPE)

\mathbf{R}_{m} = \begin{bmatrix} \cos m\theta & -\sin m\theta \\ \sin m\theta & \cos m\theta \end{bmatrix}, \qquad (\mathbf{R}_{m}\mathbf{q})^{\top}(\mathbf{R}_{n}\mathbf{k}) = \mathbf{q}^{\top}\mathbf{R}_{n-m}\,\mathbf{k}

“R m is rotation by m theta; R m q transpose times R n k equals q transpose R n minus m k”

Rotate each 2-D pair of query and key coordinates by an angle proportional to the token’s position. The attention score then depends only on the distance n - m between the tokens.

Term by term

  • m, n — positions of the query and key tokens
  • \theta — rotation frequency; each coordinate pair i has its own \theta_i = 10000^{-2i/d}
  • \mathbf{R}_{m}^{\top}\mathbf{R}_{n} = \mathbf{R}_{n-m} — rotations compose, so only the difference survives

In AI papers

Used by LLaMA, Mistral, Qwen and most open LLMs. Context-extension methods (NTK scaling, YaRN) change \theta.

Su et al., “RoFormer”, 2021

Low-rank adaptation (LoRA)

\mathbf{h} = \mathbf{W}_{0}\mathbf{x} + \frac{\alpha}{r}\,\mathbf{B}\mathbf{A}\mathbf{x}, \qquad \mathbf{B} \in \mathbb{R}^{d \times r}, \; \mathbf{A} \in \mathbb{R}^{r \times k}, \; r \ll \min(d, k)

“h equals W zero x plus alpha over r times B A x”

Freeze the pretrained weights \mathbf{W}_0 and learn only a low-rank correction \Delta\mathbf{W} = \mathbf{B}\mathbf{A}. That trains r(d + k) numbers instead of dk.

Term by term

  • \mathbf{W}_{0} \in \mathbb{R}^{d \times k} — frozen pretrained weights
  • \mathbf{B}\mathbf{A} — rank-r update; \mathbf{B} starts at zero, so training starts from the original model
  • \alpha / r — scale, so changing r needs little learning-rate re-tuning

In AI papers

With d = k = 4096 and r = 8, a full matrix has 16.8 M weights and the adapter only 65 K.

Hu et al., “LoRA: Low-Rank Adaptation of Large Language Models”, 2021

lessons.title: Multivariate Calculus
lessons.html:
Multivariate Calculus

Backpropagation, computing gradients, partial derivatives for weight updates.

Rates & slopes

Speed as a rate

\text{speed} = \frac{\text{distance}}{\text{time}}

“speed equals distance over time”

A rate says how much one quantity changes for each unit of another. 120 km in 2 hours is \frac{120}{2} = 60 km per hour.

Term by term

  • \text{distance} — how far (the change)
  • \text{time} — how long it took

In AI papers

Rates are everywhere in AI: tokens per second, loss drop per step. A derivative is a rate measured at a single instant.

Change in (Delta)

\Delta x = x_{\text{new}} - x_{\text{old}}

“delta x”

Capital delta in front of a variable means “the change in” it: new value minus old value. It is one symbol, not \Delta times x.

Example

x: 3 \to 7 \quad\Rightarrow\quad \Delta x = 4

In AI papers

\Delta\boldsymbol{\theta} is how much the weights move in one training step.

Slope of a line (rise over run)

m = \frac{\Delta y}{\Delta x} = \frac{y_{2} - y_{1}}{x_{2} - x_{1}}

“m equals delta y over delta x, y 2 minus y 1 over x 2 minus x 1”

How much y goes up for each step of 1 in x. Pick two points on the line and divide the rise by the run.

Term by term

  • (x_1, y_1), (x_2, y_2) — two points on the line
  • \Delta y — rise
  • \Delta x — run

In AI papers

A derivative is this slope, taken between two points that are infinitely close.

Limit

\lim_{x \to a} f(x) = L

“the limit of f of x as x approaches a is L”

The value f(x) gets as close to as you like when x gets close to a, even if f(a) itself is undefined.

Example

\lim_{x \to 0} \frac{\sin x}{x} = 1

In AI papers

Derivatives are limits; convergence results are limits as the number of steps T \to \infty.

Infinity and tends to

x \to \infty, \qquad f(x) \to 0

“x goes to infinity; f of x tends to zero”

\infty is not a number but a direction: “grows without bound”. \to in a limit is read “approaches” or “tends to”.

Example

\frac{1}{x} \to 0 \text{ as } x \to \infty

In AI papers

The attention mask uses -\infty because e^{-\infty} = 0: masked tokens get zero weight.

Derivatives

Derivative (Leibniz notation)

\frac{dy}{dx}, \qquad \frac{d}{dx} f(x)

“d y d x; d by d x of f of x”

The instantaneous rate of change of y as x changes: the slope of the curve at a point. It is not a fraction of two numbers, but it often behaves like one.

Example

\frac{d}{dx} x^{2} = 2x

In AI papers

Leibniz notation makes the chain rule look like cancelling fractions, which is why backprop derivations use it.

Derivative (prime and dot notation)

f'(x), \quad f''(x), \quad \dot{x}

“f prime of x; f double prime of x; x dot”

A prime is the derivative of a one-variable function; two primes, the second derivative. A dot over a variable is a derivative with respect to time (Newton's notation).

Example

f(x) = x^{3}: \quad f'(x) = 3x^{2}, \quad f''(x) = 6x

In AI papers

Activation derivatives such as \sigma'(z) appear in every backprop formula; \dot{\boldsymbol{\theta}} = -\nabla\mathcal{L} is gradient flow.

Second derivative

\frac{d^{2}y}{dx^{2}}

“d squared y d x squared”

The derivative of the derivative: how fast the slope itself is changing. Positive means the curve bends upward (convex, like a bowl).

Example

\frac{d^{2}}{dx^{2}} x^{2} = 2 > 0

In AI papers

Curvature of the loss. In many dimensions it becomes the Hessian matrix.

Definite integral

\int_{a}^{b} f(x)\,dx

“the integral from a to b of f of x d x”

The (signed) area under the curve between a and b: the continuous version of a sum. The dx says which variable is being integrated.

Example

\int_{0}^{1} 2x\,dx = 1

In AI papers

Expectations over continuous variables are integrals: \mathbb{E}[f(x)] = \int f(x)\,p(x)\,dx.

Definition of the derivative

f'(x) = \lim_{h \to 0} \frac{f(x + h) - f(x)}{h}

“f prime of x equals the limit as h goes to zero of f of x plus h minus f of x, over h”

The slope between x and a point a tiny distance h away, as that distance shrinks to zero.

Term by term

  • h — a small step
  • f(x+h) - f(x) — rise over that step
  • \lim_{h \to 0} — let the step shrink to nothing

In AI papers

Gradient checking tests backprop by computing this fraction with a small real h such as 10^{-5} (the finite-difference method).

Power rule

\frac{d}{dx} x^{n} = n\,x^{n-1}

“d by d x of x to the n equals n x to the n minus 1”

Bring the exponent down in front and reduce it by one.

Term by term

  • n — any real exponent

In AI papers

Gives the gradient of squared error: \frac{d}{d\hat{y}} (\hat{y} - y)^{2} = 2(\hat{y} - y).

Derivatives of exp and log

\frac{d}{dx} e^{x} = e^{x}, \qquad \frac{d}{dx} \ln x = \frac{1}{x}

“d by d x of e to the x is e to the x; d by d x of the natural log of x is one over x”

e^{x} is its own derivative, which is what makes e special. The log’s slope gets smaller as x grows.

Term by term

  • e^{x} — grows at a rate equal to its own value
  • 1/x — why -\log p has a large gradient when p is small

In AI papers

These two rules produce the famous clean gradient of softmax plus cross-entropy.

Product rule

\frac{d}{dx}\big[u(x)\,v(x)\big] = u'(x)\,v(x) + u(x)\,v'(x)

“the derivative of u times v equals u prime v plus u v prime”

Differentiate one factor at a time, keep the other fixed, and add the two results.

Term by term

  • u'v — change coming from u
  • uv' — change coming from v

In AI papers

Needed for gated activations such as SiLU, x\,\sigma(x), whose derivative is \sigma(x) + x\,\sigma(x)(1 - \sigma(x)).

Fundamental theorem of calculus

\int_{a}^{b} f'(x)\,dx = f(b) - f(a)

“the integral from a to b of f prime of x d x equals f of b minus f of a”
