Non-convex convergence results only promise \|\nabla f\| \le \varepsilon: an approximately stationary point.

Sharpness

\lambda_{\max}\big(\nabla^{2}\mathcal{L}(\boldsymbol{\theta})\big)

“lambda max of the Hessian of the loss”

The curvature in the steepest direction. Flat minima (small sharpness) are thought to generalise better than sharp ones.

In AI papers

Sharpness-Aware Minimization (SAM) and the “edge of stability” phenomenon are both about this quantity.

Stable learning rate on a quadratic

\mathcal{L}(\boldsymbol{\theta}) = \tfrac{1}{2}\boldsymbol{\theta}^{\top}\mathbf{H}\boldsymbol{\theta}: \qquad \boldsymbol{\theta}_{t} = (\mathbf{I} - \eta\mathbf{H})^{t}\,\boldsymbol{\theta}_{0} \to \mathbf{0} \iff \eta < \frac{2}{\lambda_{\max}(\mathbf{H})}

“on a quadratic, gradient descent converges if and only if eta is less than two over the largest eigenvalue of H”

Along each eigen-direction the error is multiplied by 1 - \eta\lambda_i every step. If any |1 - \eta\lambda_i| > 1, that direction explodes.

Term by term

  • \mathbf{H} — Hessian (curvature)
  • 1 - \eta\lambda_{i} — per-step factor in direction i
  • 2/\lambda_{\max} — the edge of stability

In AI papers

Full-batch training drifts until sharpness sits right at 2/\eta (“edge of stability”, Cohen et al., 2021).

Quadratic model of the loss

\mathcal{L}(\boldsymbol{\theta} + \boldsymbol{\delta}) \approx \mathcal{L}(\boldsymbol{\theta}) + \nabla\mathcal{L}(\boldsymbol{\theta})^{\top}\boldsymbol{\delta} + \frac{1}{2}\,\boldsymbol{\delta}^{\top}\mathbf{H}\,\boldsymbol{\delta}

“L of theta plus delta is approximately L of theta plus the gradient transpose delta plus one half delta transpose H delta”

Near the current weights the loss looks like a bowl (or saddle) described by the gradient and the Hessian.

Term by term

  • \nabla\mathcal{L}^{\top}\boldsymbol{\delta} — first-order change (slope)
  • \frac{1}{2}\boldsymbol{\delta}^{\top}\mathbf{H}\boldsymbol{\delta} — second-order change (curvature)

In AI papers

Minimising this model gives Newton’s step \boldsymbol{\delta} = -\mathbf{H}^{-1}\nabla\mathcal{L}; pruning methods (Optimal Brain Surgeon, GPTQ) use it to predict the damage from removing or rounding weights.

Classifying a stationary point

\nabla f(\mathbf{x}^{*}) = \mathbf{0} \text{ and } \begin{cases} \nabla^{2} f(\mathbf{x}^{*}) \succ 0 & \text{local minimum} \\ \nabla^{2} f(\mathbf{x}^{*}) \prec 0 & \text{local maximum} \\ \text{eigenvalues of both signs} & \text{saddle point} \end{cases}

“at a point with zero gradient, a positive definite Hessian means a minimum, negative definite a maximum, mixed signs a saddle”

The Hessian’s eigenvalues are the curvatures along its eigen-directions. Up in every direction: a minimum. Up in some and down in others: a saddle.

Term by term

  • \succ 0 — all eigenvalues positive
  • \text{mixed} — a saddle, the most common critical point in high dimensions

In AI papers

In networks with millions of parameters most critical points are saddles, and noisy SGD escapes them.

Sharpness-aware minimization (SAM)

\min_{\boldsymbol{\theta}} \; \max_{\|\boldsymbol{\epsilon}\|_{2} \le \rho} \mathcal{L}(\boldsymbol{\theta} + \boldsymbol{\epsilon}), \qquad \hat{\boldsymbol{\epsilon}} = \rho\,\frac{\nabla\mathcal{L}(\boldsymbol{\theta})}{\|\nabla\mathcal{L}(\boldsymbol{\theta})\|_{2}}

“minimise over theta the worst loss within a ball of radius rho around theta”

Look for weights whose whole neighbourhood has low loss, which is a flat minimum. In practice, take one step up the gradient to find the worst nearby point, and use the gradient there.

Term by term

  • \rho — neighbourhood radius
  • \hat{\boldsymbol{\epsilon}} — first-order approximation of the worst perturbation

In AI papers

Costs two gradient computations per step and often improves generalisation.

Foret et al., 2021

Regularization

L2 regularisation

\mathcal{L}_{\text{reg}}(\boldsymbol{\theta}) = \mathcal{L}(\boldsymbol{\theta}) + \frac{\lambda}{2}\|\boldsymbol{\theta}\|_{2}^{2} \quad\Rightarrow\quad \nabla\mathcal{L}_{\text{reg}} = \nabla\mathcal{L} + \lambda\boldsymbol{\theta}

“the regularised loss equals the loss plus lambda over two times the squared norm of theta”

Penalise large weights. Its gradient adds \lambda\boldsymbol{\theta}, which pulls every weight toward zero (“weight decay”).

Term by term

  • \lambda — regularisation strength
  • \frac{1}{2} — chosen so the gradient is simply \lambda\boldsymbol{\theta}

In AI papers

For plain SGD this equals weight decay; for Adam it does not, hence AdamW.

Gradient-norm clipping

\mathbf{g} \leftarrow \mathbf{g}\cdot\min\!\Big(1, \frac{c}{\|\mathbf{g}\|_{2}}\Big)

“g gets g times the minimum of one and c over the norm of g”

If the gradient is longer than c, shrink it to length c while keeping its direction; otherwise leave it alone.

Term by term

  • c — clipping threshold, often 1.0
  • \|\mathbf{g}\|_{2} — global norm over all parameters

In AI papers

Protects LLM training from rare loss spikes; standard in RNN training too.

Inverted dropout

\tilde{\mathbf{h}} = \frac{\mathbf{m} \odot \mathbf{h}}{1 - p}, \qquad m_{i} \overset{\text{iid}}{\sim} \operatorname{Bernoulli}(1 - p)

“h tilde equals the mask times h, divided by one minus p”

During training, zero each activation with probability p and scale the survivors up so that the expected value is unchanged: \mathbb{E}[\tilde{\mathbf{h}}] = \mathbf{h}.

Term by term

  • \mathbf{m} — random 0/1 mask
  • p — drop probability, e.g. 0.1
  • 1/(1-p) — rescaling, so nothing changes at test time

In AI papers

Used in the original Transformer; many LLM pretraining runs now set p = 0.

Srivastava et al., 2014

lessons.title: Numerical Analysis
lessons.html:
Numerical Analysis

Model quantization, FP8/BF16 training stability, memory-bound computing efficiency.

Number representation

Rounding

3.14159 \approx 3.14, \qquad 2.5 \to 2 \text{ or } 3\,?

“three point one four one five nine is approximately three point one four”

Keep the digits you need and round the last one: up if the next digit is 5 or more, down otherwise. Computers break exact ties (like 2.5) toward the even neighbour, so ties do not always round up.

Example

7.46 \approx 7.5, \qquad 7.44 \approx 7.4

In AI papers

Every floating-point operation rounds its result, which is where numerical error comes from.

Place value

347 = 3 \times 10^{2} + 4 \times 10^{1} + 7 \times 10^{0} = 300 + 40 + 7

“three hundred forty-seven equals three times ten squared plus four times ten plus seven”

Each digit is worth ten times the digit to its right. The position of a digit is its power of ten.

Term by term

  • 10^{2} = 100 — hundreds place
  • 10^{0} = 1 — ones place

In AI papers

Computers do exactly the same thing in base 2, the binary system.

Scientific notation

6.02 \times 10^{23}, \qquad 3 \times 10^{-4} = \texttt{3e-4}

“six point oh two times ten to the twenty-three; three times ten to the minus four”

A number between 1 and 10 times a power of ten. The power says how many places to move the decimal point. Code writes the power after an “e”.

Example

12{,}300 = 1.23 \times 10^{4}, \qquad 0.0005 = 5 \times 10^{-4}

In AI papers

Floating-point numbers are scientific notation in base 2: a significand times a power of two.

Size prefixes

\text{k} = 10^{3}, \;\; \text{M} = 10^{6}, \;\; \text{G} = 10^{9}, \;\; \text{T} = 10^{12}, \;\; \text{P} = 10^{15}; \qquad \text{KiB} = 2^{10}, \;\; \text{GiB} = 2^{30}

“kilo, mega, giga, tera, peta; kibibyte, gibibyte”

Thousand, million, billion, trillion, quadrillion. Memory is sometimes counted in powers of two instead: 1 GiB = 1,073,741,824 bytes, about 7% more than 1 GB.

In AI papers

A “7B” model has 7 \times 10^{9} parameters; a GPU might do 10^{15} FLOP/s (1 PFLOP/s) with 80 GB of memory.

Bits and bytes

1 \text{ byte} = 8 \text{ bits}, \qquad n \text{ bits} \Rightarrow 2^{n} \text{ values}

“one byte is eight bits; n bits give two to the n values”

A bit is a single 0 or 1. With n bits you can write 2^{n} different patterns.

Example

\text{INT8}: 2^{8} = 256 \text{ values, from } -128 \text{ to } 127

In AI papers

FP32 = 4 bytes, BF16/FP16 = 2 bytes, FP8/INT8 = 1 byte, INT4 = half a byte per number.

Binary numbers

1011_{2} = 1 \cdot 2^{3} + 0 \cdot 2^{2} + 1 \cdot 2^{1} + 1 \cdot 2^{0} = 11_{10}

“one zero one one in base two equals eleven in base ten”

In base 2 each place is worth twice the place to its right, and the only digits are 0 and 1. The subscript names the base.

Term by term

  • _{2} — base 2 (binary)
  • 2^{3}, 2^{2}, 2^{1}, 2^{0} — place values 8, 4, 2, 1

In AI papers

Binary fractions work the same way: 0.101_2 = \frac{1}{2} + \frac{1}{8} = 0.625. That is how the mantissa of a float is read.

Memory needed for a model’s weights

\text{memory} = N_{\text{params}} \times \frac{b}{8} \text{ bytes}

“memory equals the number of parameters times bits per parameter over eight bytes”

Multiply the number of weights by the bytes each one takes.

Term by term

  • N_{\text{params}} — number of parameters, e.g. 7 \times 10^{9}
  • b — bits per parameter: 32, 16, 8 or 4

In AI papers

A 7B model needs 28 GB in FP32, 14 GB in BF16, 7 GB in INT8 and 3.5 GB in INT4, which is why quantization lets it run on a laptop.

Floating-point formats

Machine epsilon

\epsilon_{\text{mach}} = 2^{-p}

“epsilon machine equals two to the minus p”

The gap between 1 and the next larger floating-point number, where p is the number of stored mantissa bits. It sets the relative precision of the format. (Some texts call half of it, the unit roundoff u, “epsilon”.)

Example

\text{FP32}: 2^{-23} \approx 1.2 \times 10^{-7}, \quad \text{FP16}: 2^{-10} \approx 9.8 \times 10^{-4}, \quad \text{BF16}: 2^{-7} \approx 7.8 \times 10^{-3}

In AI papers

BF16 is only accurate to about 2–3 decimal digits, which is why optimizer states are usually kept in FP32.

Format names (sign, exponent, mantissa bits)

\underbrace{s}_{1}\;\underbrace{e_{1}\cdots e_{E}}_{E \text{ exponent bits}}\;\underbrace{m_{1}\cdots m_{M}}_{M \text{ mantissa bits}}

“one sign bit, E exponent bits, M mantissa bits”

Exponent bits set the range (how big and how small); mantissa bits set the precision (how many significant digits).

Example

\text{FP32}{:}\,(1, 8, 23) \quad \text{FP16}{:}\,(1, 5, 10) \quad \text{BF16}{:}\,(1, 8, 7) \quad \text{E4M3}{:}\,(1, 4, 3) \quad \text{E5M2}{:}\,(1, 5, 2)

In AI papers

BF16 keeps FP32’s 8 exponent bits, so it has the same range and rarely overflows, at the cost of precision.

Value of a floating-point number

x = (-1)^{s} \times \Big(1 + \sum_{i=1}^{M} m_{i}\,2^{-i}\Big) \times 2^{\,e - \text{bias}}, \qquad \text{bias} = 2^{E-1} - 1

“x equals minus one to the s times one point m in binary times two to the e minus bias”

Sign, then a significand between 1 and 2 (the leading 1 is implicit, not stored), then a power of two. The stored exponent is offset by a bias so that it can be negative.

Term by term

  • s — sign bit
  • m_i — mantissa (fraction) bits
  • e — stored exponent; e = all zeros is reserved for zero and subnormals, all ones for ∞/NaN in IEEE formats
  • \text{bias} — 127 for FP32/BF16, 15 for FP16, 7 for E4M3

In AI papers

Precision is relative: there are as many BF16 numbers between 1 and 2 as between 1024 and 2048.

Largest FP16 number

x_{\max}^{\text{FP16}} = (2 - 2^{-10}) \times 2^{15} = 65{,}504

“the largest FP16 number is two minus two to the minus ten times two to the fifteen, which is 65,504”

With only 5 exponent bits, FP16 overflows to infinity above 65,504. BF16 and FP32 go up to about 3.4 \times 10^{38}.

Term by term

  • 2 - 2^{-10} — largest significand (all mantissa bits 1)
  • 2^{15} — largest exponent (30 - 15)

In AI papers

Why FP16 training needs loss scaling and why e^{12} \approx 162{,}755 computed in FP16 becomes \infty.

Unit in the last place

\operatorname{ulp}(x) = 2^{\lfloor \log_{2}|x| \rfloor - p}

“u l p of x”

The spacing between neighbouring floats near x. It doubles each time |x| crosses a power of two, so absolute precision gets worse for big numbers.

Example

\text{BF16}: \operatorname{ulp}(1) = 2^{-7}, \quad \operatorname{ulp}(256) = 2

In AI papers

A small update \eta g is lost entirely if it is less than half an ulp of the weight it is added to.

FP8 formats E4M3 and E5M2

\mathrm{E4M3}: \; \max = 448, \;\; \epsilon = 2^{-3} \qquad \mathrm{E5M2}: \; \max = 57{,}344, \;\; \epsilon = 2^{-2}

“E four M three, max 448; E five M two, max 57,344”

“ExMy” means x exponent and y mantissa bits. E4M3 has more precision; E5M2 has more range.

In AI papers

FP8 training usually stores weights and activations in E4M3 and gradients in E5M2, each tensor with its own scale factor.

Rounding & error

Absolute and relative error

\text{absolute error} = |\hat{x} - x|, \qquad \text{relative error} = \frac{|\hat{x} - x|}{|x|}

“absolute error is the size of x hat minus x; relative error is that divided by the size of x”

Absolute error is how far off you are; relative error is how far off compared with the size of the true value. Floats keep the relative error small.

Term by term

  • x — true value
  • \hat{x} — computed or approximate value

In AI papers

Being off by 1 matters for a weight of 0.5 but not for one of 10,000; quantization error is best judged relatively.

Floating-point rounding operator

\operatorname{fl}(x)

“f l of x, x rounded to floating point”

The nearest representable floating-point number to the real number x. Error analysis writes computed results as \operatorname{fl}(a + b) and so on.

In AI papers

\operatorname{fl}_{\text{bf16}}(w) is what a weight becomes when cast to BF16.

Standard model of floating-point arithmetic

\operatorname{fl}(a \circ b) = (a \circ b)(1 + \delta), \qquad |\delta| \le u = \tfrac{1}{2}\epsilon_{\text{mach}}, \qquad \circ \in \{+, -, \times, \div\}

“the computed result of a op b equals the exact result times one plus delta, with delta at most the unit roundoff”

Each basic operation is exact except for one final rounding, which has relative error at most u. Errors then build up over long chains of operations.

Term by term

  • \delta — relative rounding error of this one operation
  • u — unit roundoff: 2^{-24} for FP32, 2^{-8} for BF16

In AI papers

A sum of n numbers can have error around n u in the worst case, which is why long dot products accumulate in FP32.

Swamping (small numbers lost in big ones)

\operatorname{fl}_{\text{bf16}}(256 + 1) = 256, \qquad \operatorname{fl}_{\text{fp32}}\big(1 + 10^{-8}\big) = 1

“in BF16, 256 plus 1 is 256; in FP32, one plus ten to the minus eight is one”

When you add a small number to a large one, the small one can be rounded away entirely. BF16 has only 8 significant bits, so near 256 the spacing is 2 and adding 1 changes nothing.

Term by term

  • \operatorname{ulp}_{\text{bf16}}(256) = 2 — the gap between neighbouring BF16 values at 256
  • 256 + 1 — a tie, broken toward the even value 256

In AI papers

Why weights are updated in FP32 “master” copies: \boldsymbol{\theta} - \eta\mathbf{g} in BF16 would often leave \boldsymbol{\theta} unchanged.

Catastrophic cancellation

\operatorname{Var}(x) = \mathbb{E}[x^{2}] - \big(\mathbb{E}[x]\big)^{2} \quad\text{is unstable when}\quad |\mathbb{E}[x]| \gg \operatorname{Std}(x)

“variance as E of x squared minus E of x, squared, is unstable when the mean is much larger than the spread”

Subtracting two nearly equal rounded numbers cancels their leading digits and leaves mostly rounding error. The formula is exact on paper but can even return a negative variance.

Term by term

  • \mathbb{E}[x^{2}] \approx (\mathbb{E}[x])^{2} — two big, nearly equal numbers
  • \text{fix} — subtract the mean first, or use Welford’s running algorithm

In AI papers

Normalisation kernels compute variance in FP32 with a stable (two-pass or Welford) method.

Condition number of a problem

\kappa_{f}(x) = \left| \frac{x\,f^{\prime}(x)}{f(x)} \right| \approx \frac{\text{relative change in output}}{\text{relative change in input}}

“the condition number of f at x equals the absolute value of x f prime of x over f of x”

How much a problem amplifies small relative errors in its input. A large \kappa means the answer is sensitive no matter how carefully you compute it.

Term by term

  • \kappa \approx 1 — well-conditioned
  • \kappa \gg 1 — ill-conditioned: expect to lose about \log_{10}\kappa digits

In AI papers

For solving \mathbf{A}\mathbf{x} = \mathbf{b} the analogue is \kappa(\mathbf{A}) = \sigma_{\max}/\sigma_{\min}, and it also slows optimizers.

Numerical stability

Log-sum-exp trick

\log\sum_{i=1}^{K} e^{z_{i}} = m + \log\sum_{i=1}^{K} e^{z_{i} - m}, \qquad m = \max_{i} z_{i}

“log of the sum of e to the z i equals m plus log of the sum of e to the z i minus m, where m is the largest z”

Subtract the largest value before exponentiating. The biggest term becomes e^{0} = 1, so nothing overflows, and the answer is mathematically unchanged.

Term by term

  • m — the maximum logit
  • z_i - m \le 0 — every exponent is now at most 0

In AI papers

Used inside every cross-entropy and softmax kernel; without it, a logit of 100 overflows even in FP32 (e^{100} \approx 2.7 \times 10^{43}).

Shift-invariance of softmax

\operatorname{softmax}(\mathbf{z}) = \operatorname{softmax}(\mathbf{z} - c\,\mathbf{1}) \quad \text{for any } c \in \mathbb{R}

“softmax of z equals softmax of z minus c for any constant c”

Adding the same constant to every logit multiplies top and bottom by e^{-c}, which cancels. So subtracting the max is free.

Term by term

  • c = \max_i z_i — the choice that prevents overflow

In AI papers

Also why only the differences between logits matter.

Online softmax (FlashAttention)

m^{\text{new}} = \max(m, \tilde{m}), \qquad \ell^{\text{new}} = e^{m - m^{\text{new}}}\,\ell + e^{\tilde{m} - m^{\text{new}}}\,\tilde{\ell}

“the new running max is the max of the old and the block max; the new running sum rescales both sums to the new max”

Softmax can be computed one block of scores at a time: keep a running maximum m and a running sum \ell, and rescale the old sum whenever a larger maximum appears.

Term by term

  • m, \ell — running max and running sum of e^{z - m} so far
  • \tilde{m}, \tilde{\ell} — max and sum for the new block

In AI papers

Lets FlashAttention avoid ever writing the n \times n score matrix to memory, turning attention from memory-bound to compute-bound.

Milakov & Gimelshein, 2018; Dao et al., “FlashAttention”, 2022

Loss scaling for FP16

\tilde{\mathcal{L}} = S \cdot \mathcal{L}, \qquad \mathbf{g} = \frac{1}{S}\,\nabla_{\boldsymbol{\theta}}\tilde{\mathcal{L}}

“scale the loss by S before backprop, then divide the gradients by S”

Small gradients underflow to zero in FP16 (below about 6 \times 10^{-8}). Multiplying the loss by S shifts every gradient up into range; dividing afterwards (in FP32) restores the true values.

Term by term

  • S — scale, e.g. 2^{16}; halved when an overflow (inf/NaN) is detected, grown slowly otherwise

In AI papers

Dynamic loss scaling (`GradScaler`) is needed for FP16 but not for BF16, whose range matches FP32.

Micikevicius et al., “Mixed Precision Training”, 2018

Mixed-precision update with master weights

\boldsymbol{\theta}^{\text{fp32}} \leftarrow \boldsymbol{\theta}^{\text{fp32}} - \eta\,\mathbf{u}\big(\mathbf{g}^{\text{fp32}}\big), \qquad \boldsymbol{\theta}^{\text{bf16}} = \operatorname{fl}_{\text{bf16}}\big(\boldsymbol{\theta}^{\text{fp32}}\big)

“update the FP32 master weights, then cast them to BF16 for the next forward and backward pass”

Compute in low precision but accumulate updates in high precision, so that small steps are not swamped.

Term by term

  • \mathbf{u}(\cdot) — the optimizer step (e.g. Adam’s)
  • \operatorname{fl}_{\text{bf16}} — round to BF16

In AI papers

With Adam this costs about 16 bytes per parameter: 2 (BF16 weights) + 2 (grads) + 4 (master) + 4 + 4 (moments). A 7B model needs about 112 GB before activations.

Stochastic rounding

\operatorname{SR}(x) = \begin{cases} \lfloor x \rfloor & \text{with probability } 1 - (x - \lfloor x \rfloor) \\ \lfloor x \rfloor + 1 & \text{with probability } x - \lfloor x \rfloor \end{cases} \qquad \mathbb{E}[\operatorname{SR}(x)] = x

“stochastic rounding rounds up with probability equal to the fractional part”

Round randomly, in proportion to how close x is to each neighbour (here on a grid of spacing 1). On average there is no error, so many tiny updates add up correctly instead of being rounded away.

Term by term

  • x - \lfloor x \rfloor — fractional part = chance of rounding up
  • \mathbb{E}[\operatorname{SR}(x)] = x — unbiased

In AI papers

Makes pure-BF16 or FP8 weight updates workable without FP32 master weights.

RMSNorm

\operatorname{RMSNorm}(\mathbf{x}) = \frac{\mathbf{x}}{\sqrt{\frac{1}{d}\sum_{i=1}^{d} x_{i}^{2} + \epsilon}} \odot \mathbf{g}

“RMS norm of x equals x divided by the root mean square of its entries plus epsilon, times the gain g”

Rescale each token vector to unit root-mean-square size, then apply a learned per-feature gain. Cheaper than LayerNorm, with no mean subtraction.

Term by term

  • \sqrt{\frac{1}{d}\sum x_i^{2}} — root mean square of the entries
  • \epsilon — guards against division by zero (e.g. 10^{-6})
  • \mathbf{g} — learned gain

In AI papers

Used in LLaMA and most modern LLMs. Implementations compute the sum of squares in FP32 even for BF16 inputs.

Zhang & Sennrich, 2019

Quantization

Signed integer ranges

\text{INT}b: \; [-2^{b-1},\; 2^{b-1} - 1]

“a b-bit signed integer ranges from minus two to the b minus one up to two to the b minus one, minus one”

Two’s-complement integers have one more negative value than positive. The spacing is always exactly 1, unlike floats.

Example

\text{INT8}: [-128, 127], \qquad \text{INT4}: [-8, 7]

In AI papers

Symmetric quantization often uses only [-127, 127] so that zero sits exactly in the middle.

Clamp (clip)

\operatorname{clamp}(x, a, b) = \min\big(\max(x, a),\, b\big)

“clamp x between a and b”

Force x into the interval [a, b]: values below a become a, values above b become b.

Example

\operatorname{clamp}(300, -128, 127) = 127

In AI papers

Quantizers clamp to the integer range; outliers that get clamped cause large errors.

Affine (asymmetric) quantization

q = \operatorname{clamp}\!\Big( \Big\lfloor \frac{x}{s} \Big\rceil + z,\; q_{\min},\; q_{\max} \Big), \qquad \hat{x} = s\,(q - z)

“q equals x over s rounded, plus z, clamped to the integer range; x hat equals s times q minus z”

Map real numbers onto an integer grid with a scale s (the grid spacing) and a zero-point z (the integer that stands for 0.0). Dequantizing multiplies back.

Term by term

  • s = \frac{x_{\max} - x_{\min}}{q_{\max} - q_{\min}} — scale (step size)
  • z = q_{\min} - \lfloor x_{\min}/s \rceil — zero-point
  • \lfloor \cdot \rceil — round to nearest

In AI papers

Standard for INT8 activations, which are often not centred on zero (e.g. after ReLU).

Symmetric absmax quantization

s = \frac{\max_{i} |x_{i}|}{2^{b-1} - 1}, \qquad q_{i} = \Big\lfloor \frac{x_{i}}{s} \Big\rceil, \qquad \hat{x}_{i} = s\,q_{i}

“s equals the largest absolute value over two to the b minus one, minus one; q i is x i over s rounded”

Scale so the largest magnitude maps to the largest integer (127 for INT8), with zero-point 0. Simple and fast, but a single outlier makes s large and wastes resolution for all the other values.

Term by term

  • \max_i |x_i| = \|\mathbf{x}\|_{\infty} — absmax of the tensor, row or block
  • 2^{b-1} - 1 — 127 for INT8, 7 for INT4

In AI papers

Per-channel or per-block scales (e.g. one scale per 64 or 128 weights) limit the damage from outliers.

Quantization noise

e = x - \hat{x} \in \Big[-\frac{s}{2}, \frac{s}{2}\Big], \qquad \mathbb{E}[e^{2}] \approx \frac{s^{2}}{12}

“the rounding error is between minus s over 2 and s over 2, with mean square about s squared over 12”

Rounding to a grid of spacing s gives an error that behaves like uniform noise. Each extra bit halves s and cuts the noise power by 4 (about 6 dB).

Term by term

  • s — quantization step
  • s^{2}/12 — variance of a uniform distribution of width s

In AI papers

Going from INT8 to INT4 makes the step 16 times coarser, which is why 4-bit methods need careful error compensation (GPTQ, AWQ).

Block (microscaling) formats

x_{i} \approx s_{B}\cdot q_{i}, \quad i \in B, \qquad |B| = 32, \quad q_{i} \in \text{FP4 (E2M1)} = \{0, \pm 0.5, \pm 1, \pm 1.5, \pm 2, \pm 3, \pm 4, \pm 6\}

“each value is approximately the block scale times a 4-bit code”

Split a tensor into small blocks that share one scale factor, and store each element in very few bits. Small blocks adapt to local magnitude, so outliers only hurt their own block.

Term by term

  • s_{B} — shared scale for block B (a power of two in MX formats)
  • q_i — low-precision element, here 4-bit floating point

In AI papers

MXFP8/MXFP4 (OCP spec) and NVFP4 (16-element blocks with FP8 scales) are supported in hardware on recent accelerators.

OCP Microscaling Formats (MX) Specification, 2023

Per-tensor FP8 scaling

s = \frac{\operatorname{amax}(\mathbf{X})}{448}, \qquad \mathbf{X}^{\text{fp8}} = \operatorname{fl}_{\text{E4M3}}\!\big(\mathbf{X} / s\big)

“s equals the absolute max of X over 448; store X over s in E4M3”

Stretch the tensor so its largest value lands at the top of the E4M3 range (448), to use the format’s precision without overflowing. Keep s in higher precision next to the FP8 data.

Term by term

  • \operatorname{amax} — largest absolute value, often taken from a history of recent steps (“delayed scaling”)
  • 448 — largest finite E4M3 value

In AI papers

How FP8 training works on Hopper/Blackwell GPUs (Transformer Engine); DeepSeek-V3 used finer tile-wise scales.

Micikevicius et al., “FP8 Formats for Deep Learning”, 2022

Migrating outliers (SmoothQuant)

\mathbf{Y} = \mathbf{X}\mathbf{W} = \big(\mathbf{X}\operatorname{diag}(\mathbf{s})^{-1}\big)\big(\operatorname{diag}(\mathbf{s})\,\mathbf{W}\big), \qquad s_{j} = \frac{\max|\mathbf{X}_{:,j}|^{\alpha}}{\max|\mathbf{W}_{j,:}|^{1-\alpha}}

“X W equals X times diag s inverse, times diag s times W”

Divide each activation channel by s_j and multiply the matching weight row by s_j. The product is unchanged, but activation outliers shrink, so both factors quantize well.

Term by term

  • \operatorname{diag}(\mathbf{s})^{-1}\operatorname{diag}(\mathbf{s}) = \mathbf{I} — the rescaling cancels exactly
  • \alpha — how much difficulty to move from activations to weights, e.g. 0.5

In AI papers

LLM activations have a few channels up to 100× larger than the rest; this makes W8A8 inference accurate.

Xiao et al., “SmoothQuant”, 2023

Straight-through estimator

\text{forward: } \hat{x} = s\,\Big\lfloor \frac{x}{s} \Big\rceil, \qquad \text{backward: } \frac{\partial \hat{x}}{\partial x} := 1

“forward, round x to the grid; backward, pretend the rounding had derivative one”

Rounding has zero gradient almost everywhere, so training through it would learn nothing. The STE passes the gradient straight through as if rounding were the identity.

Term by term

  • \lfloor \cdot \rceil — true derivative is 0 (or undefined at jumps)
  • := 1 — a deliberate approximation

In AI papers

The basis of quantization-aware training (QAT) and of binary/ternary networks; also used in VQ-VAE.

Bengio, Léonard & Courville, 2013

Compute & memory efficiency

FLOPs versus FLOP/s

\text{FLOPs} \;(\text{work}) \qquad \text{vs.} \qquad \text{FLOP/s} \;(\text{speed})

“floating-point operations, versus floating-point operations per second”

FLOPs counts how much arithmetic a job needs; FLOP/s is how fast hardware can do it. Time ≈ FLOPs ÷ (FLOP/s × utilisation). One multiply-add counts as 2 FLOPs.

In AI papers

Model FLOPs Utilisation (MFU) is achieved FLOP/s divided by peak; 40–60% is good for LLM training.

FLOPs of a matrix multiplication

\underset{m \times n}{\mathbf{A}}\;\underset{n \times p}{\mathbf{B}}: \qquad \text{FLOPs} = 2\,m\,n\,p

“multiplying an m by n matrix by an n by p matrix costs two m n p floating-point operations”

Each of the m p outputs is a dot product of length n: n multiplies and about n adds.

Term by term

  • m\,p — number of outputs
  • 2n — one multiply and one add per term

In AI papers

A forward pass costs about 2N FLOPs per token for a model with N parameters, since every weight is used in one multiply-add.

Memory bandwidth

\beta \;[\text{bytes/s}], \qquad t_{\text{mem}} = \frac{\text{bytes moved}}{\beta}

“beta, the memory bandwidth; memory time equals bytes moved over bandwidth”

How many bytes per second can travel between memory (HBM) and the compute units. If moving the data takes longer than computing on it, the job is memory-bound.

In AI papers

An H100 SXM has about 3.35 TB/s of HBM bandwidth but about 990 TFLOP/s of dense BF16 compute.

Training compute

C \approx 6\,N\,D

“compute C is approximately six times N times D”

Total training FLOPs ≈ 6 × parameters × training tokens: 2 for the forward pass and 4 for the backward pass (which computes gradients for both activations and weights).

Term by term

  • N — number of parameters
  • D — number of training tokens
  • 6 = 2 + 4 — forward + backward

In AI papers

A 7B model on 2T tokens needs about 6 \times 7 \times 10^{9} \times 2 \times 10^{12} \approx 8.4 \times 10^{22} FLOPs. Chinchilla-optimal training uses D \approx 20N.

Kaplan et al., 2020; Hoffmann et al., 2022

Arithmetic intensity

I = \frac{\text{FLOPs}}{\text{bytes moved}}, \qquad I_{\text{matmul}}(n{\times}n{\times}n,\ \text{BF16}) = \frac{2n^{3}}{3 \cdot 2n^{2}} = \frac{n}{3}, \qquad I_{\text{matvec}} \approx 1

“arithmetic intensity is FLOPs per byte moved”

How much computing you do for each byte you fetch from memory. Large matrix products reuse each number many times; a matrix–vector product uses each weight once.

Term by term

  • 2n^{3} — FLOPs of an n \times n by n \times n product
  • 3 \cdot 2n^{2} — bytes to read A and B and write C in BF16

In AI papers

LLM decoding at batch size 1 is matrix–vector work with I \approx 1 FLOP/byte, far below the ~300 an H100 needs to be compute-bound. That is why batching many requests speeds up serving.

Roofline model

P = \min\big(\pi,\; \beta \cdot I\big), \qquad I^{*} = \frac{\pi}{\beta}

“attainable performance equals the minimum of peak compute and bandwidth times intensity”

Below the ridge point I^{*} a kernel is memory-bound (speed limited by bandwidth); above it, compute-bound (limited by peak FLOP/s).

Term by term

  • \pi — peak compute, FLOP/s
  • \beta — memory bandwidth, bytes/s
  • I^{*} — ridge point: about 990 \times 10^{12} / 3.35 \times 10^{12} \approx 295 FLOP/byte on an H100 in BF16

In AI papers

Kernel fusion, FlashAttention and quantization all aim to raise I or cut bytes moved.

Williams, Waterman & Patterson, 2009

Memory-bound decoding speed

t_{\text{token}} \ge \frac{\text{bytes of weights} + \text{bytes of KV cache}}{\beta}

“time per token is at least the bytes that must be read divided by memory bandwidth”

To generate each token, every weight must be read from memory at least once. At small batch sizes this, not arithmetic, sets the speed limit.

Term by term

  • \beta — memory bandwidth

In AI papers

A 7B model in BF16 (14 GB) at 3.35 TB/s: at least 4.2 ms per token, at most about 240 tokens/s. In INT4 (3.5 GB) the limit is about 4 times higher.

KV-cache size

\text{KV bytes} = 2 \cdot L \cdot n_{\text{kv}} \cdot d_{\text{head}} \cdot T \cdot B \cdot b_{\text{elem}}

“KV bytes equals two times layers times KV heads times head size times sequence length times batch times bytes per element”

During generation each layer stores a key and a value vector (the 2) for every past token, so later tokens do not recompute them. It grows linearly with context length and batch.

Term by term

  • L — number of layers
  • n_{\text{kv}} — number of key/value heads (fewer than query heads with GQA/MQA)
  • T, B — context length and batch size
  • b_{\text{elem}} — bytes per number: 2 for BF16, 1 for FP8

In AI papers

LLaMA-2-7B (L = 32, n_{\text{kv}} = 32, d_{\text{head}} = 128) at 4,096 tokens in BF16: exactly 2 GiB per sequence. GQA with 8 KV heads cuts that by 4.

Cost of self-attention

\text{FLOPs} \approx 4\,n^{2}\,d \;\text{ per layer}, \qquad \text{naive memory for scores} = \mathcal{O}(h\,n^{2})

“attention costs about four n squared d FLOPs per layer, and naive memory grows as n squared”

Computing \mathbf{Q}\mathbf{K}^{\top} and multiplying the weights by \mathbf{V} each cost 2n^{2}d. Both time and naive memory grow with the square of the sequence length.

Term by term

  • n — sequence length
  • d — model width (h \cdot d_k)
  • h\,n^{2} — one n \times n score matrix per head

In AI papers

Doubling the context quadruples attention cost. FlashAttention removes the n^{2} memory, but the n^{2} FLOPs remain.

lessons.title: 00. Setup and the GPU mental model
lessons.html:
00. Setup and the GPU mental model

30 min

Check the toolchain, measure the two roofs every later lab is judged against.

How this course works

Every lab follows the same loop, and the app follows it too:

  1. Write: open labs/NN_name/kernel.py and fill in the numbered TODOs. solution.py next to it is the reference; peek only when stuck.
  2. Run: python labs/NN_name/run.py checks your kernel against PyTorch, then benchmarks it. --solution runs the reference instead.
  3. Measure: type the numbers your GPU printed into the lesson. The app shows the reference from the course GB200 next to yours.
  4. Explain: the explanation unlocks once you have measured. Predict first, then read why.

Every run.py ends with four lines: CLAIM (what the lesson asserts), MEASURED, VERDICT and NEXT. When a claim fails on your hardware, that is a finding, not a bug in your reading.

The path through the course:

PartLabsYou build
Kernels01–05vector add (Triton, Gluon, CUDA), fused softmax, LayerNorm·mul, GEMM+SiLU with TMA, CUDA reductions
HSTU06–08jagged attention forward, backward, then the full model
Train09HSTU on MovieLens-1M
Serve10Triton Inference Server with dynamic batching
Systems11profiling, batch scaling, CUDA graphs, compile caches
Field notes12what the 2026 Triton conference added

A GPU in five sentences

A GPU is a grid of streaming multiprocessors (SMs; 152 on GB200). Each SM runs groups of 32 threads called warps in lockstep, and keeps many warps resident so that while one waits on memory another computes. Data moves through a hierarchy: registers (per thread) → shared memory (per block, up to 227 KB) → L2 (shared, 129 MiB) → HBM. A kernel launch is a grid of blocks (Triton calls them programs); every block runs on one SM. Performance is almost always about keeping enough bytes in flight to cover HBM latency, or enough math in flight to keep the tensor cores busy.

Write

Nothing to write yet. Create the environment once:

python -m venv venv && source venv/bin/activate
python -m pip install torch triton numpy
git clone https://github.com/venkatacrc/gpukernels && cd gpukernels

The CUDA labs compile with NVRTC through torch.cuda._compile_kernel, so no nvcc is needed; gk/bench.py finds the CUDA headers that ship inside the torch wheel.

Run
python tools/check_env.py
Measure

Run the lab and record what your GPU prints. Reference values were measured on one GB200.

MeasurementUnitReference
HBM copy bandwidthGB/s6637.0
bf16 matmul 8192³TFLOP/s1741.0
smallest kernel as timedµs6.9
number of SMsSMs152.0
Explain

Two roofs. The copy reads 1 GiB and writes 1 GiB, so it reports achievable HBM bandwidth (GB200 HBM3e is rated near 8 TB/s; reaching about 85% with a plain copy is normal). The 8192³ matmul does 2 · 81923 FLOPs and is bound by the tensor cores.

Arithmetic intensity. Divide the two: 1741 TFLOP/s ÷ 6.6 TB/s ≈ 262 FLOPs per byte. That is the ridge point of the roofline. A vector add does 1 FLOP per 12 bytes, far below the ridge, so labs 01–03 and 05 are judged in GB/s. A large GEMM does hundreds of FLOPs per byte, so Lab 04 is judged in TFLOP/s. Attention (labs 06–07) sits in between, and the whole game there is not writing the N2 matrix to memory.

The launch floor. Even a 1-element kernel costs several microseconds end to end. A model step that launches 300 small kernels pays that floor 300 times. Remember this number for Lab 11.

lessons.title: 01. Vector add three ways
lessons.html:
01. Vector add three ways

60 min · lab labs/01_vector_add

The same kernel in Triton, Gluon and CUDA; masks, layouts, vector loads, Little's law.

The simplest kernel there is: out = x + y. You will write it three times, at three levels of control:

  • Triton: you describe what one program does with a whole block of elements; the compiler decides how threads split it.
  • Gluon: Triton's lower-level dialect. Same language, but you choose the layout: which thread owns which elements.
  • CUDA: you write what one thread does. Everything else is your job.

Vector add is purely memory-bound (12 bytes moved per FLOP), so the only score is GB/s, against the copy bandwidth you measured in lesson 00.

Write

Open labs/01_vector_add/kernel.py.

Triton (TODOs 1–4). Each program owns BLOCK consecutive elements:

pid = tl.program_id(0)
offs = pid * BLOCK + tl.arange(0, BLOCK)
mask = offs < n                       # the last block runs past the end
x = tl.load(x_ptr + offs, mask=mask)
y = tl.load(y_ptr + offs, mask=mask)
tl.store(out_ptr + offs, x + y, mask=mask)

Launch with grid = (triton.cdiv(n, BLOCK),).

Gluon (TODOs 5–6). The body is identical except gl.arange needs an explicit layout. Build it in the wrapper:

layout = gl.BlockedLayout(size_per_thread=[vec], threads_per_warp=[32],
                          warps_per_cta=[num_warps], order=[0])

size_per_thread=[4] means each thread owns 4 consecutive fp32 values, which the compiler can fetch with one 16-byte load. If BLOCK is larger than vec · 32 · num_warps, the layout repeats and each thread owns several such chunks.

CUDA (TODOs 7–9). A scalar kernel (one float per thread) and a float4 kernel (16 bytes per thread):

int i = blockIdx.x * blockDim.x + threadIdx.x;
if (i < n4) { float4 a = x[i], b = y[i]; out[i] = make_float4(a.x+b.x, a.y+b.y, a.z+b.z, a.w+b.w); }
Run
python labs/01_vector_add/run.py           # your kernel.py
python labs/01_vector_add/run.py --solution

The table sweeps sizes from 2¹⁶ to 2²⁸ elements and a Gluon vec sweep.

Measure

Run the lab and record what your GPU prints. Reference values were measured on one GB200.

MeasurementUnitReference
torch add, 2²⁸ elementsGB/s7142.0
Triton add, 2²⁸GB/s7149.0
Gluon add, 2²⁸GB/s7142.0
CUDA scalar, 2²⁸GB/s4075.0
CUDA float4, 2²⁸GB/s7215.0
any kernel at 2¹⁶ elementsµs6.6
Gluon vec=1, 2²⁸GB/s7208.0
Explain

Everyone hits the same wall except scalar CUDA. Torch, Triton, Gluon and float4 CUDA all land near 7.1–7.2 TB/s, above the 6.6 TB/s copy because a copy moves 2 bytes per byte read while add moves 3, and more concurrent streams keep HBM busier. Scalar CUDA tops out near 4.1 TB/s.

Little's law explains why. To sustain bandwidth B against memory latency L, you need B × L bytes in flight. At roughly 7 TB/s and roughly 1 µs that is several MB across the chip, tens of KB per SM. A scalar CUDA thread issues one 4-byte load per input and then waits. Even with the SM full of threads, there aren't enough bytes outstanding. The float4 version puts 16 bytes per load in flight, four times more per instruction.

Then why is Gluon vec=1 still fast? Because the layout repeats. With BLOCK=4096, 4 warps and vec=1, each thread owns 4096 / 128 = 32 elements and issues 32 independent loads before waiting. Width per load matters less than total bytes in flight per thread. The vec sweep (7208 / 7174 / 7133 / 7134 GB/s for vec 1/2/4/8) shows it: once enough loads are outstanding, the width barely matters. Triton's default layout makes this choice for you; Gluon lets you see and change it.

Small sizes measure launch, not bandwidth. At 2¹⁶ elements (768 KB) every implementation takes about 6.6 µs, the launch-and-sync floor from lesson 00. The data sits in L2 anyway. Never quote GB/s for a kernel that runs in under about 10 µs.

The mask. Without mask=offs < n the last program reads and writes past the end of the buffer. On a GPU that is silent memory corruption, or an illegal-address fault if you are lucky.

lessons.title: 02. Fused softmax
lessons.html:
02. Fused softmax

45 min · lab labs/02_fused_softmax

Kernel fusion = fewer HBM round trips; one row per program, stable max, register limits.

Softmax along a row: yi = exi - m / Σj exj - m with m = maxj xj.

Written in PyTorch as separate ops (max, sub, exp, sum, div), every step reads the full matrix from HBM and writes a temporary back. That is about five reads and three writes per element. A fused kernel loads each row once into registers, does all of it there, and writes once: one read, one write.

That is the entire idea of kernel fusion: count HBM round trips and remove them.

Write

labs/02_fused_softmax/kernel.py, TODOs 1–5. One program per row:

row = tl.program_id(0)
cols = tl.arange(0, BLOCK)
mask = cols < n_cols
x = tl.load(x_ptr + row * stride + cols, mask=mask, other=-float("inf"))
x = x - tl.max(x, axis=0)
num = tl.exp(x)
out = num / tl.sum(num, axis=0)
tl.store(out_ptr + row * stride + cols, out.to(out_ptr.dtype.element_ty), mask=mask)

other=-inf matters: padded lanes must not win the max, and exp(-inf) = 0 keeps them out of the sum. BLOCK = triton.next_power_of_2(n_cols); bump num_warps as rows grow so each thread holds fewer elements.

Run
python labs/02_fused_softmax/run.py
Measure

Run the lab and record what your GPU prints. Reference values were measured on one GB200.

MeasurementUnitReference
naive (5 PyTorch ops), 16384×4096µs558.0
torch.softmax, 16384×4096µs182.0
your Triton, 16384×4096µs82.0
Triton at 16384 columnsGB/s7038.0
torch.softmax at 16384 columnsGB/s4406.0
Triton at 65536 columnsGB/s3951.0
Explain

Naive vs fused: 6.8×. The 16384×4096 fp32 matrix is 256 MiB. The naive version moves about 8 × 256 MiB; the fused one moves 2 × 256 MiB. Time ratio 558 / 82 ≈ 6.8, which is the round-trip ratio plus the saved launches.

Fused vs torch.softmax: 2.2×. PyTorch's softmax is already one fused kernel, so why is ours faster at this shape? Its generic kernel makes more than one pass over the row (max pass, then sum-and-write) and is tuned for a wide range of shapes. Ours holds the entire row in registers and reads it once. At 16384 columns we reach 7.0 TB/s, essentially HBM speed, vs 4.4 TB/s for torch.

Where it breaks: 65536 columns. A 64K-column fp32 row is 256 KB. With 32 warps that is 64 values per thread, more than the register file can hold alongside everything else, so the compiler spills to local memory, which really is HBM. Bandwidth drops to 3.95 TB/s and torch catches up (3.7 TB/s). The fix for very long rows is the online softmax: loop over chunks keeping a running max and a rescaled running sum. That is exactly the trick flash attention uses, and you will use its relative in Lab 06.

Numerical safety. Subtracting the row max keeps exp from overflowing in fp32 (it overflows above about 88) without changing the result, because the factor e-m cancels.

lessons.title: 03. LayerNorm × gate, forward and backward
lessons.html:
03. LayerNorm × gate, forward and backward

60 min · lab labs/03_layernorm_mul

Fuse a normalisation with HSTU's gating multiply; save mean/rstd; write the backward.

HSTU's output path computes y = LayerNorm(attn) * u, where u is a gate projected from the input. In PyTorch that is a LayerNorm kernel, which writes its output to HBM, and then a multiply kernel that reads it back. Fusing them saves one full read and write of the activation. It is also the first kernel in the course with a backward, so the forward must save what the backward needs.

Write

labs/03_layernorm_mul/kernel.py.

Forward (TODOs 1–6), one row per program:

x = tl.load(x_ptr + row * D + cols, mask=mask, other=0.0).to(tl.float32)
mean = tl.sum(x, axis=0) / D
xc = tl.where(mask, x - mean, 0.0)
var = tl.sum(xc * xc, axis=0) / D
rstd = 1.0 / tl.sqrt(var + eps)
y = (xc * rstd * w + b) * u
tl.store(mean_ptr + row, mean); tl.store(rstd_ptr + row, rstd)

Accumulate in fp32 even when inputs are bf16.

Backward (TODO 7), written in PyTorch inside the autograd.Function, using the saved mean and rstd. With x̂ = (x-μ) r, ℓ = x̂ w + b and y = ℓ u:

  • ∂ u = g · ℓ
  • gℓ = g · u, so ∂ w = Σrows gℓ x̂ and ∂ b = Σrows gℓ
  • gx̂ = gℓ w, then ∂ x = r (gx̂ - gx̂ - x̂ gx̂ x̂), where the overline is the mean over the row.
Run
python labs/03_layernorm_mul/run.py
Measure

Run the lab and record what your GPU prints. Reference values were measured on one GB200.

MeasurementUnitReference
smallest fused speedup in the table×2.09
largest fused speedup×2.57
bf16, 262144×512GB/s3737.0
fp32, 262144×512GB/s6086.0
Explain

Why about 2×+. Unfused: LayerNorm reads x and writes ℓ; the multiply reads ℓ and u and writes y. That is 5 activation-sized transfers. Fused: read x and u, write y, so 3 transfers, plus 8 bytes per row for mean and rstd. 5/3 ≈ 1.7× from bytes alone. The measured 2.1–2.6× is higher because PyTorch's LayerNorm also does a separate pass to compute statistics, and we save a launch.

bf16 is slower in GB/s, not in time. The same shape in bf16 moves half the bytes, but the kernel still does the same number of reductions and the same per-row work with half as many bytes to hide them behind. With D=512, a row is only 1 KB in bf16; each program is short and spends proportionally more time in the two tree reductions and the launch tail. The lesson: for narrow rows, put several rows in one program (a 2-D block) so each program moves more bytes.

Save statistics, not activations. Saving mean and rstd costs 8 bytes per row; saving ℓ would cost D·2 bytes per row. The backward recomputes x̂ from x and the stats. This recompute instead of store trade comes back in Lab 07 (attention backward) and Lab 08 (GEMM+SiLU backward).

Why the dx formula has two mean terms. Both μ and r depend on every element in the row, so each input's gradient is reduced by the gradient carried through the mean (the gx̂ term) and through the variance (the x̂ gx̂x̂ term).

lessons.title: 04. GEMM + SiLU, from tiles to TMA
lessons.html:
04. GEMM + SiLU, from tiles to TMA

90 min · lab labs/04_matmul_silu

Tiled GEMM, grouped ordering, epilogue fusion, then Blackwell TMA + persistent + warp specialization.

Every HSTU layer starts with one GEMM that produces four projections at once, followed by SiLU: UVQK = SiLU(LN(x) @ W). The HSTU shape is tall and skinny: M = tokens (tens of thousands), N = 4·d, K = d.

This lab has two steps:

  1. A pointer-based tiled GEMM, the classic Triton matmul, with the SiLU fused into the epilogue.
  2. The Blackwell version: TMA descriptors move tiles between HBM and shared memory, a persistent grid runs one program per SM, and warp specialization splits producer and consumer warps.
Write

labs/04_matmul_silu/kernel.py.

Step 1 (TODOs 1–5). Each program computes one BM×BN tile of C:

a_ptrs = a_ptr + offs_m[:, None] * sam + offs_k[None, :] * sak
b_ptrs = b_ptr + offs_k[:, None] * sbk + offs_n[None, :] * sbn
acc = tl.zeros((BM, BN), dtype=tl.float32)
for k in range(0, tl.cdiv(K, BK)):
    a = tl.load(a_ptrs, mask=..., other=0.0)
    b = tl.load(b_ptrs, mask=..., other=0.0)
    acc = tl.dot(a, b, acc)          # tensor cores, fp32 accumulate
    a_ptrs += BK * sak; b_ptrs += BK * sbk
if ACT == "silu":
    acc = acc * tl.sigmoid(acc)      # epilogue fusion: free, the tile is in registers

Grouped ordering (TODO 3). Map pid so that GROUP consecutive programs walk down a column of M-tiles before moving to the next N-tile. They reuse the same B tiles while those are still in L2.

Step 2 (TODOs 6–9). B is passed transposed (N×K) so both operands are K-contiguous:

a_d = tl.make_tensor_descriptor(a_ptr, shape=[M, K], strides=[K, 1], block_shape=[BM, BK])
b_d = tl.make_tensor_descriptor(bt_ptr, shape=[N, K], strides=[K, 1], block_shape=[BN, BK])
for tile in tl.range(tl.program_id(0), num_m * num_n, NUM_SMS, flatten=True, warp_specialize=True):
    ...
    for k in range(k_tiles):
        acc = tl.dot(a_d.load([pid_m * BM, k * BK]), b_d.load([pid_n * BN, k * BK]).T, acc)
    acc = acc / (1.0 + tl.exp2(-1.4426950408889634 * acc))     # SiLU via exp2
    c_d.store([pid_m * BM, pid_n * BN], acc.to(c_ptr.dtype.element_ty))

Descriptors need scratch memory: call triton.set_allocator(...) once. TMA requires 16-byte-aligned strides, so K and N must be multiples of 8 in bf16.

Autotune key. Key on M_BUCKET = triton.next_power_of_2(M), not M. In training M is the token count of a jagged batch, which changes every step, and keying on raw M re-runs the autotuner every step. That bug made the first version of Lab 09 hang.

Run
python labs/04_matmul_silu/run.py
Measure

Run the lab and record what your GPU prints. Reference values were measured on one GB200.

MeasurementUnitReference
cuBLAS GEMM, 65536×1024×256TFLOP/s925.0
cuBLAS GEMM, then F.siluµs95.0
step 1 pointer GEMMTFLOP/s453.0
step 2 TMA/persistent/WS GEMMTFLOP/s763.0
step 2 GEMM+SiLU fusedµs59.0
cuBLAS at 8192³TFLOP/s1778.0
step 2 at 8192³TFLOP/s1567.0
Explain

The fused epilogue is the win. For the HSTU shape, cuBLAS does the GEMM in 37 µs, but the separate SiLU reads and writes the 65536×1024 bf16 output (128 MiB each way) and the pair takes 95 µs. Our step-2 kernel does both in about 59 µs: 1.6× faster than cuBLAS + SiLU, even though our plain GEMM (763 TFLOP/s) is slower than cuBLAS's (925). On a skinny GEMM the epilogue is a large fraction of total bytes, and fusing it beats a better GEMM.

Why step 1 is slow (453 TFLOP/s). With pointer loads, the same warps compute addresses, issue loads, wait, and run MMAs. Software pipelining (num_stages) helps, but every warp still spends registers and issue slots on address math and waiting.

What step 2 changes.

  • TMA (Tensor Memory Accelerator): one thread hands a descriptor and a coordinate to a hardware copy engine, which moves the whole tile into shared memory asynchronously. No per-thread address math, bounds checks done in hardware.
  • Persistent grid: launch exactly 152 programs, one per SM. Each loops over tiles, so the pipeline stays warm across tiles and there is no tail of half-empty waves.
  • Warp specialization (warp_specialize=True): the compiler splits the program into producer warps that only issue TMA loads and consumer warps that only issue MMAs, connected by shared-memory barriers. Loads for tile k+1 overlap MMAs for tile k. An ablation on this machine: the same TMA kernel without WS reached 636 TFLOP/s; with WS, 790.
  • EPI=2: store the output tile in two halves so fewer accumulator registers are live during the store.

Total: 1.67× over step 1.

Large square GEMMs. At 8192³, cuBLAS (1778 TFLOP/s) still leads our 1567. It uses Blackwell's 2-CTA tcgen05 MMAs and hand-tuned tile schedulers. Matching it is a research project; beating it on fused workloads is the practical goal, and you just did.

The SiLU formula. x · σ(x) = x / (1 + e-x), and e-x = 2-x log2 e. exp2 maps to a single hardware instruction (MUFU.EX2), while tl.sigmoid may lower to a slower exp plus a full-precision divide.

lessons.title: 05. Reductions in raw CUDA
lessons.html:
05. Reductions in raw CUDA

60 min · lab labs/05_cuda_reduction

Coalescing, shared-memory trees, warp shuffles, float4; compiled at runtime with NVRTC.

Triton hides two things you must understand to read any kernel profile: coalescing (how the 32 threads of a warp turn their addresses into memory transactions) and intra-block communication (shared memory and warp shuffles). This lab sums each row of an M×N fp32 matrix three ways in CUDA, then once more in Triton.

The CUDA source is a Python string compiled at runtime with NVRTC:

k = torch.cuda._compile_kernel(CUDA_SRC, "rowsum_shfl")
k(grid=(m, 1, 1), block=(256, 1, 1), args=[x, out, m, n])
Write

labs/05_cuda_reduction/kernel.py.

v1, one thread per row (given). Each thread loops over its row.

v2, one block per row with a shared-memory tree (TODOs 1–4):

float s = 0.f;
for (int j = threadIdx.x; j < n; j += blockDim.x) s += r[j];     // coalesced: lane i reads r[base + i]
buf[threadIdx.x] = s; __syncthreads();
for (int stride = blockDim.x / 2; stride > 0; stride >>= 1) {
    if (threadIdx.x < stride) buf[threadIdx.x] += buf[threadIdx.x + stride];
    __syncthreads();
}
if (threadIdx.x == 0) out[blockIdx.x] = buf[0];

v3, float4 loads and warp shuffles (TODOs 5–7):

__device__ float warp_sum(float v) {
    for (int off = 16; off > 0; off >>= 1) v += __shfl_xor_sync(0xffffffff, v, off);
    return v;
}

Each thread accumulates float4s, reduces within its warp by shuffles (no shared memory, no barriers), and lane 0 of each warp writes one partial. Warp 0 then reduces the partials.

Triton (TODO 8): loop over the row in BLOCK chunks into a (BLOCK,) fp32 accumulator, then tl.sum once at the end.

Run
python labs/05_cuda_reduction/run.py
Measure

Run the lab and record what your GPU prints. Reference values were measured on one GB200.

MeasurementUnitReference
v1 thread-per-row, 16384×8192GB/s522.0
v2 shared-memory treeGB/s2362.0
v3 float4 + shufflesGB/s5823.0
Triton rowsumGB/s5533.0
torch.sum(dim=1)GB/s4480.0
v1 at 2048×65536GB/s30.0
Explain

v1 (522 GB/s, and 30 GB/s on wide rows): uncoalesced. At step j, thread t reads x[t·n + j]. The 32 lanes of a warp touch 32 different rows, n·4 bytes apart, so each lane needs its own 32-byte sector: 32 transactions to deliver 128 useful bytes. Only 1/8 of every sector is used. On wide, short matrices (2048 rows) it gets worse: only 2048 threads exist, 64 warps for 152 SMs, so most SMs sit idle: almost no parallelism and no coalescing. 30 GB/s is 0.5% of the hardware.

v2 (2362 GB/s): coalesced but under-fed. Lane i reads r[j + i], so a warp's 32 loads hit 128 contiguous bytes, perfectly coalesced. But each thread keeps only one 4-byte load in flight per loop iteration (lesson 01's Little's law again), and the tree spends log₂(256) = 8 barrier-separated steps, in which most threads sit idle.

v3 (5823 GB/s): enough bytes in flight, cheap reduction. float4 quadruples bytes per load. __shfl_xor_sync exchanges registers between lanes of a warp directly: 5 steps, no shared memory, no __syncthreads. Shared memory carries only 8 partials (one per warp). This is how production reductions (CUB, PyTorch) are written.

Triton (5533 GB/s) gets close with four lines. The (BLOCK,) accumulator means each thread holds several independent partial sums, which gives instruction-level parallelism and wide loads, and tl.sum lowers to the same shuffle tree. Torch's generic reduction (4480) handles every dtype, layout and dimension, and pays for that generality.

Takeaway. When a profile shows low bandwidth, check in this order: are warps coalesced? Are there enough bytes in flight per thread? Is the reduction serialised behind barriers?

lessons.title: 06. HSTU attention forward (jagged, fused)
lessons.html:
06. HSTU attention forward (jagged, fused)

120 min · lab labs/06_hstu_attention_fwd

Pointwise SiLU attention with a time-and-position bias, over jagged sequences, without ever storing N×N.

What HSTU attention computes

HSTU (Hierarchical Sequential Transduction Units, Zhai et al., 2024) is the generative recommender architecture behind Meta's trillion-parameter recommendation models. Each user is a sequence of interactions (here: movies, with timestamps). Its attention differs from a transformer's in three ways:

  1. Pointwise, not softmax. A = SiLU(α QKᵀ + rab) / N. No row normalisation, so no running max or sum, and each score is independent.
  2. Relative attention bias from position and time. rabij = wpos[clamp(i-j, 0, P-1)] + wts[⌊ log2 max(|ti - tj|, 1) ⌋]. How long ago you watched something matters, on a log scale.
  3. Jagged batches. Users have different history lengths. Instead of padding to the longest, sequences are concatenated into one (T, H, D) tensor with offsets[b] .. offsets[b+1] marking user b.

Causal masking keeps j ≤ i.

The fusion

A PyTorch implementation pads to (B, H, N, D), materialises the (B, H, N, N) score matrix, gathers the bias into another N×N tensor, applies SiLU, masks, and multiplies by V. That is several N² tensors in HBM, plus compute wasted on padding.

The fused kernel gives each program BM query rows of one (user, head). It streams that user's key/value blocks through shared memory, builds scores and bias in registers, and accumulates A V directly. Nothing N×N ever touches HBM, and padding never exists.

Write

labs/06_hstu_attention_fwd/kernel.py.

The bias helper (TODOs 1–3):

rel = offs_m[:, None] - offs_n[None, :]
pos_b = tl.minimum(tl.maximum(rel, 0), P - 1)
dt = tl.maximum(tl.abs(ts_m[:, None] - ts_n[None, :]).to(tl.float32), 1.0)
t_b = ((dt.to(tl.int32, bitcast=True) >> 23) & 0xFF) - 127      # floor(log2(dt)) from the exponent bits
t_b = tl.minimum(tl.maximum(t_b, 0), NT - 1)
bias = tl.load(pos_w_ptr + pos_b) + tl.load(ts_w_ptr + t_b)

The kernel (TODOs 4–8). Grid (cdiv(max_len, BM), B * H). Read start = offsets[b] and L = offsets[b+1] - start; programs with pid_m * BM >= L return immediately (that is how jaggedness costs nothing). Then:

hi = tl.minimum((pid_m + 1) * BM, L)          # causal: no key beyond this block's last query
for n0 in range(0, hi, BN):
    k, v, ts_n = ...                          # masked loads of BN keys
    s = tl.dot(q, tl.trans(k)) * alpha + bias
    a = s * tl.sigmoid(s) * inv_n
    a = tl.where((rel >= 0) & m_mask[:, None] & n_mask[None, :], a, 0.0)
    acc += tl.dot(a.to(v.dtype), v)

Use int64 for start * stride_t: with tens of millions of tokens × H × D, 32-bit offsets overflow.

Run
python labs/06_hstu_attention_fwd/run.py

The baseline is a fair dense PyTorch version: inputs already padded once (padded_inputs) so it is not charged for a Python loop, and bf16 throughout.

Measure

Run the lab and record what your GPU prints. Reference values were measured on one GB200.

MeasurementUnitReference
speedup at B=128, N≤200×10.4
dense peak memory, B=128 N≤200MB186.0
fused peak memory, B=128 N≤200MB3.0
speedup at B=64, N≤512×31.9
fused time, B=64 N≤512µs121.0
speedup at N≤2048×12.9
Explain

Where the 10–32× comes from. Three sources, roughly multiplicative:

  • Memory traffic. Dense writes and rereads B·H·N² scores, plus bias tensors and masks: 994 MB at B=64, N=512. The fused kernel only reads Q, K, V once per query block and writes the output: 8.7 MB peak.
  • Padding. Realistic histories are 45–52% padding in these batches. Dense computes all of it; fused programs past a user's length exit on their first instruction.
  • Causality. Dense computes the full N×N and masks half away. The fused loop stops at hi, skipping blocks above the diagonal, which is about half the FLOPs.

The speedup peaks near N=512 and settles at 12–13× for long sequences. At large N the dense version becomes efficient big-GEMM work, while the fused kernel becomes compute-bound on its own tl.dots.

The exponent trick is exact. A positive fp32 number is stored as 2e-127 × 1.m, so (bits >> 23) - 127 is exactly ⌊ log2 x ⌋. The reference uses torch.frexp, whose exponent is one larger; the course reference subtracts 1, and the two agree on every input. No log2, no rounding risk at exact powers of two.

Why pointwise attention fuses so well. Softmax attention (flash attention) must keep a running max and rescale the accumulator whenever the max grows. HSTU's SiLU score is independent per element, so each block's contribution simply adds to acc. That makes it simpler than flash attention, and it is why the backward in Lab 07 needs no stored row statistics at all.

Why 1/N with N = max_len. HSTU normalises by sequence length rather than by a softmax. Using the batch's max_len (as the reference does) keeps the scale identical between the dense and fused paths.

lessons.title: 07. HSTU attention backward
lessons.html:
07. HSTU attention backward

120 min · lab labs/07_hstu_attention_bwd

Recompute instead of store, two-kernel FA2 split, and why naive atomics cost 70×.

Training needs gradients for Q, K, V and for the two bias tables. The forward saved only its inputs (no N×N matrices), so the backward recomputes scores tile by tile, exactly like flash attention.

With s = α q· k + rab, σ = sigmoid(s), A = SiLU(s)/N (masked):

GradientFormula
dVAᵀ dO
dAdO Vᵀ
dSdA · σ (1 + s(1-σ)) / N, since SiLU'(s) = σ(1 + s(1-σ))
dQα dS K
dKα dSᵀ Q
dpos[b], dts[b]sum of dS over entries that fall in bucket b

Two kernels, no atomics on Q/K/V

dK and dV are sums over query rows; dQ is a sum over key rows. The FlashAttention-2 split:

  • Kernel 1 fixes a block of BN keys and loops over query blocks i ≥ j, accumulating dK and dV in registers. It also produces the bias-table gradients.
  • Kernel 2 fixes a block of BM queries and loops over key blocks j ≤ i, accumulating dQ.

Each output block has exactly one owner, so dQ, dK and dV are plain stores.

Write

labs/07_hstu_attention_bwd/kernel.py.

The shared tile (TODOs 1–3) in _ds_tile: recompute s, the bias, sig, the validity mask and a, then

da = tl.dot(do, tl.trans(v))
ds = tl.where(valid, da * sig * (1.0 + s * (1.0 - sig)) * inv_n, 0.0)

Kernel 1 (TODOs 4–5): dv += tl.dot(tl.trans(a.to(do.dtype)), do), dk += tl.dot(tl.trans(ds.to(q.dtype)), q), and scale dk by alpha once at the end.

For the bias tables, first write the obvious version: tl.atomic_add(dpos_ptr + pos_b, ds, mask=valid) into one shared table of P floats. Run it and record the time. Then give every program its own private row:

row = (pid_bh * tl.num_programs(0) + pid_n).to(tl.int64)
tl.atomic_add(dpos_ptr + row * P + pos_b, ds, mask=valid, sem="relaxed")

and sum the rows on the host side with dpos.sum(0). Size the buffer for the smallest BN in the autotune list, and add reset_to_zero=["dpos_ptr", "dts_ptr"] to the autotuner. Otherwise each benchmarking trial adds into the same buffer.

Kernel 2 (TODO 6): dq += tl.dot(ds.to(k.dtype), k).

Autograd (TODO 7): return one gradient per forward input, None for ts, offsets, max_len and alpha.

Run
python labs/07_hstu_attention_bwd/run.py
Measure

Run the lab and record what your GPU prints. Reference values were measured on one GB200.

MeasurementUnitReference
backward with one shared bias table (your first version)µs33285.0
backward with private rowsµs474.0
forward+backward speedup, B=128 N≤200×20.4
forward+backward speedup, B=64 N≤512×31.7
fused fwd+bwd peak memory, B=64 N≤512MB48.0
forward+backward speedup, N≤2048×6.5
Explain

The atomics cliff: 33 ms vs 0.47 ms. The position table has 256 entries and the time table 32. With one shared copy, every one of thousands of programs fires BM·BN atomic adds per tile into the same 288 addresses. Atomics on the same address serialise at the L2 slice that owns that cache line, so the whole GPU queues behind a few cache lines. Private rows remove all cross-program contention. Within a program, the compiler can combine lanes that hit the same address. The final sum(0) over a few thousand rows of 256 floats is a trivial reduction.

The general rule: atomics are cheap when addresses are spread out and catastrophic when they are hot. Make reductions hierarchical: private, then local, then global.

Recompute vs store. Storing A for backward would cost B·H·N² bf16 values, about 1 GB at B=64, N=512. Recomputing it costs one extra QKᵀ per tile, which the tensor cores do far faster than HBM could reload it. Fused peak memory for forward+backward is 48 MB vs 996 MB dense.

Why the speedup is larger than the forward alone (20–32×). The dense backward through PyTorch autograd also materialises dS, dA and the gathered bias gradient as N² tensors. The bias backward through advanced indexing originally took 1.26 s until the course reference switched to bincount (TableGather in gk/hstu_ref.py). The fused version adds two kernels and no new N² traffic.

Why it shrinks at N=2048 (6.5×). Each fused backward program now loops over long key or query ranges and is compute-bound, recomputing QKᵀ twice (once per kernel). The dense path, meanwhile, is doing large efficient GEMMs. Production kernels fuse dQ into kernel 1 with atomics on dQ, or use warp specialization, to claw this back.

**reset_to_zero matters.** The autotuner runs each config several times on the same buffers. Without zeroing, the accumulated bias gradients grow with every trial and your correctness check fails, but only the first time you run.

lessons.title: 08. Stitch the kernels into an HSTU model
lessons.html:
08. Stitch the kernels into an HSTU model

90 min · lab labs/08_hstu_model

One HSTU layer from Labs 03, 04, 06 and 07; autograd glue; check against plain PyTorch.

Everything so far was one kernel at a time. Now they become a model. One HSTU layer on the jagged token matrix x of shape (T, d):

h          = LayerNorm(x)
u, v, q, k = split(SiLU(h @ W_uvqk))          Lab 04: one fused GEMM + SiLU for all four projections
a          = HSTUAttention(q, k, v, ts, rab)  Labs 06 + 07: jagged fused attention, fwd + bwd
y          = LayerNorm(a) * u                 Lab 03: fused norm + gate
x          = x + Dropout(y @ W_o)

The full model embeds item ids (plus an optional learned position embedding), stacks layers, L2-normalises the output, and scores the next item by cosine similarity against the item embedding table. Item and output embeddings are tied.

gk/kernels.py loads your kernel.py from each lab when GK_KERNELS=mine is set, and the reference solution.py otherwise. So you can run the model on your own kernels end to end.

Write

labs/08_hstu_model/kernel.py.

TODO 1: MatmulSiLU backward. The forward uses the Lab 04 kernel and saves only a and w. In backward, recompute the pre-activation with cuBLAS:

z = (a @ w_t.t()).float()
sig = torch.sigmoid(z)
dz = (dy.float() * sig * (1 + z * (1 - sig))).to(a.dtype)
return dz @ w_t, dz.t() @ a

TODOs 2–4: the block forward.

uvqk = MatmulSiLU.apply(h.to(torch.bfloat16), self.w_uvqk.to(torch.bfloat16))
u, v, q, k = uvqk.split(H * dh, dim=1)
a = kernels.hstu_attention()(q, k, v, ts, offsets, max_len, self.pos_w, self.ts_w, alpha)
y = kernels.ln_mul()(a.reshape(T, H * dh), u.contiguous(), self.norm_w, self.norm_b)

TODO 5: the sampled softmax loss. Score each position's state against its true next item and num_neg shared random negatives, divide by a temperature (0.05), and take cross-entropy with the positive at index 0. Mask a negative that happens to equal the target. num_neg=0 means full softmax over the catalogue.

Run
python labs/08_hstu_model/run.py
GK_KERNELS=mine python labs/08_hstu_model/run.py     # the model on *your* kernels from labs 03/04/07
Measure

Run the lab and record what your GPU prints. Reference values were measured on one GB200.

MeasurementUnitReference
forward max abs diff vs PyTorch0.0045
worst relative gradient error0.0111
step time torch, B=128 N=200ms27.1
step time triton, B=128 N=200ms6.5
peak memory torch, B=64 N=512MB1042.0
peak memory triton, B=64 N=512MB144.0
step time triton, B=32 N=1024ms12.1
Explain

Correctness at bf16 precision. Forward outputs agree to about 4.5e-3 and every parameter gradient to about 1% relative error. That is what bf16 matmuls in two different orders produce. The check compares every parameter's gradient, including the bias tables, which is where a wrong atomic or a missing alpha shows up first.

4× faster, 7× less memory. The step includes forward, backward, the loss and AdamW. Memory is the clearer story: the dense path's peak grows with N² (365 MB at N=200 → 1042 MB at 512 → 2006 MB at 1024) while the fused path stays near 120–150 MB, because nothing N×N exists. Step-time ratios move around between runs (this GPU is shared), but the triton step is consistently 4–5× faster at N=200–512.

Why the speedup shrinks at N=1024 (about 1.3×). At B=32 the dense path is a few large batched GEMMs, efficient on tensor cores. The fused attention backward loops over 1024 keys per program and recomputes scores twice, which is the compute-bound regime from Lab 07.

What the step is made of now. At the ML-1M shape the attention kernels are no longer the bottleneck; Lab 11's profile shows the fp32 loss GEMMs, softmax, AdamW and launch overhead on top. Fusion moves the bottleneck; it never removes it.

Recompute in MatmulSiLU. Saving z (T × 4·H·dh) per layer would cost more memory than all the attention state. Recomputing it is one skinny cuBLAS GEMM, about 37 µs at the Lab 04 shape.

Why the dropout and residual stay in PyTorch. They are cheap elementwise ops on (T, d) with d=64. Fusing them would save microseconds. Always fuse in the order of bytes saved, which is the order this course followed.

lessons.title: 09. Train HSTU on MovieLens-1M
lessons.html:
09. Train HSTU on MovieLens-1M

90 min · lab train

GPU-resident jagged batches, full-ranking HR@10 / NDCG@10, and an ablation you run yourself.

Now the model learns something real. MovieLens-1M has 1,000,209 ratings from 6,040 users on 3,706 movies, each with a timestamp. The task: given a user's history in time order, predict the next movie.

Protocol (the one used in the HSTU and SASRec papers):

  • The last interaction of each user is the test target; everything before it is history.
  • Train on next-item prediction at every position of the history (teacher forcing), with up to 200 most recent events.
  • Evaluate with full ranking: score all 3,706 movies, then compute HR@10 (is the true movie in the top 10?) and NDCG@10 (rewards higher positions: 1/log₂(rank+1)).

The data pipeline is on the GPU. train/train.py loads the whole dataset as tensors once. Each batch picks random users, slices their tails with vectorised index arithmetic, and builds offsets. No DataLoader and no host-to-device copies per step: at about 8 ms per step a CPU pipeline would be the bottleneck.

Write

Nothing new to write; this lab is about experiments. Read train/train.py first: GPUSequences.batch, evaluate, and the training loop. Then download the data:

python train/data.py --dataset ml-1m        # into data/ml-1m.npz
Run

Baseline, then the experiments. Each run prints the loss, step time and tokens/s, and HR@10 / NDCG@10 every 10 epochs.

python train/train.py --epochs 100                                          # baseline: 2 layers, 512 negatives
python train/train.py --epochs 200 --pos-emb --out checkpoints/exp_pos.pt   # + position embedding
python train/train.py --epochs 200 --pos-emb --negatives 0 --out checkpoints/exp_full.pt  # + full softmax
python train/train.py --epochs 200 --pos-emb --negatives 0 --layers 4      # final recipe -> checkpoints/hstu_ml-1m.pt

Add --impl torch to any run to train the identical model without the custom kernels.

Measure

Run the lab and record what your GPU prints. Reference values were measured on one GB200.

MeasurementUnitReference
baseline HR@10, 100 epochs0.2353
baseline NDCG@100.1183
full softmax + pos emb, HR@100.2651
4 layers, full softmax, pos emb, HR@100.282
4 layers, NDCG@100.1557
seconds per epoch, 2 layerss0.4
Explain

The ablation on the course GB200 (best HR@10 / NDCG@10 over the run):

ChangeHR@10NDCG@10
baseline: 2 layers, d=64, 512 negatives, 100 epochs0.23530.1183
200 epochs0.25020.1275
+ position embedding0.25080.1308
128 negatives instead of 5120.2253—
full softmax (all 3,706 items)0.26210.1445
full softmax + position embedding0.26510.1460
d=1280.26870.1570
4 layers + full softmax + pos emb0.28200.1557
4 layers, d=1280.27500.1562
paper: SASRec0.28530.1603
paper: HSTU0.30970.1720

What each change teaches.

  • Negatives matter most. The softmax denominator over 128 random negatives is a noisy, biased estimate, because random negatives are mostly easy. Going 128 → 512 → full raises HR by 4 points. With 3,706 items, full softmax is one (T × 3706) GEMM, cheap enough, so use it. At YouTube scale (millions of items) you cannot, and the sampling strategy becomes a research topic.
  • Depth beats width here. 4 layers gains 1.7 points; doubling d gains less, and 4 layers at d=128 overfits ML-1M's 6,040 users.
  • Timestamps already encode order. The absolute position embedding adds little on top of the relative time-and-position bias.

The remaining gap to the paper's HSTU (0.31) comes from tuning (learning-rate schedule, longer training, dropout schedule and seeds). The paper reports its best configurations. Treat our numbers as a reproducible, honest baseline, not a leaderboard entry.

Throughput. About 0.4 s per epoch with 2 layers (48 steps of 128 users, about 1.6 M tokens/s); 4 layers takes about 0.85 s. The GPU is mostly idle during these steps, because the batch is small and each step launches about 280 kernels. Lab 11 measures exactly how idle, and what to do about it.

The bug this lab found. The first training run hung for minutes per step. The Lab 04 GEMM's autotune key included M, and the jagged token count changes every batch, so every step re-ran the autotuner. Bucketing M to the next power of two fixed it. Real workloads find bugs that microbenchmarks never do.

lessons.title: 10. Serve with Triton Inference Server
lessons.html:
10. Serve with Triton Inference Server

90 min · lab serving

Python-backend model repository, ragged dynamic batching into one jagged batch, load testing.

Two different things are both called "Triton". Triton the language is what you wrote kernels in. Triton Inference Server is NVIDIA's model server: it takes HTTP/gRPC requests, queues them, forms batches and runs models through backends (TensorRT, ONNX, PyTorch, Python, and others). This lab serves the trained HSTU through the Python backend, so the same Triton kernels run inside the server.

The model repository

serving/model_repository/
  hstu/            config.pbtxt + 1/model.py    dynamic batching on
  hstu_nobatch/    config.pbtxt + 1/model.py    one request at a time

Each request is one user: a variable-length list of item ids and timestamps. The key configuration:

max_batch_size: 128
input [ { name: "item_ids" data_type: TYPE_INT64 dims: [ -1 ] allow_ragged_batch: true }, ... ]
dynamic_batching { max_queue_delay_microseconds: 2000  preferred_batch_size: [ 32, 64, 128 ] }

allow_ragged_batch lets requests of different lengths be grouped. execute() (in serving/hstu_backend.py) receives the group, concatenates the histories and builds offsets. That is a jagged batch, exactly what the attention kernel wants. Batching costs zero padding.

Write

Read serving/hstu_backend.py: initialize loads the checkpoint and warms the kernels up; execute builds the jagged batch and returns top-10 items per request.

One sharp edge you will meet. Tensors cross into and out of the backend through DLPack (pb_utils.Tensor.from_dlpack, to_dlpack), not as_numpy() and pb_utils.Tensor(name, ndarray). The server's stub is compiled against the numpy 1.x C ABI. Given numpy 2 arrays, it misreads their element size and every response fails with "output tensor shape does not match size of output". DLPack bypasses numpy entirely.

Set up the server once (no Docker: it unpacks the server binaries shipped in the nvidia-pytriton wheel and builds a matching Python 3.13 for the backend stub):

bash serving/setup_tritonserver.sh
Run
bash serving/start_server.sh &                 # wait for "Started GRPCInferenceService"
python serving/client.py                       # correctness on 50 users, then the load test

The load test runs N closed-loop clients (each sends the next request when the previous returns) for 1, 8, 32 and 128 clients, against both models. Run it twice and keep the second, warm run.

Measure

Run the lab and record what your GPU prints. Reference values were measured on one GB200.

MeasurementUnitReference
users whose served top-10 equals offline top-10 (of 50)50.0
no batching, 1 clientreq/s181.0
no batching, 128 clientsreq/s270.0
no batching, 128 clients, p99ms633.0
dynamic batching, 128 clientsreq/s3940.0
dynamic batching, 128 clients, p99ms66.0
mean batch size formed, 128 clients48.4
Explain

Throughput: 270 → 3,940 req/s (14.6×) at 128 clients. Without batching, each request is one forward pass of about 5 ms: 4 layers of about 10 tiny kernels each, plus top-k, for a single user of at most 200 tokens. The GPU does almost no work per launch, so the server saturates at 1 / 5 ms ≈ 200–270 req/s no matter how many clients wait. Queueing makes p99 explode to 633 ms.

With dynamic batching, the scheduler holds requests up to 2 ms and hands execute() up to 128 at once. A batch of 48 users costs barely more GPU time than a batch of 1, because the same launches simply do more work each. That is the same launch-bound regime as training (Lab 11). Throughput grows with the batch size the scheduler forms (mean 48.4 at 128 clients), and p99 falls to 66 ms.

At 1 client batching costs a little. 181 vs 141 req/s: the batcher waits for companions that never come. max_queue_delay_microseconds is the knob between latency at low load and throughput at high load.

Cold start is real. The first, cold run showed a p99 of 1.56 s at 1 client: each model instance is its own process, and kernels it had not seen yet (new autotune keys) compiled on the first requests. initialize() warms up a few shapes; production servers warm up every shape bucket and persist the Triton cache (Lab 11, part D).

Correctness first. The client compares the served top-10 with the offline model for 50 real users: 50/50 identical. Batching changes nothing about each user's result, because the jagged kernel never mixes users.

lessons.title: 11. System optimisation
lessons.html:
11. System optimisation

90 min · lab labs/11_system_opt

Profile the whole step, find the launch-bound regime, batch scaling, CUDA graphs for jagged shapes, compile caches.

Fast kernels are necessary, not sufficient. Once the big kernels are fused, the step is made of everything between them: the CPU issuing launches, small PyTorch ops, the optimizer, the loss, and start-up compilation. This lab measures all of it in four parts:

  • A. GPU-bound or CPU-bound? Profile 20 training steps; GPU busy time ÷ wall time; kernels per step; the kernels that dominate.
  • B. Batch scaling. Step time and tokens/s from 32 to 2048 users.
  • C. CUDA graphs for jagged inference. Record the whole top-k forward once and replay it with one launch.
  • D. Compile caches. Time to the first training step in a fresh process, cold vs warm TRITON_CACHE_DIR, with and without TRITON_CACHE_AUTOTUNING=1.
Write

Read labs/11_system_opt/cuda_graphs.py (GraphedTopK). CUDA graphs need static shapes and static addresses, but jagged batches change every call. The trick:

  • Capture one graph per bucket (B users, T tokens): (1, 256), (8, 2048), (64, 16384).
  • Copy a real batch into the bucket's static buffers; unused user slots get length 0 (offsets repeat).
  • One dummy user at index B owns the unused token tail, so the jagged kernels see a consistent layout. Its outputs are thrown away.
  • Run once before capture so Triton compiles and autotunes outside the graph (compilation cannot be captured).

Exercise after the run: wire GraphedTopK into serving/hstu_backend.py and rerun the Lab 10 load test.

Run
python labs/11_system_opt/run.py

Part D spawns fresh Python processes with empty and then warm cache directories, so it takes a minute.

Measure

Run the lab and record what your GPU prints. Reference values were measured on one GB200.

MeasurementUnitReference
GPU busy fraction, triton step, B=128%22.0
kernels launched per triton step278.0
triton step time, B=128ms10.5
tokens/s at 32 usersMtok/s0.4
tokens/s at 2048 usersMtok/s7.65
eager top-10, 1 userµs2617.0
CUDA graph top-10, 1 userµs174.0
first step, cold caches17.0
