So the actual objective is: $$\max_\theta ; \mathbb{E}\big[r_\phi(x,y)\big] - \beta , \mathbb{E}\big[\mathrm{KL}(\pi_\theta(\cdot|x) ,|, \pi_{ref}(\cdot|x))\big]$$ Implemented as a per-token penalty -beta * (log pi_theta(token) - log pi_ref(token)) added to the (otherwise zero) reward at every step, with the terminal RM score added only at the final token.
  3. GAE (Generalized Advantage Estimation). A learned value head $V_\psi$ estimates expected future (KL-adjusted) reward from each prefix. GAE combines multi-step returns with the value baseline to get a lower-variance advantage estimate $\hat{A}_t$, trading off bias (small $\lambda$) vs. variance (large $\lambda$).
  4. Clipped surrogate loss. Because a rollout batch is reused for several gradient steps (PPO_EPOCHS), the policy that generated the data (old) drifts from the policy being updated (new). PPO bounds how much any single update can exploit that drift: $$L^{CLIP}(\theta) = \mathbb{E}\Big[\min\big(\rho_t \hat{A}t,\ \mathrm{clip}(\rho_t, 1-\epsilon, 1+\epsilon)\hat{A}t\big)\Big], \quad \rho_t = \frac{\pi\theta(a_t|s_t)}{\pi{old}(a_t|s_t)}$$

That's the whole algorithm. Everything else (value loss, entropy bonus, reward/advantage normalization) is stabilization detail, present in scratch/train_ppo_scratch.py and commented inline.

Files

  • scratch/train_ppo_scratch.py -- every piece above, hand-written, on lvwerra/gpt2-imdb (GPT-2 already SFT'd on movie reviews -- see lab 01 for how that step works) with lvwerra/distilbert-imdb as the reward model. Classic, fast-feedback demo: within ~100-150 PPO steps the model visibly shifts towards positive reviews.
  • trl/train_ppo_trl.py -- the same algorithm via TRL's PPOTrainer (now under trl.experimental.ppo), on Qwen2.5-0.5B, using the reward model trained in lab 02 on the TL;DR summarization task.

Run it

# from-scratch (single GPU, a few minutes)
python labs/03_ppo_rlhf/scratch/train_ppo_scratch.py

# TRL (run labs 01 and 02's TRL scripts first to get the SFT + reward-model checkpoints)
python labs/03_ppo_rlhf/trl/train_ppo_trl.py

Watch mean_reward climb and read the printed sample completion each log step -- you should see it drift from generic movie-review text towards enthusiastic, unambiguously positive language.

Things to try

  • Set KL_BETA = 0.0 in the scratch script and re-run: reward will climb faster at first, then the sample text will degrade into repetitive/nonsensical positive-sounding tokens -- textbook reward hacking (formalized in lab 08).
  • Sweep CLIP_EPS (try 0.05 vs 0.4) and watch clip_frac/approx_kl in the logged metrics -- tighter clipping should keep approx_kl smaller step-to-step, at the cost of slower reward improvement.
  • Compare GAE_LAMBDA = 1.0 (pure Monte Carlo advantage, high variance) against GAE_LAMBDA = 0.0 (pure TD/bootstrap, high bias) and see which trains more stably at this response length.
  • After running both scratch and trl versions, sample outputs from all three models -- lab 01's SFT model, this lab's PPO model, and lab 04's DPO model -- on the same prompts to build intuition for how similarly (or not) PPO and DPO shift behavior.

lessons.title: Lab 04 -- The DPO Family
lessons.html:
Lab 04 -- The DPO Family

Goal: derive Direct Preference Optimization from the same Bradley-Terry model lab 02 used for reward modeling, see that it eliminates the reward model and the RL rollout loop entirely, then compare it (and its cousin KTO) against lab 03's PPO on a shared reward-vs-KL frontier.

Theory

Lab 02's reward-model loss:

$$\mathcal{L}{RM}(\phi) = -\log\sigma\big(r\phi(x, y_w) - r_\phi(x, y_l)\big)$$

DPO's derivation starts from a fact about the KL-constrained RL objective PPO (lab 03) optimizes -- $\max_\theta \mathbb{E}[r(x,y)] - \beta , \mathrm{KL}(\pi_\theta | \pi_{ref})$ -- which has a closed-form optimal policy:

$$\pi^*(y|x) = \frac{1}{Z(x)} \pi_{ref}(y|x) \exp!\big(r(x,y)/\beta\big)$$

Solving this for $r$ gives $r(x,y) = \beta \log\frac{\pi^*(y|x)}{\pi_{ref}(y|x)} + \beta\log Z(x)$ -- i.e. any reward function is equivalent (up to a prompt-dependent constant that cancels in a pairwise comparison) to the log-ratio of some policy over the reference. Substituting this "implicit reward" into the Bradley-Terry loss above and dropping the now-cancelled $Z(x)$ terms gives the DPO loss, directly over policy parameters:

$$\mathcal{L}{DPO}(\theta) = -\log\sigma\Big(\beta\big[\log\tfrac{\pi\theta(y_w|x)}{\pi_{ref}(y_w|x)} - \log\tfrac{\pi_\theta(y_l|x)}{\pi_{ref}(y_l|x)}\big]\Big)$$

No reward model, no sampling from $\pi_\theta$ during training, no value function -- just two forward passes (policy and frozen reference) over already-collected (prompt, chosen, rejected) triples, and ordinary supervised-style backprop. The trade-off: DPO is fully off-policy (it only ever "sees" the fixed dataset's completions, never the current policy's own samples), whereas PPO/GRPO are (at least partially) on-policy, which matters when the offline preference data doesn't cover the region the policy needs to move into.

KTO relaxes DPO's need for paired preferences: instead of "y_w beats y_l for this x", it only needs independent binary desirable/undesirable labels per (prompt, completion), using a prospect-theory-inspired asymmetric loss around a reference point. Practically: pass the same paired data through unchanged and KTOTrainer will split it into unpaired examples for you (see trl/train_kto_trl.py).

Files

  • scratch/train_dpo_scratch.py -- the DPO loss above, hand-coded, on lvwerra/gpt2-imdb with the same IMDB-derived preference pairs style as lab 02's scratch reward model (so it's directly comparable to lab 03's PPO run, which starts from the same base model).
  • trl/train_dpo_trl.py / trl/train_kto_trl.py -- DPOTrainer / KTOTrainer on Qwen2.5-0.5B (from the lab-01 SFT checkpoint), on the exact same trl-lib/tldr-preference data lab 02 used for reward modeling.
  • trl/compare_ppo_dpo_kto.py -- generates from whichever of {SFT, PPO, DPO, KTO} checkpoints exist, scores them with lab 02's reward model, estimates each one's KL drift from the SFT reference, and plots the reward-vs-KL frontier.

Run it

# from-scratch (single GPU, a few minutes)
python labs/04_dpo_family/scratch/train_dpo_scratch.py

# TRL (run lab 01's TRL script first for the SFT starting checkpoint)
python labs/04_dpo_family/trl/train_dpo_trl.py
python labs/04_dpo_family/trl/train_kto_trl.py

# after running lab 03's TRL PPO script too, compare all three:
python labs/04_dpo_family/trl/compare_ppo_dpo_kto.py

Things to try

  • In the scratch script, set BETA = 0.01 vs BETA = 1.0 and compare the final margin (chosen_reward - rejected_reward) and held-out accuracy -- beta controls how sharply DPO is willing to move the policy per unit of preference signal, exactly like the KL coefficient in PPO.
  • Derive on paper (or in a scratch cell) what happens to the DPO loss as $\pi_\theta \to \pi_{ref}$ everywhere (hint: the gradient vanishes) -- this is why DPO still needs some initial preference signal exploitable near the reference policy.
  • Run compare_ppo_dpo_kto.py after only training DPO (skip PPO/KTO) and re-run again once you've trained the others -- the script gracefully skips missing checkpoints, so you can build up the comparison incrementally.
  • Try training DPO directly from the raw Qwen/Qwen2.5-0.5B base model (skip lab 01's SFT step) and compare sample quality/coherence against starting from the SFT checkpoint -- this is a hands-on version of the "why SFT first" argument from lab 01.

lessons.title: Lab 05 -- GRPO and RLVR Reasoning
lessons.html:
Lab 05 -- GRPO and RLVR Reasoning

Goal: understand the two big ideas behind how models like DeepSeek-R1 are trained: (1) GRPO -- replacing PPO's learned critic with a cheap, group-relative baseline, and (2) RLVR (RL from Verifiable Rewards) -- replacing the learned reward model with a rule that can check correctness directly (does the final answer match?).

Theory

Why drop the critic? PPO's value function $V_\psi(s)$ exists to provide a low-variance baseline for the advantage estimate. Training it well is itself hard (it's a whole extra network, prone to being wrong especially early in training) and it roughly doubles memory/compute (a second copy of the model, effectively). GRPO's insight: if you sample multiple completions for the same prompt, you get a for-free, unbiased baseline -- the group's own mean reward:

$$A_i = \frac{r_i - \mathrm{mean}(r_1, \dots, r_G)}{\mathrm{std}(r_1, \dots, r_G) + \epsilon}, \qquad i = 1, \dots, G$$

No value network, no GAE -- just: sample a group, score each member, normalize within the group. This only requires the reward to be reasonably cheap to compute many times per prompt, which brings us to:

Why verifiable rewards? A learned reward model (lab 02) is itself a noisy, exploitable proxy (lab 08). For tasks with a checkable ground truth -- math (does the number match?), code (do the tests pass?) -- you can skip the reward model entirely and score with a rule. This is dramatically cheaper (no extra forward pass through a big network per sample) and, crucially, can't be reward-hacked in the same way a learned model can, since it's checking the actual thing you care about.

The KL term moves. PPO subtracts a per-token KL penalty from the reward before computing advantages (lab 03). GRPO instead adds a KL term directly to the loss, using Schulman's k3 estimator (unbiased, always $\geq 0$, low variance):

$$\widehat{\mathrm{KL}}{k3}(\pi\theta | \pi_{ref}) = \exp(\log\pi_{ref} - \log\pi_\theta) - (\log\pi_{ref} - \log\pi_\theta) - 1$$

Otherwise the update is the same clipped-surrogate machinery as PPO.

Files

  • env/math_reward.py -- GSM8K loading + a rule-based reward: extract the model's final numeric answer, compare to ground truth (reused from common/rewards.py).
  • scratch/train_grpo_scratch.py -- GRPO hand-written on GPT-2, task: single-digit addition ("3 + 5 = " -> 8). Deliberately tiny/fast so you can watch group statistics (mean reward, fraction of "zero-signal" groups) evolve over a few hundred steps on one GPU.
  • trl/train_grpo_trl.py -- GRPOTrainer + vLLM (colocate mode) on Qwen/Qwen2.5-Math-1.5B with real GSM8K math word problems -- the DeepSeek-R1-Zero recipe at a scale you can actually run.

Run it

# from-scratch (single GPU, a few minutes)
python labs/05_grpo_rlvr_reasoning/scratch/train_grpo_scratch.py

# TRL + vLLM on Qwen2.5-Math-1.5B (single GPU)
python labs/05_grpo_rlvr_reasoning/trl/train_grpo_trl.py

# multi-GPU (more groups in flight per step)
accelerate launch --config_file configs/accelerate/deepspeed_zero3_8gpu.yaml \
    labs/05_grpo_rlvr_reasoning/trl/train_grpo_trl.py

Things to try

  • Watch zero_signal_group_frac in the scratch run's metrics: early on, most groups are "all wrong" (0 variance, 0 gradient); track how it shrinks as accuracy improves, then note it rises again as accuracy approaches ~100% (now most groups are "all right"). GRPO's signal is richest in the middle of the accuracy curve -- an important, underappreciated property of group-relative RLVR.
  • Remove the / (group_std + eps) normalization (Dr. GRPO's fix for a length/scale bias this introduces) and compare training stability -- see paper_index in TRL's docs for the precise argument.
  • Increase GROUP_SIZE (e.g. 4 -> 16) in the scratch script and see whether fewer total steps are needed to reach the same accuracy (more samples per prompt = better baseline estimate, at the cost of more compute per step).
  • In the TRL script, try removing the #### <number> format bonus from env/math_reward.py's gsm8k_reward and see whether/how much slower the model converges to a parseable answer format.
  • Compare wall-clock time for the TRL script with use_vllm=False vs. True -- this is the single biggest lever for RLVR training speed, since rollout generation (not the gradient step) dominates wall-clock time once group sizes get large.

lessons.title: Lab 06 -- RLOO and GSPO Variants
lessons.html:
Lab 06 -- RLOO and GSPO Variants

Goal: see two more points in the PPO/GRPO design space: RLOO (how much of PPO's machinery can you strip away and still learn?) and GSPO (matching the granularity of importance sampling to the granularity of the advantage).

Theory

RLOO asks: do we need PPO's clipped surrogate and multi-epoch reuse at all? Its answer is closer to the original REINFORCE algorithm:

$$\nabla_\theta J(\theta) = \mathbb{E}\big[(R - b), \nabla_\theta \log \pi_\theta(y|x)\big]$$

with the baseline $b$ chosen as the leave-one-out mean of a sampled group:

$$b_i = \frac{1}{G-1}\sum_{j \neq i} r_j, \qquad A_i = r_i - b_i$$

Excluding $r_i$ from its own baseline is what makes this exactly unbiased (the baseline is independent of the term it's subtracted from). GRPO's group-mean baseline $r_i - \mathrm{mean}(r_1..r_G)$ includes $r_i$ in its own baseline, which introduces a small $O(1/G)$ bias -- negligible for reasonable group sizes, but a genuine, precise distinction. The much bigger practical difference in this lab's scratch script: variance. Compare the logged var_naive (no baseline) against var_loo / var_group_mean and you'll see any reasonable baseline is a large win over none at all.

GSPO asks a different question: PPO/GRPO's clipped objective needs an importance ratio $\rho = \pi_\theta(\cdot)/\pi_{old}(\cdot)$ to correct for the policy having moved since the rollout was sampled. GRPO computes this per token, but the advantage it's multiplied by is a single per-sequence number (from the group). GSPO's fix: compute the ratio at the sequence level too (average the log-ratio over the completion, then exponentiate), so both halves of the update operate at the same granularity:

$$\rho^{\text{GSPO}} = \exp!\Big(\tfrac{1}{|y|}\sum_{t} \log\tfrac{\pi_\theta(y_t)}{\pi_{old}(y_t)}\Big) \quad \text{vs.} \quad \rho^{\text{GRPO}}t = \tfrac{\pi\theta(y_t)}{\pi_{old}(y_t)} ; \text{(per token)}$$

This matters most when training is even mildly off-policy (rollouts reused for more than one gradient step) and for very long completions or MoE models, where per-token ratios get noisy.

Files

  • scratch/train_rloo_scratch.py -- vanilla REINFORCE + leave-one-out baseline, on the same single-digit-addition RLVR task as lab 05, logging naive/group-mean/LOO advantage variance side-by-side every step.
  • trl/train_rloo_trl.py -- RLOOTrainer on the same GSM8K/Qwen2.5-Math-1.5B setup as lab 05's GRPO run, for a direct training-curve comparison.
  • trl/train_gspo_trl.py -- GRPOTrainer with importance_sampling_level="sequence", loss_type="grpo" (the TRL-documented GSPO recipe), same task/model as lab 05.

Run it

# from-scratch (single GPU, a few minutes)
python labs/06_rloo_and_gspo/scratch/train_rloo_scratch.py

# TRL, on Qwen2.5-Math-1.5B / GSM8K
python labs/06_rloo_and_gspo/trl/train_rloo_trl.py
python labs/06_rloo_and_gspo/trl/train_gspo_trl.py

Things to try

  • Overlay runs/lab05_grpo_scratch/metrics.csv and runs/lab06_rloo_scratch/metrics.csv (mean_reward vs step) -- on this simple task, do GRPO and RLOO converge at a meaningfully different rate?
  • In the scratch script, print the actual numeric difference between adv_group_mean and adv_loo for a few groups -- confirm it shrinks as GROUP_SIZE grows (the $O(1/G)$ bias argument, made concrete).
  • In train_gspo_trl.py, set steps_per_generation = gradient_accumulation_steps (i.e. fully on-policy) and note TRL's own docs point out sequence- vs token-level importance sampling become equivalent in that regime -- the difference only shows up once training goes even mildly off-policy.
  • Try loss_type="bnpo" instead of "grpo" in the GSPO script and watch for TRL's logged warning about token-summed loss types silently length-weighting sequences when combined with sequence-level importance sampling.

lessons.title: Lab 07 -- Capstone: Scale-Up
lessons.html:
Lab 07 -- Capstone: Scale-Up

Goal: take the GRPO/RLVR recipe from lab 05 and run it "for real" -- a 7-8B model, sharded across all 8 B200s, with vLLM colocated for rollout generation -- and measure exactly what scaling the node buys you.

This lab is intentionally light on new algorithmic content: the point is that scaling RL post-training from a 1.5B toy run to a real model is mostly an infrastructure problem (sharding, mixed precision, colocated generation, checkpointing) layered on top of the exact same algorithm you already understand from lab 05.

Files

  • train_grpo_capstone.py -- lab 05's GRPO + GSM8K recipe, parameterized for a larger model (Qwen/Qwen2.5-7B-Instruct by default), meant to be launched with accelerate across multiple GPUs.
  • throughput_worker.py / benchmark_scaling.py -- a controlled 1/2/4/8-GPU training throughput benchmark (data-parallel, not FSDP, so the per-GPU compute/memory profile stays constant across GPU counts and the comparison is apples-to-apples).

Run it

# the capstone training run itself, sharded via FSDP across all 8 GPUs
accelerate launch --config_file configs/accelerate/fsdp_8gpu.yaml \
    labs/07_capstone_scale_up/train_grpo_capstone.py

# if FSDP + colocated vLLM misbehaves on your installed versions, DeepSpeed ZeRO-3
# is the alternative (same as labs 05/06 already use):
accelerate launch --config_file configs/accelerate/deepspeed_zero3_8gpu.yaml \
    labs/07_capstone_scale_up/train_grpo_capstone.py

# throughput scaling benchmark (needs all 8 GPUs free, ~a few minutes)
python labs/07_capstone_scale_up/benchmark_scaling.py

train_grpo_capstone.py accepts --model, --per-device-batch-size, --num-generations, --gradient-accumulation-steps, and --vllm-gpu-memory-utilization if you want to point it at a different model size or tune memory usage -- see lab 00's throughput benchmark and the OOM-debugging notes in lab 05's README for guidance on what to adjust first.

Things to try

  • Run benchmark_scaling.py --model Qwen/Qwen2.5-0.5B-Instruct (matches lab 00's model) and compare scaling efficiency against the default 7B model -- smaller models are more likely to be communication-bound (gradient all-reduce dominates), so you may see worse scaling efficiency at 8 GPUs for the small model than the large one.
  • Watch nvidia-smi dmon during the capstone run: with vLLM colocated, you should see GPU utilization alternate between "training" and "generation" phases rather than a flat 100% -- that's the colocate/sleep-mode handoff happening.
  • Try --vllm-gpu-memory-utilization 0.2 vs 0.6 and see the effect on both OOM risk and rollout throughput (more vLLM memory = larger KV cache = more concurrent sequences = faster generation, at the cost of less headroom for the training step).
  • Swap Qwen/Qwen2.5-7B-Instruct for meta-llama/Llama-3.1-8B-Instruct (you'll need to accept its license on the Hugging Face Hub first) and compare GSM8K learning curves between the two base models.

lessons.title: Lab 08 -- Safety and Reward Hacking
lessons.html:
Lab 08 -- Safety and Reward Hacking

Goal: see the failure modes every previous lab has been warning about, concretely: reward hacking (Goodhart's law), the reward-vs-KL trade-off every algorithm makes implicitly, the "alignment tax" on general capability, and a minimal red-teaming harness for measuring whether alignment actually changed model behavior.

Theory recap

Every lab so far mentioned a version of the same warning:

  • Lab 02: the reward model is only trained on pairs from roughly the SFT policy's distribution -- once the policy moves elsewhere, its judgments are extrapolation.
  • Lab 03: the KL penalty exists specifically to stop the policy from drifting into regions where the reward model is wrong-but-high.
  • Lab 05: verifiable rewards are harder to hack (they check the real thing), but not impossible (a model can learn to satisfy the letter of a format check without the substance).

This lab makes each of these failure modes something you actually watch happen.

Files

  • reward_hacking_demo.py -- trains against a deliberately naive proxy reward (completion length) with little/no KL constraint, while separately monitoring (never training against) a sentiment-classifier score and a text-repetition metric. Watch the proxy reward climb while the monitored "true quality" signals stagnate or the text visibly degrades into repetitive filler.
  • kl_reward_frontier.py -- trains several short runs at different KL coefficients (beta) against the real sentiment reward, and plots the resulting reward-vs-KL Pareto frontier.
  • alignment_tax.py -- scores every available checkpoint (base, SFT, PPO, DPO, KTO) on a held-out MMLU subset via log-likelihood multiple-choice scoring, to see whether task-specific alignment cost anything on unrelated general knowledge.
  • redteam_eval.py -- a fixed set of adversarial prompts + an LLM judge classifying each response as REFUSED/COMPLIED, tallying a refusal rate per checkpoint.

Run it

python labs/08_safety_and_reward_hacking/reward_hacking_demo.py                  # kl_beta=0.0: watch it hack
python labs/08_safety_and_reward_hacking/reward_hacking_demo.py --kl-beta 0.2    # constrained: compare

python labs/08_safety_and_reward_hacking/kl_reward_frontier.py

# after training whichever of labs 01/03/04 you want compared:
python labs/08_safety_and_reward_hacking/alignment_tax.py
python labs/08_safety_and_reward_hacking/redteam_eval.py

Things to try

  • In reward_hacking_demo.py, plot proxy_reward and true_reward_sentiment on the same axes (they're both in metrics.csv) -- the growing gap between them, not either curve alone, is the real signature of reward hacking.
  • Re-run reward_hacking_demo.py with a few different --kl-beta values (0.0, 0.05, 0.2, 1.0) and see how much KL constraint is "enough" to prevent the length-hack on this task -- compare against where that beta value would land on kl_reward_frontier.py's curve.
  • In alignment_tax.py, swap in a domain-relevant eval instead of MMLU (e.g. a summarization-quality metric like ROUGE against reference TL;DRs) -- MMLU is a poor match for a model that was only ever trained/aligned on summarization, so a domain-specific eval will show the tax (or gain!) more clearly than general knowledge.
  • In redteam_eval.py, read a handful of full transcripts by hand (not just the judge's verdict) -- LLM judges have their own failure modes (e.g. being fooled by a confident-sounding refusal that actually leaks some information), and it's worth building the habit of spot-checking automated evals.
  • Combine ideas: run redteam_eval.py against a model you deliberately trained with reward_hacking_demo.py's beta=0.0 setting (reward-hacked, degenerate text) and see how the judge handles clearly broken/repetitive outputs -- a reminder that automated evals can behave unpredictably outside their expected input distribution too.

lessons.title: Quantization Learning Labs
lessons.html:
Quantization Learning Labs

A self-contained, hands-on curriculum for understanding model / LLM quantization, from the raw bit-level numerics up to serving a multi-precision, tensor-parallel model across multiple GPUs. Every lab is a plain Python script you run from the shell -- no notebook server needed, so it works cleanly over SSH on a remote GPU box.

Built and intended to be run on an 8x NVIDIA B200 (183GB) node, which is one of the first GPU generations with native FP8 and FP4 tensor cores -- so labs 05/06 in particular let you see quantization formats that are actually accelerated in hardware, not just simulated.

Curriculum

Lab Topic What you'll learn
00_fundamentals Numerics primer INT8/INT4/FP8/FP4 formats, symmetric vs asymmetric, per-tensor/channel/group scales, quantization error
01_rtn_weight_only Round-to-nearest PTQ Simplest weight-only PTQ baseline; granularity vs accuracy/memory trade-off
02_gptq GPTQ Hessian-based layer-wise weight reconstruction, from scratch + production tool comparison
03_awq AWQ Activation-aware salient-channel scaling before RTN
04_smoothquant SmoothQuant Migrating activation outliers into weights to enable true INT8 W8A8
05_fp8 FP8 (E4M3/E5M2) Native Blackwell FP8 tensor cores, per-tensor vs per-row scaling
06_fp4_nvfp4 FP4 / NVFP4 / MXFP4 OCP microscaling format, Blackwell-native FP4 inference
07_qat QAT / STE Quantization-aware fine-tuning with a straight-through estimator
08_qlora QLoRA 4-bit NF4 base + LoRA fine-tuning, memory savings
09_kv_cache_quant KV-cache quantization Quantizing the KV cache for long-context serving
10_capstone_serving_bench Capstone Multi-GPU vLLM serving benchmark across BF16/FP8/INT4/NVFP4

Each lab folder has its own README.md with the theory, how to run it, and what to look for in the output. Labs are numbered in the order they're meant to be done -- later labs reuse concepts (and sometimes results) from earlier ones.

Environment

This was designed against the environment already validated on the target node:

  • 8x NVIDIA B200, 183GB each, driver 580.126.09, CUDA 13.0, sm_100
  • torch 2.11.0+cu130, transformers 5.14.1, accelerate 1.14.0, peft 0.20.0, datasets 5.0.1, deepspeed 0.19.3, vllm 0.26.0, flash-attn 2.8.3.post1
  • HF_HOME=/raid/llm_rl_cache/hf_home (plenty of disk on /raid)

A few extra packages are needed for specific labs (bitsandbytes, GPTQ/AWQ/SmoothQuant libraries, torchao, etc). Install them with:

pip install -r requirements-extra.txt

You don't have to install everything up front -- each script checks what it needs on startup (via common/env_check.py) and tells you exactly what's missing and how to get it.

Models default to fully open, ungated Qwen2.5 checkpoints, so no HF_TOKEN or license click-through is required. Model size scales up across labs (0.5B for fast iteration in labs 00/01/07, up to 32B tensor-parallel for the lab 10 capstone) -- see common/models.py for the registry. If you'd rather use Llama or another gated family, that's a one-line change there.

Running the labs

This repo is developed locally and meant to be synced onto the GPU node, e.g.:

# on your workstation
git push origin main

# on b200-72
git clone https://github.com/venkatacrc/quantization.git
cd quantization
conda activate <your-env>       # the one with torch/transformers/vllm already installed
pip install -r requirements-extra.txt

Then run any lab directly:

python labs/00_fundamentals/lab00_numerics.py
python labs/01_rtn_weight_only/lab01_rtn.py
python labs/02_gptq/lab02_gptq_from_scratch.py
...

Each script prints progress to stdout and writes plots/tables/JSON metrics into that lab's results/ directory. Later labs (05+) expect a GPU; labs needing more than one GPU say so explicitly in their README (e.g. lab 10 launches vLLM with tensor_parallel_size > 1).

Running everything

run_all.py runs every lab in order, each as its own subprocess (so one lab's GPU memory / vLLM processes don't leak into the next), streaming output live and also saving it to run_all_logs/. It keeps going if a lab fails (e.g. a missing optional dependency) and writes a running summary (run_all_logs/summary.txt / .json) after every lab, so an interrupted run still leaves you a useful report.

python run_all.py                     # everything, in order (expect a few hours -- lab 10 dominates)
python run_all.py --dry-run           # see the planned run order without executing anything
python run_all.py --only 00,01,02,03  # just the from-scratch PTQ labs
python run_all.py --skip 10 --skip-production-comparisons   # skip the capstone + the optional lab02b/03b/05b
python run_all.py --from 06           # resume a run that died partway through

Run python run_all.py --help for the full set of options.

Repo layout

quantization/
  run_all.py         runs every lab in order (see "Running everything" above)
  common/            shared helpers used by every lab
    quant_ops.py       quantize/dequantize primitives, STE fake-quant, FP4/FP8 simulation
    models.py          model registry + load_model()/load_tokenizer()
    data.py            wikitext2/c4 calibration + eval data loaders
    eval.py            perplexity and accuracy helpers
    bench.py           latency/throughput/GPU-memory benchmarking harness
    plotting.py        matplotlib helpers that save PNGs into a lab's results/
    env_check.py       checks GPU + optional-library availability
  labs/
    00_fundamentals/ .. 10_capstone_serving_bench/
      README.md          theory + how to run
      labXX_*.py         the runnable script(s)
      results/           generated output (gitignored contents)
  requirements-extra.txt

Suggested order

Go through the labs in numeric order -- each README calls out what to compare against earlier labs. If you only have limited GPU time, the highest-signal path is: 00 -> 01 -> 02 -> 05 -> 06 -> 10, and you can come back for QAT/QLoRA/KV-cache (07-09) and AWQ/SmoothQuant (03-04) afterward.

lessons.title: Lab 00 - Quantization Numerics Fundamentals
lessons.html:
Lab 00 - Quantization Numerics Fundamentals

Goal: build intuition for what "quantization" actually does at the bit level, before touching a real model. Every later lab is a variation on the ideas here.

Runtime: a minute or two. CPU is fine; a GPU (if present) is used automatically but not required.

Background

What is quantization?

Neural network weights and activations are normally stored as 16- or 32-bit floating point numbers. Quantization maps those values onto a much smaller set of representable numbers (e.g. 256 integer levels for 8-bit, 16 levels for 4-bit) so that a tensor takes less memory and, on hardware with native low-precision arithmetic, computes faster. The core trade-off is always: fewer bits -> less memory & faster compute, but more rounding error.

Uniform integer quantization: scale + zero-point

For b bits, we pick an integer grid (e.g. [-127, 127] for 8-bit symmetric) and a real-valued scale s (and, for asymmetric quantization, a zero-point z) so that:

quantize:    q = round(x / s + z),  clamped to the integer grid
dequantize:  x_hat = (q - z) * s
  • Symmetric quantization forces z = 0 -- simpler and what most weight quantizers use, at the cost of wasting one grid code if the data isn't centered at zero.
  • Asymmetric quantization fits s and z to the tensor's actual [min, max], giving a tighter fit for skewed distributions (e.g. post-ReLU activations, which are >= 0).

Granularity: per-tensor vs per-channel vs per-group

A single (s, z) for an entire weight matrix (per-tensor) is cheap to store but forces every row to share one dynamic range -- if one output channel has much larger weights than the rest, it dominates the scale and everyone else loses precision. Per-channel quantization gives every row of a weight matrix (e.g. one scale per output feature) its own (s, z). Per-group goes further and gives every contiguous chunk of group_size elements within a row its own scale -- this is what GPTQ/AWQ/QLoRA use in practice (typical group_size is 32, 64, or 128), because even within one output channel the input dimension can have very different local scales. Finer granularity = less error, but more scale factors to store (and every stored scale eats into the memory savings you're trying to get).

Floating-point quantization: FP8 and FP4

Instead of a uniform integer grid, you can quantize onto a floating-point grid, which spaces its representable values non-uniformly (finer resolution near zero, coarser further out) -- often a better match for weight/activation distributions, which are usually peaked near zero with occasional outliers.

  • FP8 comes in two flavors: E4M3 (4 exponent bits, 3 mantissa bits, max magnitude ~448) trades dynamic range for precision, while E5M2 (5 exponent bits, 2 mantissa) trades precision for dynamic range (useful for gradients/activations that can spike). NVIDIA Blackwell GPUs (including your B200s) have native FP8 tensor cores, so FP8 isn't just a memory-saving trick here -- it's also a real speedup (see lab 05).
  • FP4 has only 16 representable magnitudes total. With 1 sign + 2 exponent + 1 mantissa bit (E2M1), the non-negative grid is exactly {0, 0.5, 1, 1.5, 2, 3, 4, 6}. To keep this usable, FP4 formats share one extra scale factor across a small block of elements (16 for NVIDIA's NVFP4, 32 for the OCP "MX" spec's MXFP4) -- this is called microscaling. NVFP4 uses an FP8 (E4M3) block scale for more precision; MXFP4 uses a power-of-two scale (E8M0, i.e. just an exponent, no mantissa) which is coarser but even cheaper. B200s have native FP4 tensor cores too -- see lab 06.

What the script does

lab00_numerics.py:

  1. Builds a synthetic weight-like tensor (Gaussian body + a few outlier rows, mimicking the heavy-tailed per-channel statistics real LLM weights show) and, if a GPU + internet are available, also pulls one real attention projection weight matrix from Qwen2.5-0.5B-Instruct for a sanity check that the synthetic tensor isn't misleading.
  2. Sweeps bit-width {8, 4, 3, 2} x {symmetric, asymmetric} at per-tensor granularity and records reconstruction error.
  3. Sweeps granularity {per_tensor, per_channel, per_group(32/64/128)} at INT4 and records error.
  4. Compares INT8 vs FP8 (E4M3, E5M2) at the same "8 bits" budget.
  5. Compares INT4 vs FP4 (NVFP4-style block=16, MXFP4-style block=32 with a power-of-two scale) at the same "4 bits" budget.
  6. Saves bar charts + an error histogram + a metrics.json summary into results/.

Run it

python labs/00_fundamentals/lab00_numerics.py

What to look for

  • Error should drop sharply from 8->4->3->2 bits, and roughly follow error ~ 2^-bits for uniform quantization of a roughly-Gaussian tensor.
  • Asymmetric quantization should look better than or equal to symmetric at every bit-width here, because the synthetic tensor isn't perfectly zero-centered.
  • Per-group should beat per-channel should beat per-tensor at INT4 -- but by a shrinking margin as group_size grows, since a smaller group means a scale factor that fits the local data better.
  • FP8 (E4M3) should have lower error than INT8 on the outlier rows specifically (check the printed per-row breakdown) even though both use 8 bits, because the floating grid adapts its spacing to magnitude.
  • FP4 should be much worse than INT4 per-element on average (only 16 total grid points vs 16 integer points is the same count, but FP4's grid is non-uniform and its block scale is shared over many more values than a typical per-group INT4 setup) -- this is exactly why lab 06 spends time on how real NVFP4/MXFP4 recipes claw that accuracy back.

lessons.title: Lab 01 - Round-to-Nearest (RTN) Weight-Only PTQ
lessons.html:
Lab 01 - Round-to-Nearest (RTN) Weight-Only PTQ

Goal: apply the simplest possible post-training quantization (PTQ) method -- round every weight to the nearest grid point, independently, with no calibration data at all -- to a real language model, and measure the actual accuracy/memory trade-off. This is the baseline every fancier method (GPTQ, AWQ, ...) in later labs tries to beat.

Runtime: ~5-10 minutes on one B200 (model download + several perplexity evaluations on Qwen2.5-0.5B-Instruct).

Background

RTN quantization is exactly the fake_quantize_int function from lab 00, applied to every nn.Linear weight matrix in the model (skipping the embedding and LM head, which are usually kept at higher precision since vocabulary-sized matrices are unusually sensitive to quantization relative to their size). No data is needed -- just the weight tensor itself.

Because it's data-free and needs no per-layer optimization, RTN is essentially free to run, which makes it the natural first thing to try and a useful baseline. Its weakness is exactly what you'd expect: it treats every weight independently and has no way to account for which weights matter most for the model's actual outputs (that's what GPTQ and AWQ add in labs 02-03).

What the script does

  1. Loads Qwen2.5-0.5B-Instruct in bf16 and measures baseline WikiText-2 perplexity + real GPU memory footprint.
  2. For a sweep of (bits, granularity) configs -- {8, 4, 3} x {per_tensor, per_channel, per_group(g=128), per_group(g=32)} -- quantizes every linear layer's weights in place with RTN, measures the new perplexity, then restores the original weights before moving to the next config (so every config starts from the same clean baseline).
  3. Estimates the theoretical packed memory footprint for each config (bits per weight + the overhead of storing one scale per group) -- the script itself keeps weights in bf16 the whole time (since PyTorch doesn't have a native int4 tensor type to just drop in), so this is a computed estimate of what a real packed-int4 kernel would use, not a measurement of this script's own memory use.
  4. Runs a short generation from the model at a couple of the more aggressive configs, so you can read the degradation, not just see it as a number.
  5. Saves a perplexity-vs-bits line chart (one line per granularity) and a memory-footprint bar chart to results/.

Run it

python labs/01_rtn_weight_only/lab01_rtn.py

What to look for

  • Perplexity should barely move at 8-bit (any granularity), start noticeably degrading at 4-bit per-tensor, and recover most of that degradation at 4-bit per-group(32) -- granularity matters more as bits shrink, exactly as lab 00 predicted on synthetic data.
  • 3-bit per-tensor is usually where RTN starts falling apart on a 0.5B model -- watch the generated text at that config for repeated tokens or incoherence.
  • The memory chart should show group-wise quantization's overhead (one scale per group) eating into its savings vs per-channel/per-tensor as group_size shrinks -- there's a real cost to finer granularity, not just a benefit.
  • Keep these numbers in mind for lab 02 (GPTQ) and lab 03 (AWQ) at the same bit-widths -- both should beat RTN's perplexity at 4-bit and especially at 3-bit, since they use calibration data to decide how to quantize instead of just rounding.

lessons.title: Lab 02 - GPTQ (Hessian-Based Layer-Wise Reconstruction)
lessons.html:
Lab 02 - GPTQ (Hessian-Based Layer-Wise Reconstruction)

Goal: implement the core GPTQ algorithm from scratch and see why it beats RTN at the same bit-width -- then reproduce the same idea with a production library and compare.

Runtime: ~15-25 minutes on one B200 (calibration forward passes + per-layer quantization + two perplexity evaluations on Qwen2.5-1.5B-Instruct). Lab 02b (production comparison) needs gptqmodel or llmcompressor installed (pip install -r requirements-extra.txt).

Background

RTN (lab 01) quantizes every weight independently -- it has no way to know that rounding one weight can be partly "corrected for" by adjusting the other, not-yet-quantized weights in the same row. GPTQ ("GPTQ: Accurate Post-Training Quantization for Generative Pre-trained Transformers", Frantar et al. 2022) fixes this with a layer-wise reconstruction: for each linear layer, quantize its weight matrix one column (input feature) at a time, and after quantizing each column, adjust every remaining column to compensate for the error just introduced -- using second-order (Hessian) information from real calibration data to know exactly how much to adjust.

Concretely, for one layer with weight W (out_features x in_features) and calibration input activations X (n_tokens x in_features), we want to minimize the squared output error ||W Xᵀ - Ŵ Xᵀ||². Because that loss is quadratic in Ŵ, its Hessian w.r.t. any one row of W is H = 2 XᵀX (the same for every row, since the loss decomposes over rows). GPTQ:

  1. Adds a small damping term to H for numerical stability, then computes H⁻¹ via Cholesky decomposition (twice: once to invert, once more to get the Cholesky factor of the inverse -- this specific two-step trick is what makes the algorithm numerically stable enough to run on full-size LLM layers, per the paper's appendix).
  2. Processes columns left to right. For column i: quantize it (RTN, but using the group's live/current values -- see below), then propagate the resulting error into every later column j > i, weighted by H⁻¹[i, j] / H⁻¹[i, i]. This is the same "compensate the neighbors" update as classical Optimal Brain Quantization (OBQ, GPTQ's predecessor), but GPTQ's fixed column order + Cholesky trick makes it run in O(d_in²) instead of OBQ's O(d_in³).
  3. Re-derives the group's scale/zero-point every group_size columns, from the (partially-corrected) live weight values at that point -- not from the original weights -- so later groups benefit from the error correction already applied to them.

A simplification this lab makes, on purpose

Real GPTQ implementations (including the ones in lab 02b) quantize transformer blocks sequentially: to build the calibration activations for block N, they run the calibration data through blocks 0..N-1 after those blocks have already been quantized, so each layer's Hessian reflects the actual (quantized) activations it will see at inference time. That's important for best-possible accuracy, but it roughly doubles the code you need (you have to interleave "run calibration forward pass one block at a time" with "quantize this block's linears") without teaching anything new about the math of GPTQ.

This lab instead captures calibration activations for every linear layer in a single forward pass through the original, unquantized model, and quantizes every layer independently from those activations. This is sometimes called "non-sequential" GPTQ. It's slightly less accurate than the real thing (errors from early layers aren't accounted for when quantizing later layers) but isolates exactly the Hessian-based reconstruction math above. Lab 02b's production-library run uses the real sequential algorithm, so the gap you measure between the two is a decent proxy for "how much does sequential error-correction actually buy you".

What the scripts do

lab02_gptq_from_scratch.py:

  1. Loads Qwen2.5-1.5B-Instruct, evaluates BF16 baseline perplexity.
  2. Runs 128 calibration sequences (512 tokens each, from WikiText-2) through the model with forward hooks on every target linear layer, accumulating each layer's Hessian H = XᵀX on the fly (never materializing the full activation tensor, just the running in_features x in_features sum).
  3. For each layer, runs the from-scratch GPTQ column-by-column reconstruction described above at INT4/group_size=128 (same bit budget as one of lab 01's RTN configs), replacing the layer's weight in place.
  4. Also computes plain RTN at the same bit budget for a direct, same-script comparison.
  5. Evaluates perplexity for both, prints per-layer reconstruction error (||W - Ŵ||_F / ||W||_F) so you can see which layers are hardest to quantize, and saves a comparison chart + metrics.json.

lab02b_compare_production_gptq.py:

  1. Checks for gptqmodel (preferred) or falls back to describing what to install if neither is present.
  2. Quantizes the same model to the same INT4/group_size=128 config using the real, sequential production algorithm, on the same calibration data.
  3. Evaluates perplexity of the resulting checkpoint and reports wall-clock quantization time, appending its numbers onto lab02's metrics.json / comparison chart.

Run it

python labs/02_gptq/lab02_gptq_from_scratch.py
# then, if you have gptqmodel or llmcompressor installed:
python labs/02_gptq/lab02b_compare_production_gptq.py

What to look for

  • From-scratch GPTQ should land between RTN and the production library on perplexity at INT4/g128 -- better than RTN (it's using calibration data and the Hessian), but not quite matching the production sequential version.
  • Per-layer error should be noticeably worse for a handful of layers (often later MLP down_proj layers) -- this is the same "some layers are much more sensitive than others" pattern that motivates mixed-precision / outlier-aware methods like AWQ (lab 03).
  • The production run's wall-clock time is usually longer than the from-scratch version despite being more optimized code, precisely because it pays for the sequential recalibration this lab skips.

lessons.title: Lab 03 - AWQ (Activation-Aware Weight Quantization)
lessons.html:
Lab 03 - AWQ (Activation-Aware Weight Quantization)

Goal: implement AWQ's core insight from scratch -- that a small number of input channels (not weights themselves) drive most of the quantization error, and that you can protect them with a per-channel rescaling instead of mixed precision -- then compare against a production AWQ implementation.

Runtime: ~10-15 minutes on one B200 (Qwen2.5-1.5B-Instruct, same model as lab 02 so the RTN/GPTQ/AWQ comparison is apples-to-apples).

Background

GPTQ (lab 02) reduces quantization error by adjusting weights after the fact, using second-order information. AWQ ("AWQ: Activation-aware Weight Quantization for LLM Compression and Acceleration", Lin et al. 2023) takes a different angle: it observes that a handful of input channels have much larger activation magnitudes than the rest (this is the same activation-outlier phenomenon SmoothQuant, lab 04, also exploits), and that the weight columns multiplying those channels are disproportionately important to get right -- even though the weights themselves aren't unusually large.

The key trick is a mathematical identity that costs nothing at inference time (once fused into the previous layer): for any per-input-channel scale vector s,

W x = (W * s) * (x / s)         # exactly equal, for any channel-wise s > 0

If we pick s_c > 1 for a salient channel c, the corresponding weight column W[:, c] gets multiplied up before quantization -- effectively giving it more "room" on the quantization grid relative to its rounding error, without changing the true mathematical output at all (since the matching x / s cancels it back out). The catch: scaling one column up also raises that row's max value, which can widen the shared scale/zero-point for the other columns in a per-channel/per-group quantizer, making their error slightly worse. So there's a real trade-off, and AWQ picks s by a small grid search that balances "protect the salient channels" against "don't hurt everyone else":

s_c(alpha) = act_scale_c ^ alpha / weight_scale_c ^ (1 - alpha)

where act_scale_c is channel c's average calibration activation magnitude and weight_scale_c is channel c's average weight magnitude. alpha is searched over a small grid (this lab uses 9 points from 0 to 1) and picked by actually measuring reconstruction error on calibration data for each candidate.

A simplification this lab makes, on purpose

In production, the x / s division is fused into whatever produced x (usually the preceding LayerNorm's weight, or the previous linear's output rows) so there's zero extra runtime cost. Implementing that fusion requires walking the specific pairs of adjacent modules in each transformer block (attention QKV comes after an RMSNorm, down_proj comes after an activation function applied to gate_proj/up_proj, etc.) -- useful production engineering, but it doesn't teach anything new about why AWQ works. This lab instead wraps each quantized linear layer in a small module that explicitly divides its input by s before the matmul. This is numerically identical to the fused version (same weights, same effective math) -- just with one extra elementwise op per forward pass instead of a free one, which is the right trade to make for a learning lab.

What the scripts do

lab03_awq_from_scratch.py:

  1. Loads Qwen2.5-1.5B-Instruct, evaluates BF16 baseline perplexity (should match lab 02's baseline).
  2. Runs calibration data through the model once, recording each target layer's mean per-channel activation magnitude and a small cached batch of raw activations (for the scale search's reconstruction-error check).
  3. For each layer: searches alpha in {0, 0.125, ..., 1.0}, and for each candidate computes the scaled+quantized weight and measures output reconstruction error directly (||Wx - Ŵ'x'||) on the cached calibration batch; keeps the best alpha.
  4. Replaces the layer with a small wrapper that applies the input scaling
    • holds the scaled/quantized weight, at the same INT4/group_size=128 budget used in labs 01/02.
  5. Evaluates perplexity, prints the picked alpha per layer (salient layers should end up wanting alpha closer to 1), and saves a comparison chart against lab 02's RTN/GPTQ numbers.

lab03b_compare_production_awq.py mirrors lab 02b: quantizes the same model with autoawq (falling back to llmcompressor's AWQModifier) and adds that number to the same comparison chart.

Run it

python labs/03_awq/lab03_awq_from_scratch.py
python labs/03_awq/lab03b_compare_production_awq.py   # needs autoawq or llmcompressor

What to look for

  • From-scratch AWQ should beat RTN and land close to (sometimes better than, on this simplified non-sequential setup) from-scratch GPTQ from lab 02, despite being conceptually much simpler -- AWQ protects the few channels that matter most instead of trying to optimize every weight.
  • Printed per-layer best alpha values: attention output projections and MLP down_proj layers (which see the widest activation distributions) usually pick larger alpha than QKV projections.
  • The production AWQ run should be noticeably faster to quantize than production GPTQ (lab 02b) for the same reason it's simpler to implement here: no Hessian, no Cholesky, just a bounded grid search per layer.

lessons.title: Lab 04 - SmoothQuant (W8A8: Weight *and* Activation Quantization)
lessons.html:
Lab 04 - SmoothQuant (W8A8: Weight and Activation Quantization)

Goal: go from weight-only quantization (labs 01-03) to quantizing activations too, which is what actually lets hardware run an INT8 x INT8 matmul instead of dequantizing back to bf16 first -- and see the real GPU speedup that unlocks, not just a memory number.

Runtime: ~15-20 minutes on one B200 (Qwen2.5-3B-Instruct, larger than labs 01-03 so the GEMM benchmark has representative matrix sizes).

Background

Every previous lab quantized weights but still computed in bf16: the quantized weight gets dequantized back to bf16 before the matmul, so you save memory (loading weights) but not compute -- the GPU still does a bf16 GEMM. To get an actual compute speedup on hardware with fast low-precision tensor cores, both operands of the matmul need to be low-precision: this is what "W8A8" (8-bit weights and 8-bit activations) means.

The problem: activations in transformer LLMs have large per-channel outliers (some input feature channels are consistently 10-100x larger than the rest, across almost every token) -- much worse outliers than the weights have. A naive per-tensor INT8 quantizer for activations gets dominated by those few channels and wrecks precision for everyone else.

SmoothQuant ("SmoothQuant: Accurate and Efficient Post-Training Quantization for Large Language Models", Xiao et al. 2022) fixes this with the same per-channel-scale identity AWQ uses (lab 03), but applied with a different goal: instead of protecting salient weight channels, it deliberately migrates difficulty from activations to weights -- weights are much easier to quantize precisely (no outliers, and they're static so you can compute an exact per-channel scale offline), so moving the outlier problem onto them is a good trade:

s_c = act_scale_c ^ alpha / weight_scale_c ^ (1 - alpha)      (alpha = 0.5 by default)

W' = W * s        (folded into the weight, offline, one time)
X' = X / s        (folded into the previous layer at deployment; explicit here, see below)

Higher alpha pushes more of the outlier magnitude onto the weights (smoother activations, lumpier weights); lower alpha does the opposite. alpha = 0.5 is the paper's default and works well across most models; this lab sweeps a few values so you can see the accuracy trade-off directly instead of taking that on faith.

After smoothing, both W' and X' are quantized to INT8:

  • Weights: per-output-channel (row) scale, computed once from the (smoothed) weight tensor itself -- call this static weight quantization, since it needs no runtime data at all.
  • Activations: this lab uses static, per-tensor quantization -- one scale, calibrated ahead of time from the smoothed activations' observed max magnitude -- which is what actually enables a real INT8 x INT8 GEMM with no runtime scale computation. (Some deployed systems instead use dynamic per-token activation quantization -- computing each batch's scale on the fly -- which is usually more accurate but needs an extra reduction op at runtime; this lab's script prints the dynamic-quant accuracy as a reference point without implementing its own fused kernel.)

The same simplification as lab 03

As in AWQ, X' = X / s is normally fused into the previous layer for free. This lab again applies it as an explicit elementwise division in a wrapper module -- numerically identical, just not fused for maximum speed.

What the script does

  1. Loads Qwen2.5-3B-Instruct, evaluates BF16 baseline perplexity.
  2. Runs calibration data through the model, recording per-channel activation scales (for smoothing) and the smoothed activations' max magnitude (for static INT8 calibration).
  3. Sweeps alpha in {0.3, 0.5, 0.7} (quick perplexity check on a handful of windows), picks the best, then does the full smoothing + INT8 weight+activation quantization at that alpha and replaces every target linear layer with a module that does a real torch._int_mm INT8 x INT8 matmul on GPU.
  4. Evaluates full perplexity of the resulting W8A8 model.
  5. GEMM microbenchmark: times a raw torch._int_mm INT8 matmul against an equivalent-shape bf16 matmul, at this model's actual layer shapes, to measure the real hardware speedup from int8 tensor cores directly (the cleanest signal for "is INT8 compute actually faster on this GPU", independent of any Python-level overhead in the whole-model wrapper).
  6. End-to-end benchmark: times text generation with the full W8A8 model vs BF16, as a rough sanity check (see the caveat below).
  7. Saves comparison charts + metrics.json.

Run it

python labs/04_smoothquant/lab04_smoothquant.py

What to look for

  • The perplexity gap between BF16 and W8A8-SmoothQuant should be small (typically well under 1 point on a 3B-class model) -- the entire point of the smoothing step is making 8-bit activations viable in the first place; compare against what happens if you skip smoothing (alpha = 0, printed as a reference row) to see how much it's actually buying you.
  • The GEMM microbenchmark should show a clear speedup for torch._int_mm over bf16 at large matrix shapes -- this is the real payoff of W8A8 that weight-only methods (labs 01-03) can't give you, since B200 has native INT8 tensor cores at roughly double the bf16 throughput.
  • Caveat: the end-to-end generation benchmark uses this lab's simple, unfused per-layer wrapper (quantize activation -> torch._int_mm -> dequantize, one Python call per linear layer), so its wall-clock number usually shows less speedup than the GEMM microbenchmark, or even a slowdown at small batch sizes -- a production W8A8 kernel (as used by vLLM/TensorRT-LLM) fuses all of that into one kernel per layer. Treat the GEMM microbenchmark as "what the hardware can do" and the end-to-end number as "what this teaching implementation does with it".

lessons.title: Lab 05 - FP8 Quantization (Native Blackwell Tensor Cores)
lessons.html:
Lab 05 - FP8 Quantization (Native Blackwell Tensor Cores)

Goal: quantize both weights and activations to FP8 and run a real FP8 matmul on your B200s, comparing E4M3 vs E5M2 and per-tensor vs per-row scaling -- and see why FP8 needs much less special handling than INT8 (lab 04) did.

Runtime: ~15-20 minutes on one B200 (Qwen2.5-7B-Instruct).

Background

Lab 00 introduced FP8's two flavors: E4M3 (more mantissa bits, less range, max magnitude ~448) and E5M2 (more range, less precision, max magnitude ~57344). NVIDIA Hopper and Blackwell GPUs (your B200s) have native FP8 tensor cores -- an FP8 x FP8 matmul isn't just a memory trick, it runs at roughly double the throughput of an equivalent bf16 matmul in hardware. PyTorch exposes this directly via torch._scaled_mm, which this lab calls straight from Python (no custom CUDA needed).

Why FP8 doesn't need SmoothQuant-style smoothing

Lab 04 showed that naive INT8 activation quantization (no smoothing) badly hurts accuracy, because a uniform integer grid gets dominated by a few outlier channels. FP8's floating-point grid is non-uniform by construction -- it naturally allocates more resolution near zero and less far from zero, which is a much better match for the "mostly small values, occasional large outlier" shape real activations have. This lab quantizes activations to FP8 directly, per-tensor, dynamically (scale computed fresh every forward pass, no calibration, no smoothing) and you'll see perplexity stay close to the bf16 baseline anyway -- a direct, hands-on illustration of why FP8 has become the default "just quantize it" format for LLM inference, while INT8 needs much more care.

What the scripts do

lab05_fp8_inference.py:

  1. Loads Qwen2.5-7B-Instruct, evaluates BF16 baseline perplexity + memory.
  2. Weight-only FP8 sweep (fake-quant, like lab 01's RTN sweep but on the FP8 grid instead of an integer grid): {E4M3, E5M2} x {per-tensor, per-row}, measuring perplexity for each.
  3. GEMM microbenchmark: times a real torch._scaled_mm FP8 x FP8 matmul against an equivalent bf16 matmul at this model's actual layer shapes and a few batch sizes -- the direct hardware speedup signal.
  4. W8A8-FP8 end-to-end: replaces every target linear layer with a module that dynamically quantizes its input activations to FP8 E4M3 (per-tensor, computed fresh each forward call -- no smoothing, no calibration) and its weights to FP8 E4M3 (static, per-row), then actually calls torch._scaled_mm. Evaluates perplexity and benchmarks generation throughput/memory against the BF16 baseline.
  5. Saves comparison charts + metrics.json.

lab05b_compare_torchao.py (needs torchao): reproduces the W8A8-FP8 setup with torchao's Float8DynamicActivationFloat8WeightConfig (a fused, production-grade implementation) and compares perplexity + throughput against this lab's from-scratch version.

Run it

python labs/05_fp8/lab05_fp8_inference.py
python labs/05_fp8/lab05b_compare_torchao.py   # needs torchao

What to look for

  • Weight-only FP8 should barely move perplexity at either E4M3 or E5M2 -- 7B-class models have plenty of headroom at 8 bits regardless of grid shape; the interesting comparison here is INT8 vs FP8 at the activation side (next point), not weights.
  • W8A8-FP8 (no smoothing) perplexity should land close to lab 04's smoothed SmoothQuant INT8 result, and clearly beat lab 04's unsmoothed INT8 reference row -- direct evidence that FP8's grid shape is doing SmoothQuant's job for free.
  • The GEMM microbenchmark should show FP8 meaningfully faster than bf16 at large token counts, and (if you ran lab 04) roughly comparable to or faster than the INT8 torch._int_mm numbers -- Blackwell's FP8 tensor cores are a first-class citizen, not a fallback path.
  • torchao's fused implementation should show a bigger end-to-end generation speedup than this lab's unfused per-layer version, for the same reason noted in lab 04: production kernels fuse the quantize/matmul/dequantize sequence into one kernel launch.

lessons.title: Lab 06 - FP4 / NVFP4 / MXFP4 (Blackwell-Native 4-Bit Formats)
lessons.html:
Lab 06 - FP4 / NVFP4 / MXFP4 (Blackwell-Native 4-Bit Formats)

Goal: understand the microscaling trick that makes 4-bit floating point usable at all, measure it from scratch, and then try the real hardware-accelerated path your B200s support.

Runtime: ~15-25 minutes on one B200 (Qwen2.5-7B-Instruct); the accelerated-path section needs nvidia-modelopt and/or torchao and may take longer depending on what's installed.

Background

Lab 00 introduced the math: a 4-bit float with 2 exponent + 1 mantissa bit (E2M1) has exactly 8 non-negative representable values, {0, 0.5, 1, 1.5, 2, 3, 4, 6}. That's a brutally coarse grid on its own -- nowhere near enough to represent a full weight tensor's dynamic range. The fix used by both NVFP4 (NVIDIA's format) and MXFP4 (the Open Compute Project's "microscaling" spec, which NVFP4 is closely related to) is to share one extra scale factor across a small block of elements (16 for NVFP4, 32 for MXFP4), so the local dynamic range within each block still gets the full 8-value grid, even though the global range across the whole tensor can be huge. NVFP4 uses an FP8 (E4M3) block scale (finer); MXFP4 uses a power-of-two-only (E8M0) block scale (coarser, cheaper -- no mantissa bits to store).

This block-sharing is exactly what makes FP4 practical -- and exactly what makes it fundamentally different from INT4 with the same group size: INT4's uniform integer grid + a per-group scale gives 16 evenly spaced levels per group, while FP4's floating grid + per-block scale gives 16 unevenly spaced levels (denser near zero) per block. Which one wins depends on how peaked the underlying data is -- you measured this directly for a synthetic tensor in lab 00; this lab measures it on a real 7B model.

B200 (Blackwell) GPUs have native FP4 tensor cores, so NVFP4/MXFP4 aren't just an extreme memory-saving trick -- like FP8 in lab 05, real FP4 compute is meaningfully faster than bf16 or even FP8 in hardware, when you use a kernel that actually exploits it (this lab's from-scratch code does not -- see the "accelerated path" section below for what does).

What the script does

  1. Loads Qwen2.5-7B-Instruct, evaluates BF16 baseline perplexity.
  2. From-scratch weight-only quantization sweep at the same "4 bits" budget: INT4 (per-group, g=32) vs NVFP4 (block=16) vs MXFP4 (block=32, power-of-two scale), using the fp4_blockwise_quantize_dequantize function from common/quant_ops.py (the same one lab 00 exercised on synthetic data) applied to every linear layer's weights.
  3. Accelerated path (best-effort): checks for nvidia-modelopt (TensorRT Model Optimizer) and, if present, runs its NVFP4 PTQ recipe on the same calibration data and evaluates perplexity; separately checks for torchao's NVFP4/MXFP4 support. Whichever is available gets run and compared; if neither is installed, the script prints exactly what to pip install and skips this section rather than failing.
  4. Pulls FP8 (lab 05) and RTN/GPTQ/AWQ (labs 01-03) numbers from their metrics.json files if those labs were already run, and charts each as relative perplexity degradation ((ppl - baseline_ppl) / baseline_ppl) rather than raw perplexity -- labs 01-03 use a smaller model than labs 05-06, so raw perplexity values aren't directly comparable across them, but "how much worse than that model's own bf16 baseline" is.
  5. Saves comparison charts + metrics.json.

Run it

python labs/06_fp4_nvfp4/lab06_fp4_blackwell.py

Run labs 01, 02, 03, and 05 first (on the same model where possible) if you want the combined "every precision so far" chart to be fully populated -- the script works fine without them, it just has fewer bars.

What to look for

  • NVFP4 (block=16, finer per-block scale) should beat MXFP4 (block=32, power-of-two scale) on perplexity -- smaller blocks adapt to local magnitude better, and a real (non-power-of-two) scale wastes less range.
  • Whether NVFP4 beats or loses to INT4 at group=32 is genuinely model/layer dependent -- report what you actually observe rather than assuming one wins; this is exactly the kind of empirical check real quantization engineers do before picking a format for production.
  • If you have nvidia-modelopt or torchao's FP4 path installed: their perplexity should beat this lab's naive weight-only FP4 (no calibration, no error correction) by a similar margin to how GPTQ/AWQ beat plain RTN in labs 02-03 -- production 4-bit recipes combine microscaling with calibration-based error correction, not just a better number format.
  • Keep this lab's numbers in mind for the lab 10 capstone, which serves an NVFP4 checkpoint (if you have the tooling) alongside BF16/FP8/INT4 across multiple GPUs and measures the actual throughput difference.

lessons.title: Lab 07 - Quantization-Aware Training (QAT) with a Straight-Through Estimator
lessons.html:
Lab 07 - Quantization-Aware Training (QAT) with a Straight-Through Estimator

Goal: instead of quantizing an already-trained model and hoping it still works (PTQ -- everything in labs 01-06), fine-tune the model while simulating quantization in the forward pass, so its weights learn to be robust to the rounding they'll experience at inference time.

Runtime: ~10-15 minutes on one B200 (Qwen2.5-0.5B-Instruct; small on purpose, since QAT needs a training loop, not just a forward pass).

Background

Every PTQ method so far (RTN, GPTQ, AWQ, SmoothQuant) starts from trained full-precision weights and tries to quantize them with minimum damage. QAT instead keeps training the model with the quantization operation inside the forward pass, so gradient descent can push the underlying full-precision weights toward values that happen to round well -- not just values that were good in full precision.

The obstacle: round() (which every quantizer in this repo uses) has zero gradient almost everywhere and an undefined one at the rounding boundaries. If you literally backprop through round(), no weight ever updates. The fix, used since the earliest quantized neural network work, is the straight-through estimator (STE): in the forward pass, actually quantize (round, clamp, dequantize -- exactly the fake_quantize_int from lab 00/01); in the backward pass, pretend the quantization step was the identity function and let the gradient flow straight through to the underlying full-precision weight, unchanged. It's a biased gradient estimator (the true function's gradient is zero almost everywhere, and STE uses 1 instead), but empirically it works well enough that it's still the standard approach.

forward:   w_q = dequantize(quantize(w))         # real rounding happens here
backward:  d(loss)/dw  ~=  d(loss)/d(w_q)          # STE: treat quantize+dequantize as identity

This lab implements that directly: common/quant_ops.py's ste_fake_quantize is a tiny torch.autograd.Function whose forward calls the exact same fake_quantize_int used everywhere else in this repo, and whose backward just returns the incoming gradient unchanged.

What the script does

  1. Loads Qwen2.5-0.5B-Instruct in full precision and evaluates a baseline perplexity (before any quantization).
  2. Wraps every target linear layer in a QATLinear module that keeps a full-precision trainable weight but always runs it through ste_fake_quantize (INT4, per-channel) before the matmul -- so from this point on, the model always "sees" the quantization at both training and eval time.
  3. Immediately evaluates perplexity in this state, before any training step -- this is exactly a PTQ/RTN baseline at the same bit-width, computed for free as a side effect of the wrapper.
  4. Fine-tunes for a few hundred steps on WikiText-2 (next-token loss, small batches, low learning rate), periodically re-evaluating perplexity on a quick subset so you get a training curve, not just a before/after number.
  5. Evaluates final perplexity on the full WikiText-2 test set.
  6. Saves a loss curve, a perplexity-over-training-steps curve, and a before/after bar chart.

Run it

python labs/07_qat/lab07_qat_lsq.py

What to look for

  • The "before training" perplexity (step 0) should look like a typical aggressive PTQ result -- noticeably worse than full precision, since INT4 per-channel with no calibration data is one of the harsher configs this curriculum has tried.
  • Perplexity should visibly recover over the first ~100-200 steps as the underlying full-precision weights adjust to round more favorably, then plateau -- QAT doesn't need nearly as many steps as original pretraining, since it's fine-tuning around an already-good minimum.
  • The loss curve should be noisier early on (large rounding jumps from a weight distribution the model wasn't trained for) and smooth out as training progresses.
  • This is real compute you're spending (a training loop, with an optimizer) to recover accuracy, unlike calibration-only methods (GPTQ, AWQ) which are a single forward-pass-worth of work -- QAT is the "spend more to get more" point on this curriculum's cost/accuracy spectrum. Compare final perplexity here against lab 02's GPTQ number on a similarly-sized model to see whether the extra training cost is worth it for your use case.

lessons.title: Lab 08 - QLoRA (NF4 4-Bit Base + LoRA Fine-Tuning)
lessons.html:
Lab 08 - QLoRA (NF4 4-Bit Base + LoRA Fine-Tuning)

Goal: see how quantization enables fine-tuning models that wouldn't otherwise fit in memory for training at all -- by freezing a 4-bit base model and only training a small set of full-precision adapter weights on top of it.

Runtime: ~15-20 minutes on one B200 (Qwen2.5-7B-Instruct). Needs bitsandbytes (pip install -r requirements-extra.txt).

Background

Labs 01-07 were all about inference: quantize a trained model, run it faster/smaller, measure the accuracy cost. QLoRA ("QLoRA: Efficient Finetuning of Quantized LLMs", Dettmers et al. 2023) uses quantization to make training cheaper instead: it freezes the entire base model in 4-bit and only trains a small number of extra parameters (LoRA adapters -- low rank matrices inserted alongside each frozen linear layer), so training memory is dominated by the tiny frozen base model plus the adapters' gradients/optimizer state, not the full model's.

Two things specific to QLoRA, beyond "just" 4-bit weights:

  • NF4 ("NormalFloat4"): instead of a uniform integer grid (INT4, labs 01-03) or a floating-point exponent/mantissa grid (FP4, lab 06), NF4 picks its 16 representable values as quantiles of a standard normal distribution -- i.e. the grid points that would be information-optimal if the data were exactly Gaussian. Real neural network weights are approximately Gaussian, so this tends to beat both INT4 and FP4 at the same bit-width for weight-only quantization specifically (this lab verifies that on a real weight tensor before doing anything else).
  • LoRA on top of a frozen quantized base: peft's prepare_model_for_kbit_training + LoraConfig inserts trainable low-rank A/B matrices (rank 16 by default here) next to each target linear layer; the frozen 4-bit base weight W and the LoRA update BA are summed at forward time (y = Wx + BAx), so only A/B (and their optimizer state) need full-precision memory and gradients.

What the script does

  1. Quick from-scratch check: quantizes one real weight tensor from Qwen2.5-7B-Instruct to INT4 (per-group, g=64), NF4 (block=64, matching bitsandbytes' default), and NVFP4 (block=16, its own native block size) and reports reconstruction error for each -- a direct, real-model version of lab 00's format comparison.
  2. Loads the full model with transformers' BitsAndBytesConfig(load_in_4bit=True, bnb_4bit_quant_type="nf4", bnb_4bit_use_double_quant=True) and measures actual GPU memory used, compared against an estimate of what loading the same model in bf16 would take.
  3. Wraps the model with peft's prepare_model_for_kbit_training + LoRA adapters (rank 16, targeting every attention/MLP projection), reports how many parameters are actually trainable (should be well under 1% of the total).
  4. Fine-tunes on a small slice of the Alpaca instruction dataset (a few hundred steps, small batches) with a plain PyTorch training loop, tracking the loss curve and peak GPU memory during training.
  5. Compares peak training memory actually observed against a rough estimate of what full-precision full fine-tuning (weights + gradients + Adam optimizer state, no quantization, no LoRA) would require for the same model.
  6. Generates a couple of instruction-following completions before/after fine-tuning so you can see the adapter's effect qualitatively, not just as a loss number.
  7. Saves comparison charts + metrics.json.

Run it

python labs/08_qlora/lab08_qlora_finetune.py

What to look for

  • NF4 should show the lowest reconstruction error of the three 4-bit formats on a real weight tensor (step 1) -- this is the concrete payoff of designing a codebook around the actual data distribution instead of a generic uniform/floating-point grid.
  • The measured 4-bit memory footprint should be roughly a quarter of the bf16 estimate (4 bits vs 16, plus a little overhead for double-quantized scale factors) -- and the trainable parameter count should be tiny (LoRA rank 16 on a 7B model is typically well under 1% of total parameters).
  • Peak training memory should be dramatically lower than the full fine-tuning estimate -- this is the whole point of QLoRA: it's not just "a smaller model", it's "fine-tuning became possible on hardware that couldn't otherwise hold this model's gradients and optimizer state".
  • Loss should decrease over training steps even with this few adapters training and this little data -- LoRA's whole premise is that most fine-tuning updates live in a low-rank subspace, so a small number of steps is often enough to see a clear, visible shift in behavior.

lessons.title: Lab 09 - KV-Cache Quantization
lessons.html:
Lab 09 - KV-Cache Quantization

Goal: quantize the KV cache (not the weights, not the activations that flow through a linear layer -- the per-token key/value tensors saved during autoregressive generation) and measure both the memory savings and the accuracy cost, then compare a from-scratch implementation against vLLM's native support.

Runtime: ~15-20 minutes on one B200 (Qwen2.5-7B-Instruct). The vLLM comparison section needs vllm (already in your base environment).

Background

During autoregressive generation, a transformer caches every previous token's key and value projections per layer/head so it doesn't have to recompute them at every new step -- that's the "KV cache". For long contexts and/or large batches, this cache can dominate GPU memory more than the model's weights do:

kv_cache_bytes = 2 (K and V) x num_layers x num_kv_heads x head_dim x seq_len x batch_size x bytes_per_element

Halving bytes_per_element (bf16 -> int8, or bf16 -> fp8) directly halves that memory, which either lets you serve longer contexts, larger batches, or both, with the same GPU memory. Unlike weight quantization, this cost is paid fresh, every request (the cache is per-conversation, not a one-time offline step), so KV-cache quantization has to be cheap enough to do at generation time, not just accurate.

Why this is a slightly different problem than weight quantization

Keys and values are activations, computed on the fly from the current context -- there's no "calibrate once offline" step like GPTQ/AWQ get to do. The standard approach (used by vLLM, TensorRT-LLM, and this lab) is per-token dynamic quantization: whenever a new token's key/value is computed, quantize it (with a scale derived from that token's own values) before writing it into the cache, then dequantize when reading it back out for attention. This lab implements exactly that, using the same fake_quantize_int / fp8_quantize_dequantize primitives from lab 00, applied per-token by subclassing transformers' DynamicCache.

What the script does

  1. Computes and charts the theoretical KV-cache memory for Qwen2.5-7B-Instruct at a few context lengths (4K/32K/128K tokens), comparing bf16 vs INT8 vs FP8 cache storage -- purely arithmetic, no GPU needed, but it's the clearest way to see why this matters before context length gets long.
  2. Implements QuantizedKVCache, a small subclass of transformers' DynamicCache that quantizes every key/value tensor (INT8 or FP8, per-token dynamic scale) the moment it's written to the cache, then dequantizes it back before returning it for attention -- so the rest of the model is completely unaware anything is quantized.
  3. Re-runs this lab's own version of the sliding-window WikiText-2 perplexity evaluation (from common/eval.py), but this time passing the quantized cache explicitly, so every window's self-attention actually reads back quantized-and-dequantized keys/values -- a genuine test of the accuracy cost, not just a memory estimate.
  4. Compares BF16 cache (baseline), INT8 cache, and FP8 (E4M3) cache.
  5. Production comparison: launches vLLM twice (kv_cache_dtype="auto" vs kv_cache_dtype="fp8") on the same model, and compares actual reported GPU memory usage and generation throughput.
  6. Saves comparison charts + metrics.json.

Run it

python labs/09_kv_cache_quant/lab09_kv_cache_quant.py

What to look for

  • The theoretical memory chart should make it obvious that at long enough context, the KV cache -- not the weights -- becomes the memory bottleneck; this is exactly why vLLM/TensorRT-LLM support KV-cache quantization as a first-class serving option, independent of whatever precision the weights are in.
  • INT8 KV-cache perplexity degradation should be small but non-zero; FP8 should be even closer to the bf16 baseline, for the same reason FP8 activations needed no smoothing in lab 05 -- keys/values have outlier structure too, and FP8's non-uniform grid absorbs it better than INT8's uniform one.
  • The vLLM comparison should show a measurable memory reduction with kv_cache_dtype="fp8" at the same gpu_memory_utilization setting -- in production this memory gets reinvested as more available KV cache blocks, i.e. more concurrent requests or longer contexts, not just a smaller footprint for its own sake.

lessons.title: Lab 10 - Capstone: Multi-Precision, Multi-GPU Serving Benchmark
lessons.html:
Lab 10 - Capstone: Multi-Precision, Multi-GPU Serving Benchmark

Goal: bring every precision this curriculum covered together in one place, served the way it would actually be deployed -- through vLLM, with tensor parallelism across multiple B200s -- and measure the real throughput/latency/memory/quality trade-off between them.

Runtime: this is the capstone and genuinely takes a while: expect 45-90 minutes for the full sweep (4 precisions x 3 concurrency levels, each needing its own vLLM engine startup + weight loading across multiple GPUs). See "Scoping this down" below if you want a faster run.

What this pulls together

Precision How it's produced here Which earlier lab covered the technique
BF16 vLLM's default, no quantization the baseline in every previous lab
FP8 vLLM's built-in on-the-fly FP8 weight quantization (quantization="fp8") lab 05
INT4 vLLM's built-in on-the-fly bitsandbytes NF4 quantization (quantization="bitsandbytes") labs 01-03 (RTN/GPTQ/AWQ) and lab 08 (NF4 specifically)
NVFP4 vLLM's modelopt-style FP4 quantization path, best-effort -- see below lab 06

This lab deliberately uses vLLM's on-the-fly quantization options (load a normal bf16 checkpoint, quantize during engine startup) instead of pre-producing separate quantized checkpoints with the libraries from labs 02/03/05/06 -- that keeps this already-long capstone from also needing a 32B-scale offline quantization pass per precision. The accuracy/format trade-offs you already measured in those labs on smaller models still apply; this lab's job is to show the serving-time trade-off (throughput, latency, memory) that those techniques exist to unlock in the first place.

NVFP4 is best-effort: whether vLLM's installed version exposes a working on-the-fly FP4 quantization path for this model depends heavily on your vllm/nvidia-modelopt versions and the specific model architecture. The script tries it, and if it fails, skips that one row of the comparison with a clear message and a suggestion (build a pre-quantized NVFP4 checkpoint with nvidia-modelopt, the way lab 06's accelerated path does, then point --model at that checkpoint) rather than blocking the rest of the lab.

What the script does
