  1. DNS: the client resolves api.example.com. GeoDNS / latency-based DNS returns the IP of the nearest healthy region; health checks remove failed regions. Caveat: DNS answers are cached for the record TTL (keep it short, 30-60 s, for failover) and resolvers may be far from users.
  2. Anycast: the same IP is announced via BGP from many locations; the internet routes each client to the topologically nearest one. Global load balancers and CDNs use anycast front ends that terminate TLS at the edge and forward over the provider's backbone.
  3. Edge / CDN: points of presence close to users terminate TCP+TLS (saving round trips), apply WAF/DDoS protection, and keep long-lived connections to origin regions. LLM responses aren't cacheable like images, but edge termination still cuts the connection-setup latency and protects the origin. Streaming (SSE) must pass through without buffering.
user ─► DNS (GeoDNS) ─► anycast edge PoP (TLS, WAF, DDoS) ─► provider backbone
     ─► regional L7 load balancer / API gateway ─► inference cluster (llm-d router) ─► GPUs

Routing policy across regions

  • Latency-based: nearest region by measured RTT.
  • Weighted: split traffic (e.g. 90/10 for a canary region).
  • Failover: primary/secondary with health checks.
  • Capacity-aware: send overflow to regions with spare GPUs (needs a global view of queue depth or saturation - the same signals the llm-d EPP uses inside a cluster, aggregated up).
  • Data residency: EU users' prompts must stay in EU regions (GDPR, customer contracts), which overrides latency.

Multi-region active-active

Each region runs a full stack (gateway, router, model servers) and serves live traffic. Requirements: identical model versions everywhere (artifact registry replication), configuration as code, per-region capacity for failover (N+1: if one region of N fails, the rest absorb its load), and state that is either regional (conversation KV caches are regional and rebuildable) or replicated (user accounts, quotas).

lessons.title: Load balancers, API gateways and admission control
lessons.html:
Load balancers, API gateways and admission control

L4 vs L7

  • L4 (transport) load balancers forward TCP/UDP connections by IP/port. Fast and simple, but one long-lived HTTP/2 connection carrying thousands of requests lands on one backend.
  • L7 (application) load balancers / proxies (Envoy, NGINX, cloud ALBs) parse HTTP, so they can route per request, by path or header, retry, apply timeouts, and terminate TLS. Classic policies: round-robin, least-request, consistent hashing (session affinity).
  • Inference-aware L7 (llm-d EPP via Envoy ext_proc, Gateway API Inference Extension) adds model-server state: queue depth, KV-cache usage, prefix-cache locality, predicted latency, P/D roles, LoRA adapters loaded. llm-d lab 01 shows why this beats round-robin and least-request.

The API gateway layer

In front of the inference router, a production API usually has an API gateway that does what the GPUs shouldn't:

Concern How
Authentication API keys, OAuth/JWT validation, mTLS for service-to-service
Tenant identity derive tenant/tier from the token, strip client-supplied x-llm-d-* headers, inject authoritative x-llm-d-inference-fairness-id / x-llm-d-inference-objective
Rate limiting requests/min and tokens/min per key (token-bucket); prompt tokens can be counted up front, output tokens charged as they stream
Quotas & billing per-tenant token accounting, usage events to a billing pipeline
Model routing map public model names to pools/versions, A/B and canary splits
Safety input/output moderation, PII filtering, prompt-injection defenses
Observability request ids, traces (W3C traceparent), access logs

Admission control and backpressure

Accepting more work than you can serve only converts overload into timeouts. Layers of defense:

  1. Gateway rate limits per tenant (protects everyone from one tenant).
  2. Router flow control (llm-d lab 03): per-tenant fair queues with priorities; hold requests in the router while the pool is saturated; reject (429) when a band's queue or TTL limits are hit.
  3. Engine limits: --max-num-seqs, --max-num-batched-tokens, preemption when KV runs out.
  4. Client behavior: retries with exponential backoff and jitter, and respecting Retry-After; otherwise retry storms amplify overload.

Shedding low-priority (batch, best-effort) traffic first keeps interactive latency within SLO during spikes.

Streaming through proxies

Every proxy on the path must stream SSE without buffering, allow long request durations (minutes for long generations), and propagate client disconnects so the engine can abort the request and free its KV cache.

lessons.title: GPU capacity, autoscaling and cost
lessons.html:
GPU capacity, autoscaling and cost

Capacity planning from first principles

  1. Traffic model: peak requests/s, input and output token distributions, prefix reuse, diurnal pattern per region.
  2. Per-replica capacity at SLO: from benchmarks (the labs), the maximum requests/s one replica sustains while meeting p99 TTFT and TPOT targets - goodput, not peak throughput.
  3. Replicas = peak load / per-replica goodput, plus headroom for failures (N+1 per AZ/region) and deploys.
  4. Memory check: weights + KV for the concurrency implied by Little's law (concurrency = rate × latency) must fit, per replica.

Cost per million tokens

cost per 1M output tokens = (GPU $/hour × GPUs) ÷ (output tokens/s × 3600) × 1,000,000

Illustrative: 8 GPUs at $5/GPU-hour = $40/h. At 20,000 output tokens/s sustained that is 72M tokens/h → ≈ $0.56 per 1M output tokens. At 30% average utilization the effective cost is ~3x higher. Every optimization in the engine labs moves this number: FP8 (~1.5-2x tokens/s), prefix caching (fewer prefill FLOPs), speculative decoding (lower latency at low load), and routing (higher cache hit rates per GPU).

Input tokens are cheaper than output tokens (prefill is parallel and compute-efficient), which is why providers price them separately and why cached input tokens are discounted further.

Buying GPUs

Option Trade-off
On-demand flexible, most expensive, may be unavailable for large GPUs
Reservations / committed use cheaper per hour, you pay whether used or not
Spot / preemptible cheapest, can be reclaimed with short notice: batch and offline inference
Multi-cloud / neoclouds more capacity, more operational surface

Common pattern: reserved capacity for the baseline, on-demand or another region for peaks, spot for batch jobs (llm-d's batch gateway / async processing fits here).

Autoscaling LLM services

  • Scale on leading signals: router in-flight requests, queue size, pool saturation, KV-cache pressure - not GPU utilization, which reads ~100% under any batching load (llm-d lab 09).
  • Startup latency dominates: image pull + weight load + compile + CUDA graph capture can take minutes. Mitigations: pre-pulled images, weights on node-local NVMe or a fast distributed cache, compile caches, model streaming loaders, sleep/wake (fast model actuation: keep a vLLM process with weights parked in host memory, wake in seconds).
  • Scale-down carefully: drain in-flight requests (--shutdown-timeout, preStop hooks); scaling a pool with warm prefix caches down loses those caches.
  • Cluster autoscaler / node provisioning adds GPU nodes when pods are pending; for GPUs this can take many minutes, so keep warm spare nodes for bursty traffic.
  • Scale to zero suits rarely used models (KEDA), at the cost of a cold start on the first request.

Multi-model and multi-tenant efficiency

  • LoRA adapters: serve many fine-tunes on one base model; the router can prefer replicas with the adapter loaded.
  • Model variants across accelerator types (H100, B200, MI355X) with the router picking the cheapest pool that meets the SLO.
  • Priority tiers: interactive traffic first, batch fills the gaps.

lessons.title: Reliability, rollouts and observability
lessons.html:
Reliability, rollouts and observability

SLOs and error budgets

  • SLI (indicator): a measured ratio, e.g. "fraction of requests with TTFT < 1 s and no 5xx".
  • SLO (objective): the target, e.g. 99.5% over 28 days.
  • Error budget: 1 − SLO = 0.5% of requests may miss. While budget remains, ship features; when it's burning fast, freeze risky changes and fix reliability. Alert on burn rate (budget consumed per hour), not on single blips.

For LLM APIs, define separate SLOs for availability (non-5xx), TTFT and TPOT, per tier (interactive vs batch).

Failure modes specific to LLM serving

Failure Symptom Mitigation
GPU Xid / ECC / NVLink errors pod crash, NCCL hang health checks, node auto-repair, LWS group restart
KV cache exhaustion preemptions, TTFT spikes admission control, KV offload, more replicas
Hot prefix / hot tenant one replica saturated load-aware scoring (not pure affinity), flow control
Slow cold starts autoscale too late warm pools, sleep/wake, scale on queue signals
Model/tokenizer mismatch garbage output, failed tool parsing pinned images and artifacts, canaries with eval checks
Retry storms load doubles under failure backoff + jitter, retry budgets, 429 with Retry-After
Long requests during deploy dropped streams graceful drain (--shutdown-timeout, preStop), connection draining

Safe rollouts

  • Rolling update: replace pods a few at a time; readiness probes gate traffic.
  • Blue/green: stand up the new version beside the old, switch traffic, keep the old one for instant rollback.
  • Canary: send 1-5% of traffic (weighted HTTPRoute, gateway split) to the new model/engine version and compare SLIs and quality metrics (eval scores, refusal rates, tool-call parse errors) before ramping.
  • Shadow traffic: mirror requests to the new version without returning its responses, to measure performance safely.
  • Treat model weights, chat templates, engine version and flags as one versioned artifact - a change in any of them is a deploy.

Observability

  • Metrics (Prometheus): engine metrics (vllm:num_requests_running, vllm:num_requests_waiting, vllm:kv_cache_usage_perc, vllm:prefix_cache_hits_total, TTFT/ITL histograms), router metrics (EPP in-flight, flow-control queues, scheduling decisions), GPU metrics (DCGM exporter: SM activity, memory, power, Xid errors), gateway metrics.
  • Logs: structured, sampled; never log prompts by default (privacy).
  • Traces (OpenTelemetry → Jaeger/Tempo): one trace per request across gateway → Envoy → EPP → model server shows where time went (queueing vs prefill vs decode vs network).
  • Dashboards per layer and an SLO dashboard; llm-d ships Grafana dashboards for the router and model servers.

Disaster recovery

Define RTO (how fast you must recover) and RPO (how much data you may lose). Inference is mostly stateless, so DR is about capacity and artifacts: model weights replicated to every region's registry, infra as code to rebuild a cluster, tested regional failover (game days), and enough quota in the fallback regions.

lessons.title: Security, privacy and multi-tenancy
lessons.html:
Security, privacy and multi-tenancy

Threats to an LLM service

  • Abuse: credential stuffing, scraping, denial of wallet (expensive long prompts), DDoS. → WAF/DDoS at the edge, auth, token-based rate limits.
  • Tenant isolation failures: one tenant seeing another's data. Shared prefix caches are safe in content terms (a cache hit requires the exact same tokens) but can leak timing (a fast TTFT reveals that someone sent that prefix). Mitigations: per-tenant cache salting/namespaces for sensitive tenants, dedicated pools for regulated customers.
  • Prompt injection / tool abuse: untrusted content steering an agent to call tools. → least-privilege tools, output validation, human approval for risky actions. (Structured outputs help parsing, not trust.)
  • Supply chain: malicious model files (pickle), compromised images or Python packages. → safetensors only, signed and scanned images, pinned digests, private registries and model mirrors.
  • Secrets: HF tokens, API keys in env vars or logs. → secret managers, Kubernetes Secrets with RBAC, never in images or command lines.

Data handling

  • Encrypt in transit (TLS at the edge, mTLS inside the mesh) and at rest (model registry, logs, KV offload tiers on disk).
  • Minimize retention: don't log prompts/responses by default; if you must (debugging, abuse review), redact PII and set short retention.
  • Data residency: keep prompts, logs and KV tiers in the user's region; route by geography at DNS/gateway level.
  • Offloaded KV on shared filesystems is user data - apply the same access controls and encryption as any other data store.

Network and cluster hygiene

  • Model servers and the EPP should not be reachable from the internet; only the gateway is. Use NetworkPolicies so only the router can reach model pods, and only the EPP can scrape them.
  • RBAC: the EPP only needs to watch pods/InferencePools in its namespace.
  • Run containers as non-root where possible; restrict privileged mounts (RDMA devices, host paths) to the pods that need them.

lessons.title: The life of one request
lessons.html:
The life of one request

A user in Berlin sends a chat message to api.example.com. Here is every hop, what it costs, and which lab or module covers it.

 ① DNS          ② Edge PoP          ③ Regional gateway      ④ llm-d router          ⑤ Model server         ⑥ GPU
 GeoDNS ──► anycast TLS/WAF ──► auth, quotas, tenant ──► Envoy + EPP pick ──► vLLM/SGLang schedule ──► prefill, decode
   ~10 ms*      ~5-20 ms           ~1-5 ms                 ~1-3 ms                queue: 0 .. seconds     ms .. seconds
                                                                                    ◄──── tokens stream back over SSE ────

* cached DNS answers cost ~0.

  1. DNS (Cloud 1). GeoDNS answers with the anycast IP of the global load balancer; the EU region is chosen for latency and data residency.
  2. Edge (Cloud 1). The nearest PoP terminates TCP+TLS (saving ~2 round trips to the origin), applies WAF/DDoS rules, and forwards over the provider backbone to eu-west.
  3. API gateway (Cloud 2, 5). Validates the API key/JWT, looks up the tenant (tier: premium), checks token-rate limits, strips any client x-llm-d-* headers and injects x-llm-d-inference-fairness-id: acme and x-llm-d-inference-objective: premium-traffic, starts a trace, maps model chat-large → InferencePool qwen3-32b-prod.
  4. llm-d router (llm-d labs 01-03). Envoy receives the request and streams it to the EPP over ext_proc. The EPP:
    • classifies the flow (tenant + priority) and, if the pool is saturated, queues it fairly (flow control);
    • hashes the prompt's blocks: the 3,000-token system prompt of this app is cached on replicas 3 and 7 (prefix-cache affinity);
    • filters to those, scores by queued prompt tokens (token load), picks replica 7, and returns x-gateway-destination-endpoint: 10.4.2.17:8000. In P/D mode it picks a prefill pod and a decode pod instead (llm-d lab 05).
  5. Model server (vLLM/SGLang labs). The API server applies the chat template and tokenizes. The scheduler admits the request into the next continuous batch if KV blocks are available (else it waits or preempts). Prefix caching finds 3,000 tokens already cached; only the new 150 tokens are prefilled (chunked so running decodes aren't stalled).
  6. GPU (Foundations 1-5). Prefill runs compute-bound GEMMs and FlashAttention-4 kernels; then each decode step streams all weights (FP8: half the bytes) plus this sequence's KV from HBM, inside a captured CUDA graph, verifying 3 EAGLE-3 draft tokens per step when acceptance is high.
  7. Streaming back. Each detokenized chunk is sent as an SSE event through Envoy, the gateway and the edge. The gateway counts output tokens for billing; the trace records TTFT and TPOT per hop.
  8. After the response. The KV blocks stay in the prefix cache (and are offloaded to CPU RAM when evicted) so the user's next turn hits the cache
    • as long as the router sends it back to replica 7 or its CPU tier.

Where the latency goes (typical 32B model, warm cache)

Component Budget
Network to region (TLS at edge) 20-60 ms
Gateway + router 2-8 ms
Queueing 0 ms at healthy load; seconds when overloaded
Prefill 150 new tokens (3K cached) ~20-40 ms
Prefill 3K tokens uncached ~150-300 ms
Decode, per token 10-30 ms

The single biggest lever on TTFT is usually not recomputing the prefix (cache + cache-aware routing); on TPOT it is bytes per step (precision, batch, speculation); on tail latency it is queueing (capacity, flow control, autoscaling).

lessons.title: Reference architecture for a global LLM service
lessons.html:
Reference architecture for a global LLM service

                           ┌──────────────────────── Global ────────────────────────┐
  clients ─► GeoDNS ─► anycast edge (TLS, WAF, DDoS) ─► global LB (latency/geo/capacity)
                           └───────────────┬──────────────────────┬─────────────────┘
                                           ▼                      ▼
            ┌────────────── Region us-east ──────────┐   ┌──── Region eu-west ────┐
            │ API gateway: authn, quotas, tenant hdrs│   │ (same stack; EU data   │
            │ model routing, moderation, metering    │   │  stays in EU)          │
            │                   │                    │   └────────────────────────┘
            │   ┌───────── Kubernetes cluster(s) ─────────────────────────┐      │
            │   │ llm-d router (Envoy + EPP, 2+ replicas, HA)              │      │
            │   │   flow control → filters → scorers → picker              │      │
            │   │ InferencePool A: Qwen3-32B FP8, aggregated, TP=2 × N     │      │
            │   │ InferencePool B: DeepSeek MoE, P/D + wide-EP (LWS)       │      │
            │   │ KV tiers: HBM → CPU RAM → NVMe/shared FS                  │      │
            │   │ KEDA autoscaling on EPP metrics; warm/sleeping replicas  │      │
            │   └──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘      │
            │ Model registry mirror · image registry · secrets manager           │
            │ Prometheus/Grafana · OTel traces · logs · SLO alerts               │
            └─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘
  Control plane: GitOps (Helm/Kustomize) · CI with perf + eval gates · canary controller

Layer responsibilities

Layer Owns Course
Global traffic DNS, anycast, edge TLS, region selection, failover Cloud 1
Gateway identity, quotas, tenant/priority headers, model mapping, safety, billing Cloud 2, 5
Inference router (llm-d) replica choice (cache/load/latency aware), P/D scheduling, fair queuing, pool discovery llm-d 01-05, 08
Model server (vLLM/SGLang) batching, KV paging and caching, kernels, quantization, speculation, parallelism vLLM & SGLang tracks
Accelerators HBM, tensor cores, NVLink, RDMA NICs Foundations 1-3
Platform Kubernetes, LWS, GPU operators, autoscaling, observability, rollouts Foundations 7, llm-d 07-09, Cloud 3-4

Design decisions and defaults

  • Engine: vLLM for breadth of models, hardware and features; SGLang for RadixAttention-heavy workloads, structured generation and some MoE/DeepSeek optimizations. llm-d supports both behind the same router.
  • Precision: BF16 to validate, then FP8 (W8A8 + FP8 KV) as the production default on Hopper/Blackwell; FP4 (NVFP4/MXFP4) where evals allow.
  • Topology: smallest TP that fits with KV headroom; DP replicas behind the llm-d optimized baseline. Add P/D when prompts are long and TPOT SLOs strict; wide-EP for large MoE models across nodes.
  • Caching: prefix caching always on; cache-aware routing; CPU KV tier for multi-turn/agentic traffic; precise prefix routing when the pool is large.
  • Admission: gateway rate limits + router flow control with priority bands; batch traffic as best-effort or through a batch API.
  • Scaling: KEDA on EPP queue/saturation signals; warm capacity sized to startup time × growth rate.
  • Release safety: perf and eval gates in CI; canaries per region; model, template, engine and flags versioned together.

lessons.title: The optimization playbook
lessons.html:
The optimization playbook

A checklist that maps symptoms to the lab that fixes them.

Single replica (vLLM / SGLang)

Symptom Likely cause Try Lab
Very low tokens/s, GPU underused FP32 or naive HF loop, static batching BF16, a real engine with continuous batching vLLM 00-02, SGLang 01-02
Few concurrent sequences fit KV cache too big FP8 KV, GQA model, smaller max-model-len, more GPUs vLLM 08, Foundations 2
High TTFT with shared system prompts prefix recomputation prefix caching / RadixAttention vLLM 04, SGLang 05
TPOT spikes when long prompts arrive prefill interrupting decode chunked prefill, tune max-num-batched-tokens; later P/D vLLM 05, SGLang 06, llm-d 05
Slow decode at low concurrency launch overhead, eager mode CUDA graphs, -O2, overlap scheduling vLLM 06, SGLang 07
Slow decode at low concurrency, graphs on memory-bound weights FP8/MXFP8/FP4 or INT4 weights; speculative decoding vLLM 07-09, SGLang 03, 08
Long-prompt prefill slow attention kernel FA4 / FlashInfer / TRT-LLM backends vLLM 03, SGLang 12
Model doesn't fit / latency too high single-GPU limits tensor parallelism (inside NVLink) vLLM 10, SGLang 04
MoE model inefficient TP slicing experts DP attention + expert parallelism, EPLB SGLang 10, llm-d 06
JSON outputs invalid unconstrained sampling structured outputs (grammar backends) SGLang 09

Fleet (llm-d)

Symptom Try Lab
Prefix hit rate low despite shared prompts prefix-cache-aware routing llm-d 01
One replica hot, others idle load-aware scorers with affinity, calibrate peakPrefillThroughput llm-d 02
One tenant's burst hurts everyone flow control with fairness + priorities llm-d 03
Multi-turn sessions miss cache after a while CPU/NVMe KV tier + tier-aware routing llm-d 04, SGLang 13
Approximate cache routing mispredicts at scale precise prefix-cache routing (KV events) llm-d 08
Long prompts + strict TPOT P/D disaggregation, scale P and D separately llm-d 05, 08
Big MoE across nodes wide-EP with DeepEP + P/D llm-d 06
Latency SLOs differ per request predicted-latency routing with SLO headers llm-d 08
Capacity lags demand KEDA on EPP signals, warm pools, sleep/wake llm-d 09

Order of operations

  1. Measure a baseline with the target workload shape (lengths, prefix reuse), not just random tokens.
  2. Get the engine basics right: BF16 → FP8, prefix caching, chunked prefill, CUDA graphs, right TP.
  3. Scale out with DP replicas behind an inference-aware router.
  4. Add the specialised paths only when their symptom shows up: P/D, KV tiers, wide-EP, flow control, predicted latency.
  5. Re-measure after each change, including quality.

cards.label: Quiz · Sliding Window Pattern
cards.front:
When is the Sliding Window pattern typically preferred over a naive nested loop approach?

  1. When checking all possible contiguous subarrays or substrings of a specific or variable length
  2. When working with non-contiguous subsets or permutations of elements
  3. When elements must be sorted and compared pairwise across the entire list
  4. When solving tree traversal or hierarchical network problems
cards.back:
A. When checking all possible contiguous subarrays or substrings of a specific or variable length

Sliding Window is highly optimized for contiguous blocks (subarrays or substrings) because it allows updating the window's state incrementally (O(1) average time per slide) instead of recalculating from scratch (O(k) or O(N^2)).

cards.label: Quiz · Sliding Window Pattern
cards.front:
For a variable-size sliding window, what condition causes the left pointer to advance?

  1. When the current window is invalid or has met/exceeded the target condition
  2. When the right pointer reaches the end of the array
  3. When the right pointer encounters a duplicate character
  4. When the time limit of the current slide expires
cards.back:
A. When the current window is invalid or has met/exceeded the target condition

In variable-size window problems (like Minimum Window Substring), we expand the right pointer to find a valid state, then contract the left pointer as long as the condition remains valid to find the minimum/optimal window size.

cards.label: Quiz · Sliding Window Pattern
cards.front:
What is the worst-case space complexity of a sliding window algorithm using a hash map to track character frequencies?

  1. O(K) or O(1) where K is the size of the alphabet
  2. O(N) where N is the total elements in the array
  3. O(N log N) due to hashing collisions
  4. O(N^2) because of nested index tracking
cards.back:
A. O(K) or O(1) where K is the size of the alphabet

The space complexity is determined by the size of the character frequency map. Since there are a fixed number of unique characters (e.g., 26 for English letters, 128 or 256 for standard ASCII), the space complexity is O(K), which simplifies to O(1) if K is bounded.

cards.label: Quiz · Two Pointers Pattern
cards.front:
In what state must the array be to successfully apply the classic two-pointer approach (e.g., target sum)?

  1. Sorted (ascending or descending order)
  2. Fully shuffled to guarantee uniform access
  3. Homogeneous (all elements must have the same sign)
  4. Partially populated with null values at index boundaries
cards.back:
A. Sorted (ascending or descending order)

The classic two-pointer technique for finding a target sum requires a sorted array. This allows us to move pointers inward: increment the left pointer to increase the sum, or decrement the right pointer to decrease it.

cards.label: Quiz · Two Pointers Pattern
cards.front:
What is the time complexity of the Floyd's Cycle Detection (Tortoise and Hare) algorithm?

  1. O(N) time complexity
  2. O(N log N) time complexity
  3. O(1) time complexity
  4. O(N^2) time complexity
cards.back:
A. O(N) time complexity

Floyd's Cycle Finding algorithm runs in O(N) time because the fast pointer (moving 2 steps) and slow pointer (moving 1 step) will meet inside the cycle of size C in at most N steps.

cards.label: Quiz · NumPy Tutorial – Arrays, Broadcasting & Linear Algebra
cards.front:
What does NumPy's 'broadcasting' do?

  1. Allows arithmetic operations on arrays of different shapes without copying data
  2. Distributes array computations across multiple CPU cores in parallel
  3. Converts multi-dimensional arrays into flat 1D views
  4. Performs fast serialization of arrays to binary files on disk
cards.back:
A. Allows arithmetic operations on arrays of different shapes without copying data

Broadcasting automatically stretches compatible dimensions of arrays (virtually, without duplicating memory) so they can participate in element-wise operations together.

cards.label: Quiz · NumPy Tutorial – Arrays, Broadcasting & Linear Algebra
cards.front:
Under what condition are two dimensions compatible for broadcasting?

  1. They are equal, or one of them is 1
  2. They are both prime numbers or multiples of 2
  3. Their sum is equal to the total rank (ndim) of the target array
  4. One dimension is exactly double the other dimension
cards.back:
A. They are equal, or one of them is 1

Numpy aligns dimensions starting from the rightmost (trailing) axis. Two dimensions are compatible if they are equal, or if one of them is 1.

cards.label: Quiz · NumPy Tutorial – Arrays, Broadcasting & Linear Algebra
cards.front:
What is the difference between `a.ravel()` and `a.flatten()` in NumPy?

  1. `ravel()` returns a view when possible; `flatten()` always returns a copy
  2. `ravel()` always returns a copy; `flatten()` returns an in-place reference
  3. `ravel()` only works on 2D arrays; `flatten()` works on any N-dimensional array
  4. `ravel()` is slower because it allocates memory; `flatten()` is instantaneous
cards.back:
A. `ravel()` returns a view when possible; `flatten()` always returns a copy

`ravel()` returns a contiguous flattened view if possible, which shares the underlying buffer. `flatten()` always creates a brand new copy of the data, consuming more memory.

cards.label: Quiz · PyTorch Tutorial – Karpathy Repos
cards.front:
Why is tracking gradients manually in deep learning frameworks obsolete?

  1. PyTorch uses Autograd to dynamically build a directed acyclic graph during the forward pass and perform backpropagation automatically
  2. Stochastic gradient descent operates perfectly without any gradient tracking
  3. GPUs perform gradient calculations at a hardware level without software layers
  4. Weight initialization techniques make active optimization gradients unnecessary
cards.back:
A. PyTorch uses Autograd to dynamically build a directed acyclic graph during the forward pass and perform backpropagation automatically

PyTorch's Autograd engine records all operations performed on tensors that have `requires_grad=True`, building a dynamic computation graph. Calling `.backward()` computes the gradients of these variables automatically.

cards.label: Quiz · PyTorch Tutorial – Karpathy Repos
cards.front:
What does the `loss.backward()` method do in PyTorch?

  1. Computes the gradient of the loss with respect to all leaf nodes (tensors) in the computation graph
  2. Resets all parameters and optimization weights back to random initialization values
  3. Updates parameter weights by subtracting learning rate times the gradient
  4. Reverses the neural network's layers for inference mode
cards.back:
A. Computes the gradient of the loss with respect to all leaf nodes (tensors) in the computation graph

`loss.backward()` computes gradients using backpropagation. To actually update the weights using those gradients, you call `optimizer.step()`.

cards.label: Quiz · PyTorch Tutorial – Karpathy Repos
cards.front:
What is the purpose of `torch.no_grad()`?

  1. Disables gradient calculation, reducing memory consumption and speeding up calculations during inference/evaluation
  2. Forces the model to calculate gradients strictly on the CPU instead of GPU
  3. Filters out NaN or infinite gradient errors from backpropagation logs
  4. Prevents the optimizer from updating specific layers in a frozen network
cards.back:
A. Disables gradient calculation, reducing memory consumption and speeding up calculations during inference/evaluation

`with torch.no_grad():` is a context manager that disables gradient tracking. This is highly recommended for evaluation and validation loops because it reduces memory usage and speeds up model forward passes.

cards.label: Quiz · System Design – State-of-the-Art AI Agents
cards.front:
What is a major architectural difference between single-agent systems and multi-agent routing systems?

  1. Multi-agent architectures decompose complex, monolithic tasks into specialized, cooperative nodes with distinct instructions, tools, and states
  2. Single-agent systems are always slower because they cannot run asynchronous calls
  3. Multi-agent networks store their persistent state entirely inside local database instances rather than in-memory context
  4. Single-agent systems rely exclusively on fine-tuned transformer weights, whereas multi-agent setups do not
cards.back:
A. Multi-agent architectures decompose complex, monolithic tasks into specialized, cooperative nodes with distinct instructions, tools, and states

Multi-agent systems break down a large, fragile prompt/task into small, specialized agents. Each agent has narrow context, dedicated tools, and specific instructions, increasing success rates and simplifying debugging.

cards.label: Quiz · System Design – State-of-the-Art AI Agents
cards.front:
How does the 'ReAct' (Reasoning and Acting) prompting framework work in AI agent design?

  1. It iterates between a 'Thought' phase (analyzing state) and an 'Action' phase (calling a tool or querying an API) in a loop
  2. It converts user natural language directly into database SQL commands in a single pass
  3. It trains the model weights iteratively in real-time as users interact with the system
  4. It strictly separates coding agents from logical planning agents
cards.back:
A. It iterates between a 'Thought' phase (analyzing state) and an 'Action' phase (calling a tool or querying an API) in a loop

ReAct prompts the LLM to generate both reasoning traces ('Thought') and task-specific actions ('Action'). The agent executes the action, receives an 'Observation' from the environment, and repeats the loop until it achieves the goal.

cards.label: Quiz · Python — Robust software at billion-user scale
cards.front:
What is the Global Interpreter Lock (GIL) in Python (CPython) and how does it affect concurrency?

  1. A mutex that prevents multiple native threads from executing Python bytecodes at once, making CPU-bound multi-threading ineffective
  2. A security layer that blocks unauthorized socket connections in async servers
  3. An automatic garbage collection system that runs exclusively when memory limits are exceeded
  4. A compiler lock that speeds up single-threaded mathematical computations
cards.back:
A. A mutex that prevents multiple native threads from executing Python bytecodes at once, making CPU-bound multi-threading ineffective

The GIL ensures only one thread executes Python bytecode at a time. Therefore, multi-threading is great for I/O-bound tasks (network/file access), but for CPU-bound tasks (computations), you must use multi-processing or C extensions.

cards.label: Quiz · Python — Robust software at billion-user scale
cards.front:
Why is `asyncio` highly scalable for network-heavy Python services compared to traditional multi-threading?

  1. It uses single-threaded cooperative multitasking with an event loop, eliminating context switching overhead of operating system threads
  2. It bypasses the CPython GIL entirely, allowing full parallel CPU scaling
  3. It compiles Python code into optimized native machine instructions at runtime
  4. It automatically creates redundant network channels to prevent connection packet drops
cards.back:
A. It uses single-threaded cooperative multitasking with an event loop, eliminating context switching overhead of operating system threads

`asyncio` uses an event loop to run cooperative tasks. When a task awaits an I/O operation, it yields control back to the loop, letting other tasks execute. This allows a single process to handle thousands of concurrent open sockets efficiently.

cards.label: Quiz · Data Pipelines – Pandas, PySpark & Distributed Optimizations
cards.front:
In PySpark, what is the difference between a Transformation and an Action?

  1. Transformations are lazy and only build a logical execution plan (DAG); Actions trigger the actual execution of computations
  2. Transformations instantly execute calculations; Actions are cached in memory for later lookup
  3. Transformations modify the schema on disk; Actions modify the values in memory
  4. Transformations only run on CPU nodes; Actions run exclusively on GPU nodes
cards.back:
A. Transformations are lazy and only build a logical execution plan (DAG); Actions trigger the actual execution of computations

PySpark is lazily evaluated. Transformations (like `.filter()` or `.select()`) are added to a Directed Acyclic Graph (DAG) without running them. An Action (like `.count()` or `.collect()`) forces Spark to compile and execute the DAG across the cluster.

cards.label: Quiz · Data Pipelines – Pandas, PySpark & Distributed Optimizations
cards.front:
Why is calling `.collect()` on a large Spark DataFrame in production considered dangerous?

  1. It pulls all distributed data into the driver node's single memory space, potentially causing an Out-Of-Memory (OOM) crash
  2. It locks the entire distributed cluster, preventing other scheduled pipelines from running
  3. It modifies the raw source files on disk, making operations non-idempotent
  4. It forces the DataFrame to lose its schema partitions and index maps
cards.back:
A. It pulls all distributed data into the driver node's single memory space, potentially causing an Out-Of-Memory (OOM) crash

`.collect()` retrieves all data from the worker partitions across the cluster and sends it to the central driver node. If the dataset is larger than the driver's RAM, the driver process will crash with an OOM error. Use `.take(n)` or write results to a storage layer instead.

cards.label: Quiz · Hugging Face Transformers – Architecture Study Guide
cards.front:
What is the primary formula for scaled dot-product attention in the original Transformer architecture?

  1. softmax(Q K^T / sqrt(d_k)) V
  2. sigmoid(Q K^T) * V
  3. tanh(Q K^T * d_k) + V
  4. softmax(Q V^T / d_k) K
cards.back:
A. softmax(Q K^T / sqrt(d_k)) V

Scaled dot-product attention calculates similarity scores between Queries (Q) and Keys (K), divides by the square root of Key dimension (d_k) to prevent vanishing gradients in softmax, and multiplies by Values (V) to aggregate context.

cards.label: Quiz · Hugging Face Transformers – Architecture Study Guide
cards.front:
What is the difference between BERT and GPT architectural styles?

  1. BERT is an encoder-only model using bi-directional attention; GPT is a decoder-only model using causal (masked) attention
  2. BERT is a sequence-to-sequence model; GPT only processes single inputs at a time
  3. BERT does not use positional embeddings, whereas GPT relies heavily on them
  4. BERT uses convolutional blocks; GPT uses pure recurrent layers
cards.back:
A. BERT is an encoder-only model using bi-directional attention; GPT is a decoder-only model using causal (masked) attention

BERT (Bidirectional Encoder Representations from Transformers) attends to both left and right contexts, making it perfect for understanding/classification. GPT (Generative Pre-trained Transformer) masks future tokens so attention only flows forward, making it perfect for auto-regressive generation.

cards.label: Quiz · SQL Study Guide - Essential Patterns
cards.front:
How does the `ROW_NUMBER()` window function differ from the `RANK()` and `DENSE_RANK()` window functions?

  1. `ROW_NUMBER()` assigns sequential unique integers; `RANK()` leaves gaps on duplicates; `DENSE_RANK()` does not leave gaps
  2. `ROW_NUMBER()` sorts elements descending; `RANK()` sorts ascending; `DENSE_RANK()` sorts randomly
  3. `ROW_NUMBER()` requires a `GROUP BY` clause; `RANK()` and `DENSE_RANK()` require an `ORDER BY` clause
  4. `ROW_NUMBER()` operates across table partitions; `RANK()` and `DENSE_RANK()` only operate within one partition
cards.back:
A. `ROW_NUMBER()` assigns sequential unique integers; `RANK()` leaves gaps on duplicates; `DENSE_RANK()` does not leave gaps

For duplicate values, `ROW_NUMBER()` still assigns different consecutive numbers (e.g., 1, 2, 3). `RANK()` assigns the same rank but skips values (e.g., 1, 2, 2, 4). `DENSE_RANK()` assigns the same rank without skipping (e.g., 1, 2, 2, 3).

cards.label: Quiz · SQL Study Guide - Essential Patterns
cards.front:
In what order does a SQL query logically execute (regardless of how database engines optimize it under the hood)?

  1. FROM → JOIN → WHERE → GROUP BY → HAVING → SELECT → ORDER BY → LIMIT
  2. SELECT → FROM → WHERE → GROUP BY → HAVING → ORDER BY → LIMIT
  3. FROM → SELECT → WHERE → GROUP BY → HAVING → ORDER BY → LIMIT
  4. LIMIT → SELECT → FROM → WHERE → GROUP BY → ORDER BY
cards.back:
A. FROM → JOIN → WHERE → GROUP BY → HAVING → SELECT → ORDER BY → LIMIT

The logical processing order of SQL begins with identifying the tables (`FROM`, `JOIN`), filtering rows (`WHERE`), grouping (`GROUP BY`), filtering groups (`HAVING`), evaluating return expressions (`SELECT`), ordering results (`ORDER BY`), and finally slicing (`LIMIT`).

cards.label: Compute — the Workers · brick
cards.front:
Virtual Machines

AWS EC2 · Google Compute Engine · Azure VMs
cards.back:
The standard 2×4 rectangular brick: sturdy and fully customizable, but heavy. You own everything from the operating system up.

A hypervisor slices one physical server into isolated guests, each running its own kernel and operating system. You pick the CPU, memory, disk and image, and you are responsible for patching, configuring and scaling what runs inside.

Reach for it when

  • The software needs a full OS, a custom kernel module, GPUs, or licensed software tied to a machine.
  • You run long-lived, steady workloads where reserved or committed-use pricing beats paying per request.
  • You host your own databases, message brokers or Kubernetes worker nodes.

Trade-offs

  • Boots in tens of seconds to minutes, so scaling reacts slowly to sudden spikes.
  • You patch the OS, rotate credentials and fight configuration drift between machines.
  • You pay for idle capacity unless an autoscaling group shrinks the fleet.

How it breaks

  • The physical host fails and takes the VM with it. Spread instances across availability zones behind a load balancer.
  • Hand-patched 'pet' servers drift apart until one behaves differently in production. Build immutable images (Packer, AMIs) and replace instead of repair.
  • Noisy neighbours on shared hardware cause unpredictable latency.

Remember

  • Classic trio: machine image + autoscaling group + load balancer with health checks.
  • Treat servers as cattle, not pets.

Read more

  • Xen and the Art of Virtualization (SOSP 2003) — The paravirtualization paper behind early EC2
  • AWS Nitro System — How modern EC2 offloads virtualization to dedicated hardware
  • Static stability using Availability Zones — Amazon Builders' Library

cards.label: Compute — the Workers · brick
cards.front:
Containers

Docker · containerd · OCI images
cards.back:
Uniformly sized modular bricks that stack perfectly on any baseplate, because each brick carries its own dependencies inside.

A container is an ordinary process isolated with Linux namespaces and limited with cgroups. It shares the host kernel, so it starts in about a second and packs densely. The image bundles the app with its libraries, so the same artifact runs on a laptop, in CI and in production.

Reach for it when

  • You deploy stateless web services and microservices.
  • You want 'works on my machine' to mean 'works everywhere', with the same image in development, CI and production.
  • You want to pack many small services onto fewer machines.

Trade-offs

  • Isolation is weaker than a VM because every container shares one kernel.
  • One container is easy; hundreds need an orchestrator for placement, networking, secrets and rollouts.
  • State must live outside the container, in a database, cache or volume.

How it breaks

  • The container restarts and its local disk is gone. Never keep the only copy of data inside it.
  • It is OOM-killed when it exceeds its memory limit, often in a restart loop.
  • Bloated images slow down every deploy and scale-out.

Remember

  • Twelve-Factor rules: stateless processes, configuration in environment variables, logs to stdout.
  • Container = process + namespaces + cgroups + an image filesystem.

Read more

  • Docker overview
  • The Twelve-Factor App: Processes — Why services should be stateless and share nothing
  • The Twelve-Factor App — The whole checklist for container-friendly services

cards.label: Compute — the Workers · brick
cards.front:
Container Orchestration

Kubernetes · Amazon ECS · Nomad
cards.back:
The baseplate plus a robot that reads the instructions. You declare what the finished model should look like, and it keeps rebuilding it whenever a piece falls off.

You declare the desired state: which images, how many replicas, how much CPU and memory. Controllers keep reconciling reality toward it. They restart crashed pods, reschedule them off failed nodes, roll out new versions gradually, give services stable DNS names, and autoscale on metrics.

Reach for it when

  • You run many services that need rolling deploys, service discovery and autoscaling.
  • You want to use machines efficiently by bin-packing many workloads onto shared nodes.
  • You need one deployment model across clouds or on-premises.

Trade-offs

  • Operating it is a job in itself: networking, upgrades, RBAC and YAML sprawl.
  • For one or two services, a managed platform or serverless is usually cheaper and simpler.

How it breaks

  • A misconfigured liveness probe restarts healthy pods, which can cascade across the service.
  • Missing resource requests and limits cause noisy neighbours and surprise evictions.
  • A control-plane outage leaves running pods serving (static stability) but blocks deploys and scaling.

Read more

  • Borg, Omega, and Kubernetes (ACM Queue) — Lessons from a decade of container management at Google
  • Large-scale cluster management at Google with Borg (EuroSys 2015)
  • Kubernetes overview

cards.label: Compute — the Workers · brick
cards.front:
Serverless Functions

AWS Lambda · Cloudflare Workers · Google Cloud Run functions
cards.back:
Tiny micro-bricks that appear the instant two pieces need connecting, then disappear. You never store or maintain them.

You upload a function and choose what triggers it: an HTTP request, a queue message, an object landing in S3, or a schedule. The platform runs one instance per concurrent event, scales to zero when idle, and bills per millisecond. Lambda isolates each function in a Firecracker microVM; Cloudflare Workers use V8 isolates, which start in under a millisecond at the edge.

Reach for it when

  • Traffic is spiky or rare, so paying for idle servers is wasteful.
  • You need glue between managed services, such as 'image uploaded to S3, so resize it'.
  • Event handlers, webhooks, scheduled jobs and edge logic (redirects, auth checks, A/B tests).

Trade-offs

  • Cold starts: the first request to a new instance can take from about 100 ms to several seconds, depending on runtime and package size.
  • Hard limits: Lambda runs at most 15 minutes and has memory, payload and concurrency caps.
  • Functions are stateless, harder to debug locally, and tie you to the vendor.
  • At steady high load, per-request billing can cost more than containers.

How it breaks

  • A traffic spike launches thousands of instances that exhaust the database's connections. Put a queue or a connection proxy (such as RDS Proxy) in between.
  • Asynchronous invocations are retried, so side effects can run twice. Make handlers idempotent.
  • Account concurrency limits throttle unrelated functions that share them.

Read more

  • Firecracker: Lightweight Virtualization for Serverless Applications (NSDI 2020) — How AWS Lambda isolates functions
  • Cloud Computing without Containers — Cloudflare on V8 isolates
  • Serverless Computing: One Step Forward, Two Steps Back — A sharp critique from Berkeley (CIDR 2019)
  • Cloud Programming Simplified: A Berkeley View on Serverless Computing

cards.label: Storage & Databases — the Memory · brick
cards.front:
Relational Databases

PostgreSQL · MySQL · Amazon Aurora
cards.back:
The rigid LEGO grid: every piece must click into clean rows and columns, and nothing that doesn't fit is allowed on the board.

Data lives in tables with a fixed schema. You query it with SQL, joining tables as needed. Indexes (usually B-trees) keep lookups fast, and constraints such as foreign keys and uniqueness protect integrity. ACID transactions (atomicity, consistency, isolation, durability) make a group of writes all-or-nothing, even with many concurrent users.

Reach for it when

  • Money, orders, inventory and bookings: anything where a half-applied change is a bug.
  • You need ad-hoc queries, reports and joins across entities.
  • The shape of the data is known and relationships matter. This is the default choice until proven otherwise.

Trade-offs

  • Writes scale vertically until you add sharding (Vitess, Citus) or move to distributed SQL (Spanner, CockroachDB).
  • Schema migrations on big tables need care: online migrations, backfills and dual writes.
  • Read replicas scale reads but serve slightly stale data (replication lag).

How it breaks

  • A burst of clients exhausts connections. Use a pooler such as PgBouncer and cap the size of the app's pool.
  • Hot rows, such as one inventory counter in a flash sale, serialize on locks.
  • A missing index turns a 1 ms lookup into a full table scan that drags down everything else.
  • Reading your own write from a lagging replica shows the user old data.

Read more

  • A Relational Model of Data for Large Shared Data Banks (Codd, 1970) — Where the grid came from
  • Architecture of a Database System — Hellerstein, Stonebraker and Hamilton: how a database works inside
  • PostgreSQL: Concurrency control and MVCC
  • Why Uber Engineering switched from Postgres to MySQL — Replication and write amplification at scale
  • How Figma's databases team lived to tell the scale — Horizontally sharding Postgres

cards.label: Storage & Databases — the Memory · brick
cards.front:
NoSQL & Document Databases

DynamoDB · MongoDB · Cassandra · Bigtable
cards.back:
Flexible Bionicle pieces that morph into whatever shape you're storing, as long as you decide in advance how you'll pick them up.

There are four families: key-value (DynamoDB, Redis), document (MongoDB), wide-column (Cassandra, Bigtable) and graph (Neo4j). Most scale horizontally by hashing a partition key across many nodes and allow flexible, schema-on-read records. You model the data around your access patterns, not around entities, and usually denormalize.

Reach for it when

  • The scale is huge but access is simple and known: get by key, or a range inside one partition.
  • Write throughput is very high: messages, events, IoT readings, activity logs.
  • Records carry flexible, evolving attributes, such as product catalogs, user profiles, carts and sessions.

Trade-offs

  • Joins and ad-hoc queries are weak or missing. Adding a new access pattern can mean a new index or a copy of the data.
  • Many are eventually consistent by default, and multi-item transactions are limited.
  • The partition key is the most important design decision and hard to change later.

How it breaks

  • A hot partition, such as a celebrity's key or everything written under today's date, throttles while other nodes sit idle.
  • Full-table scans are slow and expensive.
  • Schema-on-read drift: old records in shapes the code no longer expects.

Read more

  • Dynamo: Amazon's Highly Available Key-value Store (SOSP 2007) — Consistent hashing, quorums, vector clocks
  • Amazon DynamoDB: A Scalable, Predictably Performant, and Fully Managed NoSQL Database Service (USENIX ATC 2022)
  • The What, Why, and When of Single-Table Design with DynamoDB — Alex DeBrie on access-pattern-first modeling
  • How Discord Stores Trillions of Messages — Cassandra to ScyllaDB, hot partitions
  • MongoDB data modeling

cards.label: Storage & Databases — the Memory · brick
cards.front:
Object Storage

Amazon S3 · Google Cloud Storage · Azure Blob Storage
cards.back:
Huge storage bins where you dump media, raw text and massive static assets. Each bin has a label, and you fetch things by label.

A flat namespace of buckets and keys, each pointing to an immutable blob plus metadata, accessed over HTTP. Capacity is effectively unlimited and cheap, and S3 is designed for 11 nines of durability. It is not a filesystem: you replace whole objects rather than editing them in place.

Reach for it when

  • Images, video, audio, documents, backups, logs, ML datasets, a data lake.
  • Static website assets served through a CDN.
  • Any large blob: put the bytes in object storage and keep only the key and metadata in your database.

Trade-offs

  • Each request takes tens of milliseconds, far slower than local disk or a cache.
  • You cannot edit part of an object; you rewrite it. Listing huge buckets is slow.
  • There are request-rate limits per key prefix, so spread hot keys across prefixes.

How it breaks

  • A misconfigured public bucket leaks data. Block public access by default.
  • Routing uploads through your servers wastes bandwidth and CPU. Hand clients presigned URLs so they upload directly.
  • Event notifications are at-least-once, so the same upload may trigger processing twice. Consumers must be idempotent.

Remember

  • S3 has provided strong read-after-write consistency since December 2020.
  • Lifecycle rules move old objects to cheaper tiers such as Glacier automatically.

Read more

  • Building and operating a pretty big storage system called S3 — Werner Vogels (Andy Warfield's keynote)
  • Finding a needle in Haystack: Facebook's photo storage (OSDI 2010)
  • The Google File System (SOSP 2003) — The ancestor of large-scale blob storage

cards.label: Storage & Databases — the Memory · brick
cards.front:
Wide-Column Stores: Cassandra

Apache Cassandra · ScyllaDB · Google Bigtable · HBase
cards.back:
A huge rack of labelled drawers spread over many tables. Every table can take new pieces at any moment, and each drawer keeps its pieces sorted.

A masterless, Dynamo-style cluster with a Bigtable-style data model. Rows are placed on a consistent-hash ring by partition key and replicated to N nodes (typically 3, across racks or zones). Any node can coordinate a request, and the consistency level is chosen per query (ONE, QUORUM, LOCAL_QUORUM, ALL). Writes go to a commit log and memtable and are flushed to immutable SSTables that are compacted later (an LSM tree), so writes are very fast. Inside a partition, rows are sorted by clustering columns, which makes 'latest N items for X' queries cheap.

Reach for it when

  • Write-heavy, always-on workloads: messages, events, time series, activity feeds, IoT, audit logs.
  • Multi-datacenter active-active with local-quorum latency.
  • Access patterns are known up front: design one table per query.

Data modeling rules

  • Primary key = (partition key, clustering columns…). The partition key spreads load; clustering columns sort rows inside it.
  • Bound partition size (roughly under 100 MB) by adding a time bucket to the key, for example (channel_id, day).
  • Denormalize: write the same data into several query-shaped tables. There are no joins.

Trade-offs

  • No joins, limited secondary indexes, and ad-hoc queries are expensive.
  • Lightweight transactions (Paxos-based compare-and-set) exist but are slow. Use them sparingly.
  • Repairs, compaction tuning, JVM garbage collection pauses (Cassandra) and tombstones take real operational care.

How it breaks

  • Hot or oversized partitions (a mega-channel or celebrity key) overload a few replicas.
  • Tombstone buildup from heavy deletes makes reads scan dead data and time out.
  • Skipped anti-entropy repair leaves replicas silently diverged, and deleted data can reappear.

Similar blocks

  • ScyllaDB: Cassandra-compatible, rewritten in C++ with a shard-per-core design. Discord moved to it from Cassandra.
  • Google Bigtable and HBase: range-partitioned wide-column stores with a single master for metadata. Row-key design is the whole game.
  • Amazon DynamoDB: a managed service with similar partition and sort-key modeling.

Read more

  • Cassandra: A Decentralized Structured Storage System (LADIS 2009) — Lakshman and Malik, Facebook
  • Apache Cassandra: Dynamo architecture — Ring, replication, tunable consistency
  • Apache Cassandra documentation — Includes the data-modeling guide
  • How Discord Stores Trillions of Messages — Cassandra to ScyllaDB, hot partitions
  • Bigtable: A Distributed Storage System for Structured Data

cards.label: Storage & Databases — the Memory · brick
cards.front:
Distributed SQL (NewSQL)

Google Spanner · CockroachDB · YugabyteDB · Amazon Aurora
cards.back:
The rigid LEGO grid, but built from many baseplates snapped together, and it still feels like one board.

Relational databases that keep SQL and ACID transactions but scale out horizontally. Data is split into ranges or tablets, each replicated with Raft or Paxos, and transactions that span ranges use a distributed commit protocol. Spanner uses TrueTime for external consistency; CockroachDB and YugabyteDB use hybrid logical clocks. Aurora takes a different route: one writer, with a shared, replicated storage layer that scales reads and durability.

Reach for it when

  • You've outgrown a single Postgres or MySQL primary but still need transactions and SQL.
  • Multi-region deployments with strong consistency and automatic failover.
  • You want to avoid hand-rolled application-level sharding.

Trade-offs

  • Every write pays for consensus. Cross-region transactions add tens to hundreds of milliseconds.
  • Hot ranges (sequential primary keys) still bottleneck. Use hashed or UUID keys.
  • Costs more and has more moving parts than a single-node database.

Read more

  • Spanner: Google's Globally-Distributed Database
  • CockroachDB: The Resilient Geo-Distributed SQL Database (SIGMOD 2020)
  • Amazon Aurora: Design Considerations for High Throughput Cloud-Native Relational Databases (SIGMOD 2017) — The log is the database
  • YugabyteDB documentation

cards.label: Storage & Databases — the Memory · brick
cards.front:
Search Engines

Elasticsearch · OpenSearch · Apache Solr · Lucene
cards.back:
The index at the back of the instruction booklet: look up a word and it tells you every page it appears on.

Search engines build an inverted index (term → list of documents), plus BM25 relevance scoring, analyzers for tokenizing and stemming, facets and aggregations, and increasingly vector search too. An index is split into shards with replicas across nodes. It is fed from the source-of-truth database, usually asynchronously through change data capture or events, and is almost never the system of record.

Reach for it when

  • Full-text product and catalog search, typeahead, log search and analytics, faceted filtering.

Trade-offs

  • Near-real-time rather than instant: refresh intervals of about 1 s. Reindexing after a mapping change is costly.
  • The index drifts from the database if the update pipeline drops events. Plan full rebuilds.

How it breaks

  • Too many small shards overload the cluster state. Deep pagination and heavy aggregations exhaust memory.
  • Split-brain from bad quorum settings on older versions.

Read more

  • Elasticsearch
  • OpenSearch documentation
  • Apache Lucene — The library under Elasticsearch, OpenSearch and Solr
  • How we rebuilt the Walmart Autocomplete Backend — Walmart Global Tech: a prefix index served from a distributed cache

cards.label: Storage & Databases — the Memory · brick
cards.front:
Vector Databases

pgvector · Milvus · Vertex AI Vector Search · FAISS · Pinecone
cards.back:
A bin sorted by shape-similarity instead of by label: hold up a piece and it hands you the ones that look most like it.

Vector databases store embeddings (dense vectors from a model) and answer 'k nearest neighbours' queries with approximate nearest neighbour (ANN) indexes. HNSW is a graph index: fast with high recall, but memory-hungry. IVF plus product quantization clusters and compresses vectors, so it is cheaper at billion scale. Metadata filters and hybrid search (combined with BM25) narrow the results. They are the retrieval brick behind RAG, semantic search, recommendations and deduplication.

Reach for it when

  • Retrieval-augmented generation (RAG) for LLM apps, semantic or product search, similar-item recommendations.
  • Start with pgvector if you already run Postgres. Move to a dedicated engine for more than about 100 million vectors or very high QPS.

Trade-offs

  • Recall vs latency vs memory is tuned through index parameters (HNSW M and efSearch, IVF nlist and nprobe).
  • Re-embedding the whole corpus when the embedding model changes is a batch job to plan for.

Read more

  • Efficient and robust approximate nearest neighbor search using HNSW graphs — Malkov and Yashunin
  • Billion-scale similarity search with GPUs (FAISS)
  • pgvector
  • Milvus documentation
  • Retrieval-Augmented Generation for Knowledge-Intensive NLP Tasks — The original RAG paper

cards.label: Storage & Databases — the Memory · brick
cards.front:
Coordination Services

ZooKeeper · etcd · Consul · Google Chubby
cards.back:
The small, trusted referee's notebook that every builder checks to find out who's in charge and which instructions are current.

Coordination services are small, strongly consistent (consensus-replicated) key-value stores for coordination, not bulk data. They provide leader election, distributed locks and leases, service discovery, configuration, and cluster membership through watches and ephemeral keys. etcd stores all Kubernetes state. ZooKeeper historically coordinated Kafka, HBase and Hadoop; Kafka has replaced it with its own KRaft quorum.

Use it well

  • Keep data tiny (KBs to MBs), and keep writes infrequent.
  • A lock needs a fencing token (a monotonic number checked by the resource). Otherwise a paused client can act on an expired lease.

How it breaks

  • Losing quorum (for example 2 of 3 nodes) blocks all writes and leader changes. Run 3 or 5 nodes across zones.
  • Abusing it as a general database causes slow disks, huge snapshots and election storms.

Read more

  • ZooKeeper: Wait-free coordination for Internet-scale systems (USENIX ATC 2010)
  • The Chubby lock service for loosely-coupled distributed systems — Mike Burrows, OSDI 2006
  • etcd documentation
  • How to do distributed locking — Martin Kleppmann on fencing tokens

cards.label: Storage & Databases — the Memory · brick
cards.front:
Google Cloud Storage Buckets

GCS · gs:// · the data lake and model store on GCP
cards.back:
Google's version of the giant storage bins, with a choice of how close to the front door each bin sits (and what it costs to open).

GCS is Google Cloud's object store. Objects live in buckets under a flat namespace with '/' only as a naming convention. Location types are region, dual-region and multi-region. Storage classes are Standard, Nearline (30-day minimum), Coldline (90-day) and Archive (365-day), with Autoclass available to tier automatically. It offers strong global consistency for object reads, writes and listing, IAM with uniform bucket-level access, signed URLs, object versioning, lifecycle rules, and Pub/Sub notifications. It is the default landing zone for data lakes, Spark and Dataproc jobs, BigQuery external tables, training data and model artifacts.

Reach for it when

  • Raw and curated data-lake zones (Parquet or Iceberg files), batch pipeline inputs and outputs.
  • ML datasets, checkpoints and model weights. Mount with Cloud Storage FUSE, or stream with parallel readers.
  • Media and static assets behind Cloud CDN. Backups and logs with lifecycle rules to cheaper classes.

Design tips

  • Co-locate buckets with compute (same region) to avoid egress cost and latency.
  • Ramp request rates gradually. Very high QPS on sequential names (timestamps) can hot-spot, so prefer random or hashed prefixes.
  • Use Pub/Sub notifications or Eventarc to trigger pipelines when objects land. Delivery is at-least-once, so make consumers idempotent.
  • Many small files hurt Spark and BigQuery. Compact them into files of about 128 MB to 1 GB.

How it breaks

  • Early deletion fees and retrieval costs on cold classes surprise batch jobs that reread old data.
  • A publicly readable bucket through a mistaken IAM binding. Enforce public access prevention.
  • Loading model weights from GCS on every pod start slows GPU autoscaling. Cache or pre-stage the weights.

Read more

  • Storage classes — Google Cloud
  • Bucket locations
  • Request rate and access distribution guidelines — Avoiding hot-spotting
  • Cloud Storage consistency
  • Pub/Sub notifications for Cloud Storage
  • Object Lifecycle Management
  • Signed URLs
  • Cloud Storage FUSE — Mount buckets for training and serving

cards.label: Networking & Routing — the Connectors · brick
cards.front:
DNS & Global Traffic Routing

Amazon Route 53 · Cloudflare DNS · Google Cloud DNS
cards.back:
The address printed on the box lid. Before anyone can touch your model, they have to find which table it's sitting on.

DNS turns names into IP addresses through a hierarchy of cached lookups, and each record has a TTL. Managed DNS can also route: by latency or geography to the nearest region, by weight for canaries and blue/green deploys, and by failover when health checks fail.

Reach for it when

  • This is always the first hop: every request starts with a lookup.
  • Multi-region active-active or active-passive failover.
  • Weighted shifts of traffic between old and new stacks.

Trade-offs

  • Caching makes changes slow to propagate. They take at least the TTL to spread, and some clients ignore TTLs.
  • Short TTLs mean faster failover but more lookups and more dependence on the DNS provider.

How it breaks

  • An outage at the DNS provider makes healthy services unreachable, as in the 2016 Dyn attack.
  • A long TTL on a record pointing at a dead region keeps sending users there.

Read more

  • What is DNS? (Cloudflare Learning Center)
  • Route 53 routing policies — Latency, geolocation, weighted, failover

cards.label: Networking & Routing — the Connectors · brick
cards.front:
Load Balancers

AWS ALB/NLB · NGINX · HAProxy · Envoy
cards.back:
The traffic manager that splits an incoming stream of LEGO pegs evenly across many identical worker bricks, and stops feeding any brick that has cracked.

A load balancer spreads requests across a pool of healthy targets. Layer 4 balancers route raw TCP or UDP connections and are fast and simple. Layer 7 balancers understand HTTP: they route by path or header, terminate TLS, and retry. Common algorithms are round-robin, least-connections and consistent hashing (for stickiness). Health checks eject failing targets.

Reach for it when

  • You scale any stateless tier horizontally, whether web servers, APIs or workers behind RPC.
  • You want TLS termination in one place, zero-downtime deploys, and blue/green or canary releases.

Trade-offs

  • The balancer itself must be highly available: use a managed service, or a redundant pair with a floating IP or anycast.
  • Sticky sessions undermine even distribution and make scaling in painful. Prefer stateless servers.

How it breaks

  • A health check that is too shallow keeps a server in rotation that returns 200 while its database is gone.
  • A health check that is too deep (it checks the database) means one database blip ejects every target and causes a total outage.
  • Long-lived connections (WebSockets, gRPC) stay pinned to old servers, so newly added servers get no load.

Read more

  • Maglev: A Fast and Reliable Software Network Load Balancer (NSDI 2016) — Google's L4 balancer and consistent hashing
  • Load Balancing in the Datacenter (Google SRE book)
  • Implementing health checks — Amazon Builders' Library on shallow vs deep checks
  • NGINX HTTP load balancing
  • What is Envoy — The L7 proxy behind most service meshes

cards.label: Networking & Routing — the Connectors · brick
cards.front:
API Gateway

Amazon API Gateway · Kong · Apigee · Envoy Gateway
cards.back:
The single front-door stud every piece must pass through. It checks your ticket, limits how fast you can push, and routes you to the right sub-assembly.

A single entry point in front of many backend services. It handles cross-cutting concerns in one place: authentication and authorization, rate limits and quotas, routing by path or version, request and response transformation, protocol translation (REST to gRPC), and metrics and tracing. A Backend-for-Frontend (BFF) is a gateway tailored to one client, such as mobile.

Reach for it when

  • Mobile and web clients talk to many microservices, and you don't want each client to know about each service.
  • You expose public APIs that need keys, quotas and usage plans.
  • You want auth, throttling and observability configured once rather than in every service.

Trade-offs

  • It adds a network hop and a component that must scale and stay highly available.
  • Business logic tends to creep in. Keep the gateway thin.

How it breaks

  • One bad routing or auth config change takes every API down at once. Roll out config gradually.
  • Without per-client limits, one noisy client starves everyone else.

Read more

  • Pattern: API Gateway / Backends for Frontends — Chris Richardson, microservices.io
  • Scaling your API with rate limiters — Stripe's four kinds of limiter
  • What is Amazon API Gateway?

cards.label: Networking & Routing — the Connectors · brick
cards.front:
Content Delivery Network

Amazon CloudFront · Cloudflare · Akamai · Fastly
cards.back:
Small caching outposts built on every block of the city, so kids grab pieces from the corner shop instead of walking to the main warehouse.

A CDN is a global network of edge servers (points of presence, or PoPs) that cache content close to users. It cuts latency and offloads your origin. It serves static assets, video segments and downloads, can cache some dynamic responses, terminates TLS near the user, and absorbs DDoS attacks. Edge compute such as Workers or Lambda@Edge runs logic there.

Reach for it when

  • Images, JS/CSS, fonts, video (HLS/DASH segments), software downloads.
  • You have a global audience, or you need DDoS protection and a web application firewall at the edge.

Trade-offs

  • Invalidation is hard. Prefer versioned, content-hashed filenames (app.3f9a.js) with long TTLs.
  • Personalized or rapidly changing responses cache poorly.

How it breaks

  • A global purge or a cold cache sends every miss to the origin at once. Add an origin shield or tiered cache.
  • Caching private responses (a missing Cache-Control: private) leaks one user's data to another.
  • Stale assets after a deploy break the page if HTML and JS versions mismatch.

Read more

  • What is a CDN? (Cloudflare Learning Center)
  • The Akamai Network: A Platform for High-Performance Internet Applications — ACM SIGOPS Operating Systems Review, 2010
  • Netflix Open Connect — Netflix's own CDN, placed inside ISPs

cards.label: Networking & Routing — the Connectors · brick
cards.front:
Service Mesh: Istio

Istio · Envoy · Linkerd · ambient mode
cards.back:
A clip-on connector attached to every brick, so every connection between bricks is locked, counted and steerable without redesigning the bricks themselves.

A service mesh moves service-to-service networking out of application code into a proxy layer. In sidecar mode an Envoy proxy runs next to every pod; in ambient mode per-node ztunnel proxies handle L4 and optional waypoint proxies handle L7. The control plane (istiod) pushes configuration to the proxies. You get mutual TLS and workload identity, fine-grained traffic management (weighted canaries, header routing, retries, timeouts, circuit breaking, fault injection, mirroring), authorization policy, and uniform metrics and traces.

Reach for it when

  • Many microservices on Kubernetes need zero-trust mTLS and consistent retries, timeouts and telemetry.
  • Progressive delivery: shift 1% → 10% → 100% of traffic to a new version, or mirror production traffic to a shadow model.
  • Chaos drills: inject delays and aborts with a VirtualService, no code changes needed.

Key resources

  • Gateway (ingress and egress), VirtualService (routing rules), DestinationRule (subsets, load balancing, outlier detection), PeerAuthentication and AuthorizationPolicy (mTLS and access).

Trade-offs

  • Sidecars add memory and CPU per pod and extra latency per hop, which ambient mode reduces.
  • Mesh-level retries stacked on client retries multiply load. Own retries in one layer.
  • A bad mesh config push can break traffic cluster-wide. Canary your control-plane changes.

Read more

  • What is Istio?
  • Istio traffic management
  • Istio security (mTLS, identity, authorization)
  • Istio ambient mode overview — Sidecar-less mesh
  • What is Envoy

cards.label: Networking & Routing — the Connectors · brick
cards.front:
Torbit: Walmart's Edge Platform

Edge proxy · L7 routing · edge caching and security
cards.back:
Walmart's own front gate and sorting station at the edge of the city. Every visitor passes through it before reaching any building, and it decides which building they go to.

Torbit began as a web-performance startup (real-user monitoring and dynamic front-end optimization) that Walmart Labs acquired in 2013. The team went on to build Walmart's in-house edge infrastructure: proxies, load balancers, edge security and real-user monitoring. Walmart engineers use Torbit for edge traffic control such as path-based routing between legacy and new services. Conceptually it plays the role of a CDN or edge proxy plus L7 load balancer in front of the origin: TLS termination, caching, request routing and rewriting, bot and WAF protection, and gradual traffic shifting.

Where it sits

  • Client → DNS → Torbit edge (TLS, cache, security, routing) → regional load balancers or ingress (Istio gateway) → services.
  • The public equivalent is Cloudflare, Akamai or Fastly, combined with an Envoy or NGINX edge tier.

Use it for

  • Path-based migration: route /api/cart/* to the new microservice at 10%, then increase, with instant rollback at the edge.
  • Shielding origins from flash-sale spikes with caching, rate limits and request collapsing.

How it breaks

  • An edge misconfiguration affects everything behind it. Stage and canary routing changes.
  • Caching personalized responses leaks data. Split what is cacheable from what is personalized.

Read more

  • Walmart Labs scoops up site-speed optimizer Torbit (TechCrunch, 2013)
  • Faster is Better: How We Are Optimizing Walmart.com — @WalmartLabs announcement
  • Farewell Torbit / Walmart — Co-founder on proxies, load balancers, edge infrastructure and edge security
  • Fine-Grained Traffic Routing for Microservice Migration — Walmart Global Tech: path-based routing with Torbit

cards.label: Integration & Communication — the Glue · brick
cards.front:
Message Queues

Amazon SQS · RabbitMQ · Google Cloud Tasks
cards.back:
A buffer tray between two builders. When one passes pieces faster than the next can snap them in, the pieces wait safely in the tray instead of falling on the floor.

Producers put messages on a durable queue and consumers pull them, process them, and then acknowledge (delete) them. Each message goes to one consumer (point-to-point). The queue decouples the producer from the consumer's speed and availability, levels out bursts, and makes retries easy. Most queues deliver at least once, so a message can arrive more than once.

Reach for it when

  • Background jobs: emails, video encoding, report generation, order fulfilment.
  • Load leveling: absorb a 10× spike and drain it at the rate the database can handle.
  • Spreading work across a pool of workers that you scale on queue depth.

Trade-offs

  • Processing becomes asynchronous: the user sees 'processing…' and the result arrives later.
  • Ordering is not guaranteed unless you use FIFO queues or message groups, which limit throughput.
  • At-least-once delivery means duplicates, so handlers must be idempotent.

How it breaks

  • A poison message fails forever and blocks or wastes workers. Move it to a dead-letter queue (DLQ) after N attempts.
  • If the visibility timeout is shorter than processing time, the message reappears and is processed twice.
  • If consumers are permanently slower than producers, the backlog grows without bound. Queues absorb bursts; they don't fix sustained overload.

Read more

  • Queues Don't Fix Overload — Fred Hebert: a must-read before adding a queue
  • Avoiding insurmountable queue backlogs — Amazon Builders' Library
  • Amazon SQS visibility timeout
  • Amazon SQS dead-letter queues
  • RabbitMQ tutorials — Work queues, pub/sub, routing, RPC

cards.label: Integration & Communication — the Glue · brick
cards.front:
Event Streams

Apache Kafka · Amazon Kinesis · Redpanda · Google Pub/Sub
cards.back:
A central conveyor belt that constantly carries every change past every station. Each station takes what it needs, and the belt remembers what went by so a station can rewind.

A stream is an append-only log, split into partitions and replicated across brokers. Consumers track their own offsets, so many independent consumer groups can read the same events at their own pace. Retention lets you replay history. Order is guaranteed within a partition, and all events with the same key land in the same partition.

Reach for it when

  • Fan-out: one event (OrderPlaced, DriverMoved) feeds many services such as billing, analytics, search and notifications.
  • Change data capture from a database, real-time analytics, activity and telemetry pipelines.
  • Event sourcing, or rebuilding a read model by replaying history.

Trade-offs

  • Clusters, partitions and schemas are heavy to operate.
  • Order holds only within a partition, and consumer parallelism is capped at the partition count.
  • Exactly-once processing needs idempotent producers plus transactions or idempotent sinks.

How it breaks

  • Consumer lag grows until data ages out of retention before a slow consumer reads it.
  • A skewed key (one busy city, one mega-customer) creates a hot partition.
  • Rebalancing storms pause every consumer in the group while partitions are reassigned.

Queue vs stream

  • Queue: a message is consumed once, then deleted. Good for work distribution.
  • Stream: an event is retained, read by many, and can be replayed. Good for broadcasting facts.

Read more

  • The Log: What every software engineer should know about real-time data's unifying abstraction — Jay Kreps, the essay behind Kafka
  • Apache Kafka design
  • Exactly-once Semantics Are Possible: Here's How Kafka Does It — Confluent
  • What do you mean by 'Event-Driven'? — Martin Fowler: four different patterns under one name

cards.label: Integration & Communication — the Glue · brick
cards.front:
Caches

Redis · Memcached · Valkey · in-process caches
cards.back:
An ultra-fast shelf at arm's reach for the pieces you grab most, so you don't open the heavy bottom drawer (the database) every time.

A cache is an in-memory key-value store that answers in under a millisecond. The common patterns are cache-aside (the app reads the cache, and on a miss loads from the database and fills the cache), read-through, write-through and write-behind. Entries expire by TTL and are evicted by LRU or LFU. Redis adds data structures such as sorted sets for leaderboards, geo indexes, counters, streams and pub/sub.

Reach for it when

  • Reads far outnumber writes and the same hot data is read over and over.
  • Sessions, rate-limit counters, leaderboards, feature flags, computed or aggregated results.
  • Fast geo lookups, such as nearby drivers, with Redis GEO.

Trade-offs

  • Staleness: you choose how wrong the data is allowed to be, and for how long.
  • Invalidation adds complexity, and memory costs more than disk.
  • It is another system that can fail or disagree with the source of truth.

How it breaks

  • Stampede (thundering herd): a hot key expires and thousands of requests hit the database at once. Fix with request coalescing, locks or leases, or early refresh.
  • A cold cache after a restart or failover sends the full read load to the database.
  • Treating the cache as the source of truth loses data on eviction or restart.

Remember

  • Main memory ≈ 100 ns, SSD read ≈ 100 µs, a same-datacenter round trip ≈ 0.5 ms.
  • Track the hit ratio. Going from a 90% to a 99% hit rate cuts database load 10×.

Read more

  • Scaling Memcache at Facebook (NSDI 2013) — Leases, stampedes and regional replication
  • TAO: Facebook's Distributed Data Store for the Social Graph (USENIX ATC 2013)
  • Caching challenges and strategies — Amazon Builders' Library
  • Redis documentation
