With a one-hot target every term but one is zero, so the loss is just minus the log-probability of the correct class.

Term by term

  • \mathbf{e}_{y} — one-hot target for class y
  • z_y — logit of the correct class
  • \log \sum_{j} e^{z_j} — log-sum-exp, computed stably in practice

In AI papers

`F.cross_entropy(logits, y)` in PyTorch computes this directly from logits.

cards.label: Cross-entropy · Undergraduate
cards.front:
Binary cross-entropy

\mathcal{L}_{\text{BCE}}(y, \hat{y}) = -\big[\, y \log \hat{y} + (1 - y)\log(1 - \hat{y}) \,\big], \qquad \hat{y} = \sigma(z)
cards.back:
“B C E equals minus the quantity y log y hat plus one minus y times log of one minus y hat”

Cross-entropy for a yes/no label. Only one term is active: -\log \hat{y} if the answer is yes, -\log(1 - \hat{y}) if no.

Term by term

  • y \in \{0, 1\} — true label
  • \hat{y} \in (0, 1) — predicted probability of 1

In AI papers

Used for multi-label classification, reward models and discriminators.

cards.label: Mutual information & information gain · Undergraduate
cards.front:
Information gain

\operatorname{IG}(Y, A) = H(Y) - \sum_{a} \frac{|S_{a}|}{|S|}\,H(Y \mid A = a)
cards.back:
“the information gain of splitting on A equals the entropy of Y minus the weighted average entropy of Y in each branch”

How much a question (the feature A) reduces uncertainty about the label Y. Decision trees split on the feature with the highest gain.

Term by term

  • H(Y) — uncertainty before the split
  • S_a — examples where A = a
  • H(Y \mid A = a) — uncertainty left in that branch

In AI papers

The second term is H(Y \mid A), so information gain is the mutual information I(Y; A). Active learning picks the data whose label would give the most information gain.

Quinlan, ID3, 1986

cards.label: Cross-entropy · Masters
cards.front:
Language-modeling loss

\mathcal{L}(\boldsymbol{\theta}) = -\frac{1}{T}\sum_{t=1}^{T} \log p_{\boldsymbol{\theta}}(x_{t} \mid x_{<t})
cards.back:
“L of theta equals minus one over T times the sum over t of log p theta of x t given x before t”

Average, over every position, the surprise of the actual next token. It is cross-entropy between the text and the model, and its exponential is perplexity.

Term by term

  • x_t — the true next token
  • x_{<t} — the context the model sees
  • \frac{1}{T} — average per token

In AI papers

The pretraining objective of every GPT-style model.

cards.label: Cross-entropy · Masters
cards.front:
Gradient of softmax cross-entropy

\frac{\partial \mathcal{L}_{\text{CE}}}{\partial \mathbf{z}} = \operatorname{softmax}(\mathbf{z}) - \mathbf{e}_{y} = \mathbf{p} - \mathbf{y}
cards.back:
“the gradient of the cross-entropy loss with respect to the logits equals the predicted probabilities minus the one-hot target”

The gradient is simply “prediction minus truth”: push down every wrong class by its probability and push up the correct class by 1 - p_y.

Term by term

  • \mathbf{p} — predicted probabilities
  • \mathbf{y} = \mathbf{e}_y — one-hot target

In AI papers

This clean form is why softmax and cross-entropy are always fused in code: faster and numerically stable.

cards.label: Cross-entropy · Masters
cards.front:
Label smoothing

\mathbf{y}^{\text{LS}} = (1 - \varepsilon)\,\mathbf{e}_{y} + \frac{\varepsilon}{K}\,\mathbf{1}
cards.back:
“y L S equals one minus epsilon times the one-hot target, plus epsilon over K on every class”

Replace the hard one-hot target with a slightly softened one, so the model is never pushed toward probability exactly 1.

Term by term

  • \varepsilon — smoothing amount, e.g. 0.1
  • \frac{\varepsilon}{K}\mathbf{1} — a little probability spread over all K classes

In AI papers

Improves calibration; used in the original Transformer and in Inception.

Szegedy et al., 2016

cards.label: KL divergence · Masters
cards.front:
KL divergence

D_{\mathrm{KL}}(p \,\|\, q)
cards.back:
“the KL divergence of p from q, or KL of p parallel q”

How much worse it is to use q when the truth is p, in extra bits or nats. It is 0 only when p = q, and D_{\mathrm{KL}}(p \| q) \ne D_{\mathrm{KL}}(q \| p) in general. Also written \mathrm{KL}(p \| q).

In AI papers

Keeps a fine-tuned model close to its reference model in RLHF; regularises the latent space in VAEs.

cards.label: KL divergence · Masters
cards.front:
Forward and reverse KL

D_{\mathrm{KL}}(p \,\|\, q_{\theta}) \;\;\text{vs.}\;\; D_{\mathrm{KL}}(q_{\theta} \,\|\, p)
cards.back:
“forward KL versus reverse KL”

Forward KL (data first) punishes q_{\theta} for missing any region where p has mass, so it spreads out to cover everything (“mass-covering”). Reverse KL punishes q_{\theta} for putting mass where p has none, so it locks onto one mode (“mode-seeking”).

In AI papers

MLE minimises forward KL; the KL penalty in RLHF and variational inference use reverse KL.

cards.label: KL divergence · Masters
cards.front:
KL divergence formula

D_{\mathrm{KL}}(p \,\|\, q) = \sum_{x} p(x)\,\log\frac{p(x)}{q(x)} = \mathbb{E}_{x \sim p}\big[\log p(x) - \log q(x)\big] \ge 0
cards.back:
“the KL divergence of p from q equals the sum over x of p of x times log of p of x over q of x”

The expected log-ratio between the two distributions, weighted by p. It is never negative (Gibbs’ inequality).

Term by term

  • \log\frac{p(x)}{q(x)} — how much more likely x is under p than under q
  • \mathbb{E}_{x \sim p} — averaged over samples from p

In AI papers

In RLHF it is estimated per token from samples: \log \pi_\theta(y_t \mid \cdot) - \log \pi_{\text{ref}}(y_t \mid \cdot).

cards.label: KL divergence · Masters
cards.front:
Cross-entropy = entropy + KL

H(p, q) = H(p) + D_{\mathrm{KL}}(p \,\|\, q)
cards.back:
“the cross-entropy of p and q equals the entropy of p plus the KL divergence of p from q”

Cross-entropy splits into the unavoidable uncertainty in the data, H(p), plus the extra cost of the model being wrong, the KL.

Term by term

  • H(p) — irreducible: fixed by the data
  • D_{\mathrm{KL}}(p \| q) — reducible: what training shrinks

In AI papers

Explains why LM loss never reaches zero, and the constant E (irreducible loss) in scaling laws.

cards.label: KL divergence · Masters
cards.front:
Evidence lower bound (ELBO)

\log p_{\theta}(\mathbf{x}) \;\ge\; \mathbb{E}_{q_{\phi}(\mathbf{z} \mid \mathbf{x})}\big[\log p_{\theta}(\mathbf{x} \mid \mathbf{z})\big] - D_{\mathrm{KL}}\big(q_{\phi}(\mathbf{z} \mid \mathbf{x}) \,\|\, p(\mathbf{z})\big)
cards.back:
“log p theta of x is at least the expected reconstruction log-likelihood minus the KL divergence of the encoder from the prior”

The true log-likelihood is intractable, but this lower bound is not. Its first term rewards good reconstructions; the KL keeps the codes close to the prior.

Term by term

  • q_{\phi}(\mathbf{z} \mid \mathbf{x}) — encoder: approximate posterior
  • p_{\theta}(\mathbf{x} \mid \mathbf{z}) — decoder
  • p(\mathbf{z}) = \mathcal{N}(\mathbf{0}, \mathbf{I}) — prior over latent codes

In AI papers

The VAE objective; the diffusion training loss is also derived from an ELBO.

Kingma & Welling, 2014

cards.label: KL divergence · Masters
cards.front:
Knowledge distillation

\mathcal{L}_{\text{KD}} = \tau^{2}\,D_{\mathrm{KL}}\big(\operatorname{softmax}(\mathbf{z}_{T} / \tau) \,\|\, \operatorname{softmax}(\mathbf{z}_{S} / \tau)\big)
cards.back:
“the distillation loss equals tau squared times the KL divergence between the teacher’s and the student’s softened distributions”

Train a small student to match the full output distribution of a large teacher, not just the top answer. A temperature \tau > 1 exposes how the teacher ranks the wrong answers.

Term by term

  • \mathbf{z}_T, \mathbf{z}_S — teacher and student logits
  • \tau — distillation temperature
  • \tau^{2} — keeps gradient size comparable as \tau changes

In AI papers

How many small open models are trained from larger ones.

Hinton, Vinyals & Dean, “Distilling the Knowledge in a Neural Network”, 2015

cards.label: Mutual information & information gain · Masters
cards.front:
Conditional entropy

H(Y \mid X)
cards.back:
“the entropy of Y given X”

The uncertainty left in Y after you learn X, averaged over the values of X.

In AI papers

A perfect classifier has H(Y \mid X) = 0: once you see the input, the label is certain.

cards.label: Mutual information & information gain · Masters
cards.front:
Mutual information

I(X; Y)
cards.back:
“the mutual information between X and Y”

How much knowing one variable reduces uncertainty about the other. Note the semicolon; it is symmetric: I(X; Y) = I(Y; X).

In AI papers

Contrastive learning (InfoNCE) maximises a lower bound on the mutual information between two views of the same data.

cards.label: Mutual information & information gain · Masters
cards.front:
Mutual information

I(X; Y) = H(X) - H(X \mid Y) = D_{\mathrm{KL}}\big(p(x, y) \,\|\, p(x)\,p(y)\big)
cards.back:
“I of X and Y equals H of X minus H of X given Y, which is the KL divergence of the joint from the product of the marginals”

The reduction in uncertainty about X from knowing Y. Equivalently, how far the joint distribution is from what it would be if they were independent.

Term by term

  • H(X \mid Y) — uncertainty in X that remains after seeing Y
  • p(x)\,p(y) — the joint if X and Y were independent

In AI papers

Zero if and only if X and Y are independent. Used in feature selection, the information bottleneck, and interpretability probes.

cards.label: Mutual information & information gain · Masters
cards.front:
InfoNCE (contrastive) loss

\mathcal{L}_{\text{InfoNCE}} = -\log \frac{\exp\!\big(\operatorname{sim}(\mathbf{q}, \mathbf{k}^{+}) / \tau\big)}{\sum_{i=0}^{K} \exp\!\big(\operatorname{sim}(\mathbf{q}, \mathbf{k}_{i}) / \tau\big)}
cards.back:
“InfoNCE equals minus log of e to the similarity of the query and its positive key over tau, over the sum across all keys”

A softmax classification problem: pick out the one matching item \mathbf{k}^{+} from K distractors. Minimising it maximises a lower bound on mutual information.

Term by term

  • \mathbf{k}^{+} — positive: another view of the same example
  • \mathbf{k}_{i} — all candidates, including the positive
  • \operatorname{sim} — usually cosine similarity
  • \tau — temperature, e.g. 0.07

In AI papers

CLIP trains image and text encoders with this loss; so do SimCLR and dense retrievers.

van den Oord et al., “Representation Learning with Contrastive Predictive Coding”, 2018

cards.label: Alignment objectives · Masters
cards.front:
Reward-model loss (Bradley–Terry)

\mathcal{L}_{R}(\phi) = -\,\mathbb{E}_{(x, y_{w}, y_{l}) \sim \mathcal{D}}\Big[ \log \sigma\big( r_{\phi}(x, y_{w}) - r_{\phi}(x, y_{l}) \big) \Big]
cards.back:
“L R equals minus the expectation over preference pairs of log sigma of the reward of the winner minus the reward of the loser”

Humans compared two answers. Train a reward model so that the probability “winner beats loser”, \sigma(\Delta r), is high: binary cross-entropy on the reward difference.

Term by term

  • y_w, y_l — preferred (winning) and rejected (losing) responses
  • r_{\phi}(x, y) — scalar reward for response y to prompt x
  • \sigma(r_w - r_l) — Bradley–Terry probability that y_w is preferred

In AI papers

Stage 2 of classic RLHF (InstructGPT).

Ouyang et al., “Training language models to follow instructions with human feedback”, 2022

cards.label: Alignment objectives · Masters
cards.front:
KL-regularised RLHF objective

\max_{\pi_{\theta}} \; \mathbb{E}_{x \sim \mathcal{D},\, y \sim \pi_{\theta}(\cdot \mid x)}\big[ r_{\phi}(x, y) \big] \;-\; \beta\, D_{\mathrm{KL}}\big( \pi_{\theta}(\cdot \mid x) \,\|\, \pi_{\text{ref}}(\cdot \mid x) \big)
cards.back:
“maximise over the policy pi theta the expected reward of its answers, minus beta times the KL divergence of the policy from the reference model”

Make the model produce answers the reward model likes, but pay a penalty for drifting far from the original model. That prevents “reward hacking” and keeps the language fluent.

Term by term

  • \pi_{\theta} — the policy: the LLM being tuned
  • \pi_{\text{ref}} — frozen reference (the SFT model)
  • r_{\phi} — learned reward model
  • \beta — strength of the KL leash

In AI papers

Optimised with PPO in InstructGPT; GRPO and DPO start from the same objective.

Ouyang et al., 2022; Ziegler et al., 2019

cards.label: Alignment objectives · Masters
cards.front:
Optimal KL-regularised policy

\pi^{*}(y \mid x) = \frac{1}{Z(x)}\,\pi_{\text{ref}}(y \mid x)\,\exp\!\Big(\frac{1}{\beta}\,r(x, y)\Big)
cards.back:
“pi star of y given x equals one over Z of x times pi ref of y given x times e to the reward over beta”

The exact solution of the RLHF objective: reweight the reference model’s answers by the exponential of their reward. Z(x) normalises, and cannot be computed directly.

Term by term

  • Z(x) = \sum_{y} \pi_{\text{ref}}(y \mid x)\,e^{r(x, y)/\beta} — partition function
  • \beta \to 0 — pure reward maximisation
  • \beta \to \infty — stay exactly at \pi_{\text{ref}}

In AI papers

Solving for r gives r = \beta \log\frac{\pi^{*}}{\pi_{\text{ref}}} + \beta\log Z, the key step in deriving DPO.

Rafailov et al., 2023

cards.label: Alignment objectives · Masters
cards.front:
Direct Preference Optimization (DPO)

\mathcal{L}_{\text{DPO}}(\theta) = -\,\mathbb{E}_{(x, y_{w}, y_{l})}\left[ \log \sigma\!\left( \beta \log\frac{\pi_{\theta}(y_{w} \mid x)}{\pi_{\text{ref}}(y_{w} \mid x)} - \beta \log\frac{\pi_{\theta}(y_{l} \mid x)}{\pi_{\text{ref}}(y_{l} \mid x)} \right) \right]
cards.back:
“L DPO equals minus the expectation of log sigma of beta times the log-ratio for the winner minus beta times the log-ratio for the loser”

Skip the reward model and RL. The policy’s own log-ratio against the reference acts as an implicit reward, and the Bradley–Terry loss is applied to it directly.

Term by term

  • \beta \log \frac{\pi_{\theta}(y \mid x)}{\pi_{\text{ref}}(y \mid x)} — implicit reward of response y
  • y_w, y_l — preferred and rejected responses
  • \log\sigma(\cdot) — Bradley–Terry log-likelihood (the \log Z terms cancel)

In AI papers

A widely used preference-tuning method for open models, because it is just supervised training on pairs.

Rafailov et al., “Direct Preference Optimization”, 2023

cards.label: Alignment objectives · Masters
cards.front:
PPO clipped objective

\mathcal{L}^{\text{CLIP}}(\theta) = \mathbb{E}_{t}\Big[ \min\big( \rho_{t}(\theta)\,\hat{A}_{t},\; \operatorname{clip}(\rho_{t}(\theta), 1 - \epsilon, 1 + \epsilon)\,\hat{A}_{t} \big) \Big], \qquad \rho_{t}(\theta) = \frac{\pi_{\theta}(a_{t} \mid s_{t})}{\pi_{\theta_{\text{old}}}(a_{t} \mid s_{t})}
cards.back:
“L clip equals the expectation over steps of the minimum of rho t times A hat t and the clipped rho t times A hat t”

Raise the probability of actions that did better than expected (positive advantage) and lower the others, but clip the probability ratio so that no update moves the policy too far.

Term by term

  • \rho_t — probability ratio of new to old policy
  • \hat{A}_t — advantage: how much better than average the action was
  • \epsilon — clip range, e.g. 0.2

In AI papers

The RL algorithm in InstructGPT-style RLHF. For LLMs an “action” is a token and the “state” is the prompt plus the tokens so far.

Schulman et al., “Proximal Policy Optimization Algorithms”, 2017

cards.label: Alignment objectives · Masters
cards.front:
Group-relative advantage (GRPO)

\hat{A}_{i} = \frac{r_{i} - \operatorname{mean}(r_{1}, \ldots, r_{G})}{\operatorname{std}(r_{1}, \ldots, r_{G})}
cards.back:
“A hat i equals r i minus the mean of the group’s rewards, over their standard deviation”

Sample G answers to the same prompt and score each against its siblings, instead of training a separate value network to estimate the baseline.

Term by term

  • G — group size: answers sampled per prompt
  • r_i — reward of answer i (e.g. 1 if a maths answer is correct)

In AI papers

Used to train reasoning models (DeepSeekMath, DeepSeek-R1) with verifiable rewards.

Shao et al., “DeepSeekMath”, 2024

cards.label: Minima & objectives · High school
cards.front:
Minimum of a parabola

f(x) = a x^{2} + b x + c, \;\; a > 0 \quad\Rightarrow\quad x^{*} = -\frac{b}{2a}, \quad f(x^{*}) = c - \frac{b^{2}}{4a}
cards.back:
“for f of x equals a x squared plus b x plus c with a positive, the minimum is at x star equals minus b over 2 a”

An upward parabola has one lowest point, the vertex. It is where the slope 2ax + b equals zero.

Term by term

  • a > 0 — opens upward, so there is a minimum
  • x^{*} — the minimiser (arg min)
  • f(x^{*}) — the minimum value

In AI papers

Near a minimum, every smooth loss looks like a parabola; that local picture drives learning-rate theory.

cards.label: Minima & objectives · High school
cards.front:
Mean squared error

\operatorname{MSE} = \frac{1}{n}\sum_{i=1}^{n} \big(y_{i} - \hat{y}_{i}\big)^{2}
cards.back:
“M S E equals one over n times the sum over i of y i minus y hat i, squared”

Average of the squared differences between true values and predictions. Squaring makes all errors positive and punishes big misses more.

Term by term

  • y_i — true value
  • \hat{y}_i — prediction
  • (\cdot)^{2} — squared error

In AI papers

The loss for regression, value functions and diffusion noise prediction.

cards.label: Minima & objectives · Undergraduate
cards.front:
Optimisation problem

\min_{\boldsymbol{\theta} \in \mathbb{R}^{d}} \; \mathcal{L}(\boldsymbol{\theta})
cards.back:
“minimise L of theta over theta in R d”

Find the parameters that make the loss as small as possible. The subscript names the variables you are allowed to change, and where they may live.

In AI papers

Every training run is an attempt to solve this problem, only approximately.

cards.label: Minima & objectives · Undergraduate
cards.front:
Global and local minima

f(\mathbf{x}^{*}) \le f(\mathbf{x}) \;\; \forall \mathbf{x} \qquad \text{vs.} \qquad \forall \mathbf{x} \in B_{r}(\mathbf{x}^{*})
cards.back:
“global minimum, for every x; local minimum, for every x in a small ball around x star”

A global minimum is the lowest point anywhere; a local minimum is the lowest point in its neighbourhood, a small ball B_r of radius r.

In AI papers

Neural losses have many minima; in large networks most local minima turn out to be nearly as good as the global one.

cards.label: Minima & objectives · Undergraduate
cards.front:
Empirical risk minimisation

\boldsymbol{\theta}^{*} = \arg\min_{\boldsymbol{\theta}} \; \frac{1}{N}\sum_{i=1}^{N} \ell\big(f_{\boldsymbol{\theta}}(\mathbf{x}^{(i)}),\, y^{(i)}\big)
cards.back:
“theta star is the arg min over theta of the average loss over the training set”

Choose the parameters with the smallest average loss on the training data. The average stands in for the true expected loss (the risk), which we cannot compute.

Term by term

  • \ell — per-example loss, e.g. cross-entropy
  • f_{\boldsymbol{\theta}}(\mathbf{x}^{(i)}) — model prediction
  • \frac{1}{N}\sum — empirical average over the dataset

In AI papers

The formal statement of “training a model”.

cards.label: Gradient descent · Undergraduate
cards.front:
Iterates and the update arrow

\boldsymbol{\theta}_{t}, \quad \boldsymbol{\theta}_{t+1}, \quad \boldsymbol{\theta} \leftarrow \boldsymbol{\theta} - \eta\,\mathbf{g}
cards.back:
“theta at step t; theta at step t plus 1; theta gets theta minus eta g”

A subscript t counts optimisation steps. The left arrow is assignment in an algorithm (like `=` in code), not a mathematical equality.

In AI papers

Optimizer pseudocode in papers (Adam, AdamW, Lion) is written with these conventions.

cards.label: Gradient descent · Undergraduate
cards.front:
Learning rate

\eta, \quad \alpha, \quad \eta_{t}
cards.back:
“eta (or alpha), the learning rate; eta t, the learning rate at step t”

The step size: how far to move against the gradient. A subscript t means it changes during training according to a schedule.

In AI papers

Typical peak values: 10^{-3} for small models, 3 \times 10^{-4} to 10^{-4} for LLM pretraining, 10^{-5} for fine-tuning.

cards.label: Gradient descent · Undergraduate
cards.front:
Gradient at step t

\mathbf{g}_{t} = \nabla_{\boldsymbol{\theta}}\,\mathcal{L}(\boldsymbol{\theta}_{t-1})
cards.back:
“g t, the gradient at step t”

Shorthand for the (usually stochastic) gradient used in step t. Adam’s paper evaluates it at \boldsymbol{\theta}_{t-1}, the weights before the update.

In AI papers

\mathbf{g}_t^{2} in optimizer papers means the element-wise square \mathbf{g}_t \odot \mathbf{g}_t, not a dot product.

cards.label: Gradient descent · Undergraduate
cards.front:
Gradient descent

\boldsymbol{\theta}_{t+1} = \boldsymbol{\theta}_{t} - \eta\,\nabla_{\boldsymbol{\theta}}\mathcal{L}(\boldsymbol{\theta}_{t})
cards.back:
“theta t plus 1 equals theta t minus eta times the gradient of L at theta t”

Take a small step downhill, in the direction opposite to the gradient, and repeat.

Term by term

  • \boldsymbol{\theta}_{t} — current parameters
  • \eta — learning rate (step size)
  • -\nabla\mathcal{L} — steepest-descent direction

In AI papers

The basis of every neural-network optimizer.

cards.label: SGD & momentum · Undergraduate
cards.front:
Minibatch

\mathcal{B}_{t} \subset \{1, \ldots, N\}, \quad |\mathcal{B}_{t}| = B
cards.back:
“B t, the minibatch at step t, of size B”

A small random subset of the training examples used to estimate the gradient at one step.

In AI papers

LLM batch sizes are often quoted in tokens, e.g. 4 M tokens per step.

cards.label: SGD & momentum · Undergraduate
cards.front:
Stochastic gradient descent (SGD)

\boldsymbol{\theta}_{t+1} = \boldsymbol{\theta}_{t} - \eta\,\frac{1}{|\mathcal{B}_{t}|}\sum_{i \in \mathcal{B}_{t}} \nabla_{\boldsymbol{\theta}}\,\ell\big(\mathbf{x}^{(i)}, y^{(i)}; \boldsymbol{\theta}_{t}\big)
cards.back:
“theta t plus 1 equals theta t minus eta times the average gradient over the minibatch”

Use the average gradient of a small random batch instead of the whole dataset. It is a noisy but unbiased estimate, and far cheaper.

Term by term

  • \mathcal{B}_{t} — random minibatch
  • \ell(\cdot; \boldsymbol{\theta}) — per-example loss
  • \mathbb{E}[\hat{\mathbf{g}}] = \nabla\mathcal{L} — unbiased estimate of the full gradient

In AI papers

The gradient noise also helps escape saddle points and sharp minima.

cards.label: SGD & momentum · Undergraduate
cards.front:
Exponential moving average

m_{t} = \beta\, m_{t-1} + (1 - \beta)\, g_{t}
cards.back:
“m t equals beta m t minus 1 plus one minus beta times g t”

A running average that forgets old values gradually. Each step keeps a fraction \beta of the old average; it averages over roughly the last \frac{1}{1 - \beta} values.

Term by term

  • \beta — decay, e.g. 0.9 ≈ last 10 steps, 0.999 ≈ last 1000
  • (1 - \beta)\,g_t — weight on the newest value

In AI papers

Adam’s moments, BatchNorm running statistics and EMA copies of weights all use this formula.

cards.label: Loss landscape · Undergraduate
cards.front:
Stationary (critical) point

\nabla f(\mathbf{x}^{*}) = \mathbf{0}
cards.back:
“the gradient of f at x star is the zero vector”

A flat point: a minimum, a maximum or a saddle. Gradient descent stops moving there.

In AI papers

Non-convex convergence results only promise \|\nabla f\| \le \varepsilon: an approximately stationary point.

cards.label: Regularization · Undergraduate
cards.front:
L2 regularisation

\mathcal{L}_{ ext{reg}}( oldsymbol{ heta}) = \mathcal{L}( oldsymbol{ heta}) + rac{\lambda}{2}\| oldsymbol{ heta}\|_{2}^{2} \quad\Rightarrow\quad abla\mathcal{L}_{ ext{reg}} = abla\mathcal{L} + \lambda oldsymbol{ heta}
cards.back:
“the regularised loss equals the loss plus lambda over two times the squared norm of theta”

Penalise large weights. Its gradient adds \lambda\boldsymbol{\theta}, which pulls every weight toward zero (“weight decay”).

Term by term

  • \lambda — regularisation strength
  • \frac{1}{2} — chosen so the gradient is simply \lambda\boldsymbol{\theta}

In AI papers

For plain SGD this equals weight decay; for Adam it does not, hence AdamW.

cards.label: Minima & objectives · Masters
cards.front:
Constrained problem

\min_{\mathbf{x}} f(\mathbf{x}) \quad \text{s.t.} \quad g(\mathbf{x}) \le 0
cards.back:
“minimise f of x subject to g of x at most zero”

“s.t.” means “subject to”: only points satisfying the constraint count. Lagrange multipliers turn this into an unconstrained problem.

In AI papers

Trust-region methods (TRPO) constrain the step by a KL budget; RLHF’s KL penalty is the Lagrangian form of such a constraint.

cards.label: Gradient descent · Masters
cards.front:
Descent lemma

\mathcal{L}(\boldsymbol{\theta}_{t+1}) \le \mathcal{L}(\boldsymbol{\theta}_{t}) - \eta\Big(1 - \frac{L\eta}{2}\Big)\big\|\nabla\mathcal{L}(\boldsymbol{\theta}_{t})\big\|_{2}^{2}
cards.back:
“the next loss is at most the current loss minus eta times one minus L eta over two times the squared gradient norm”

For an L-smooth loss, a gradient step is guaranteed to lower the loss as long as \eta < 2/L. With \eta = 1/L, the loss drops by at least \frac{1}{2L}\|\nabla\mathcal{L}\|^{2}.

Term by term

  • L — smoothness constant (maximum curvature)
  • 1 - L\eta/2 > 0 — requires \eta < 2/L

In AI papers

The first step of almost every convergence proof; explains why too large a learning rate makes the loss blow up.

cards.label: SGD & momentum · Masters
cards.front:
SGD with momentum

\mathbf{v}_{t+1} = \mu\,\mathbf{v}_{t} + \mathbf{g}_{t}, \qquad \boldsymbol{\theta}_{t+1} = \boldsymbol{\theta}_{t} - \eta\,\mathbf{v}_{t+1}
cards.back:
“v t plus 1 equals mu v t plus g t; theta t plus 1 equals theta t minus eta v t plus 1”

Keep a velocity that accumulates past gradients, like a heavy ball rolling downhill. Consistent directions speed up; zig-zags cancel out.

Term by term

  • \mathbf{v} — velocity (running sum of gradients)
  • \mu — momentum, typically 0.9

In AI papers

This is PyTorch’s form. With \mu = 0.9 the effective step is about 10\eta in a steady direction.

Polyak, 1964; Sutskever et al., 2013

cards.label: Adam & AdamW · Masters
cards.front:
Adam hyper-parameters

\beta_{1} = 0.9, \quad \beta_{2} = 0.999, \quad \epsilon = 10^{-8}
cards.back:
“beta one, beta two, epsilon”

\beta_1 is the decay rate of the running mean of gradients, \beta_2 of the running mean of squared gradients. \beta^{t} with a superscript t is a power, used in bias correction.

In AI papers

LLM training often uses \beta_2 = 0.95 for stability.

cards.label: Adam & AdamW · Masters
cards.front:
Adam

\begin{aligned} \mathbf{m}_{t} &= \beta_{1}\mathbf{m}_{t-1} + (1 - \beta_{1})\,\mathbf{g}_{t} \\ \mathbf{v}_{t} &= \beta_{2}\mathbf{v}_{t-1} + (1 - \beta_{2})\,\mathbf{g}_{t}^{2} \\ \hat{\mathbf{m}}_{t} &= \mathbf{m}_{t} / (1 - \beta_{1}^{t}), \qquad \hat{\mathbf{v}}_{t} = \mathbf{v}_{t} / (1 - \beta_{2}^{t}) \\ \boldsymbol{\theta}_{t} &= \boldsymbol{\theta}_{t-1} - \eta\,\hat{\mathbf{m}}_{t} / \big(\sqrt{\hat{\mathbf{v}}_{t}} + \epsilon\big) \end{aligned}
cards.back:
“m t is a moving average of gradients; v t is a moving average of squared gradients; divide each by one minus beta to the t; step by eta times m hat over root v hat plus epsilon”

Momentum (the first moment \mathbf{m}) sets the direction; the running average of squared gradients (second moment \mathbf{v}) sets a separate step size for each parameter, so rarely-updated or low-gradient weights still move.

Term by term

  • \mathbf{g}_{t}^{2} — element-wise square
  • 1 - \beta^{t} — bias correction (\beta^t is a power; the moments start at 0)
  • \sqrt{\hat{\mathbf{v}}_t} — per-parameter scale of recent gradients
  • \epsilon — avoids division by zero

In AI papers

The default optimizer of deep learning. Each step moves each weight by roughly \eta at most, regardless of the gradient’s scale.

Kingma & Ba, “Adam: A Method for Stochastic Optimization”, 2015

cards.label: Adam & AdamW · Masters
cards.front:
Why Adam corrects bias

\mathbf{m}_{t} = (1 - \beta_{1})\sum_{s=1}^{t} \beta_{1}^{\,t-s}\,\mathbf{g}_{s} \quad\Rightarrow\quad \mathbb{E}[\mathbf{m}_{t}] = (1 - \beta_{1}^{t})\,\mathbb{E}[\mathbf{g}] \;\;\text{(if the gradient distribution is stationary)}
cards.back:
“m t is a weighted sum of past gradients whose weights add to one minus beta one to the t”

Starting the average at zero makes early estimates too small. The weights sum to 1 - \beta_1^{t}, so dividing by it fixes the average.

Term by term

  • \beta_{1}^{\,t-s} — older gradients fade geometrically
  • 1 - \beta_{1}^{t} — total weight so far; tends to 1 as t grows

In AI papers

Without the correction for \mathbf{v} (with \beta_2 = 0.999), the first steps would be about 30 times too large.

cards.label: Adam & AdamW · Masters
cards.front:
AdamW (decoupled weight decay)

\boldsymbol{\theta}_{t} = \boldsymbol{\theta}_{t-1} - \eta_{t}\left( \frac{\hat{\mathbf{m}}_{t}}{\sqrt{\hat{\mathbf{v}}_{t}} + \epsilon} + \lambda\,\boldsymbol{\theta}_{t-1} \right)
cards.back:
“theta t equals theta t minus 1 minus eta t times the Adam step plus lambda theta t minus 1”

Shrink the weights directly by \lambda at each step, outside the adaptive scaling. Putting L2 into the loss instead would divide the decay by \sqrt{\hat{\mathbf{v}}} and weaken it for large-gradient weights.

Term by term

  • \lambda\,\boldsymbol{\theta}_{t-1} — decoupled weight decay (e.g. \lambda = 0.1)
  • \eta_{t} — scheduled learning rate, which also scales the decay

In AI papers

The standard optimizer for training Transformers and LLMs.

Loshchilov & Hutter, “Decoupled Weight Decay Regularization”, 2019

cards.label: Learning-rate schedules · Masters
cards.front:
Linear warm-up

\eta_{t} = \eta_{\max}\cdot\min\!\Big(1, \frac{t}{T_{\text{warm}}}\Big)
cards.back:
“eta t equals eta max times the minimum of one and t over T warm”

Start with a tiny learning rate and ramp up linearly for the first T_{\text{warm}} steps. Early on Adam’s \hat{\mathbf{v}} is noisy and the weights are in a sharp region, so large steps diverge.

Term by term

  • T_{\text{warm}} — warm-up length, e.g. 2,000 steps
  • \eta_{\max} — peak learning rate

In AI papers

Used for almost all Transformer training.

cards.label: Learning-rate schedules · Masters
cards.front:
Cosine decay

\eta_{t} = \eta_{\min} + \frac{1}{2}\big(\eta_{\max} - \eta_{\min}\big)\left(1 + \cos\!\Big(\frac{t}{T}\,\pi\Big)\right)
cards.back:
“eta t equals eta min plus one half of eta max minus eta min times one plus cosine of t over T times pi”

Glide the learning rate from \eta_{\max} at t = 0 down to \eta_{\min} at t = T along half a cosine wave: slow at first, fastest in the middle, gentle at the end.

Term by term

  • \cos(0) = 1 — start: \eta = \eta_{\max}
  • \cos(\pi) = -1 — end: \eta = \eta_{\min}
  • T — total number of decay steps

In AI papers

The most common LLM schedule (after warm-up), often with \eta_{\min} = 0.1\,\eta_{\max}.

Loshchilov & Hutter, “SGDR”, 2017

cards.label: Learning-rate schedules · Masters
cards.front:
The original Transformer schedule

\eta_{t} = d_{\text{model}}^{-0.5}\cdot\min\!\big(t^{-0.5},\; t\cdot T_{\text{warm}}^{-1.5}\big)
cards.back:
“eta t equals d model to the minus one half times the minimum of t to the minus one half and t times T warm to the minus three halves”

Linear warm-up for T_{\text{warm}} steps, then decay proportional to 1/\sqrt{t}. The two branches meet at t = T_{\text{warm}}.

Term by term

  • t \cdot T_{\text{warm}}^{-1.5} — rising branch (warm-up)
  • t^{-0.5} — falling branch (inverse square root)

In AI papers

Vaswani et al. used T_{\text{warm}} = 4000; inverse-square-root decay is still used for open-ended training.

Vaswani et al., 2017

cards.label: Convexity & convergence rates · Masters
cards.front:
Convex function

f \text{ convex} \iff f(\lambda\mathbf{x} + (1 - \lambda)\mathbf{y}) \le \lambda f(\mathbf{x}) + (1 - \lambda) f(\mathbf{y}), \;\; \lambda \in [0, 1]
cards.back:
“f is convex if and only if f of a blend of x and y is at most the blend of f of x and f of y”

The chord between any two points on the graph lies on or above the graph: a bowl with no dents. Every local minimum of a convex function is global.

Example

x^{2}, \; |x|, \; e^{x}, \; -\log x \text{ are convex}

In AI papers

Linear and logistic regression are convex; deep networks are not, but convex theory still explains a lot of optimizer behaviour.

cards.label: Convexity & convergence rates · Masters
cards.front:
L-smooth (Lipschitz gradient)

\| abla f(\mathbf{x}) - abla f(\mathbf{y})\|_{2} \le L\,\|\mathbf{x} - \mathbf{y}\|_{2}
cards.back:
“the gradient of f is L-Lipschitz”

The gradient cannot change faster than rate L. For twice-differentiable f this means every Hessian eigenvalue is at most L in size. Here L is a constant, not the loss.

In AI papers

Sets the safe step size: gradient descent with \eta \le 1/L always decreases the loss.

cards.label: Convexity & convergence rates · Masters
cards.front:
Strong convexity

f(\mathbf{y}) \ge f(\mathbf{x}) + \nabla f(\mathbf{x})^{\top}(\mathbf{y} - \mathbf{x}) + \frac{\mu}{2}\|\mathbf{y} - \mathbf{x}\|_{2}^{2}
cards.back:
“f is mu-strongly convex”

The function curves upward at least as much as a parabola with curvature \mu. Every Hessian eigenvalue is at least \mu > 0.

In AI papers

Adding L2 regularisation \frac{\lambda}{2}\|\boldsymbol{\theta}\|^{2} to a convex loss makes it \lambda-strongly convex.

cards.label: Convexity & convergence rates · Masters
cards.front:
Condition number

\kappa = \frac{L}{\mu} = \frac{\lambda_{\max}(\mathbf{H})}{\lambda_{\min}(\mathbf{H})}
cards.back:
“kappa equals L over mu”

The ratio of the steepest to the flattest curvature. A large \kappa is a long narrow valley, where plain gradient descent zig-zags and is slow.

In AI papers

Momentum, Adam and normalisation layers all help by reducing the effective condition number.

cards.label: Convexity & convergence rates · Masters
cards.front:
Convergence rates

\mathcal{O}\big(1/\sqrt{T}\big), \quad \mathcal{O}(1/T), \quad \mathcal{O}(1/T^{2}), \quad \mathcal{O}\big(\rho^{T}\big) \; (\rho < 1)
cards.back:
“order one over root T; order one over T; order one over T squared; order rho to the T”

How fast the error shrinks with the number of steps T. Sublinear rates (the first three) need about 1/\varepsilon^{2}, 1/\varepsilon or 1/\sqrt{\varepsilon} steps to reach error \varepsilon; a linear rate \rho^{T} needs only about \log(1/\varepsilon).

In AI papers

SGD on convex problems: 1/\sqrt{T}; gradient descent on smooth convex: 1/T; Nesterov acceleration: 1/T^{2}; strongly convex: linear.

cards.label: Convexity & convergence rates · Masters
cards.front:
Gradient descent rate (smooth convex)

f(\mathbf{x}_{T}) - f^{*} \le \frac{L\,\|\mathbf{x}_{0} - \mathbf{x}^{*}\|_{2}^{2}}{2T} = \mathcal{O}\Big(\frac{1}{T}\Big) \qquad (\eta = 1/L)
cards.back:
“the gap between f of x T and the optimum is at most L times the squared starting distance over 2 T”

On a convex, L-smooth function, the excess loss after T steps shrinks like 1/T: ten times more steps, ten times smaller gap.

Term by term

  • f^{*} — optimal value
  • \|\mathbf{x}_{0} - \mathbf{x}^{*}\| — distance from the start to a solution
  • \mathcal{O}(1/T) — sublinear rate

In AI papers

The baseline that accelerated and adaptive methods are measured against.

cards.label: Convexity & convergence rates · Masters
cards.front:
Linear convergence (strongly convex)

\|\mathbf{x}_{T} - \mathbf{x}^{*}\|_{2}^{2} \le \Big(1 - \frac{\mu}{L}\Big)^{T}\,\|\mathbf{x}_{0} - \mathbf{x}^{*}\|_{2}^{2} = \Big(1 - \frac{1}{\kappa}\Big)^{T}\,\|\mathbf{x}_{0} - \mathbf{x}^{*}\|_{2}^{2}
cards.back:
“the squared distance to the optimum after T steps is at most one minus mu over L to the T times the starting squared distance”

With strong convexity the error shrinks by a constant factor every step: geometric (“linear”) convergence. The factor is close to 1, so progress is slow, when the condition number \kappa is large.

Term by term

  • \mu — strong-convexity constant (minimum curvature)
  • L — smoothness (maximum curvature)
  • \kappa = L/\mu — condition number: about \kappa\log(1/\varepsilon) steps are needed

In AI papers

Why preconditioning (Adam, Shampoo, normalisation) matters: it reduces \kappa.

cards.label: Convexity & convergence rates · Masters
cards.front:
SGD rate (convex, noisy gradients)

\mathbb{E}\big[f(\bar{\mathbf{x}}_{T})\big] - f^{*} \le \frac{R\,G}{\sqrt{T}}, \qquad \eta = \frac{R}{G\sqrt{T}}, \qquad \bar{\mathbf{x}}_{T} = \frac{1}{T}\sum_{t=1}^{T}\mathbf{x}_{t}
cards.back:
“the expected gap of the averaged iterate is at most R G over root T”

With noisy gradients the rate drops to 1/\sqrt{T}: to halve the error you need four times as many steps. The step size has to shrink to cancel the noise.

Term by term

  • R — distance from start to solution
  • G — bound on the stochastic gradient norm
  • \bar{\mathbf{x}}_{T} — average of the iterates (Polyak averaging)

In AI papers

Motivates learning-rate decay at the end of training and weight averaging (EMA, SWA).

cards.label: Convexity & convergence rates · Masters
cards.front:
Non-convex guarantee

\min_{0 \le t < T} \big\|\nabla f(\mathbf{x}_{t})\big\|_{2}^{2} \le \frac{2L\,\big(f(\mathbf{x}_{0}) - f^{*}\big)}{T} \qquad (\eta = 1/L)
cards.back:
“the smallest squared gradient norm over T steps is at most 2 L times the initial gap over T”

For non-convex losses, gradient descent can only promise to find a nearly flat point (small gradient), not the global minimum.

Term by term

  • \|\nabla f\|^{2} — stationarity measure
  • f(\mathbf{x}_0) - f^{*} — how far the start is from the best value

In AI papers

The kind of guarantee proved for Adam-style methods on neural networks.

cards.label: Loss landscape · Masters
cards.front:
Sharpness

\lambda_{\max}\big(\nabla^{2}\mathcal{L}(\boldsymbol{\theta})\big)
cards.back:
“lambda max of the Hessian of the loss”

The curvature in the steepest direction. Flat minima (small sharpness) are thought to generalise better than sharp ones.

In AI papers

Sharpness-Aware Minimization (SAM) and the “edge of stability” phenomenon are both about this quantity.

cards.label: Loss landscape · Masters
cards.front:
Stable learning rate on a quadratic

\mathcal{L}(\boldsymbol{\theta}) = \tfrac{1}{2}\boldsymbol{\theta}^{\top}\mathbf{H}\boldsymbol{\theta}: \qquad \boldsymbol{\theta}_{t} = (\mathbf{I} - \eta\mathbf{H})^{t}\,\boldsymbol{\theta}_{0} \to \mathbf{0} \iff \eta < \frac{2}{\lambda_{\max}(\mathbf{H})}
cards.back:
“on a quadratic, gradient descent converges if and only if eta is less than two over the largest eigenvalue of H”

Along each eigen-direction the error is multiplied by 1 - \eta\lambda_i every step. If any |1 - \eta\lambda_i| > 1, that direction explodes.

Term by term

  • \mathbf{H} — Hessian (curvature)
  • 1 - \eta\lambda_{i} — per-step factor in direction i
  • 2/\lambda_{\max} — the edge of stability

In AI papers

Full-batch training drifts until sharpness sits right at 2/\eta (“edge of stability”, Cohen et al., 2021).

cards.label: Loss landscape · Masters
cards.front:
Quadratic model of the loss

\mathcal{L}(\boldsymbol{\theta} + \boldsymbol{\delta}) \approx \mathcal{L}(\boldsymbol{\theta}) + \nabla\mathcal{L}(\boldsymbol{\theta})^{\top}\boldsymbol{\delta} + \frac{1}{2}\,\boldsymbol{\delta}^{\top}\mathbf{H}\,\boldsymbol{\delta}
cards.back:
“L of theta plus delta is approximately L of theta plus the gradient transpose delta plus one half delta transpose H delta”

Near the current weights the loss looks like a bowl (or saddle) described by the gradient and the Hessian.

Term by term

  • abla\mathcal{L}^{ op} oldsymbol{\delta} — first-order change (slope)
  • rac{1}{2} oldsymbol{\delta}^{ op}\mathbf{H} oldsymbol{\delta} — second-order change (curvature)

In AI papers

Minimising this model gives Newton’s step oldsymbol{\delta} = -\mathbf{H}^{-1} abla\mathcal{L}; pruning methods (Optimal Brain Surgeon, GPTQ) use it to predict the damage from removing or rounding weights.

cards.label: Loss landscape · Masters
cards.front:
Classifying a stationary point

abla f(\mathbf{x}^{*}) = \mathbf{0} ext{ and } egin{cases} abla^{2} f(\mathbf{x}^{*}) \succ 0 & ext{local minimum} \ abla^{2} f(\mathbf{x}^{*}) \prec 0 & ext{local maximum} \ ext{eigenvalues of both signs} & ext{saddle point} \end{cases}
cards.back:
“at a point with zero gradient, a positive definite Hessian means a minimum, negative definite a maximum, mixed signs a saddle”

The Hessian’s eigenvalues are the curvatures along its eigen-directions. Up in every direction: a minimum. Up in some and down in others: a saddle.

Term by term

  • \succ 0 — all eigenvalues positive
  • \text{mixed} — a saddle, the most common critical point in high dimensions

In AI papers

In networks with millions of parameters most critical points are saddles, and noisy SGD escapes them.

cards.label: Loss landscape · Masters
cards.front:
Sharpness-aware minimization (SAM)

\min_{ oldsymbol{ heta}} \; \max_{\| oldsymbol{\epsilon}\|_{2} \le ho} \mathcal{L}( oldsymbol{ heta} + oldsymbol{\epsilon}), \qquad \hat{ oldsymbol{\epsilon}} = ho\, rac{ abla\mathcal{L}( oldsymbol{ heta})}{\| abla\mathcal{L}( oldsymbol{ heta})\|_{2}}
cards.back:
“minimise over theta the worst loss within a ball of radius rho around theta”

Look for weights whose whole neighbourhood has low loss, which is a flat minimum. In practice, take one step up the gradient to find the worst nearby point, and use the gradient there.

Term by term

  • \rho — neighbourhood radius
  • \hat{\boldsymbol{\epsilon}} — first-order approximation of the worst perturbation

In AI papers

Costs two gradient computations per step and often improves generalisation.

Foret et al., 2021

cards.label: Regularization · Masters
cards.front:
Gradient-norm clipping

\mathbf{g} \leftarrow \mathbf{g}\cdot\min\!\Big(1, \frac{c}{\|\mathbf{g}\|_{2}}\Big)
cards.back:
“g gets g times the minimum of one and c over the norm of g”

If the gradient is longer than c, shrink it to length c while keeping its direction; otherwise leave it alone.

Term by term

  • c — clipping threshold, often 1.0
  • \|\mathbf{g}\|_{2} — global norm over all parameters

In AI papers

Protects LLM training from rare loss spikes; standard in RNN training too.

cards.label: Regularization · Masters
cards.front:
Inverted dropout

\tilde{\mathbf{h}} = \frac{\mathbf{m} \odot \mathbf{h}}{1 - p}, \qquad m_{i} \overset{\text{iid}}{\sim} \operatorname{Bernoulli}(1 - p)
cards.back:
“h tilde equals the mask times h, divided by one minus p”

During training, zero each activation with probability p and scale the survivors up so that the expected value is unchanged: \mathbb{E}[\tilde{\mathbf{h}}] = \mathbf{h}.

Term by term

  • \mathbf{m} — random 0/1 mask
  • p — drop probability, e.g. 0.1
  • 1/(1-p) — rescaling, so nothing changes at test time

In AI papers

Used in the original Transformer; many LLM pretraining runs now set p = 0.

Srivastava et al., 2014

cards.label: Number representation · Grade 5–6
cards.front:
Rounding

3.14159 \approx 3.14, \qquad 2.5 \to 2 \text{ or } 3\,?
cards.back:
“three point one four one five nine is approximately three point one four”

Keep the digits you need and round the last one: up if the next digit is 5 or more, down otherwise. Computers break exact ties (like 2.5) toward the even neighbour, so ties do not always round up.

Example

7.46 \approx 7.5, \qquad 7.44 \approx 7.4

In AI papers

Every floating-point operation rounds its result, which is where numerical error comes from.

cards.label: Number representation · Grade 5–6
cards.front:
Place value

347 = 3 \times 10^{2} + 4 \times 10^{1} + 7 \times 10^{0} = 300 + 40 + 7
cards.back:
“three hundred forty-seven equals three times ten squared plus four times ten plus seven”

Each digit is worth ten times the digit to its right. The position of a digit is its power of ten.

Term by term

  • 10^{2} = 100 — hundreds place
  • 10^{0} = 1 — ones place

In AI papers

Computers do exactly the same thing in base 2, the binary system.

cards.label: Number representation · Grade 7–8
cards.front:
Scientific notation

6.02 \times 10^{23}, \qquad 3 \times 10^{-4} = \texttt{3e-4}
cards.back:
“six point oh two times ten to the twenty-three; three times ten to the minus four”

A number between 1 and 10 times a power of ten. The power says how many places to move the decimal point. Code writes the power after an “e”.

Example

12{,}300 = 1.23 \times 10^{4}, \qquad 0.0005 = 5 \times 10^{-4}

In AI papers

Floating-point numbers are scientific notation in base 2: a significand times a power of two.

cards.label: Number representation · Grade 7–8
cards.back:
“kilo, mega, giga, tera, peta; kibibyte, gibibyte”

Thousand, million, billion, trillion, quadrillion. Memory is sometimes counted in powers of two instead: 1 GiB = 1,073,741,824 bytes, about 7% more than 1 GB.

In AI papers

A “7B” model has 7 \times 10^{9} parameters; a GPU might do 10^{15} FLOP/s (1 PFLOP/s) with 80 GB of memory.

cards.label: Number representation · Grade 7–8
cards.front:
Bits and bytes

1 \text{ byte} = 8 \text{ bits}, \qquad n \text{ bits} \Rightarrow 2^{n} \text{ values}
cards.back:
“one byte is eight bits; n bits give two to the n values”

A bit is a single 0 or 1. With n bits you can write 2^{n} different patterns.

Example

\text{INT8}: 2^{8} = 256 \text{ values, from } -128 \text{ to } 127

In AI papers

FP32 = 4 bytes, BF16/FP16 = 2 bytes, FP8/INT8 = 1 byte, INT4 = half a byte per number.

cards.label: Number representation · Grade 7–8
cards.front:
Binary numbers

1011_{2} = 1 \cdot 2^{3} + 0 \cdot 2^{2} + 1 \cdot 2^{1} + 1 \cdot 2^{0} = 11_{10}
cards.back:
“one zero one one in base two equals eleven in base ten”

In base 2 each place is worth twice the place to its right, and the only digits are 0 and 1. The subscript names the base.

Term by term

  • _{2} — base 2 (binary)
  • 2^{3}, 2^{2}, 2^{1}, 2^{0} — place values 8, 4, 2, 1

In AI papers

Binary fractions work the same way: 0.101_2 = \frac{1}{2} + \frac{1}{8} = 0.625. That is how the mantissa of a float is read.

cards.label: Number representation · High school
cards.front:
Memory needed for a model’s weights

\text{memory} = N_{\text{params}} \times \frac{b}{8} \text{ bytes}
cards.back:
“memory equals the number of parameters times bits per parameter over eight bytes”

Multiply the number of weights by the bytes each one takes.

Term by term

  • N_{\text{params}} — number of parameters, e.g. 7 \times 10^{9}
  • b — bits per parameter: 32, 16, 8 or 4

In AI papers

A 7B model needs 28 GB in FP32, 14 GB in BF16, 7 GB in INT8 and 3.5 GB in INT4, which is why quantization lets it run on a laptop.

cards.label: Rounding & error · High school
cards.front:
Absolute and relative error

\text{absolute error} = |\hat{x} - x|, \qquad \text{relative error} = \frac{|\hat{x} - x|}{|x|}
cards.back:
“absolute error is the size of x hat minus x; relative error is that divided by the size of x”

Absolute error is how far off you are; relative error is how far off compared with the size of the true value. Floats keep the relative error small.

Term by term

  • x — true value
  • \hat{x} — computed or approximate value

In AI papers

Being off by 1 matters for a weight of 0.5 but not for one of 10,000; quantization error is best judged relatively.

cards.label: Floating-point formats · Undergraduate
cards.front:
Machine epsilon

\epsilon_{\text{mach}} = 2^{-p}
cards.back:
“epsilon machine equals two to the minus p”

The gap between 1 and the next larger floating-point number, where p is the number of stored mantissa bits. It sets the relative precision of the format. (Some texts call half of it, the unit roundoff u, “epsilon”.)

Example

\text{FP32}: 2^{-23} \approx 1.2 \times 10^{-7}, \quad \text{FP16}: 2^{-10} \approx 9.8 \times 10^{-4}, \quad \text{BF16}: 2^{-7} \approx 7.8 \times 10^{-3}

In AI papers

BF16 is only accurate to about 2–3 decimal digits, which is why optimizer states are usually kept in FP32.

cards.label: Floating-point formats · Undergraduate
cards.front:
Format names (sign, exponent, mantissa bits)

\underbrace{s}_{1}\;\underbrace{e_{1}\cdots e_{E}}_{E \text{ exponent bits}}\;\underbrace{m_{1}\cdots m_{M}}_{M \text{ mantissa bits}}
cards.back:
“one sign bit, E exponent bits, M mantissa bits”

Exponent bits set the range (how big and how small); mantissa bits set the precision (how many significant digits).

Example

\text{FP32}{:}\,(1, 8, 23) \quad \text{FP16}{:}\,(1, 5, 10) \quad \text{BF16}{:}\,(1, 8, 7) \quad \text{E4M3}{:}\,(1, 4, 3) \quad \text{E5M2}{:}\,(1, 5, 2)

In AI papers

BF16 keeps FP32’s 8 exponent bits, so it has the same range and rarely overflows, at the cost of precision.

cards.label: Floating-point formats · Undergraduate
cards.front:
Value of a floating-point number

x = (-1)^{s} \times \Big(1 + \sum_{i=1}^{M} m_{i}\,2^{-i}\Big) \times 2^{\,e - \text{bias}}, \qquad \text{bias} = 2^{E-1} - 1
cards.back:
“x equals minus one to the s times one point m in binary times two to the e minus bias”

Sign, then a significand between 1 and 2 (the leading 1 is implicit, not stored), then a power of two. The stored exponent is offset by a bias so that it can be negative.

Term by term

  • s — sign bit
  • m_i — mantissa (fraction) bits
  • e — stored exponent; e = all zeros is reserved for zero and subnormals, all ones for ∞/NaN in IEEE formats
  • \text{bias} — 127 for FP32/BF16, 15 for FP16, 7 for E4M3

In AI papers

Precision is relative: there are as many BF16 numbers between 1 and 2 as between 1024 and 2048.

cards.label: Floating-point formats · Undergraduate
cards.front:
Largest FP16 number

x_{\max}^{\text{FP16}} = (2 - 2^{-10}) \times 2^{15} = 65{,}504
cards.back:
“the largest FP16 number is two minus two to the minus ten times two to the fifteen, which is 65,504”

With only 5 exponent bits, FP16 overflows to infinity above 65,504. BF16 and FP32 go up to about 3.4 \times 10^{38}.

Term by term

  • 2 - 2^{-10} — largest significand (all mantissa bits 1)
  • 2^{15} — largest exponent (30 - 15)

In AI papers

Why FP16 training needs loss scaling and why e^{12} \approx 162{,}755 computed in FP16 becomes \infty.

cards.label: Quantization · Undergraduate
cards.front:
Signed integer ranges

\text{INT}b: \; [-2^{b-1},\; 2^{b-1} - 1]
cards.back:
“a b-bit signed integer ranges from minus two to the b minus one up to two to the b minus one, minus one”

Two’s-complement integers have one more negative value than positive. The spacing is always exactly 1, unlike floats.

Example

\text{INT8}: [-128, 127], \qquad \text{INT4}: [-8, 7]

In AI papers

Symmetric quantization often uses only [-127, 127] so that zero sits exactly in the middle.

cards.label: Quantization · Undergraduate
cards.front:
Clamp (clip)

\operatorname{clamp}(x, a, b) = \min\big(\max(x, a),\, b\big)
cards.back:
“clamp x between a and b”

Force x into the interval [a, b]: values below a become a, values above b become b.

Example

\operatorname{clamp}(300, -128, 127) = 127

In AI papers

Quantizers clamp to the integer range; outliers that get clamped cause large errors.

cards.label: Compute & memory efficiency · Undergraduate
cards.front:
FLOPs versus FLOP/s

\text{FLOPs} \;(\text{work}) \qquad \text{vs.} \qquad \text{FLOP/s} \;(\text{speed})
cards.back:
“floating-point operations, versus floating-point operations per second”

FLOPs counts how much arithmetic a job needs; FLOP/s is how fast hardware can do it. Time ≈ FLOPs ÷ (FLOP/s × utilisation). One multiply-add counts as 2 FLOPs.

In AI papers

Model FLOPs Utilisation (MFU) is achieved FLOP/s divided by peak; 40–60% is good for LLM training.

cards.label: Compute & memory efficiency · Undergraduate
cards.front:
FLOPs of a matrix multiplication

\underset{m \times n}{\mathbf{A}}\;\underset{n \times p}{\mathbf{B}}: \qquad \text{FLOPs} = 2\,m\,n\,p
cards.back:
“multiplying an m by n matrix by an n by p matrix costs two m n p floating-point operations”

Each of the m p outputs is a dot product of length n: n multiplies and about n adds.

Term by term

  • m\,p — number of outputs
  • 2n — one multiply and one add per term

In AI papers

A forward pass costs about 2N FLOPs per token for a model with N parameters, since every weight is used in one multiply-add.

cards.label: Floating-point formats · Masters
cards.front:
Unit in the last place

\operatorname{ulp}(x) = 2^{\lfloor \log_{2}|x| \rfloor - p}
cards.back:
“u l p of x”

The spacing between neighbouring floats near x. It doubles each time |x| crosses a power of two, so absolute precision gets worse for big numbers.

Example

\text{BF16}: \operatorname{ulp}(1) = 2^{-7}, \quad \operatorname{ulp}(256) = 2

In AI papers

A small update \eta g is lost entirely if it is less than half an ulp of the weight it is added to.

cards.label: Floating-point formats · Masters
cards.front:
FP8 formats E4M3 and E5M2

\mathrm{E4M3}: \; \max = 448, \;\; \epsilon = 2^{-3} \qquad \mathrm{E5M2}: \; \max = 57{,}344, \;\; \epsilon = 2^{-2}
cards.back:
“E four M three, max 448; E five M two, max 57,344”

“ExMy” means x exponent and y mantissa bits. E4M3 has more precision; E5M2 has more range.

In AI papers

FP8 training usually stores weights and activations in E4M3 and gradients in E5M2, each tensor with its own scale factor.

cards.label: Rounding & error · Masters
cards.front:
Floating-point rounding operator

\operatorname{fl}(x)
cards.back:
“f l of x, x rounded to floating point”

The nearest representable floating-point number to the real number x. Error analysis writes computed results as \operatorname{fl}(a + b) and so on.

In AI papers

\operatorname{fl}_{\text{bf16}}(w) is what a weight becomes when cast to BF16.

cards.label: Rounding & error · Masters
cards.front:
Standard model of floating-point arithmetic

\operatorname{fl}(a \circ b) = (a \circ b)(1 + \delta), \qquad |\delta| \le u = \tfrac{1}{2}\epsilon_{\text{mach}}, \qquad \circ \in \{+, -, \times, \div\}
cards.back:
“the computed result of a op b equals the exact result times one plus delta, with delta at most the unit roundoff”

Each basic operation is exact except for one final rounding, which has relative error at most u. Errors then build up over long chains of operations.

Term by term

  • \delta — relative rounding error of this one operation
  • u — unit roundoff: 2^{-24} for FP32, 2^{-8} for BF16

In AI papers

A sum of n numbers can have error around n u in the worst case, which is why long dot products accumulate in FP32.

cards.label: Rounding & error · Masters
cards.front:
Swamping (small numbers lost in big ones)

\operatorname{fl}_{\text{bf16}}(256 + 1) = 256, \qquad \operatorname{fl}_{\text{fp32}}\big(1 + 10^{-8}\big) = 1
cards.back:
“in BF16, 256 plus 1 is 256; in FP32, one plus ten to the minus eight is one”

When you add a small number to a large one, the small one can be rounded away entirely. BF16 has only 8 significant bits, so near 256 the spacing is 2 and adding 1 changes nothing.

Term by term

  • \operatorname{ulp}_{\text{bf16}}(256) = 2 — the gap between neighbouring BF16 values at 256
  • 256 + 1 — a tie, broken toward the even value 256

In AI papers

Why weights are updated in FP32 “master” copies: \boldsymbol{\theta} - \eta\mathbf{g} in BF16 would often leave \boldsymbol{\theta} unchanged.

cards.label: Rounding & error · Masters
cards.front:
Catastrophic cancellation

\operatorname{Var}(x) = \mathbb{E}[x^{2}] - \big(\mathbb{E}[x]\big)^{2} \quad\text{is unstable when}\quad |\mathbb{E}[x]| \gg \operatorname{Std}(x)
cards.back:
“variance as E of x squared minus E of x, squared, is unstable when the mean is much larger than the spread”

Subtracting two nearly equal rounded numbers cancels their leading digits and leaves mostly rounding error. The formula is exact on paper but can even return a negative variance.

Term by term

  • \mathbb{E}[x^{2}] \approx (\mathbb{E}[x])^{2} — two big, nearly equal numbers
  • \text{fix} — subtract the mean first, or use Welford’s running algorithm

In AI papers

Normalisation kernels compute variance in FP32 with a stable (two-pass or Welford) method.

cards.label: Rounding & error · Masters
cards.front:
Condition number of a problem

\kappa_{f}(x) = \left| \frac{x\,f^{\prime}(x)}{f(x)} \right| \approx \frac{\text{relative change in output}}{\text{relative change in input}}
cards.back:
“the condition number of f at x equals the absolute value of x f prime of x over f of x”

How much a problem amplifies small relative errors in its input. A large \kappa means the answer is sensitive no matter how carefully you compute it.

Term by term

  • \kappa \approx 1 — well-conditioned
  • \kappa \gg 1 — ill-conditioned: expect to lose about \log_{10}\kappa digits

In AI papers

For solving \mathbf{A}\mathbf{x} = \mathbf{b} the analogue is \kappa(\mathbf{A}) = \sigma_{\max}/\sigma_{\min}, and it also slows optimizers.

cards.label: Numerical stability · Masters
cards.front:
Log-sum-exp trick

\log\sum_{i=1}^{K} e^{z_{i}} = m + \log\sum_{i=1}^{K} e^{z_{i} - m}, \qquad m = \max_{i} z_{i}
cards.back:
“log of the sum of e to the z i equals m plus log of the sum of e to the z i minus m, where m is the largest z”

Subtract the largest value before exponentiating. The biggest term becomes e^{0} = 1, so nothing overflows, and the answer is mathematically unchanged.

Term by term

  • m — the maximum logit
  • z_i - m \le 0 — every exponent is now at most 0

In AI papers

Used inside every cross-entropy and softmax kernel; without it, a logit of 100 overflows even in FP32 (e^{100} \approx 2.7 \times 10^{43}).

cards.label: Numerical stability · Masters
cards.front:
Shift-invariance of softmax

\operatorname{softmax}(\mathbf{z}) = \operatorname{softmax}(\mathbf{z} - c\,\mathbf{1}) \quad \text{for any } c \in \mathbb{R}
cards.back:
“softmax of z equals softmax of z minus c for any constant c”

Adding the same constant to every logit multiplies top and bottom by e^{-c}, which cancels. So subtracting the max is free.

Term by term

  • c = \max_i z_i — the choice that prevents overflow

In AI papers

Also why only the differences between logits matter.

cards.label: Numerical stability · Masters
cards.front:
Online softmax (FlashAttention)

m^{\text{new}} = \max(m, \tilde{m}), \qquad \ell^{\text{new}} = e^{m - m^{\text{new}}}\,\ell + e^{\tilde{m} - m^{\text{new}}}\,\tilde{\ell}
cards.back:
“the new running max is the max of the old and the block max; the new running sum rescales both sums to the new max”

Softmax can be computed one block of scores at a time: keep a running maximum m and a running sum \ell, and rescale the old sum whenever a larger maximum appears.

Term by term

  • m, \ell — running max and running sum of e^{z - m} so far
  • \tilde{m}, \tilde{\ell} — max and sum for the new block

In AI papers

Lets FlashAttention avoid ever writing the n \times n score matrix to memory, turning attention from memory-bound to compute-bound.

Milakov & Gimelshein, 2018; Dao et al., “FlashAttention”, 2022

cards.label: Numerical stability · Masters
cards.front:
Loss scaling for FP16

\tilde{\mathcal{L}} = S \cdot \mathcal{L}, \qquad \mathbf{g} = \frac{1}{S}\,\nabla_{\boldsymbol{\theta}}\tilde{\mathcal{L}}
cards.back:
“scale the loss by S before backprop, then divide the gradients by S”

Small gradients underflow to zero in FP16 (below about 6 \times 10^{-8}). Multiplying the loss by S shifts every gradient up into range; dividing afterwards (in FP32) restores the true values.

Term by term

  • S — scale, e.g. 2^{16}; halved when an overflow (inf/NaN) is detected, grown slowly otherwise

In AI papers

Dynamic loss scaling (`GradScaler`) is needed for FP16 but not for BF16, whose range matches FP32.

Micikevicius et al., “Mixed Precision Training”, 2018

cards.label: Numerical stability · Masters
cards.front:
Mixed-precision update with master weights

\boldsymbol{\theta}^{\text{fp32}} \leftarrow \boldsymbol{\theta}^{\text{fp32}} - \eta\,\mathbf{u}\big(\mathbf{g}^{\text{fp32}}\big), \qquad \boldsymbol{\theta}^{\text{bf16}} = \operatorname{fl}_{\text{bf16}}\big(\boldsymbol{\theta}^{\text{fp32}}\big)
cards.back:
“update the FP32 master weights, then cast them to BF16 for the next forward and backward pass”

Compute in low precision but accumulate updates in high precision, so that small steps are not swamped.

Term by term

  • \mathbf{u}(\cdot) — the optimizer step (e.g. Adam’s)
  • \operatorname{fl}_{\text{bf16}} — round to BF16

In AI papers

With Adam this costs about 16 bytes per parameter: 2 (BF16 weights) + 2 (grads) + 4 (master) + 4 + 4 (moments). A 7B model needs about 112 GB before activations.

cards.label: Numerical stability · Masters
cards.front:
Stochastic rounding

\operatorname{SR}(x) = \begin{cases} \lfloor x \rfloor & \text{with probability } 1 - (x - \lfloor x \rfloor) \\ \lfloor x \rfloor + 1 & \text{with probability } x - \lfloor x \rfloor \end{cases} \qquad \mathbb{E}[\operatorname{SR}(x)] = x
cards.back:
“stochastic rounding rounds up with probability equal to the fractional part”

Round randomly, in proportion to how close x is to each neighbour (here on a grid of spacing 1). On average there is no error, so many tiny updates add up correctly instead of being rounded away.

Term by term

  • x - \lfloor x \rfloor — fractional part = chance of rounding up
  • \mathbb{E}[\operatorname{SR}(x)] = x — unbiased

In AI papers

Makes pure-BF16 or FP8 weight updates workable without FP32 master weights.

cards.label: Numerical stability · Masters
cards.front:
RMSNorm

\operatorname{RMSNorm}(\mathbf{x}) = \frac{\mathbf{x}}{\sqrt{\frac{1}{d}\sum_{i=1}^{d} x_{i}^{2} + \epsilon}} \odot \mathbf{g}
cards.back:
“RMS norm of x equals x divided by the root mean square of its entries plus epsilon, times the gain g”

Rescale each token vector to unit root-mean-square size, then apply a learned per-feature gain. Cheaper than LayerNorm, with no mean subtraction.

Term by term

  • \sqrt{\frac{1}{d}\sum x_i^{2}} — root mean square of the entries
  • \epsilon — guards against division by zero (e.g. 10^{-6})
  • \mathbf{g} — learned gain

In AI papers

Used in LLaMA and most modern LLMs. Implementations compute the sum of squares in FP32 even for BF16 inputs.

Zhang & Sennrich, 2019

cards.label: Quantization · Masters
cards.front:
Affine (asymmetric) quantization

q = \operatorname{clamp}\!\Big( \Big\lfloor \frac{x}{s} \Big\rceil + z,\; q_{\min},\; q_{\max} \Big), \qquad \hat{x} = s\,(q - z)
cards.back:
“q equals x over s rounded, plus z, clamped to the integer range; x hat equals s times q minus z”

Map real numbers onto an integer grid with a scale s (the grid spacing) and a zero-point z (the integer that stands for 0.0). Dequantizing multiplies back.

Term by term

  • s = \frac{x_{\max} - x_{\min}}{q_{\max} - q_{\min}} — scale (step size)
  • z = q_{\min} - \lfloor x_{\min}/s \rceil — zero-point
  • \lfloor \cdot \rceil — round to nearest

In AI papers

Standard for INT8 activations, which are often not centred on zero (e.g. after ReLU).

cards.label: Quantization · Masters
cards.front:
Symmetric absmax quantization

s = \frac{\max_{i} |x_{i}|}{2^{b-1} - 1}, \qquad q_{i} = \Big\lfloor \frac{x_{i}}{s} \Big\rceil, \qquad \hat{x}_{i} = s\,q_{i}
cards.back:
“s equals the largest absolute value over two to the b minus one, minus one; q i is x i over s rounded”

Scale so the largest magnitude maps to the largest integer (127 for INT8), with zero-point 0. Simple and fast, but a single outlier makes s large and wastes resolution for all the other values.

Term by term

  • \max_i |x_i| = \|\mathbf{x}\|_{\infty} — absmax of the tensor, row or block
  • 2^{b-1} - 1 — 127 for INT8, 7 for INT4

In AI papers

Per-channel or per-block scales (e.g. one scale per 64 or 128 weights) limit the damage from outliers.

cards.label: Quantization · Masters
cards.front:
Quantization noise

e = x - \hat{x} \in \Big[-\frac{s}{2}, \frac{s}{2}\Big], \qquad \mathbb{E}[e^{2}] \approx \frac{s^{2}}{12}
cards.back:
“the rounding error is between minus s over 2 and s over 2, with mean square about s squared over 12”

Rounding to a grid of spacing s gives an error that behaves like uniform noise. Each extra bit halves s and cuts the noise power by 4 (about 6 dB).

Term by term

  • s — quantization step
  • s^{2}/12 — variance of a uniform distribution of width s

In AI papers

Going from INT8 to INT4 makes the step 16 times coarser, which is why 4-bit methods need careful error compensation (GPTQ, AWQ).

cards.label: Quantization · Masters
cards.front:
Block (microscaling) formats

x_{i} \approx s_{B}\cdot q_{i}, \quad i \in B, \qquad |B| = 32, \quad q_{i} \in \text{FP4 (E2M1)} = \{0, \pm 0.5, \pm 1, \pm 1.5, \pm 2, \pm 3, \pm 4, \pm 6\}
cards.back:
“each value is approximately the block scale times a 4-bit code”

Split a tensor into small blocks that share one scale factor, and store each element in very few bits. Small blocks adapt to local magnitude, so outliers only hurt their own block.

Term by term

  • s_{B} — shared scale for block B (a power of two in MX formats)
  • q_i — low-precision element, here 4-bit floating point

In AI papers

MXFP8/MXFP4 (OCP spec) and NVFP4 (16-element blocks with FP8 scales) are supported in hardware on recent accelerators.

OCP Microscaling Formats (MX) Specification, 2023

cards.label: Quantization · Masters
cards.front:
Per-tensor FP8 scaling

s = \frac{\operatorname{amax}(\mathbf{X})}{448}, \qquad \mathbf{X}^{\text{fp8}} = \operatorname{fl}_{\text{E4M3}}\!\big(\mathbf{X} / s\big)
cards.back:
“s equals the absolute max of X over 448; store X over s in E4M3”

Stretch the tensor so its largest value lands at the top of the E4M3 range (448), to use the format’s precision without overflowing. Keep s in higher precision next to the FP8 data.

Term by term

  • \operatorname{amax} — largest absolute value, often taken from a history of recent steps (“delayed scaling”)
  • 448 — largest finite E4M3 value

In AI papers

How FP8 training works on Hopper/Blackwell GPUs (Transformer Engine); DeepSeek-V3 used finer tile-wise scales.

Micikevicius et al., “FP8 Formats for Deep Learning”, 2022

cards.label: Quantization · Masters
cards.front:
Migrating outliers (SmoothQuant)

\mathbf{Y} = \mathbf{X}\mathbf{W} = \big(\mathbf{X}\operatorname{diag}(\mathbf{s})^{-1}\big)\big(\operatorname{diag}(\mathbf{s})\,\mathbf{W}\big), \qquad s_{j} = \frac{\max|\mathbf{X}_{:,j}|^{\alpha}}{\max|\mathbf{W}_{j,:}|^{1-\alpha}}
cards.back:
“X W equals X times diag s inverse, times diag s times W”

Divide each activation channel by s_j and multiply the matching weight row by s_j. The product is unchanged, but activation outliers shrink, so both factors quantize well.

Term by term

  • \operatorname{diag}(\mathbf{s})^{-1}\operatorname{diag}(\mathbf{s}) = \mathbf{I} — the rescaling cancels exactly
  • \alpha — how much difficulty to move from activations to weights, e.g. 0.5

In AI papers

LLM activations have a few channels up to 100× larger than the rest; this makes W8A8 inference accurate.

Xiao et al., “SmoothQuant”, 2023

cards.label: Quantization · Masters
cards.front:
Straight-through estimator

\text{forward: } \hat{x} = s\,\Big\lfloor \frac{x}{s} \Big\rceil, \qquad \text{backward: } \frac{\partial \hat{x}}{\partial x} := 1
cards.back:
“forward, round x to the grid; backward, pretend the rounding had derivative one”

Rounding has zero gradient almost everywhere, so training through it would learn nothing. The STE passes the gradient straight through as if rounding were the identity.

Term by term

  • \lfloor \cdot \rceil — true derivative is 0 (or undefined at jumps)
  • := 1 — a deliberate approximation

In AI papers

The basis of quantization-aware training (QAT) and of binary/ternary networks; also used in VQ-VAE.

Bengio, Léonard & Courville, 2013

cards.label: Compute & memory efficiency · Masters
cards.front:
Memory bandwidth

\beta \;[\text{bytes/s}], \qquad t_{\text{mem}} = \frac{\text{bytes moved}}{\beta}
cards.back:
“beta, the memory bandwidth; memory time equals bytes moved over bandwidth”

How many bytes per second can travel between memory (HBM) and the compute units. If moving the data takes longer than computing on it, the job is memory-bound.

In AI papers

An H100 SXM has about 3.35 TB/s of HBM bandwidth but about 990 TFLOP/s of dense BF16 compute.

cards.label: Compute & memory efficiency · Masters
cards.front:
Training compute

C \approx 6\,N\,D
cards.back:
“compute C is approximately six times N times D”

Total training FLOPs ≈ 6 × parameters × training tokens: 2 for the forward pass and 4 for the backward pass (which computes gradients for both activations and weights).

Term by term

  • N — number of parameters
  • D — number of training tokens
  • 6 = 2 + 4 — forward + backward

In AI papers

A 7B model on 2T tokens needs about 6 \times 7 \times 10^{9} \times 2 \times 10^{12} \approx 8.4 \times 10^{22} FLOPs. Chinchilla-optimal training uses D \approx 20N.

Kaplan et al., 2020; Hoffmann et al., 2022

cards.label: Compute & memory efficiency · Masters
cards.front:
Arithmetic intensity

I = \frac{\text{FLOPs}}{\text{bytes moved}}, \qquad I_{\text{matmul}}(n{\times}n{\times}n,\ \text{BF16}) = \frac{2n^{3}}{3 \cdot 2n^{2}} = \frac{n}{3}, \qquad I_{\text{matvec}} \approx 1
cards.back:
“arithmetic intensity is FLOPs per byte moved”

How much computing you do for each byte you fetch from memory. Large matrix products reuse each number many times; a matrix–vector product uses each weight once.

Term by term

  • 2n^{3} — FLOPs of an n \times n by n \times n product
  • 3 \cdot 2n^{2} — bytes to read A and B and write C in BF16

In AI papers

LLM decoding at batch size 1 is matrix–vector work with I \approx 1 FLOP/byte, far below the ~300 an H100 needs to be compute-bound. That is why batching many requests speeds up serving.

cards.label: Compute & memory efficiency · Masters
cards.front:
Roofline model

P = \min\big(\pi,\; \beta \cdot I\big), \qquad I^{*} = \frac{\pi}{\beta}
cards.back:
“attainable performance equals the minimum of peak compute and bandwidth times intensity”

Below the ridge point I^{*} a kernel is memory-bound (speed limited by bandwidth); above it, compute-bound (limited by peak FLOP/s).

Term by term

  • \pi — peak compute, FLOP/s
  • \beta — memory bandwidth, bytes/s
  • I^{*} — ridge point: about 990 \times 10^{12} / 3.35 \times 10^{12} \approx 295 FLOP/byte on an H100 in BF16

In AI papers

Kernel fusion, FlashAttention and quantization all aim to raise I or cut bytes moved.

Williams, Waterman & Patterson, 2009

cards.label: Compute & memory efficiency · Masters
cards.front:
Memory-bound decoding speed

t_{\text{token}} \ge \frac{\text{bytes of weights} + \text{bytes of KV cache}}{\beta}
cards.back:
“time per token is at least the bytes that must be read divided by memory bandwidth”

To generate each token, every weight must be read from memory at least once. At small batch sizes this, not arithmetic, sets the speed limit.

Term by term

  • \beta — memory bandwidth

In AI papers

A 7B model in BF16 (14 GB) at 3.35 TB/s: at least 4.2 ms per token, at most about 240 tokens/s. In INT4 (3.5 GB) the limit is about 4 times higher.

cards.label: Compute & memory efficiency · Masters
cards.front:
KV-cache size

\text{KV bytes} = 2 \cdot L \cdot n_{\text{kv}} \cdot d_{\text{head}} \cdot T \cdot B \cdot b_{\text{elem}}
cards.back:
“KV bytes equals two times layers times KV heads times head size times sequence length times batch times bytes per element”

During generation each layer stores a key and a value vector (the 2) for every past token, so later tokens do not recompute them. It grows linearly with context length and batch.

Term by term

  • L — number of layers
  • n_{\text{kv}} — number of key/value heads (fewer than query heads with GQA/MQA)
  • T, B — context length and batch size
  • b_{\text{elem}} — bytes per number: 2 for BF16, 1 for FP8

In AI papers

LLaMA-2-7B (L = 32, n_{\text{kv}} = 32, d_{\text{head}} = 128) at 4,096 tokens in BF16: exactly 2 GiB per sequence. GQA with 8 KV heads cuts that by 4.

cards.label: Compute & memory efficiency · Masters
cards.front:
Cost of self-attention

\text{FLOPs} \approx 4\,n^{2}\,d \;\text{ per layer}, \qquad \text{naive memory for scores} = \mathcal{O}(h\,n^{2})
cards.back:
“attention costs about four n squared d FLOPs per layer, and naive memory grows as n squared”

Computing \mathbf{Q}\mathbf{K}^{\top} and multiplying the weights by \mathbf{V} each cost 2n^{2}d. Both time and naive memory grow with the square of the sequence length.

Term by term

  • n — sequence length
  • d — model width (h \cdot d_k)
  • h\,n^{2} — one n \times n score matrix per head

In AI papers

Doubling the context quadruples attention cost. FlashAttention removes the n^{2} memory, but the n^{2} FLOPs remain.

cards.label: Lesson 00 · Setup and the GPU mental model
cards.front: What is the ridge point of a roofline, and how do you compute it?
cards.back: Peak FLOP/s divided by peak bytes/s. Kernels below it (in FLOPs per byte moved) are memory-bound, above it compute-bound. On the course GB200: about 1741 TFLOP/s ÷ 6.6 TB/s ≈ 262 FLOP/byte.

cards.label: Lesson 00 · Setup and the GPU mental model
cards.front: What does one Triton program correspond to in CUDA?
cards.back: One thread block. It runs on a single SM; the threads inside it are managed by the compiler according to num_warps.

cards.label: Lesson 00 · Setup and the GPU mental model
cards.front: Why does a GPU keep many warps resident on each SM?
cards.back: To hide memory latency: while one warp waits hundreds of cycles for HBM, the scheduler issues instructions from another warp that is ready.

cards.label: Lesson 00 · Setup and the GPU mental model
cards.front: List the GPU memory hierarchy from fastest to slowest.
cards.back: Registers (per thread) → shared memory / L1 (per SM, up to 227 KB per block on GB200) → L2 (129 MiB, shared by all SMs) → HBM.

cards.label: Lesson 00 · Setup and the GPU mental model
cards.front: Which four lines does every lab's run.py print at the end?
cards.back: CLAIM, MEASURED, VERDICT, NEXT.

cards.label: Lesson 01 · Vector add three ways
cards.front: In Triton, what does tl.arange(0, BLOCK) inside a program represent?
cards.back: The vector of BLOCK lane offsets that this one program processes. The compiler maps those lanes onto the program's threads; you never index threads directly.

cards.label: Lesson 01 · Vector add three ways
cards.front: What does Gluon's BlockedLayout(size_per_thread=[4], threads_per_warp=[32], warps_per_cta=[4], order=[0]) mean?
cards.back: Each thread owns 4 consecutive elements, 32 threads per warp, 4 warps per program: one layout tile covers 4·32·4 = 512 elements, repeated to fill BLOCK.

cards.label: Lesson 01 · Vector add three ways
cards.front: State Little's law for memory bandwidth.
cards.back: Bytes in flight = bandwidth × latency. To reach peak HBM bandwidth you must keep about (TB/s × µs) bytes outstanding, which means many wide or independent loads per thread.

cards.label: Lesson 01 · Vector add three ways
cards.front: Why does scalar CUDA add reach only about 4.1 TB/s while float4 reaches 7.2 TB/s?
cards.back: Each scalar thread keeps only 4 bytes per stream in flight. float4 issues 16-byte loads, four times more bytes outstanding per instruction, enough to cover HBM latency.

cards.label: Lesson 01 · Vector add three ways
cards.front: Why is GB/s meaningless for a 2¹⁶-element add?
cards.back: The kernel finishes in about 6.6 µs, dominated by launch and synchronization overhead, and the data is L2-resident; you are measuring the launch floor.

cards.label: Lesson 01 · Vector add three ways
cards.front: What happens if you drop the mask on the last Triton block?
cards.back: Out-of-bounds loads and stores: silent memory corruption or an illegal memory access error.

cards.label: Lesson 02 · Fused softmax
cards.front: What is kernel fusion, in terms of memory traffic?
cards.back: Combining several elementwise or reduction steps into one kernel so intermediates stay in registers or shared memory instead of making HBM round trips. Count bytes moved before and after.

cards.label: Lesson 02 · Fused softmax
cards.front: Why load masked lanes with other=-inf in softmax?
cards.back: So padded lanes never become the row max, and exp(-inf) = 0 keeps them out of the denominator.

cards.label: Lesson 02 · Fused softmax
cards.front: Why does the one-row-per-program softmax slow down at 65536 columns?
cards.back: The row no longer fits in registers; the compiler spills to local memory (which lives in HBM), adding traffic. Use an online (chunked) softmax instead.

cards.label: Lesson 02 · Fused softmax
cards.front: What is the online softmax?
cards.back: Process a row in chunks keeping running max m and sum s; when the max grows, rescale: s ← s·e^(m_old − m_new) + Σ e^(x − m_new). One pass, bounded registers; the core of flash attention.

cards.label: Lesson 02 · Fused softmax
cards.front: Why subtract the max before exp?
cards.back: To avoid overflow (exp overflows fp32 above about 88). The common factor e^(−max) cancels between numerator and denominator.

cards.label: Lesson 03 · LayerNorm × gate, forward and backward
cards.front: Why save mean and rstd in LayerNorm's forward rather than the normalised output?
cards.back: They cost 8 bytes per row instead of D values per row; the backward recomputes x̂ = (x − mean)·rstd cheaply from x.

cards.label: Lesson 03 · LayerNorm × gate, forward and backward
cards.front: How many activation-sized HBM transfers does LayerNorm-then-multiply take unfused vs fused?
cards.back: Unfused 5 (read x, write ℓ, read ℓ, read u, write y); fused 3 (read x, read u, write y).

cards.label: Lesson 03 · LayerNorm × gate, forward and backward
cards.front: Give dx for LayerNorm in terms of g_x̂ = g·w.
cards.back: dx = rstd · (g_x̂ − mean(g_x̂) − x̂ · mean(g_x̂ · x̂)), means taken over the row.

cards.label: Lesson 03 · LayerNorm × gate, forward and backward
cards.front: Why accumulate LayerNorm statistics in fp32 for bf16 inputs?
cards.back: bf16 has only 8 bits of mantissa; summing hundreds of values loses precision and the variance can even go negative from cancellation.

cards.label: Lesson 03 · LayerNorm × gate, forward and backward
cards.front: The bf16 version reaches lower GB/s than fp32 at D=512. What would you change?
cards.back: Process several rows per program (2-D block) so each program moves more bytes and the fixed per-program reduction and launch costs amortise.

cards.label: Lesson 04 · GEMM + SiLU, from tiles to TMA
cards.front: Why does GEMM+SiLU fused beat cuBLAS GEMM followed by F.silu on the HSTU shape even though cuBLAS's GEMM is faster?
cards.back: The separate SiLU reads and writes the whole output (128 MiB each way at 65536×1024 bf16). On a skinny GEMM that traffic rivals the GEMM itself; fusing it into the epilogue removes it.

cards.label: Lesson 04 · GEMM + SiLU, from tiles to TMA
cards.front: What does TMA do?
cards.back: The Tensor Memory Accelerator copies a whole tile between global and shared memory asynchronously, from a descriptor (base, shape, strides, block shape) and a coordinate. No per-thread address arithmetic, hardware bounds handling.

cards.label: Lesson 04 · GEMM + SiLU, from tiles to TMA
cards.front: What is a persistent kernel?
cards.back: A grid of exactly one program per SM; each program loops over many output tiles. Removes wave-quantization tails and keeps pipelines warm across tiles.

cards.label: Lesson 04 · GEMM + SiLU, from tiles to TMA
cards.front: What does warp_specialize=True do in a Triton tl.range loop?
cards.back: Splits warps into producers (issue TMA loads) and consumers (issue MMAs), communicating through shared-memory barriers, so loads for the next tile overlap math on the current one.

cards.label: Lesson 04 · GEMM + SiLU, from tiles to TMA
