cards.front: Why must the GEMM autotune key be bucketed for jagged training?
cards.back: The token count M changes every batch; keying on raw M re-runs autotuning (dozens of compile+bench runs) on every step. Key on next_power_of_2(M).

cards.label: Lesson 04 · GEMM + SiLU, from tiles to TMA
cards.front: What does grouped tile ordering buy?
cards.back: L2 reuse: GROUP consecutive programs share the same B column-tiles (and nearby A row-tiles) while those are still cached, cutting HBM reads.

cards.label: Lesson 04 · GEMM + SiLU, from tiles to TMA
cards.front: Why SiLU as x / (1 + exp2(-x·log2 e))?
cards.back: exp2 is a single MUFU instruction; it avoids a slower exp and a separate sigmoid then multiply.

cards.label: Lesson 05 · Reductions in raw CUDA
cards.front: What does it mean for a warp's loads to be coalesced?
cards.back: The 32 lanes access contiguous (or at least the same few 32-byte sectors of) memory, so the hardware serves the warp with a handful of transactions instead of 32.

cards.label: Lesson 05 · Reductions in raw CUDA
cards.front: Why is thread-per-row summation slow on a row-major matrix?
cards.back: At each step neighbouring threads read addresses a full row apart: every lane needs its own sector, wasting 7/8 of each 32-byte transaction.

cards.label: Lesson 05 · Reductions in raw CUDA
cards.front: What does __shfl_xor_sync(0xffffffff, v, off) do?
cards.back: Each lane receives v from lane (laneId XOR off) in the same warp, register to register, no shared memory. Five rounds (16, 8, 4, 2, 1) give a full warp sum in every lane.

cards.label: Lesson 05 · Reductions in raw CUDA
cards.front: Why does a shared-memory tree reduction leave performance on the table?
cards.back: log₂(blockDim) steps each separated by __syncthreads, with half the remaining threads idle at each step; plus a shared-memory round trip per step.

cards.label: Lesson 05 · Reductions in raw CUDA
cards.front: How does torch.cuda._compile_kernel let you write CUDA without nvcc?
cards.back: It compiles a CUDA C++ source string at runtime with NVRTC and returns a launchable kernel: k(grid=..., block=..., args=[...], shared_mem=...).

cards.label: Lesson 05 · Reductions in raw CUDA
cards.front: Why does the Triton rowsum keep a (BLOCK,) accumulator instead of summing each chunk to a scalar?
cards.back: Independent per-lane partial sums keep many adds and loads in flight (ILP) and defer the expensive cross-lane reduction to a single tl.sum at the end.

cards.label: Lesson 06 · HSTU attention forward (jagged, fused)
cards.front: Write the HSTU attention formula.
cards.back: A = SiLU(α·QKᵀ + rab) / N, causal (j ≤ i), output A·V; rab = w_pos[clamp(i−j)] + w_ts[floor(log2 max(|t_i − t_j|, 1))].

cards.label: Lesson 06 · HSTU attention forward (jagged, fused)
cards.front: What is a jagged batch?
cards.back: Variable-length sequences concatenated into one (T, …) tensor with an offsets array: user b owns rows offsets[b] … offsets[b+1]. No padding.

cards.label: Lesson 06 · HSTU attention forward (jagged, fused)
cards.front: How does the fused kernel avoid wasting work on short users?
cards.back: The grid covers max_len query blocks for every user; programs whose block starts at or after the user's length L return immediately.

cards.label: Lesson 06 · HSTU attention forward (jagged, fused)
cards.front: How do you compute floor(log2(x)) for positive fp32 x without calling log2?
cards.back: Reinterpret the bits as int32: ((bits >> 23) & 0xFF) − 127, the unbiased exponent.

cards.label: Lesson 06 · HSTU attention forward (jagged, fused)
cards.front: Why is HSTU attention easier to fuse than softmax attention?
cards.back: Scores are pointwise (SiLU), with no row-wise normalisation, so there is no running max or sum to maintain and no rescaling; block contributions just add.

cards.label: Lesson 06 · HSTU attention forward (jagged, fused)
cards.front: Name the three sources of the fused kernel's speedup over dense PyTorch.
cards.back: No N×N tensors in HBM, no compute on padding, and skipping key blocks above the causal diagonal.

cards.label: Lesson 06 · HSTU attention forward (jagged, fused)
cards.front: Why compute the base address in int64?
cards.back: start·stride_t can exceed 2³¹ for large jagged batches (tokens × H × D), silently wrapping a 32-bit offset.

cards.label: Lesson 07 · HSTU attention backward
cards.front: Give the derivative of SiLU(s) in terms of σ = sigmoid(s).

cards.label: Lesson 07 · HSTU attention backward
cards.front: Why does the HSTU backward use two kernels?
cards.back: dK/dV reduce over queries and dQ reduces over keys. One kernel per reduction direction gives each output block a single owner, so no atomics on Q/K/V gradients (the FlashAttention-2 split).

cards.label: Lesson 07 · HSTU attention backward
cards.front: Why were atomic adds into one shared bias table about 70× slower than private rows?
cards.back: Thousands of programs hammered the same 288 addresses; same-address atomics serialise at their L2 slice. Private rows remove contention, then one cheap sum reduces them.

cards.label: Lesson 07 · HSTU attention backward
cards.front: What is "recompute instead of store" in attention backward?
cards.back: Do not save the N×N attention matrix; rebuild each score tile from Q, K and the bias inside the backward kernel. Costs FLOPs, saves O(N²) memory and traffic.

cards.label: Lesson 07 · HSTU attention backward
cards.front: Why add reset_to_zero to the autotuner of a kernel that accumulates with atomics?
cards.back: Autotuning runs the kernel many times on the same output buffer; without zeroing between trials, the accumulated values are wrong.

cards.label: Lesson 07 · HSTU attention backward
cards.front: Rule of thumb for atomics on GPUs?
cards.back: Cheap when addresses are spread out, catastrophic when they are hot. Reduce hierarchically: registers → private buffers → one final reduction.

cards.label: Lesson 08 · Stitch the kernels into an HSTU model
cards.front: List the four stages of one HSTU layer and which lab's kernel implements each.
cards.back: SiLU(LN(x)·W_uvqk) (Lab 04 fused GEMM+SiLU) → jagged HSTU attention (Labs 06/07) → LayerNorm(a)·u (Lab 03) → residual + dropout + output projection (PyTorch).

cards.label: Lesson 08 · Stitch the kernels into an HSTU model
cards.front: How do you check a model built on custom kernels is correct?
cards.back: Run the same weights through a plain-PyTorch implementation and compare forward outputs and every parameter's gradient (relative error), with a tolerance matched to the precision (about 1e-2 for bf16).

cards.label: Lesson 08 · Stitch the kernels into an HSTU model
cards.front: Why does the fused model's peak memory stay flat as N grows, while dense grows quadratically?
cards.back: Nothing of size N×N is ever materialised: attention scores live in registers, and backward recomputes them.

cards.label: Lesson 08 · Stitch the kernels into an HSTU model
cards.front: What does sampled softmax with shared negatives compute?
cards.back: For each position: logits = [⟨s, e_target⟩, ⟨s, e_neg1⟩ … ⟨s, e_negK⟩] / τ, cross-entropy with label 0. One random set of negatives is shared by the whole batch, so it is a single GEMM.

cards.label: Lesson 08 · Stitch the kernels into an HSTU model
cards.front: Why recompute z = a·Wᵀ in MatmulSiLU's backward instead of saving it?
cards.back: z is a (T × 4·H·dh) activation per layer; one extra skinny GEMM is cheaper than that much memory, and memory is what limits batch size.

cards.label: Lesson 09 · Train HSTU on MovieLens-1M
cards.front: Define HR@10 and NDCG@10.
cards.back: HR@10: fraction of users whose true next item ranks in the top 10. NDCG@10: average of 1/log₂(rank+1) when the item is in the top 10 (0 otherwise); it rewards higher ranks.

cards.label: Lesson 09 · Train HSTU on MovieLens-1M
cards.front: What is the leave-one-out protocol for sequential recommendation?
cards.back: Hold out each user's last interaction as the test target, train on everything before it, and rank the target against the whole catalogue (full ranking, not sampled).

cards.label: Lesson 09 · Train HSTU on MovieLens-1M
cards.front: Why did full softmax beat 512 sampled negatives on ML-1M?
cards.back: Sampled negatives give a noisy, biased estimate of the partition function (random negatives are mostly easy); with only 3,706 items the full softmax is one cheap GEMM.

cards.label: Lesson 09 · Train HSTU on MovieLens-1M
cards.front: Why keep the training data pipeline on the GPU?
cards.back: Steps take about 8 ms; building jagged batches on the CPU and copying them would take longer than the step. GPU-side slicing keeps the GPU fed.

cards.label: Lesson 09 · Train HSTU on MovieLens-1M
cards.front: Why did keying the GEMM autotuner on M make training hang?
cards.back: The token count M of a jagged batch changes every step, so every step triggered a full autotune (compiling and benchmarking every config).

cards.label: Lesson 10 · Serve with Triton Inference Server
cards.front: What does allow_ragged_batch: true enable in a Triton Inference Server config?
cards.back: The dynamic batcher may group requests whose inputs have different shapes (here, history lengths); the backend receives them as separate tensors and decides how to combine them.

cards.label: Lesson 10 · Serve with Triton Inference Server
cards.front: Why does HSTU serving batch without padding?
cards.back: execute() concatenates the ragged histories into one jagged tensor plus offsets, which is exactly the input format of the fused attention kernel.

cards.label: Lesson 10 · Serve with Triton Inference Server
cards.front: Why does throughput without batching saturate near 1 / (per-request latency)?
cards.back: One model instance processes one request at a time; each small forward is launch-bound, so extra concurrent clients only queue (p99 grows) without raising throughput.

cards.label: Lesson 10 · Serve with Triton Inference Server
cards.front: What trade-off does max_queue_delay_microseconds control?
cards.back: How long the scheduler waits to fill a batch: longer waits mean bigger batches and higher throughput under load, at the cost of added latency at low load.

cards.label: Lesson 10 · Serve with Triton Inference Server
cards.front: Why use DLPack rather than as_numpy() in the course's Python backend?
cards.back: The bundled backend stub is built against the numpy 1.x C ABI and misreads numpy 2 arrays (wrong element size → "output tensor shape does not match"); DLPack hands buffers across without numpy.

cards.label: Lesson 10 · Serve with Triton Inference Server
cards.front: Why can a served model's first requests be very slow?
cards.back: JIT compilation and autotuning of kernels for shapes not covered by warm-up; fix by warming every shape bucket and persisting compile/autotune caches.

cards.label: Lesson 11 · System optimisation
cards.front: How do you tell whether a training step is launch-bound?
cards.back: Profile it: if summed GPU kernel time is far below wall time (low GPU-busy fraction) and the step has hundreds of small kernels, the CPU's launch rate is the limit.

cards.label: Lesson 11 · System optimisation
cards.front: Name three cures for a launch-bound model.
cards.back: Bigger batches (more work per launch), CUDA graphs (one launch per captured sequence), and fusing small ops into fewer kernels (or torch.compile).

cards.label: Lesson 11 · System optimisation
cards.front: How do you use CUDA graphs with jagged, variable-shape inputs?
cards.back: Capture one graph per (users, tokens) bucket with static buffers; copy each batch into the smallest bucket that fits, give unused users length 0, and let a dummy user absorb the unused token tail.

cards.label: Lesson 11 · System optimisation
cards.front: Why must you run a Triton model once before capturing a CUDA graph?
cards.back: JIT compilation and autotuning (allocations, benchmarking, host syncs) cannot happen inside graph capture; they must be done before.

cards.label: Lesson 11 · System optimisation
cards.front: What do TRITON_CACHE_DIR and TRITON_CACHE_AUTOTUNING=1 save?
cards.back: The cache dir stores compiled kernels (skip compilation); TRITON_CACHE_AUTOTUNING also stores the chosen autotune config (skip re-benchmarking): 17 s → 2.7 s to first step here.

cards.label: Lesson 11 · System optimisation
cards.front: A profile shows cutlass…simt_sgemm_f32… near the top. What does that tell you?
cards.back: An fp32 GEMM is running on CUDA cores rather than tensor cores; switch it to bf16/TF32 or fuse it away (here: the loss logits).

cards.label: Lesson 12 · Field notes from Triton Developer Conference 2026
cards.front: Why does an exact-match autotune cache miss after a trivial source edit in Helion, and what is the fix?
cards.back: The key includes a hash of the kernel source. The loose key uses specialisation (dtypes, shapes, strides), hardware and a structural config-space hash, then warm-starts the search from cached winners (FROM_BEST_AVAILABLE): 1238 s → 92 s.

cards.label: Lesson 12 · Field notes from Triton Developer Conference 2026
cards.front: What does CompileIQ tune that Triton's autotuner does not?
cards.back: PTXAS's internal controls (register allocation, instruction scheduling, unrolling), searched evolutionarily and applied with ptx_options="--apply-controls=best.acf": 5% geomean on B200.

cards.label: Lesson 12 · Field notes from Triton Developer Conference 2026
cards.front: How do TritonPPM and Diode cut autotuning cost?
cards.back: Both predict runtime per config without running it (TritonPPM: static-analysis features + XGBoost; Diode: an MLP on shape/config features) and benchmark only the top-k.

cards.label: Lesson 12 · Field notes from Triton Developer Conference 2026
cards.front: What problem does AOT-Tensor solve?
cards.back: JIT Triton needs Python and compile time at serving; AOT-T records specialisations and autotune picks in one forward pass, compiles cubins ahead of time into one .so per kernel with guards, for C++ serving.

cards.label: Lesson 12 · Field notes from Triton Developer Conference 2026
cards.front: Why do non-power-of-two tiles (e.g. N=192) help on Hopper and Blackwell?
cards.back: Model shapes like head_dim 192 waste MMA work and shared memory when padded to 256; exact tiles let a 3-stage pipeline fit in 192 KB, where padded 256 needs 256 KB (over the limit).

cards.label: Lesson 12 · Field notes from Triton Developer Conference 2026
cards.front: Which course lesson does vLLM's 8-byte-copy fix mirror?
cards.back: Lab 01: wider loads per thread put more bytes in flight (float4 vs scalar), turning a latency-bound copy into a bandwidth-bound one.

cards.label: Lesson 12 · Field notes from Triton Developer Conference 2026
cards.front: What does convert_layout(..., assert_trivial=True) buy a Gluon programmer?
cards.back: A compile-time guarantee that the layout conversion moves no data (no shared-memory round trip); it errors otherwise.

cards.label: Distillation labs
cards.front: What is the core idea of Lab 00 - Setup & the Taxonomy of Distillation?
cards.back:
In both classical ML and LLMs, knowledge distillation (KD) means training a smaller/cheaper student model to reproduce the behavior of a larger/more-capable teacher model, so you end up with something that is faster and cheaper to run while retaining as much of the teacher's capability as possible. The term comes from Hinton, Vinyals, and Dean's 2015 paper "Distilling the Knowledge in a Neural Network" (lab01 implements their method exactly).

The rest of this curriculum is organized around a few independent axes you can mix and match:

cards.label: Distillation labs
cards.front: What is the core idea of Lab 01 - Classic Knowledge Distillation (Hinton et al. 2015)?
cards.back:
A trained classifier's raw output logits, once you look past the single predicted class, encode rich information: how confident the model is, and which wrong classes it considers "almost right" (Hinton calls this "dark knowledge"). A one-hot hard label throws all of that away.

KD trains a student to match the teacher's full output distribution instead of just the argmax label. Concretely, given teacher logits (z_t) and student logits (z_s) for the same input:

cards.label: Distillation labs
cards.front: What is the core idea of Lab 02 - The KD Loss Landscape: Forward KL, Reverse KL, and Jensen-Shannon?
cards.back: Lab04 trains a real student with TRL's GKDTrainer, which exposes exactly the beta (JSD interpolation) and lmbda (on-policy vs. off-policy data mix) knobs this lab lets you reason about in isolation first. If you've internalized "forward KL over-covers, reverse KL under-covers" from this lab, the beta sweep results in lab04 should not be surprising.

cards.label: Distillation labs
cards.front: What is the core idea of Lab 03 - Response-Based / SFT Distillation?
cards.back:
Word/token-level KD (lab02/lab04) requires teacher and student to share a tokenizer, and requires holding both models' logits (a full vocab-sized vector per token) - expensive at scale. Response-based/sequence-level distillation sidesteps both problems entirely:

  • Teacher and student can be any models, even different tokenizer families - you only ever need the teacher's generated text.
  • Data generation (teacher inference) and student training are fully decoupled - generate once with vLLM, train as many student configurations as you like against the same cached data.
  • The downside: the student only sees one sampled trajectory per prompt (not the full distribution over what the teacher could have said), so it can't learn as much about the teacher's uncertainty. It's also strictly offline - the student never sees its own mistakes during training (that gap is exactly what lab04's on-policy GKD addresses).

cards.label: Distillation labs
cards.front: What is the core idea of Lab 04 - On-Policy Distillation (GKD)?
cards.back:
In lab03, the student is trained via teacher-forcing on teacher-written text: at every position, it sees the correct (teacher's) prefix, even if its own greedy/sampled prefix would have diverged. At inference time, though, the student conditions on its own previous tokens - so once it makes one mistake, it's now in a part of input space it never trained on, and errors compound ("exposure bias" / train-test distribution mismatch).

On-policy distillation addresses this directly: let the student generate a full rollout during training, then have the teacher tell it, at every position the student actually visited, what distribution it should have produced. The student is now training exactly on the states it will encounter at inference time.

cards.front: What is the core idea of Lab 05 - Structured Pruning + Distillation Recovery?
cards.back:
Goal: build a small model from a big one by physically removing the most redundant transformer layers, then use knowledge distillation against the original uncompressed model to recover most of the quality lost in pruning. This is the recipe behind NVIDIA's Minitron family and similar "prune-then-distill" compact models.

Hardware: 2-4 GPUs, ~60 minutes.

cards.label: Distillation labs
cards.front: What is the core idea of Lab 07 - Distillation vs. RL Ablation (Reproducing DeepSeek-R1's Table 6)?
cards.back: Group Relative Policy Optimization (Shao et al. 2024) is the RL algorithm behind DeepSeek's models. For each prompt, sample a group of G completions, score each with a reward function, and compute each completion's advantage as its reward standardized against the group's own mean/std - no learned value network needed (contrast with PPO). The policy is updated to increase the probability of above-average completions in the group and decrease below-average ones, with a KL penalty keeping it close to a reference policy. Our reward here is as simple as it gets: 1.0 if the final numeric answer is correct, 0.0 otherwise (implemented with common.eval_harness.gsm8k_correct, the exact same correctness check used to filter traces in lab06) - a "rule-based reward" in the paper's terminology, requiring no learned reward model at all.

cards.label: Distillation labs
cards.front: What is the core idea of Lab 08 - Scaled, Disaggregated Teacher/Student Pipeline?
cards.back:
Labs 01-07 all load the teacher and student in the same Python process on the same GPU(s). That's simple and fine up to a point, but it couples two things that don't need to be coupled:

  • Teacher inference wants an inference-optimized serving stack (continuous batching, prefix/KV caching, tensor parallelism for latency) running continuously and independently of whatever training code is iterating on the student.
  • Student training wants a training-optimized stack (gradient checkpointing, ZeRO sharding, mixed precision, a completely different memory profile) that can be restarted, debugged, or scaled without touching the teacher at all.

cards.label: LLM RL alignment labs
cards.front: What is the core idea of Lab 00 -- Setup and GPU Tour?
cards.back:
Goal: confirm the whole stack (torch, CUDA 13.0, all 8 B200s, transformers, trl, vLLM) works before you spend any time debugging an RL algorithm that's actually failing because of an environment issue.

No RL yet -- this lab is pure infrastructure. But it's worth doing properly: three of the most common "my RLHF run is behaving weirdly" bugs are actually (a) NCCL/interconnect issues, (b) an accidentally-CPU or accidentally-fp32 model, and (c) a mismatched torch/vllm CUDA build. This lab catches all three up front.

cards.label: LLM RL alignment labs
cards.front: What is the core idea of Lab 01 -- SFT Warmup?
cards.back: Goal: understand why every RLHF/RLVR pipeline starts with supervised fine-tuning (SFT), and build/run the training loop (prompt masking, loss computation) that every later lab either reuses directly or conceptually depends on.

cards.label: LLM RL alignment labs
cards.front: What is the core idea of Lab 02 -- Reward Modeling?
cards.back: Goal: understand how a scalar reward model is trained from pairwise human (or rule-based) preferences via the Bradley-Terry model -- this is the reward signal PPO (lab 03) optimizes, and the thing DPO (lab 04) shows you can skip entirely.

cards.label: LLM RL alignment labs
cards.front: What is the core idea of Lab 03 -- PPO / Classic RLHF?
cards.back: Goal: implement the InstructGPT recipe end-to-end -- rollout generation, reward model scoring, a KL penalty against the reference policy, GAE, and the clipped PPO surrogate loss -- and see it visibly shift a policy's behavior.

cards.label: LLM RL alignment labs
cards.front: What is the core idea of Lab 04 -- The DPO Family?
cards.back: Goal: derive Direct Preference Optimization from the same Bradley-Terry model lab 02 used for reward modeling, see that it eliminates the reward model and the RL rollout loop entirely, then compare it (and its cousin KTO) against lab 03's PPO on a shared reward-vs-KL frontier.

cards.label: LLM RL alignment labs
cards.front: What is the core idea of Lab 05 -- GRPO and RLVR Reasoning?
cards.back: Goal: understand the two big ideas behind how models like DeepSeek-R1 are trained: (1) GRPO -- replacing PPO's learned critic with a cheap, group-relative baseline, and (2) RLVR (RL from Verifiable Rewards) -- replacing the learned reward model with a rule that can check correctness directly (does the final answer match?).

cards.label: LLM RL alignment labs
cards.front: What is the core idea of Lab 06 -- RLOO and GSPO Variants?
cards.back: Goal: see two more points in the PPO/GRPO design space: RLOO (how much of PPO's machinery can you strip away and still learn?) and GSPO (matching the granularity of importance sampling to the granularity of the advantage).

cards.label: LLM RL alignment labs
cards.front: What is the core idea of Lab 07 -- Capstone: Scale-Up?
cards.back:
Goal: take the GRPO/RLVR recipe from lab 05 and run it "for real" -- a 7-8B model, sharded across all 8 B200s, with vLLM colocated for rollout generation -- and measure exactly what scaling the node buys you.

This lab is intentionally light on new algorithmic content: the point is that scaling RL post-training from a 1.5B toy run to a real model is mostly an infrastructure problem (sharding, mixed precision, colocated generation, checkpointing) layered on top of the exact same algorithm you already understand from lab 05.

cards.label: LLM RL alignment labs
cards.front: What is the core idea of Lab 08 -- Safety and Reward Hacking?
cards.back: Goal: see the failure modes every previous lab has been warning about, concretely: reward hacking (Goodhart's law), the reward-vs-KL trade-off every algorithm makes implicitly, the "alignment tax" on general capability, and a minimal red-teaming harness for measuring whether alignment actually changed model behavior.

cards.label: Quantization labs
cards.front: What is the core idea of Lab 00 - Quantization Numerics Fundamentals?
cards.back:
Neural network weights and activations are normally stored as 16- or 32-bit floating point numbers. Quantization maps those values onto a much smaller set of representable numbers (e.g. 256 integer levels for 8-bit, 16 levels for 4-bit) so that a tensor takes less memory and, on hardware with native low-precision arithmetic, computes faster. The core trade-off is always: fewer bits -> less memory & faster compute, but more rounding error.

For b bits, we pick an integer grid (e.g. [-127, 127] for 8-bit symmetric) and a real-valued scale s (and, for asymmetric quantization, a zero-point z) so that:

cards.label: Quantization labs
cards.front: What is the core idea of Lab 01 - Round-to-Nearest (RTN) Weight-Only PTQ?
cards.back:
RTN quantization is exactly the fake_quantize_int function from lab 00, applied to every nn.Linear weight matrix in the model (skipping the embedding and LM head, which are usually kept at higher precision since vocabulary-sized matrices are unusually sensitive to quantization relative to their size). No data is needed -- just the weight tensor itself.

Because it's data-free and needs no per-layer optimization, RTN is essentially free to run, which makes it the natural first thing to try and a useful baseline. Its weakness is exactly what you'd expect: it treats every weight independently and has no way to account for which weights matter most for the model's actual outputs (that's what GPTQ and AWQ add in labs 02-03).

cards.label: Quantization labs
cards.front: What is the core idea of Lab 02 - GPTQ (Hessian-Based Layer-Wise Reconstruction)?
cards.back:
RTN (lab 01) quantizes every weight independently -- it has no way to know that rounding one weight can be partly "corrected for" by adjusting the other, not-yet-quantized weights in the same row. GPTQ ("GPTQ: Accurate Post-Training Quantization for Generative Pre-trained Transformers", Frantar et al. 2022) fixes this with a layer-wise reconstruction: for each linear layer, quantize its weight matrix one column (input feature) at a time, and after quantizing each column, adjust every remaining column to compensate for the error just introduced -- using second-order (Hessian) information from real calibration data to know exactly how much to adjust.

Concretely, for one layer with weight W (out_features x in_features) and calibration input activations X (n_tokens x in_features), we want to minimize the squared output error ||W Xᵀ - Ŵ Xᵀ||². cards.label: Quantization labs
cards.front: What is the core idea of Lab 03 - AWQ (Activation-Aware Weight Quantization)?
cards.back:
GPTQ (lab 02) reduces quantization error by adjusting weights after the fact, using second-order information. AWQ ("AWQ: Activation-aware Weight Quantization for LLM Compression and Acceleration", Lin et al. 2023) takes a different angle: it observes that a handful of input channels have much larger activation magnitudes than the rest (this is the same activation-outlier phenomenon SmoothQuant, lab 04, also exploits), and that the weight columns multiplying those channels are disproportionately important to get right -- even though the weights themselves aren't unusually large.

cards.label: Quantization labs
cards.front: What is the core idea of Lab 04 - SmoothQuant (W8A8: Weight *and* Activation Quantization)?
cards.back:
Every previous lab quantized weights but still computed in bf16: the quantized weight gets dequantized back to bf16 before the matmul, so you save memory (loading weights) but not compute -- the GPU still does a bf16 GEMM. To get an actual compute speedup on hardware with fast low-precision tensor cores, both operands of the matmul need to be low-precision: this is what "W8A8" (8-bit weights and 8-bit activations) means.

The problem: activations in transformer LLMs have large per-channel outliers (some input feature channels are consistently 10-100x larger than the rest, across almost every token) -- much worse outliers than the weights have. A naive per-tensor INT8 quantizer for activations gets dominated by those few channels and wrecks precision for everyone else.

cards.label: Quantization labs
cards.front: What is the core idea of Lab 05 - FP8 Quantization (Native Blackwell Tensor Cores)?
cards.back:
Lab 00 introduced FP8's two flavors: E4M3 (more mantissa bits, less range, max magnitude ~448) and E5M2 (more range, less precision, max magnitude ~57344). NVIDIA Hopper and Blackwell GPUs (your B200s) have native FP8 tensor cores -- an FP8 x FP8 matmul isn't just a memory trick, it runs at roughly double the throughput of an equivalent bf16 matmul in hardware. PyTorch exposes this directly via torch._scaled_mm, which this lab calls straight from Python (no custom CUDA needed).

Lab 04 showed that naive INT8 activation quantization (no smoothing) badly hurts accuracy, because a uniform integer grid gets dominated by a few outlier channels. FP8's floating-point grid is non-uniform by construction -- it naturally allocates more resolution near zero and less far from zero, which is a much better match for the "mostly small values, occasional large outlier" shape real activations have. This lab quantizes activations to FP8 directly, per-tensor, dynamically (scale computed fresh every forward pass, no calibration, no smoothing) and you'll see perplexity stay close to the bf16 baseline anyway -- a direct, hands-on illustration of why FP8 has become the default "just quantize it" format for LLM inference, while INT8 needs much more care.

cards.label: Quantization labs
cards.front: What is the core idea of Lab 06 - FP4 / NVFP4 / MXFP4 (Blackwell-Native 4-Bit Formats)?
cards.back:
Lab 00 introduced the math: a 4-bit float with 2 exponent + 1 mantissa bit (E2M1) has exactly 8 non-negative representable values, {0, 0.5, 1, 1.5, 2, 3, 4, 6}. That's a brutally coarse grid on its own -- nowhere near enough to represent a full weight tensor's dynamic range. The fix used by both NVFP4 (NVIDIA's format) and MXFP4 (the Open Compute Project's "microscaling" spec, which NVFP4 is closely related to) is to share one extra scale factor across a small block of elements (16 for NVFP4, 32 for MXFP4), so the local dynamic range within each block still gets the full 8-value grid, even though the global range across the whole tensor can be huge. NVFP4 uses an FP8 (E4M3) block scale (finer); MXFP4 uses a power-of-two-only (E8M0) block scale (coarser, cheaper -- no mantissa bits to store).

This block-sharing is exactly what makes FP4 practical -- and exactly what makes it fundamentally different from INT4 with the same group size: INT4's uniform integer grid + a per-group scale gives 16 evenly spaced levels per group, while FP4's floating grid + per-block scale gives 16 unevenly spaced levels (denser near zero) per block. Which one wins depends on how peaked the underlying data is -- you measured this directly for a synthetic tensor in lab 00; this lab measures it on a real 7B model.

cards.label: Quantization labs
cards.front: What is the core idea of Lab 07 - Quantization-Aware Training (QAT) with a Straight-Through Estimator?
cards.back:
Every PTQ method so far (RTN, GPTQ, AWQ, SmoothQuant) starts from trained full-precision weights and tries to quantize them with minimum damage. QAT instead keeps training the model with the quantization operation inside the forward pass, so gradient descent can push the underlying full-precision weights toward values that happen to round well -- not just values that were good in full precision.

The obstacle: round() (which every quantizer in this repo uses) has zero gradient almost everywhere and an undefined one at the rounding boundaries. If you literally backprop through round(), no weight ever updates. The fix, used since the earliest quantized neural network work, is the straight-through estimator (STE): in the forward pass, actually quantize (round, clamp, dequantize -- exactly the fake_quantize_int from lab 00/01); in the backward pass, pretend the quantization step was the identity function and let the gradient flow straight through to the underlying full-precision weight, unchanged. It's a biased gradient estimator (the true function's gradient is zero almost everywhere, and STE uses 1 instead), but empirically it works well enough that it's still the standard approach.

cards.label: Quantization labs
cards.front: What is the core idea of Lab 08 - QLoRA (NF4 4-Bit Base + LoRA Fine-Tuning)?
cards.back:
Labs 01-07 were all about inference: quantize a trained model, run it faster/smaller, measure the accuracy cost. QLoRA ("QLoRA: Efficient Finetuning of Quantized LLMs", Dettmers et al. 2023) uses quantization to make training cheaper instead: it freezes the entire base model in 4-bit and only trains a small number of extra parameters (LoRA adapters -- low rank matrices inserted alongside each frozen linear layer), so training memory is dominated by the tiny frozen base model plus the adapters' gradients/optimizer state, not the full model's.

cards.label: Quantization labs
cards.front: What is the core idea of Lab 09 - KV-Cache Quantization?
cards.back:
During autoregressive generation, a transformer caches every previous token's key and value projections per layer/head so it doesn't have to recompute them at every new step -- that's the "KV cache". For long contexts and/or large batches, this cache can dominate GPU memory more than the model's weights do:

Halving bytes_per_element (bf16 -> int8, or bf16 -> fp8) directly halves that memory, which either lets you serve longer contexts, larger batches, or both, with the same GPU memory. Unlike weight quantization, this cost is paid fresh, every request (the cache is per-conversation, not a one-time offline step), so KV-cache quantization has to be cheap enough to do at generation time, not just accurate.

cards.label: Start here
cards.front: What are the three layers this course optimizes, from inside out?
cards.back: A single model server (engine: vLLM or SGLang), a fleet of replicas behind an inference-aware router (llm-d), and the global service around it (regions, edge, gateways, autoscaling).

cards.label: Start here
cards.front: Which track covers prefill/decode disaggregation and inference-aware routing?
cards.back: The llm-d track (llmd/).

cards.label: Start here
cards.front: Why is there both a vLLM and an SGLang track?
cards.back: They are the two leading open-source engines; doing the same optimizations in both shows which ideas are universal (batching, paging, caching, quantization, speculation) and which are engine-specific (RadixAttention, overlap scheduler, HiCache vs OffloadingConnector).

cards.label: GPU architecture for inference
cards.front: What is the arithmetic-intensity ridge point of a B200 in BF16, roughly?
cards.back: About 280 FLOP/byte (≈2.2 PFLOP/s ÷ ≈8 TB/s). Kernels below it are memory-bound, above it compute-bound.

cards.label: GPU architecture for inference
cards.front: Why is LLM decode memory-bound?
cards.back: Each step generates one token per sequence, so a linear layer does about B FLOPs per weight byte (B = batch size), far below the ridge point; the step time is dominated by streaming all weights (and each sequence's KV cache) from HBM.

cards.label: GPU architecture for inference
cards.front: Lower bound on decode step time for an 8B BF16 model on one B200?
cards.back: About 2 ms: 16 GB of weights ÷ 8 TB/s of HBM bandwidth.

cards.label: GPU architecture for inference
cards.front: Why does batching more sequences increase decode throughput almost for free?
cards.back: The weights are read once per step regardless of batch size, so until the batch approaches the ridge point, extra sequences add FLOPs without adding much memory traffic.

cards.label: GPU architecture for inference
cards.front: What are tensor cores and which formats do Blackwell's support?
cards.back: Matrix-multiply-accumulate units inside each SM that do almost all LLM FLOPs; Blackwell's 5th-gen tensor cores support FP64/TF32/BF16/FP16/FP8/FP6/FP4 including microscaling (MX) block formats.

cards.label: GPU architecture for inference
cards.front: Why is FP32 inference so slow on modern GPUs?
cards.back: FP32 math runs on regular CUDA cores (~80 TFLOP/s on B200) instead of tensor cores (~2.2 PFLOP/s BF16), and it moves twice the bytes of BF16.

cards.label: GPU architecture for inference
cards.front: What problem do CUDA graphs solve?
cards.back: CPU launch overhead: a decode step launches hundreds of small kernels; a graph replays the recorded sequence with one launch so the GPU is not starved at small batch sizes.

cards.label: GPU architecture for inference
cards.front: Name the GPU memory hierarchy from fastest to slowest.
cards.back: Registers → shared memory/L1 (and TMEM on Blackwell) → L2 → HBM → host DRAM (PCIe/C2C) → NVMe/network.

cards.label: Transformer inference and the KV cache
cards.front: Formula for KV-cache bytes per token?
cards.back: 2 × layers × KV heads × head dim × bytes per element (2 for K and V).

cards.label: Transformer inference and the KV cache
cards.front: KV cache per token for Llama-3.1-8B in BF16?
cards.back: 2 × 32 × 8 × 128 × 2 B = 128 KiB, so an 8K-token sequence needs about 1 GiB.

cards.label: Transformer inference and the KV cache
cards.front: Which phase sets TTFT and which sets TPOT?
cards.back: Prefill (processing the prompt) sets time to first token; decode (one token per step) sets time per output token.

cards.label: Transformer inference and the KV cache
cards.front: What problem does a paged KV cache solve?
cards.back: Fragmentation and over-reservation: KV is stored in fixed-size blocks allocated on demand instead of one contiguous max-length buffer per sequence, so many more sequences fit.

cards.label: Transformer inference and the KV cache
cards.front: How does GQA reduce KV cache size?
cards.back: Several query heads share one key/value head (e.g. 32 query heads, 8 KV heads), shrinking KV by the group factor.

cards.label: Transformer inference and the KV cache
cards.front: What is MLA?
cards.back: Multi-head Latent Attention (DeepSeek): K and V are compressed into a small per-token latent vector, cutting KV size dramatically; it needs dedicated kernels.

cards.label: Transformer inference and the KV cache
cards.front: What is continuous batching?
cards.back: Re-forming the batch at every decode step so finished sequences leave and new ones join immediately, instead of waiting for a whole static batch to finish.

cards.label: Transformer inference and the KV cache
cards.front: Why does prefix caching speed up TTFT?
cards.back: Requests sharing a prompt prefix reuse already-computed KV blocks, so prefill only runs on the new suffix.

cards.label: Transformer inference and the KV cache
cards.front: In MoE models, what does the router do?
cards.back: For each token it selects the top-k of E expert MLPs (e.g. 8 of 128), so only a fraction of parameters is active per token.

cards.label: Interconnects, collectives and parallelism
cards.front: Why should tensor parallelism stay inside one node?
cards.back: TP needs two all-reduces per layer; NVLink/NVSwitch gives ~1.8 TB/s per GPU inside a node, but inter-node links are ~10x slower, so cross-node TP is communication-bound.

cards.label: Interconnects, collectives and parallelism
cards.front: Which collective does expert parallelism depend on?
cards.back: All-to-all: tokens are dispatched to the GPUs that own their experts and the results combined back.

cards.label: Interconnects, collectives and parallelism
cards.front: What is RDMA and why does P/D disaggregation need it?
cards.back: Remote direct memory access: the NIC reads or writes remote (GPU) memory without the remote CPU. Moving GBs of KV cache per request between prefill and decode pods needs that bandwidth and latency.

cards.label: Interconnects, collectives and parallelism
cards.front: Difference between TP and DP for serving?
cards.back: TP splits each layer across GPUs to serve one batch faster (lower latency, communication every layer); DP runs independent replicas that serve different requests (more throughput, no communication).

cards.label: Interconnects, collectives and parallelism
cards.front: What does NVSwitch provide in an HGX B200 node?
cards.back: Full-bandwidth all-to-all NVLink connectivity between all 8 GPUs (1.8 TB/s per GPU).

cards.label: Interconnects, collectives and parallelism
cards.front: Rule of thumb for choosing TP size?
cards.back: The smallest TP that fits the weights with enough KV-cache headroom; then scale out with data-parallel replicas behind a router.

cards.label: Interconnects, collectives and parallelism
cards.front: What is pipeline parallelism's main inefficiency?
cards.back: Pipeline bubbles: stages sit idle unless enough micro-batches are in flight.

cards.label: CUDA execution, kernels and compilation
cards.front: What is a CUDA stream?
cards.back: An ordered queue of GPU work; kernels in one stream run in order and asynchronously to the CPU, and different streams can overlap.

cards.label: CUDA execution, kernels and compilation
cards.front: Why do engines pad decode batches to fixed sizes?
cards.back: CUDA graphs are captured for specific shapes; padding a batch of 13 to the captured size 16 lets the step replay a graph instead of launching kernels individually.

cards.label: CUDA execution, kernels and compilation
cards.front: Difference between PIECEWISE and FULL CUDA graph modes in vLLM?
cards.back: PIECEWISE captures everything except attention (which runs eagerly between graph pieces); FULL also captures attention, which needs a graph-compatible attention backend.

cards.label: CUDA execution, kernels and compilation
cards.front: What does FlashAttention avoid?
cards.back: Materializing the N×N attention score matrix in HBM: it tiles Q, K, V through on-chip memory and computes softmax online.

cards.label: CUDA execution, kernels and compilation
cards.front: What do vLLM's -O0 to -O3 flags control?
cards.back: Optimization level: -O0 none, -O1 simple fusions and PIECEWISE graphs, -O2 (default) more fusions and FULL_AND_PIECEWISE graphs, -O3 aggressive (currently same as -O2).

cards.label: CUDA execution, kernels and compilation
cards.front: What is the overlap scheduler?
cards.back: Preparing the next batch on the CPU while the GPU executes the current one, hiding scheduling overhead (SGLang's default; vLLM has async scheduling).

cards.label: CUDA execution, kernels and compilation
cards.front: Why does startup time matter for serving?
cards.back: It bounds how quickly autoscaling can add capacity and how fast a crashed replica recovers; compile caches, graph capture and weight loading dominate it.

cards.label: CUDA execution, kernels and compilation
cards.front: What is Triton?
cards.back: A Python-embedded language and compiler for writing block-level GPU kernels, used by torch.compile's Inductor and as a portable attention backend.

cards.label: Number formats and quantization
cards.front: Why is BF16 preferred over FP16 for inference?
cards.back: BF16 has FP32's exponent range (8 bits), so activations don't overflow; FP16 has more mantissa precision but a max of 65504.

cards.label: Number formats and quantization
cards.front: What is microscaling (MX)?
cards.back: A block format where each group of 32 elements shares an 8-bit power-of-two (E8M0) scale, e.g. MXFP8, MXFP4; Blackwell tensor cores apply the scales in hardware.

cards.label: Number formats and quantization
cards.front: Difference between W4A16 and W8A8?
cards.back: W4A16 stores weights in 4 bits but computes in 16-bit (saves bytes); W8A8 quantizes weights and activations to 8 bits and uses FP8 tensor cores (saves bytes and FLOPs).

cards.label: Number formats and quantization
cards.front: Online vs offline quantization?
cards.back: Online quantizes BF16 weights at load time with dynamic activation scales (no calibration); offline uses calibration data to choose scales and saves a quantized checkpoint (AWQ, GPTQ, llm-compressor).

cards.label: Number formats and quantization
cards.front: What does FP8 KV cache buy you?
cards.back: Half the KV bytes per token, so roughly twice as many tokens/sequences fit in the same memory, plus less bandwidth per decode step.

cards.label: Number formats and quantization
cards.front: Why do outliers matter for per-tensor scaling?
cards.back: One large value forces a large scale, so most small values lose precision; finer-grained (per-channel/per-block) scales contain the damage.

cards.label: Number formats and quantization
cards.front: Why does weight quantization speed up decode almost proportionally?
cards.back: Decode is memory-bound on reading weights, so fewer bytes per weight means proportionally less HBM time per step.

cards.label: Processes, networking and the serving API
cards.front: Why do the labs kill the whole process group of a server?
cards.back: Engines spawn child processes (workers, engine core) that hold GPU memory; killing only the parent can leave orphans, so they start with setsid and signal the group.

cards.label: Processes, networking and the serving API
cards.front: What is SSE and why does LLM serving use it?
cards.back: Server-Sent Events: an HTTP response that streams data: chunks; it lets clients see tokens as they are generated (so TTFT matters to users).

cards.label: Processes, networking and the serving API
cards.front: What does Envoy's ext_proc filter do in llm-d?
cards.back: It streams each request's headers/body to the EPP over gRPC; the EPP replies with a header naming the destination replica, which Envoy's ORIGINAL_DST cluster forwards to.

cards.label: Processes, networking and the serving API
cards.front: What does a chat template do?
cards.back: Converts the messages list into the single prompt string (with role markers and special tokens) the model was trained on.

cards.label: Processes, networking and the serving API
cards.front: Why must containers running NCCL get a large /dev/shm?
cards.back: NCCL and multi-process engines use shared memory for intra-node communication; the Docker default (64 MB) is too small.

cards.label: Processes, networking and the serving API
cards.front: SIGTERM vs SIGKILL?
cards.back: SIGTERM requests graceful shutdown (drain in-flight requests); SIGKILL terminates immediately and cannot be handled.

cards.label: Processes, networking and the serving API
cards.front: Why can mismatched keep-alive timeouts break proxies?
cards.back: If the server closes an idle connection before the proxy's idle timeout, the proxy may reuse a closed connection and get a TCP reset.

cards.label: Containers and Kubernetes for GPU serving
cards.front: What does the NVIDIA Container Toolkit do?
cards.back: Injects the host GPU driver libraries and device files into containers so --gpus works, without baking the driver into images.

cards.label: Containers and Kubernetes for GPU serving
cards.front: What does a Kubernetes readiness probe protect against in LLM serving?
cards.back: Routing traffic to a pod whose model is still loading/compiling; the pod receives requests only after the probe (e.g. GET /v1/models) succeeds.

cards.label: Containers and Kubernetes for GPU serving
cards.front: What is an InferencePool?
cards.back: A Gateway API Inference Extension CRD naming the set of model-server pods (label selector) and the endpoint picker (EPP) that chooses among them.

cards.label: Containers and Kubernetes for GPU serving
cards.front: Why does wide-EP need LeaderWorkerSet?
cards.back: One model replica spans several pods/nodes that must be scheduled, restarted and upgraded as a unit; LWS manages that group.

cards.label: Containers and Kubernetes for GPU serving
cards.front: Helm vs Kustomize?
cards.back: Helm renders templated charts from values files; Kustomize patches and overlays plain YAML. llm-d uses Helm for the router and Kustomize for model servers.

cards.label: Containers and Kubernetes for GPU serving
cards.front: What does KEDA add to the HPA?
cards.back: Scalers that read external metrics (e.g. Prometheus queries on EPP metrics), exposing them to the HPA, plus scale-to-zero.

cards.label: Containers and Kubernetes for GPU serving
cards.front: How do pods request GPUs?
cards.back: Via the extended resource nvidia.com/gpu: N advertised by the NVIDIA device plugin (or DRA resource claims).

cards.label: Measuring LLM serving performance
cards.front: Define TTFT, TPOT and ITL.
cards.back: TTFT: time from sending the request to the first output token. ITL: time between consecutive streamed tokens. TPOT: average time per output token after the first, (E2E − TTFT)/(n − 1).

cards.label: Measuring LLM serving performance
cards.front: What is goodput?
cards.back: The rate of requests that meet the latency SLO; throughput that violates the SLO doesn't count.

cards.label: Measuring LLM serving performance
cards.front: State Little's law and apply it to 20 req/s at 5 s latency.
cards.back: L = λ × W, so 20 × 5 = 100 requests in flight on average.

cards.label: Measuring LLM serving performance
cards.front: Closed-loop vs open-loop load generation?
cards.back: Closed loop keeps a fixed number of requests outstanding (concurrency); open loop sends at a fixed arrival rate regardless of completions, which exposes queue growth past capacity.

cards.label: Measuring LLM serving performance
cards.front: Why report p99 rather than mean latency?
cards.back: Means hide the tail; p99 is what 1% of users see, and tails compound across multi-call agentic workflows.

cards.label: Measuring LLM serving performance
cards.front: Why do random-token benchmarks understate prefix caching?
cards.back: Random prompts share no prefixes, so cache hit rate is ~0; real chat/RAG/agent traffic reuses system prompts, documents and history heavily.

cards.label: Measuring LLM serving performance
cards.front: Why run inference services below 100% utilization?
cards.back: Queueing delay grows like ρ/(1−ρ): at 90% utilization waits are ~9 service times, so headroom keeps tail latency bounded.

cards.label: Lab 00: FP32 baseline
cards.front: What is the core idea of vLLM Lab 00: FP32 baseline?
cards.back:
Every other lab in this suite measures itself against this one. We serve the primary model (meta-llama/Llama-3.1-8B-Instruct) with vLLM at full FP32 precision - no quantization, no speculative decoding, nothing clever - and record:

  • Memory: weights alone are 8B params x 4 bytes = ~32GB.
  • Throughput: output tokens/sec and requests/sec under a fixed synthetic workload.
  • Latency: mean/P99 time-to-first-token (TTFT) and time-per-output-token (TPOT).

cards.label: Lab 00: FP32 baseline
cards.front: What should you observe in the results of vLLM Lab 00: FP32 baseline?
cards.back:
• Peak GPU memory usage (nvidia-smi snapshot printed before/after server start) - this is your reference point for "how much does precision / quantization actually save".
  • Note the achieved throughput is already using vLLM's continuous batching and paged KV cache - the "fp32" in this lab's name refers only to model precision, not to which serving techniques are enabled. Lab 02 is where we isolate the batching technique itself.

cards.label: Lab 01: Precision reduction (FP32 -> FP16 / BF16)
cards.front: What is the core idea of vLLM Lab 01: Precision reduction (FP32 -> FP16 / BF16)?
cards.back:
The single biggest, lowest-risk win in serving efficiency is simply not using FP32. Halving the bytes per parameter:

  • Halves weight memory (32GB -> 16GB for the 8B model), leaving far more headroom for KV cache (i.e. more concurrent requests).
  • Roughly doubles achievable throughput, since most modern GPU tensor cores (including B200's) are dramatically faster at FP16/BF16 matmuls than FP32.
  • Unlocks vLLM's fast attention backends entirely: FlashInfer and FlashAttention only support FP16/BF16 (see Lab 00's note and Lab 03).

cards.label: Lab 01: Precision reduction (FP32 -> FP16 / BF16)
cards.front: What should you observe in the results of vLLM Lab 01: Precision reduction (FP32 -> FP16 / BF16)?
cards.back:
• Memory drop after server start (nvidia-smi snapshot) - should be roughly half of Lab 00's.
  • output_throughput (tokens/sec) - typically ~1.5-2x FP32 on B200.
  • Which attention backend vLLM selects now that FP16/BF16 is available (check the server log) - this is worth comparing to Lab 00's log.

cards.label: Lab 02: Continuous batching + paged KV cache
cards.front: What is the core idea of vLLM Lab 02: Continuous batching + paged KV cache?
cards.back: This is the idea that made vLLM famous, so it's worth being precise about what it actually is (a scheduling + memory-management technique) versus what it's called in the code today (see the callout below).

cards.label: Lab 02: Continuous batching + paged KV cache
cards.front: What should you observe in the results of vLLM Lab 02: Continuous batching + paged KV cache?
cards.back:
• hf_naive_static_batch vs vllm_max_num_seqs_8: same effective concurrency limit, but vLLM should still substantially outperform HF's generate() loop because it isn't blocked by the slowest sequence in each fixed batch.
  • vllm_max_num_seqs_8 vs vllm_default: shows the throughput you leave on the table by artificially constraining concurrency.

cards.label: Lab 03: High-efficiency attention backends
cards.front: What is the core idea of vLLM Lab 03: High-efficiency attention backends?
cards.back:
As covered in Lab 02: the original standalone PagedAttention kernel is gone (removed in vLLM v0.25.0, July 2026). What's left to tune is which attention backend vLLM uses, since paged KV-cache management now lives inside each backend's own kernels. On NVIDIA Blackwell (B200, SM100), the backends you can pick for a standard GQA decoder like Llama-3.1-8B are:

Backend Notes
FLASH_ATTN FlashAttention. Version is selectable with --attention-config.flash_attn_version=2/3/4; FA4 is the default on SM100+, FA3 on Hopper, FA2 elsewhere. Automatic selection tries FlashAttention first.
FLASHINFER FlashInfer. On SM100 it uses the trtllm-gen decode kernels (with attention-sink support and native FP8 KV); disable with --attention-config.use_trtllm_attention=0. Part of vLLM's Blackwell fallback order (TRT-LLM ragged → FlashInfer → ...).
TRITON_ATTN Pure-Triton attention kernel. Slower than the two above but has no extra native-kernel dependency and supports dtypes/shapes the others don't (e.g. FP32, used unavoidably in Lab 00).
FLEX_ATTENTION PyTorch's flex_attention, compiled via torch.compile. Flexible (custom masks/score-mods) but generally the slowest for plain causal attention.

cards.label: Lab 03: High-efficiency attention backends
cards.front: What should you observe in the results of vLLM Lab 03: High-efficiency attention backends?
cards.back:
• FA4 vs FA2 on the prefill-heavy run: FA4 is written for Blackwell's tensor memory and async TMA pipeline, so the gap should be largest on long prompts.
  • Decode-heavy mean_tpot_ms (time per output token) is usually where the backends differentiate most sharply.
  • Check results/logs/lab03_<backend>_*.log for the line where vLLM reports the backend it actually selected.

cards.label: Lab 04: Automatic prefix caching (APC)
cards.front: What is the core idea of vLLM Lab 04: Automatic prefix caching (APC)?
cards.back: Many real workloads send requests that share a long common prefix: a system prompt, a few-shot example block, a RAG context chunk reused across several questions, or successive turns of the same chat. Without prefix caching, vLLM re-runs the full prefill computation for that shared prefix on every single request. With automatic prefix caching, the paged KV blocks for a prefix are kept around (as long as memory allows) and reused by any later request whose tokens start with the same prefix - turning an O(prefix length) prefill into an O(1) cache lookup for every request after the first.

cards.label: Lab 04: Automatic prefix caching (APC)
cards.front: What should you observe in the results of vLLM Lab 04: Automatic prefix caching (APC)?
cards.back:
• mean_ttft_ms and p99_ttft_ms: should drop substantially with prefix caching on, since ~79/80 requests skip re-prefilling the shared 1500 tokens.
  • output_throughput: caching frees up GPU compute that was being spent on redundant prefill, so overall throughput should also improve, not just latency.

cards.label: Lab 05: Chunked prefill
cards.front: What is the core idea of vLLM Lab 05: Chunked prefill?
cards.back: Prefill (processing a prompt's tokens for the first time) and decode (generating one new token per sequence) have very different compute profiles: prefill is compute-bound and scales with prompt length, decode is comparatively cheap but latency-sensitive. Without chunked prefill, a single very long prompt's prefill can occupy an entire scheduler step, during which no other sequence's decode step runs - so a handful of short, latency-sensitive requests can get stuck behind one long document being ingested.

cards.label: Lab 05: Chunked prefill
cards.front: What should you observe in the results of vLLM Lab 05: Chunked prefill?
cards.back:
• chunked_prefill_off_short vs chunked_prefill_on_short: look at p99_ttft_ms specifically - the tail latency of short requests is where the "blocked behind a long prefill" effect shows up most clearly.
  • The _long rows are there for context (throughput on the long-document stream itself), not the main point of the lab.

cards.label: Lab 06: CUDA graphs / compilation
cards.front: What is the core idea of vLLM Lab 06: CUDA graphs / compilation?
cards.back: Every forward pass through a model involves launching hundreds of small CUDA kernels. At small batch sizes (the common case for low-latency, low-concurrency decode), the CPU-side overhead of launching those kernels can rival or exceed the GPU time actually spent computing them.

cards.label: Lab 06: CUDA graphs / compilation
cards.front: What should you observe in the results of vLLM Lab 06: CUDA graphs / compilation?
cards.back:
• eager_low vs O2_default_low: mean_tpot_ms should be noticeably higher (worse) under --enforce-eager.
  • O1_piecewise vs O2_default: the extra gain from capturing attention inside full graphs.
  • The _high runs: the gaps shrink as each step does more GPU work.
  • Startup time in results/logs/lab06_*.log: compilation and graph capture add tens of seconds (cached under ~/.cache/vllm/torch_compile_cache on later runs) - the tradeoff for faster steady-state decode.

cards.label: Lab 07: Weight-only quantization (AWQ / GPTQ)
cards.front: What is the core idea of vLLM Lab 07: Weight-only quantization (AWQ / GPTQ)?
cards.back:
BF16 halved FP32's memory footprint; weight-only quantization goes further by storing weights in 4 bits instead of 16, while keeping activations in a higher-precision compute dtype. Two popular post-training quantization methods:

  • AWQ (Activation-aware Weight Quantization): protects the small fraction of "salient" weight channels most sensitive to quantization error (identified from activation statistics) by keeping them at higher effective precision, quantizing the rest to INT4.
  • GPTQ: a one-shot weight quantization method that greedily minimizes layer-wise reconstruction error using second-order (Hessian) information, quantizing to INT4 (or INT8) with typically small accuracy loss.

cards.label: Lab 07: Weight-only quantization (AWQ / GPTQ)
cards.front: What should you observe in the results of vLLM Lab 07: Weight-only quantization (AWQ / GPTQ)?
cards.back:
• GPU memory snapshot right after each server starts: weights should drop from ~16GB (bf16) to roughly 5-6GB (INT4) for the 8B model.
  • output_throughput: INT4 quantization reduces memory-bandwidth pressure (fewer bytes moved per weight read), which often increases throughput even though there's dequantization overhead - especially at memory-bandwidth-bound batch sizes.
  • This lab does not measure output quality/accuracy - that requires a task benchmark (e.g. lm-eval-harness), which is out of scope here. Quantization always trades some accuracy for memory/speed; AWQ and GPTQ are both designed to minimize that loss, not eliminate it.

cards.label: Lab 08: FP8 quantization (Blackwell-native)
cards.front: What is the core idea of vLLM Lab 08: FP8 quantization (Blackwell-native)?
cards.back: B200 (Blackwell, SM100) has native FP8 tensor cores - unlike AWQ/GPTQ INT4 (Lab 07), FP8 quantization here needs no pre-quantized checkpoint or calibration step: vLLM can quantize a BF16 checkpoint to FP8 dynamically at load time with --quantization fp8 (per-tensor/per-channel dynamic scales computed on the fly). This gets you roughly half the weight memory of BF16 with much less accuracy risk than INT4, backed by hardware that runs FP8 matmuls at full speed.

cards.label: Lab 08: FP8 quantization (Blackwell-native)
cards.front: What should you observe in the results of vLLM Lab 08: FP8 quantization (Blackwell-native)?
cards.back:
• GPU memory after server start: FP8 weights should be roughly half of BF16's; adding FP8 KV cache reduces it further, most visibly at higher concurrency where KV cache (not weights) dominates memory.
  • output_throughput: FP8 matmuls on B200 should outperform BF16, unlike a non-native-FP8 GPU where the dequantization overhead could eat the memory savings.
  • Check the server log for which attention backend was selected - if FlashInfer is available, FP8 attention should be running through the trtllm-gen path discussed in Lab 03.

cards.label: Lab 09: Speculative decoding
cards.front: What is the core idea of vLLM Lab 09: Speculative decoding?
cards.back: Normal decoding generates exactly one token per forward pass per sequence. Speculative decoding has a cheap "proposer" guess several tokens ahead, then verifies all of them in a single forward pass of the real (target) model - if the target model agrees with a guessed token, you get it for free; the first disagreement is the fallback point. Because verification is one batched forward pass regardless of how many tokens were proposed, you can get multiple tokens per target-model step when the proposer guesses well, at zero cost in output distribution (the outputs are mathematically identical to standard decoding, provided the acceptance rule is used correctly).

cards.label: Lab 09: Speculative decoding
cards.front: What should you observe in the results of vLLM Lab 09: Speculative decoding?
cards.back:
• no_spec_low vs draft_model_spec_low / ngram_spec_low: mean_tpot_ms should drop (fewer wall-clock ms per output token) when speculation is accepted often.
  • The same comparison at _high: the gap should be much smaller, or even favor no_spec.
  • vLLM logs speculative acceptance metrics (mean acceptance length, per-position acceptance rate) in the server log and on /metrics (vllm:spec_decode_*) - compare EAGLE-3 vs the draft model there.
  • Beyond this lab, upstream also has MTP heads (for models trained with multi-token prediction such as DeepSeek-V3), suffix decoding, and dynamic speculation (num_speculative_tokens_per_batch_size) that shrinks k as concurrency grows.

cards.label: Lab 10: Tensor parallelism
cards.front: What is the core idea of vLLM Lab 10: Tensor parallelism?
cards.back: Every other lab uses the 8B primary model, which comfortably fits on one B200. This lab switches to Qwen/Qwen2.5-32B-Instruct (ungated, ~64GB in BF16) specifically to make tensor parallelism (TP) worth doing.

cards.label: Lab 10: Tensor parallelism
cards.front: What should you observe in the results of vLLM Lab 10: Tensor parallelism?
cards.back:
• Throughput scaling from TP=1 -> 2 -> 4 -> 8: expect solid gains from 1->2 and 1->4, with diminishing returns by TP=8 as all-reduce communication overhead starts to compete with the compute time saved per GPU.
  • mean_tpot_ms at each TP size: more GPUs means each one does less compute per step, but pays a fixed communication cost every layer - latency doesn't necessarily improve as much as raw throughput does.
  • Whether the FP32/TP=1 bonus variant succeeded or OOM'd, and if it succeeded, how small the achievable KV cache / concurrency was compared to the BF16 variants - this is the "why you'd reach for TP or quantization" moment for large models.

cards.label: Lab 11: Capstone - the full optimization stack
cards.front: What is the core idea of vLLM Lab 11: Capstone - the full optimization stack?
cards.back:
This lab doesn't introduce a new technique - it pulls together everything from Labs 00-10 into the "fp32 -> fully optimized" journey, on both models.

One thing worth internalizing by this point: most of the optimizations in this suite are already the default in modern vLLM. Continuous batching, paged KV cache, prefix caching, chunked prefill, and CUDA graphs are all on unless you explicitly disable them. The knobs you actually have to reach for in practice are the ones this capstone varies: precision / quantization, and (for models too large for one GPU) tensor parallelism. Everything else, vLLM is already doing for you.

cards.label: Lab 11: Capstone - the full optimization stack
cards.front: What should you observe in the results of vLLM Lab 11: Capstone - the full optimization stack?
cards.back:
• The total speedup from fp32 to fp8_weights_and_kv on the 8B model - this is the number that answers the original question ("how much can I actually speed up serving a base fp32 model with vLLM on B200?").
  • Whether tp4_fp8 beats tp4_bf16 by roughly the same margin FP8 gave the 8B model - quantization and parallelism are largely orthogonal levers and should compose.
  • Check results/SUMMARY.md after this lab runs: it now contains every lab's table plus this final rollup, in one file.

cards.label: Lab 00 - Environment Setup
cards.front: What is the core idea of SGLang Lab 00 - Environment Setup?
cards.back: Goal: get a clean, isolated SGLang install working on your 8xB200 node, and pre-download every model the rest of the curriculum needs.

cards.label: Lab 00 - Environment Setup
cards.front: What should you observe in the results of SGLang Lab 00 - Environment Setup?
cards.back:
• Why SGLang benefits from an isolated environment on multi-framework research nodes.
  • The two SGLang benchmarking entry points you'll use throughout the curriculum: python -m sglang.launch_server (the OpenAI-compatible server) and python -m sglang.bench_serving (the async load generator).
  • Where model weights and results live ($HF_HOME, results/).

cards.label: Lab 01 - The Naive FP32 Baseline
cards.front: What is the core idea of SGLang Lab 01 - The Naive FP32 Baseline?
cards.back: The task says "take a base FP32 precision model." In practice almost no model is published in true FP32 anymore (checkpoints on the Hub are usually BF16), so we treat FP32 as our deliberately-naive starting point: we force the model to load and run its weights and activations in float32 (--dtype float32 in SGLang, torch_dtype=torch.float32 in transformers). This is exactly what you'd get if someone handed you a model and you served it with zero thought about efficiency.

cards.label: Lab 01 - The Naive FP32 Baseline
cards.front: What should you observe in the results of SGLang Lab 01 - The Naive FP32 Baseline?
cards.back:
• results/lab01_fp32_baseline/hf_naive.json -- per-request latency and overall output_throughput (tokens/sec) for the naive loop.
  • results/lab01_fp32_baseline/bench_conc1.log and bench_conc64.log -- console output from sglang.bench_serving, including TTFT (time to first token) and TPOT (time per output token) percentiles.
  • Compare output_throughput_tok_s across the three rows in results/summary.csv for lab=lab01_fp32_baseline.

cards.label: Lab 02 - Precision: FP32 vs FP16 vs BF16
cards.front: What is the core idea of SGLang Lab 02 - Precision: FP32 vs FP16 vs BF16?
cards.back:
B200 (Blackwell) tensor cores deliver dramatically higher FLOPs for bf16/fp16 than for fp32 (and higher still for fp8/fp4, covered in lab03). Halving bytes-per-parameter (4 bytes -> 2 bytes) also halves:

  • The GPU memory needed to hold the weights.
  • The size of the KV cache per token, which means SGLang's memory allocator (--mem-fraction-static) can fit a larger max_running_requests and a deeper RadixAttention prefix-cache tree in the same GPU memory.

cards.label: Lab 02 - Precision: FP32 vs FP16 vs BF16
cards.front: What should you observe in the results of SGLang Lab 02 - Precision: FP32 vs FP16 vs BF16?
cards.back:
• bfloat16 and float16 should use roughly half the GPU memory of float32 for weights, and show meaningfully higher output_throughput_tok_s in results/summary.csv.
  • The three qualitative samples in results/lab02_precision/sample_*.txt should be very close in content (Qwen2.5 was trained in bf16, so bf16 is the "native" precision; fp32 is a lossless upcast of those same weights; fp16 can occasionally diverge more due to its narrower dynamic range, though for a 7B chat model at greedy decoding this is usually imperceptible).
  • This is the cheapest possible win in the entire curriculum: one flag change, no retraining, no accuracy-tuning required to go from FP32 to BF16. Always start here before reaching for quantization.

cards.label: Lab 03 - Quantization: FP8 and INT4
cards.front: What is the core idea of SGLang Lab 03 - Quantization: FP8 and INT4?
cards.back:
• FP8 (--quantization fp8): SGLang casts the bf16 weights to FP8 (E4M3) on the fly when the server starts. B200's tensor cores have native FP8 matmul support (2x the FLOPs of bf16 on the same silicon), so this is typically the best throughput-per-accuracy-lost trade available on Blackwell. No calibration dataset or offline step required.
  • AWQ (Activation-aware Weight Quantization) / GPTQ: both quantize weights down to INT4, but need an offline calibration pass against sample data to decide how to round weights with minimal output error. We use community pre-quantized checkpoints (Qwen/Qwen2.5-7B-Instruct-AWQ and -GPTQ-Int4) so this lab doesn't need to run its own calibration job -- SGLang auto-detects the quantization method from the checkpoint's config.json, so you do not pass --quantization for these.
  • Weight-only INT4 quantization keeps activations/KV-cache at higher precision and dequantizes weights on the fly during the matmul, so it saves memory more than it saves compute -- useful when you're memory-bound rather than compute-bound.

cards.label: Lab 03 - Quantization: FP8 and INT4
cards.front: What should you observe in the results of SGLang Lab 03 - Quantization: FP8 and INT4?
cards.back:
• Memory: bf16 > fp8 > awq-int4 ~= gptq-int4, roughly in a 4 : 2 : 1 : 1 ratio for weights (KV cache size is unaffected by weight quantization, so total memory savings will be somewhat less dramatic than a pure 4x).
  • Throughput: on B200, fp8-online should show a clear throughput win over bf16-baseline with a barely perceptible quality difference in sample_fp8-online.txt vs sample_bf16-baseline.txt. INT4 methods often show even higher throughput at low/medium concurrency (memory-bandwidth bound decode phase moves less data per token), but the gap narrows or can even reverse at very high concurrency where compute-bound prefill dominates and dequantization overhead starts to matter.
  • Read all four sample_*.txt files side by side. This is the most important habit to build for production quantization work: never ship a quantized model without eyeballing (and ideally running a proper eval harness against) its outputs.

cards.label: Lab 04 - Tensor Parallelism (TP) Scaling
cards.front: What is the core idea of SGLang Lab 04 - Tensor Parallelism (TP) Scaling?
cards.back: Tensor parallelism splits individual weight matrices (attention QKVO projections, MLP up/down projections) across GPUs, so each GPU only holds 1/TP of the parameters and does 1/TP of the matmul FLOPs for those layers. After each attention block and each MLP block, the partial results must be combined with an all-reduce across the TP group before the next layer can run. That all-reduce is pure communication overhead with no useful compute -- it's the tax you pay for splitting the model.

cards.label: Lab 04 - Tensor Parallelism (TP) Scaling
cards.front: What should you observe in the results of SGLang Lab 04 - Tensor Parallelism (TP) Scaling?
cards.back:
• Total throughput should increase from TP=1 to TP=8, but per-GPU throughput (total_throughput / TP) should decrease as TP grows -- the script prints a "scaling efficiency" table making this explicit.
  • The drop-off is the NCCL all-reduce tax. It grows with TP size (more ranks to synchronize) and shrinks relative to compute as the model gets bigger (more FLOPs to amortize the fixed communication cost against) -- this is why TP is usually reserved for models that don't fit on fewer GPUs, or where you specifically need the lower per-request latency that splitting compute across more GPUs buys you.
  • Compare TTFT (median_ttft_ms) across TP sizes too: TP mainly helps latency per request (the prefill/decode for one sequence is now spread over more GPUs), which is a different axis from the throughput-via-batching win you saw in lab01. Production sizing is a joint decision over both.

cards.label: Lab 05 - RadixAttention: Automatic Prefix Caching
cards.front: What is the core idea of SGLang Lab 05 - RadixAttention: Automatic Prefix Caching?
cards.back: Every LLM request starts with a "prefill" phase (process the whole input prompt to build its KV cache) followed by a "decode" phase (generate output tokens one at a time, extending that KV cache). Prefill cost scales with prompt length -- for a workload with long, repeated system prompts (chat assistants, RAG pipelines, few-shot prompting, agent scaffolding), most GPUs end up repeatedly re-computing KV cache for tokens that are byte-for-byte identical to what a previous request already computed.

cards.label: Lab 05 - RadixAttention: Automatic Prefix Caching
cards.front: What should you observe in the results of SGLang Lab 05 - RadixAttention: Automatic Prefix Caching?
cards.back:
• median_ttft_ms (time to first token) should be dramatically lower with RadixAttention enabled: after the first request in each group "warms" the cache for that system prompt, every subsequent request in the same group only needs to prefill the short, unique question -- not the full ~2048-token shared prefix.
  • output_throughput_tok_s should also be higher with caching enabled, since GPU time that would have been spent redundantly re-prefilling identical tokens is instead available for decoding other requests.
  • This benefit is "free" -- it required zero changes to how you structure requests, as long as your client sends the same token sequence for the shared portion (same system prompt text, same tokenizer, no non-deterministic templating). It's why designing your prompts to put static/shared content first and per-request/dynamic content last is a best practice for any RadixAttention-based server.
  • Try increasing GSP_SYSTEM_PROMPT_LEN (e.g. GSP_SYSTEM_PROMPT_LEN=8192 ./run_lab.sh) to see the gap widen further -- the longer the shared prefix relative to the unique suffix, the bigger RadixAttention's win.

cards.label: Lab 06 - Continuous Batching & Scheduler Knobs
cards.front: What is the core idea of SGLang Lab 06 - Continuous Batching & Scheduler Knobs?
cards.back:
SGLang's scheduler runs a loop: at every iteration, decide which requests (new prefills and in-flight decodes) to run together as one GPU batch. Three knobs shape this:

  • Overlap scheduling (on by default): the CPU thread that decides the next batch runs concurrently with the GPU executing the current batch, instead of waiting for the GPU to finish first. This hides scheduling and Python-side overhead behind GPU compute -- pure upside on GPUs with fast CPUs, at the cost of one extra batch of "lookahead" latency for aborts/rate limiting to take effect.
  • Chunked prefill (--chunked-prefill-size N): normally, prefilling a very long prompt is one big matmul-heavy step. If a 4096-token prompt needs prefilling right when 30 other requests are mid-decode, the naive approach makes those 30 requests wait for the entire prefill to finish. Chunked prefill splits long prefills into N-token pieces and interleaves them with other requests' decode steps, trading a bit of total throughput for dramatically better tail latency.
  • Schedule policy (--schedule-policy): controls which queued request is picked next. fcfs (first-come-first-served) is simple and fair. lpm (longest-prefix-match) instead prioritizes requests that share a RadixAttention prefix with what's currently cached/running, improving cache locality (fewer evictions, more reuse) under prefix-heavy traffic at some cost to strict request-arrival fairness.

cards.label: Lab 06 - Continuous Batching & Scheduler Knobs
cards.front: What should you observe in the results of SGLang Lab 06 - Continuous Batching & Scheduler Knobs?
cards.back:
• [A] Overlap scheduling should give a small, consistent throughput/TPOT improvement with no real downside -- there's rarely a reason to disable it in production; it exists mainly as a debugging knob.
  • [B] Look at p99_ttft_ms in results/lab06_scheduling_batching/bench_chunked_off.log vs bench_chunked_on.log: disabling chunked prefill should show occasional very high tail latencies for requests unlucky enough to be queued behind a long prompt's prefill. Total throughput may be similar or even slightly higher without chunking (less scheduling overhead) -- this is a genuine throughput-vs-tail-latency trade-off, not a strict win either way.
  • [C] lpm should match or beat fcfs on throughput/TTFT for the prefix-heavy workload, since it actively schedules cache-friendly requests together instead of processing strictly in arrival order.
  • None of these knobs require touching the model or its weights at all -- they're pure serving-layer tuning, and usually the first place to look before reaching for more GPUs or a smaller model.

cards.label: Lab 07 - CUDA Graphs & torch.compile
cards.front: What is the core idea of SGLang Lab 07 - CUDA Graphs & torch.compile?
cards.back:
• CUDA graphs: capture the full sequence of GPU kernel launches for a given batch shape once, then replay the whole graph with a single lightweight API call on every subsequent step, instead of re-dispatching each kernel individually from Python/C++ every time. This eliminates per-kernel CPU launch overhead, which matters a lot during decode (many small kernels, once per token, per request in the batch) and much less during prefill (a handful of large matmuls that are compute-bound regardless of launch overhead). SGLang captures graphs for a set of common batch sizes at server startup (you'll see a "Capturing cuda graph" log line listing batch sizes) and falls back to eager execution for uncaptured shapes.
