  • torch.compile: PyTorch's JIT compiler traces the model's forward pass and generates fused, specialized kernels (via TorchInductor) for it. This is complementary to CUDA graphs (which just replay whatever kernels already exist) since it can create better kernels in the first place. SGLang's docs currently mark --enable-torch-compile as an experimental, lightly-maintained feature that can fail for some model/version combinations -- this lab treats it as best-effort and continues even if it fails to start.

cards.label: Lab 07 - CUDA Graphs & torch.compile
cards.front: What should you observe in the results of SGLang Lab 07 - CUDA Graphs & torch.compile?
cards.back:
• median_tpot_ms (time per output token = decode step cost) should be visibly higher with CUDA graphs disabled -- this is the metric CUDA graphs target directly.
  • median_ttft_ms (time to first token = prefill cost) should barely move between the two CUDA-graph configurations, confirming that prefill is matmul-bound rather than launch-overhead-bound.
  • If the torch-compile-on row is present in results/summary.csv, compare median_tpot_ms against cuda-graph-on -- gains beyond what CUDA graphs already provide are usually modest for a 7B model at these batch sizes, since CUDA graphs already remove most launch overhead; torch.compile mainly helps when there's additional kernel-fusion opportunity (e.g. fusing normalization + activation ops) that raw graph replay can't provide.

cards.label: Lab 08 - Speculative Decoding (N-gram)
cards.front: What is the core idea of SGLang Lab 08 - Speculative Decoding (N-gram)?
cards.back: Decoding is memory-bandwidth bound: generating one token means reading the entire model's weights (and KV cache) from HBM for a batch that's often small relative to the GPU's compute capacity. Speculative decoding exploits this by having a cheap "drafter" propose several candidate future tokens, then running one forward pass of the real target model to verify all of them simultaneously (a form of prefill-shaped, parallel computation). Since that verification pass costs about the same as generating a single token normally, every additional accepted draft token is close to free.

cards.label: Lab 08 - Speculative Decoding (N-gram)
cards.front: What should you observe in the results of SGLang Lab 08 - Speculative Decoding (N-gram)?
cards.back:
• ngram-spec-general vs no-spec-general: expect a real but modest output_throughput_tok_s improvement.
  • ngram-spec-repetitive vs no-spec-repetitive: expect a much larger improvement -- this is the workload shape where speculative decoding earns its keep in production (e.g. code-editing assistants, "reformat this data" tools, autocomplete).
  • Check the server log (server_ngram.log) for any lines mentioning acceptance rate / accept length if your SGLang version logs them -- higher accepted-tokens-per-step directly explains the throughput gain.
  • If you have access to a compatible EAGLE checkpoint for your target model in a real deployment, prefer it over NGRAM: EAGLE's learned drafter generalizes far better across content types than n-gram matching.

cards.label: Lab 09 - Structured Output / Grammar-Guided Decoding
cards.front: What is the core idea of SGLang Lab 09 - Structured Output / Grammar-Guided Decoding?
cards.back: LLMs are surprisingly good at producing JSON when asked, but "surprisingly good" isn't "guaranteed" -- extra prose before/after the JSON, trailing commas, unescaped quotes, or truncated output at max_tokens are all common failure modes that show up more often than you'd like in production at scale.

cards.label: Lab 09 - Structured Output / Grammar-Guided Decoding
cards.front: What should you observe in the results of SGLang Lab 09 - Structured Output / Grammar-Guided Decoding?
cards.back:
• constrained should show num_valid_json / num_requests at or very close to 100%. unconstrained will likely show at least one failure (extra commentary text, a stray field, wrong type for age, etc.) even though the model is generally well-behaved -- this gap is exactly why production extraction/tool-calling pipelines should use constrained decoding instead of prompt-and-pray plus a JSON parser wrapped in retry logic.
  • mean_latency_s should be modestly higher for the constrained case (extra grammar-mask computation per step), but usually far cheaper than the latency of a failed parse + retry round-trip would have been.
  • If the load-test rows are present in results/summary.csv, compare median_tpot_ms between plain-decoding-load and constrained-decoding-load to see the per-token overhead in a concurrent, throughput-oriented setting rather than one-request-at-a-time.

cards.label: Lab 10 - Mixture-of-Experts: Expert Parallelism & DP Attention
cards.front: What is the core idea of SGLang Lab 10 - Mixture-of-Experts: Expert Parallelism & DP Attention?
cards.back:
$MOE_MODEL (Qwen3-30B-A3B) is a MoE model: it has ~30B total parameters organized into many small expert MLPs, but a per-token router activates only a handful of experts per forward pass (~3B "active" parameters worth of compute per token). This changes the parallelism trade-offs vs a dense model like the ones in labs 01-04:

  • Plain TP shards every expert's weight matrix across all GPUs (same as it would for a dense model's single MLP). Simple, but wasteful: each GPU stores and computes against a slice of experts that a given token may not have even been routed to.
  • Expert Parallelism (EP) instead places whole experts on specific GPUs, and uses an all-to-all communication step to route each token's hidden state to whichever GPU(s) hold its selected expert(s), then another all-to-all to bring results back. In SGLang, --ep "subdivides" the TP group (--tp 8 --ep 8 uses the 8-GPU TP group to host 8 distinct expert shards). This avoids redundant expert compute, at the cost of all-to-all communication instead of all-reduce.
  • DP Attention (--enable-dp-attention --dp-size N) targets a different inefficiency: attention layers are relatively small compared to a MoE model's total FLOPs, so tensor-parallelizing them (which requires an all-reduce and duplicates KV cache management overhead across ranks) is wasteful. DP attention instead runs each GPU's attention layers on its own independent slice of requests (true data parallelism, no cross-GPU communication for attention), while the larger FFN/expert layers still use TP or EP.

cards.label: Lab 10 - Mixture-of-Experts: Expert Parallelism & DP Attention
cards.front: What should you observe in the results of SGLang Lab 10 - Mixture-of-Experts: Expert Parallelism & DP Attention?
cards.back:
• tp8-ep8 should generally outperform tp8-baseline for this model, since it eliminates redundant per-GPU expert computation -- the gap should be larger at higher concurrency (more tokens per all-to-all round = better amortized communication cost) and smaller (or even reversed) at very low concurrency.
  • tp8-dp8-attention should show its benefit mainly in memory efficiency (no duplicated KV cache management across the attention TP group) and can particularly help at high concurrency / long context, where attention's KV cache footprint becomes a bigger fraction of total memory pressure.
  • Try re-running with BENCH_MAX_CONCURRENCY=16 ./run_lab.sh and then BENCH_MAX_CONCURRENCY=128 ./run_lab.sh to see how the ranking between these three strategies shifts with load -- there is no universally "best" MoE parallelism strategy independent of your expected traffic pattern.

cards.label: Lab 11 - Capstone: Stack the Wins
cards.front: What is the core idea of SGLang Lab 11 - Capstone: Stack the Wins?
cards.back: Goal: combine the broadly-applicable optimizations from the earlier labs into one server configuration, and put a single number on the total speedup from "naive FP32, one request at a time" to "SGLang, tuned."

cards.label: Lab 11 - Capstone: Stack the Wins
cards.front: What should you observe in the results of SGLang Lab 11 - Capstone: Stack the Wins?
cards.back:
• The concurrency=1 comparison isolates the pure "better engine + better precision" win with no batching involved -- expect this alone to be a multi-x speedup over the naive HF loop.
  • The concurrency=$BENCH_MAX_CONCURRENCY comparison additionally captures continuous batching's throughput multiplier on top of that -- expect this to be the largest speedup number in the whole curriculum.
  • Look at results/plots/throughput.png for a single chart spanning every lab you've run, from the naive FP32 baseline all the way to this recipe.
  • The real lesson: optimization is not one silver bullet, it's a stack of mostly-independent, mostly-compatible levers (engine choice, precision, parallelism, scheduling, caching, speculative decoding), and the right combination depends on your model size, hardware, and traffic pattern -- which is exactly why each lab isolated one lever at a time instead of just handing you a single "optimal" config.

cards.label: Lab 12: Attention backends on Blackwell
cards.front: What is the core idea of SGLang Lab 12: Attention backends on Blackwell?
cards.back:
The attention kernel is the one part of the transformer forward pass whose cost grows with context length, and it is also the part that reads the paged KV cache. SGLang exposes the kernel library as a server argument:

Current choices include triton, torch_native, flex_attention, fa3, fa4, flashinfer, trtllm_mha, and MLA-specific backends (flashmla, trtllm_mla, cutedsl_mla, ...) for DeepSeek-style models. On B200 the four worth comparing for a GQA model are:

Backend What it is
fa4 FlashAttention 4, written in CuTe-DSL for Blackwell's tensor memory (TMEM) and 2-CTA MMA.
flashinfer FlashInfer's paged attention (JIT-compiled, plan/run split for CUDA graphs).
trtllm_mha TensorRT-LLM's hand-tuned Blackwell MHA kernels, exposed via FlashInfer.
triton Portable Triton kernels - the reference point.

cards.label: Lab 12: Attention backends on Blackwell
cards.front: What should you observe in the results of SGLang Lab 12: Attention backends on Blackwell?
cards.back:
• Prefill rows: median_ttft_ms. FA4 should lead on long prompts.
  • Decode rows: median_tpot_ms. trtllm_mha is tuned for small-batch decode.
  • This is the same experiment as vLLM lab 03 - compare the two engines' numbers for similar backends.

cards.label: Lab 13: HiCache - hierarchical KV cache (GPU -> CPU)
cards.front: What is the core idea of SGLang Lab 13: HiCache - hierarchical KV cache (GPU -> CPU)?
cards.back: RadixAttention (Lab 05) reuses KV cache for shared prefixes, but only while those prefixes are still resident in GPU memory. Real traffic often has a working set of prefixes much larger than HBM: thousands of tenants with their own system prompts, RAG over many documents, long multi-turn agent sessions that come back minutes later. Once the radix tree evicts a prefix, the next request pays the full prefill again.

cards.label: Lab 13: HiCache - hierarchical KV cache (GPU -> CPU)
cards.front: What should you observe in the results of SGLang Lab 13: HiCache - hierarchical KV cache (GPU -> CPU)?
cards.back:
• median_ttft_ms: HiCache should sit close to what lab05 shows for a fully-resident cache, while GPU-only radix falls back towards the no-cache floor.
  • Server log of the HiCache run: host-tier hit/load statistics.
  • The KV math in the script header - redo it for your model (layers x KV heads x head_dim x 2 x bytes) to size GPU vs host tiers.

cards.label: llm-d Lab 01: Why LLM traffic needs an inference-aware router
cards.front: What is the core idea of llm-d Lab 01: Why LLM traffic needs an inference-aware router?
cards.back:
A classic load balancer assumes requests are roughly interchangeable and replicas are stateless. LLM serving breaks both assumptions:

  • Requests differ by orders of magnitude. A 50-token chat turn and a 30,000-token RAG prompt cost wildly different amounts of prefill compute, and output length is unknown up front. "Number of open connections" is a poor proxy for load.
  • Replicas are stateful. Each vLLM replica holds a prefix cache (KV blocks for prompts it has seen). Sending a request to the replica that already holds its 6,000-token system prompt skips that prefill entirely. Sending it anywhere else recomputes it and evicts something useful.

cards.label: llm-d Lab 01: Why LLM traffic needs an inference-aware router
cards.front: What should you observe in the results of llm-d Lab 01: Why LLM traffic needs an inference-aware router?
cards.back:
• prefix_hit_rate: round-robin should be far below the EPP.
  • ttft_p50_ms / ttft_p99_ms: the EPP should cut TTFT sharply.
  • max_replica_share: should stay close to 0.25 with the EPP; prefix affinity without load awareness would create hot replicas (see lab 02).
  • Least-request vs round-robin: load awareness alone fixes queueing imbalance but not cache misses.

cards.label: llm-d Lab 02: Inside the scheduler - filters, scorers, pickers
cards.front: What is the core idea of llm-d Lab 02: Inside the scheduler - filters, scorers, pickers?
cards.back:
For each request the EPP runs one or more scheduling profiles. A profile is a pipeline:

  1. Filters drop ineligible endpoints (wrong role in P/D, unhealthy, saturated, not cache-warm enough).
  2. Scorers give each remaining endpoint a score in [0, 1]; scores are combined with the configured weights.
  3. A picker chooses (max-score-picker, weighted-random-picker, ...).

cards.label: llm-d Lab 02: Inside the scheduler - filters, scorers, pickers
cards.front: What should you observe in the results of llm-d Lab 02: Inside the scheduler - filters, scorers, pickers?
cards.back:
• The tension between cache affinity and load balance: prefix-only wins on prefix_hit_rate but loses on ttft_p99_ms and max_replica_share; load-only is the reverse; the combined profiles should get most of both.
  • Calibration: the affinity filter's default peakPrefillThroughput (15928 tokens/s) was measured for Qwen3-32B TP=2 on H100. A B200 has ~2x the prefill throughput, so the filter spills too early. Re-measure with upstream guides/recipes/router/calibration and set it in configs/epp/affinity-token-load.yaml.
  • epp-*.log: per-request scheduling decisions at --v=2.

cards.label: llm-d Lab 03: Flow control and multi-tenancy
cards.front: What is the core idea of llm-d Lab 03: Flow control and multi-tenancy?
cards.back: When offered load exceeds capacity, requests queue somewhere. Without flow control they queue inside each vLLM replica's scheduler, which is FIFO across all users: a batch job that dumps 2,000 requests makes every interactive user wait behind it. Once a request is committed to a replica's queue it is also stuck there even if another replica frees up first.

cards.label: llm-d Lab 03: Flow control and multi-tenancy
cards.front: What should you observe in the results of llm-d Lab 03: Flow control and multi-tenancy?
cards.back:
• quiet tenant ttft_p99_ms: large drop with flow control.
  • ALL throughput: about the same - flow control reorders work, it does not create capacity.
  • Tune maxConcurrency in the config: too high and nothing queues in the EPP; too low and replicas idle.

cards.label: llm-d Lab 04: Tiered prefix cache (HBM -> CPU RAM -> storage)
cards.front: What is the core idea of llm-d Lab 04: Tiered prefix cache (HBM -> CPU RAM -> storage)?
cards.back: A B200 has 178 GB of HBM, but a node has ~2 TB of DRAM and tens of TB of NVMe. KV cache for Qwen3-32B costs ~256 KB per token (64 layers x 8 KV heads x 128 dim x 2 (K,V) x 2 bytes), so one 8K-token conversation is ~2 GB. A few hundred concurrent agentic sessions overflow HBM quickly.

cards.label: llm-d Lab 04: Tiered prefix cache (HBM -> CPU RAM -> storage)
cards.front: What should you observe in the results of llm-d Lab 04: Tiered prefix cache (HBM -> CPU RAM -> storage)?
cards.back:
• prefix_hit_rate and ttft_p50_ms: should improve sharply with the CPU tier.
  • ext_hits per replica in results/lab04_tiered_kv_cache/*.json.
  • Host memory: free -g during run 2 shows the pinned CPU tier.
  • Compare with SGLang lab 13 (HiCache), the same idea in SGLang.

cards.label: llm-d Lab 05: Prefill/decode (P/D) disaggregation
cards.front: What is the core idea of llm-d Lab 05: Prefill/decode (P/D) disaggregation?
cards.back:
Prefill and decode want different hardware behaviour:

Prefill Decode
Work per step thousands of tokens of one prompt one token for each of many sequences
Bottleneck tensor-core FLOPs (compute-bound) HBM bandwidth reading weights + KV (memory-bound)
Best parallelism low TP, many replicas higher TP / large batch
SLO it drives TTFT TPOT / ITL

cards.label: llm-d Lab 05: Prefill/decode (P/D) disaggregation
cards.front: What should you observe in the results of llm-d Lab 05: Prefill/decode (P/D) disaggregation?
cards.back:
• tpot_p50_ms lower/steadier with P/D, at the price of a transfer hop in TTFT.
  • Prefill-pool saturation in 1P1D and the fix in 2P1D: the "scale P and D independently" argument.
  • Decoder log lines about NIXL handshakes and transfers.
  • Kubernetes version of this lab: lab08 deploys the upstream pd-disaggregation guide unchanged.

cards.label: llm-d Lab 06: Wide expert parallelism
cards.front: What is the core idea of llm-d Lab 06: Wide expert parallelism?
cards.back: Mixture-of-Experts models (DeepSeek-V3/R1, Qwen3-MoE, gpt-oss, Kimi) replace each dense FFN with many experts, of which a router activates a few per token. DeepSeek-R1 has 671B parameters but only ~37B are active per token, so the model needs a lot of memory but relatively little compute per token.

cards.label: llm-d Lab 06: Wide expert parallelism
cards.front: What should you observe in the results of llm-d Lab 06: Wide expert parallelism?
cards.back:
• Throughput at high concurrency: DP+EP > TP.
  • Latency at low concurrency: TP can win.
  • EPLB: small gain on synthetic random tokens (expert routing is close to uniform); larger gains on real skewed traffic.

cards.label: llm-d Lab 07: A Kubernetes cluster for llm-d on one 8xB200 node
cards.front: What is the core idea of llm-d Lab 07: A Kubernetes cluster for llm-d on one 8xB200 node?
cards.back:
Labs 01-06 wired everything by hand: container names, ports, GPU indices, an endpoints file. That works on one box, but a production fleet needs:

  • Scheduling onto GPUs: the NVIDIA device plugin advertises nvidia.com/gpu as a node resource; pods request nvidia.com/gpu: 2 and the scheduler places them. (DRA, resource.k8s.io/v1, is the newer model for richer device claims.)
  • Self-healing and rollouts: Deployments/LeaderWorkerSets restart crashed replicas, probes gate traffic until the model is loaded, rollouts drain gracefully (--shutdown-timeout, preStop).
  • Service discovery: the EPP watches an InferencePool (pods selected by label) instead of a YAML file.
  • Multi-pod replicas: a LeaderWorkerSet (LWS) treats a group of pods (e.g. one model replica spanning 2 nodes) as one unit; a DisaggregatedSet bundles prefill and decode LWS roles so they roll out together.
  • Autoscaling: HPA/KEDA scale replicas on metrics (lab 09).

cards.label: llm-d Lab 08: The well-lit paths on Kubernetes
cards.front: What is the core idea of llm-d Lab 08: The well-lit paths on Kubernetes?
cards.back:
llm-d packages its optimizations as well-lit paths: guides with tested manifests, a validated reference model/topology, and nightly end-to-end CI. Each guide is the same three steps (deploy_guide.sh does them for you):

Guide Reference topology (NVIDIA) What it adds
optimized-baseline Qwen3-32B, 2 replicas x TP=2 prefix-cache-affinity-filter + token-load-scorer; the default to start from.
precise-prefix-cache-routing same Model servers publish KV-cache events over ZMQ; the router's KV indexer knows exactly which blocks each pod holds. The router renders (tokenizes) each prompt to look it up.
tiered-prefix-cache same, 300 GiB CPU tier per pod vLLM OffloadingConnector (or SGLang HiCache / LMCache) plus a router scorer for the CPU tier.
pd-disaggregation gpt-oss-120b, 1P (TP=1) + 1D (TP=4) Prefill/decode pools in one DisaggregatedSet, NIXL KV transfer, router schedules each request twice.
predicted-latency-routing Qwen3-32B, 2 x TP=2 XGBoost sidecars trained online predict TTFT/TPOT per pod; optional SLO headers (x-llm-d-slo-ttft-ms).
flow-control Qwen3-32B Per-tenant fair queuing with priority bands (InferenceObjective).
wide-ep DeepSeek-R1, 32 GPUs DP+EP across nodes with DeepEP + P/D (multi-node; see lab 06 for the single-node version).

cards.label: llm-d Lab 08: The well-lit paths on Kubernetes
cards.front: What should you observe in the results of llm-d Lab 08: The well-lit paths on Kubernetes?
cards.back:
• *-pod-metrics.txt: requests and prefix hits concentrated per prefix group (optimized-baseline, precise), CPU-tier hits (tiered), prefill vs decode roles (P/D).
  • flow-control: premium tenant latency vs batch.
  • Compare against the Docker labs 01-05: same mechanisms, now with discovery, health probes, rollouts and Helm-managed config.
  • Calibration (guides/recipes/router/calibration) - the reference peakPrefillThroughput is for H100; measure it for B200.

cards.label: llm-d Lab 09: Observability and SLO-aware autoscaling
cards.front: What is the core idea of llm-d Lab 09: Observability and SLO-aware autoscaling?
cards.back:
Why CPU/GPU utilization is the wrong autoscaling signal for LLMs. During continuous batching the GPU reports close to 100% utilization almost regardless of load, so utilization says nothing about whether users are waiting. By the time latency visibly degrades, requests are already queueing. Good signals are leading and inference-aware:

Signal Source Meaning
in-flight requests EPP (llm_d_epp_inflight_requests) demand currently in the system
flow-control queue size EPP (llm_d_epp_flow_control_queue_size) demand the pool cannot absorb right now
pool saturation EPP (llm_d_epp_flow_control_pool_saturation) fraction of capacity used
waiting requests / KV-cache usage vLLM (vllm:num_requests_waiting, vllm:kv_cache_usage_perc) per-replica pressure

cards.label: llm-d Lab 09: Observability and SLO-aware autoscaling
cards.front: What should you observe in the results of llm-d Lab 09: Observability and SLO-aware autoscaling?
cards.back:
• Lag between desired rising and ready rising (startup cost).
  • KEDA's currentMetrics vs the target value.
  • In Grafana: queueing at the EPP vs inside vLLM as replicas come up.

cards.label: Regions, DNS and global traffic
cards.front: What is an availability zone?
cards.back: An independent datacenter (separate power, cooling, network) within a region, a few ms from the others, used to survive single-datacenter failures.

cards.label: Regions, DNS and global traffic
cards.front: Minimum round-trip time New York ↔ Frankfurt?
cards.back: About 60 ms at the speed of light in fiber (~200 km/ms for ~6,200 km each way); real paths are ~80-90 ms.

cards.label: Regions, DNS and global traffic
cards.front: How does GeoDNS route users?
cards.back: It returns different IPs depending on the resolver's location (or measured latency) and region health, sending users to the nearest healthy region.

cards.label: Regions, DNS and global traffic
cards.front: What is anycast?
cards.back: Announcing the same IP from many locations via BGP so each client reaches the topologically nearest one; used by global load balancers and CDNs.

cards.label: Regions, DNS and global traffic
cards.front: Why use an edge PoP for LLM APIs if responses aren't cacheable?
cards.back: Terminating TCP/TLS near the user saves round trips, the edge filters attacks (WAF, DDoS), and traffic rides the provider's backbone to the GPU region.

cards.label: Regions, DNS and global traffic
cards.front: Why keep DNS TTLs short for failover?
cards.back: Clients and resolvers cache answers for the TTL; a long TTL keeps sending users to a failed region.

cards.label: Regions, DNS and global traffic
cards.front: What does N+1 capacity mean for multi-region?
cards.back: Provision enough spare capacity that if any one region fails, the remaining regions can absorb its traffic.

cards.label: Regions, DNS and global traffic
cards.front: What can override latency-based routing?
cards.back: Data residency/sovereignty rules (e.g. EU prompts must be processed in EU regions) and capacity constraints.

cards.label: Load balancers, API gateways and admission control
cards.front: Why is L4 load balancing a poor fit for LLM APIs?
cards.back: It balances connections, not requests; long-lived HTTP/2 connections carrying many requests pin to one backend, and it can't see request cost or server state.

cards.label: Load balancers, API gateways and admission control
cards.front: What does an inference-aware router consider that a classic L7 LB doesn't?
cards.back: Model-server queue depth, KV-cache utilization, which replica holds the prompt's prefix, predicted TTFT/TPOT, P/D role and loaded adapters.

cards.label: Load balancers, API gateways and admission control
cards.front: Why should the API gateway strip client-supplied x-llm-d-* headers?
cards.back: Otherwise clients could claim another tenant's identity or premium priority; the gateway derives tenant/tier from the authenticated token and injects trusted headers.

cards.label: Load balancers, API gateways and admission control
cards.front: Why rate-limit tokens per minute, not just requests?
cards.back: Request cost varies by orders of magnitude with prompt and output length; token limits track actual GPU work.

cards.label: Load balancers, API gateways and admission control
cards.front: What is the point of router-level flow control vs engine queues?
cards.back: The router can queue fairly per tenant with priorities and dispatch to the best replica when capacity frees up, instead of FIFO queues stuck inside individual replicas.

cards.label: Load balancers, API gateways and admission control
cards.front: Why must proxies propagate client disconnects?
cards.back: So the engine aborts the generation and frees its KV cache instead of computing tokens nobody will read.

cards.label: Load balancers, API gateways and admission control
cards.front: What client behavior prevents retry storms?
cards.back: Exponential backoff with jitter and honoring Retry-After on 429/503 responses.

cards.label: GPU capacity, autoscaling and cost
cards.front: Formula for cost per 1M output tokens?
cards.back: (GPU $/hour × number of GPUs) ÷ (output tokens/s × 3600) × 1,000,000.

cards.label: GPU capacity, autoscaling and cost
cards.front: 8 GPUs at $5/hour sustaining 20k output tokens/s: cost per 1M tokens?
cards.back: $40/h ÷ 72M tokens/h ≈ $0.56 per 1M output tokens (at full utilization).

cards.label: GPU capacity, autoscaling and cost
cards.front: Why is GPU utilization a bad autoscaling signal for LLM serving?
cards.back: Continuous batching keeps the GPU busy (~100%) at almost any load, so it neither rises before latency degrades nor distinguishes light from heavy load.

cards.label: GPU capacity, autoscaling and cost
cards.front: What dominates autoscaling reaction time for LLM pods?
cards.back: Startup latency: image pull, loading tens of GB of weights, torch.compile and CUDA graph capture.

cards.label: GPU capacity, autoscaling and cost
cards.front: What is fast model actuation (sleep/wake)?
cards.back: Keeping a model-server process with weights offloaded to host memory so it can wake and serve in seconds instead of cold-starting.

cards.label: GPU capacity, autoscaling and cost
cards.front: Where do spot GPUs fit in an LLM platform?
cards.back: Interruptible batch/offline inference and evaluation jobs; not latency-critical interactive serving.

cards.label: GPU capacity, autoscaling and cost
cards.front: How do you size replicas for a service?
cards.back: Peak load ÷ per-replica goodput at the SLO (from benchmarks), plus headroom for failures and deployments, checked against KV memory for the implied concurrency.

cards.label: GPU capacity, autoscaling and cost
cards.front: Why are input tokens priced lower than output tokens?
cards.back: Prefill processes prompt tokens in parallel and is compute-efficient, while each output token needs its own memory-bound decode step.

cards.label: Reliability, rollouts and observability
cards.front: What is an error budget?
cards.back: The allowed unreliability (1 − SLO); e.g. a 99.5% SLO allows 0.5% of requests to miss. It governs the trade-off between shipping changes and reliability work.

cards.label: Reliability, rollouts and observability
cards.front: Why alert on burn rate instead of individual errors?
cards.back: Burn rate measures how fast the error budget is being consumed, catching sustained problems quickly while ignoring harmless blips.

cards.label: Reliability, rollouts and observability
cards.front: What should a canary for a new model version check besides latency?
cards.back: Quality: eval scores, refusal rates, tool-call/JSON parse errors and user feedback signals.

cards.label: Reliability, rollouts and observability
cards.front: Which vLLM metrics show overload before users complain?
cards.back: vllm:num_requests_waiting rising, vllm:kv_cache_usage_perc near 1, preemptions, and TTFT histogram tails.

cards.label: Reliability, rollouts and observability
cards.front: What do distributed traces add over metrics?
cards.back: Per-request breakdown across hops (gateway, router, queue, prefill, decode), showing where an individual slow request spent its time.

cards.label: Reliability, rollouts and observability
cards.front: Define RTO and RPO.
cards.back: RTO: maximum acceptable time to restore service. RPO: maximum acceptable data loss measured in time.

cards.label: Reliability, rollouts and observability
cards.front: Why treat weights, chat template, engine version and flags as one artifact?
cards.back: Any of them can change outputs or performance; versioning them together makes rollouts and rollbacks reproducible.

cards.label: Security, privacy and multi-tenancy
cards.front: Can a shared prefix cache leak data across tenants?
cards.back: Not content directly (a hit needs identical tokens), but timing can reveal that a prefix was recently sent; sensitive tenants can get salted cache keys or dedicated pools.

cards.label: Security, privacy and multi-tenancy
cards.front: What is "denial of wallet"?
cards.back: Abuse that drives up cost (e.g. very long prompts or outputs) rather than availability; mitigated with token-based quotas and limits.

cards.label: Security, privacy and multi-tenancy
cards.front: Why prefer safetensors over pickle checkpoints?
cards.back: Pickle files can execute arbitrary code when loaded; safetensors is a pure tensor format.

cards.label: Security, privacy and multi-tenancy
cards.front: Which component should be internet-facing in an llm-d deployment?
cards.back: Only the gateway/edge; the router (Envoy/EPP) and model servers stay internal, protected by network policies.

cards.label: Security, privacy and multi-tenancy
cards.front: Where do prompts end up that need data-residency controls?
cards.back: Model-server memory, KV caches and offload tiers, logs, traces, and any request analytics pipeline.

cards.label: The life of one request
cards.front: What does the API gateway inject for llm-d flow control?
cards.back: The authoritative x-llm-d-inference-fairness-id (tenant) and x-llm-d-inference-objective (priority class) headers, after stripping client-supplied ones.

cards.label: The life of one request
cards.front: How does the EPP tell Envoy which replica to use?
cards.back: It returns the x-gateway-destination-endpoint header with the chosen pod's address; Envoy's ORIGINAL_DST cluster forwards there.

cards.label: The life of one request
cards.front: Biggest lever on TTFT for multi-turn chat?
cards.back: Avoiding prefix recomputation: prefix caching on the server plus routing the next turn to the replica (or CPU tier) that holds the conversation's KV.

cards.label: The life of one request
cards.front: Biggest lever on TPOT?
cards.back: Bytes moved per decode step: lower-precision weights/KV, good batching, CUDA graphs, and speculative decoding.

cards.label: The life of one request
cards.front: What drives tail latency under load?
cards.back: Queueing: too little capacity, unfair FIFO queues, and slow autoscaling.

cards.label: The life of one request
cards.front: Why does the edge PoP reduce latency even though GPUs are in one region?
cards.back: TCP and TLS handshakes complete with a nearby PoP (short RTT), and the request then travels over a warm, optimized backbone connection.

cards.label: Reference architecture for a global LLM service
cards.front: Which layer decides which GPU replica serves a request?
cards.back: The inference router: llm-d's EPP (behind Envoy) using cache, load and latency signals over the InferencePool.

cards.label: Reference architecture for a global LLM service
cards.front: Which layer enforces tenant identity and quotas?
cards.back: The API gateway, before traffic reaches the inference router.

cards.label: Reference architecture for a global LLM service
cards.front: Default precision recommendation on Blackwell for production?
cards.back: FP8 weights and activations plus FP8 KV cache, after validating quality against BF16; FP4 where evals allow.

cards.label: Reference architecture for a global LLM service
cards.front: When should you add P/D disaggregation?
cards.back: Long prompts, large models and strict TPOT SLOs where prefill interference hurts decode; for short prompts aggregated serving usually wins.

cards.label: Reference architecture for a global LLM service
cards.front: Why run the router with multiple replicas?
cards.back: It's on the request path for every request; HA (2+ replicas) avoids a single point of failure. Precise prefix routing has every router replica subscribe to every pod's KV events.

cards.label: Reference architecture for a global LLM service
cards.front: What goes in the platform control plane?
cards.back: GitOps-managed manifests (Helm/Kustomize), CI with performance and quality gates, and a canary/rollout controller.

cards.label: The optimization playbook
cards.front: First fix for TTFT problems with shared system prompts?
cards.back: Turn on prefix caching (vLLM) / RadixAttention (SGLang); at fleet level, add prefix-cache-aware routing.

cards.label: The optimization playbook
cards.front: Fix for TPOT spikes when long prompts arrive?
cards.back: Chunked prefill with a tuned token budget; if that's not enough, prefill/decode disaggregation.

cards.label: The optimization playbook
cards.front: Fix when one tenant's burst raises everyone's latency?
cards.back: Router flow control: per-tenant fair queues with priority bands, plus gateway rate limits.

cards.label: The optimization playbook
cards.front: Fix when multi-turn sessions lose their cache over time?
cards.back: Add a CPU (and optionally NVMe/shared FS) KV tier and route with tier awareness.

cards.label: The optimization playbook
cards.front: What should you measure before optimizing?
cards.back: A baseline on the real workload shape (input/output lengths, prefix reuse, concurrency), with latency percentiles and quality.

problems.title: Product of Array Except Self
problems.prompt: Return out where out[i] is the product of every element except nums[i], in O(n) and without division.
problems.solution:
def product_except_self(nums):
    n = len(nums)
    out = [1] * n
    prefix = 1
    for i in range(n):            # out[i] = product of everything left of i
        out[i] = prefix
        prefix *= nums[i]
    suffix = 1
    for i in range(n - 1, -1, -1):  # times everything right of i
        out[i] *= suffix
        suffix *= nums[i]
    return out
problems.tests:
check(product_except_self([1, 2, 3, 4]), [24, 12, 8, 6])
check(product_except_self([-1, 1, 0, -3, 3]), [0, 0, 9, 0, 0])
check(product_except_self([0, 0]), [0, 0])

problems.title: Minimum Window Substring
problems.prompt: Return the shortest substring of s that contains every character of t (with multiplicity), or "".
problems.solution:
from collections import Counter

def min_window(s, t):
    need = Counter(t)
    missing = len(t)
    left = 0
    best = (float("inf"), 0, 0)
    for right, ch in enumerate(s):
        if need[ch] > 0:
            missing -= 1
        need[ch] -= 1
        while missing == 0:                       # window is valid: shrink it
            if right - left + 1 < best[0]:
                best = (right - left + 1, left, right + 1)
            need[s[left]] += 1
            if need[s[left]] > 0:
                missing += 1
            left += 1
    return s[best[1]:best[2]] if best[0] != float("inf") else ""
problems.tests:
check(min_window("ADOBECODEBANC", "ABC"), "BANC")
check(min_window("a", "a"), "a")
check(min_window("a", "aa"), "")
check(min_window("aaflslflsldkalskaaa", "aaa"), "aaa")

problems.title: Remove Nth Node From End
problems.prompt: Remove the n-th node from the end in one pass and return the head.
problems.solution:
from dc import ListNode

def remove_nth_from_end(head, n):
    dummy = ListNode(0, head)
    fast = slow = dummy
    for _ in range(n + 1):           # open a gap of n nodes
        fast = fast.next
    while fast:
        fast, slow = fast.next, slow.next
    slow.next = slow.next.next
    return dummy.next
problems.tests:
check(list_values(remove_nth_from_end(make_list([1, 2, 3, 4, 5]), 2)), [1, 2, 3, 5])
check(list_values(remove_nth_from_end(make_list([1]), 1)), [])
check(list_values(remove_nth_from_end(make_list([1, 2]), 2)), [2])

problems.title: Kth Smallest Element in a BST
problems.prompt: Return the k-th smallest value (1-indexed). Stop as soon as you find it.
problems.solution:
def kth_smallest(root, k):
    stack, node = [], root
    while True:
        while node:                  # iterative in-order traversal
            stack.append(node)
            node = node.left
        node = stack.pop()
        k -= 1
        if k == 0:
            return node.val
        node = node.right
problems.tests:
check(kth_smallest(make_tree([3, 1, 4, None, 2]), 1), 1)
check(kth_smallest(make_tree([5, 3, 6, 2, 4, None, None, 1]), 3), 3)
check(kth_smallest(make_tree([5, 3, 6, 2, 4, None, None, 1]), 6), 6)

problems.title: Merge K Sorted Lists
problems.prompt: Merge k sorted linked lists into one sorted list in O(N log k).
problems.solution:
import heapq
from dc import ListNode

def merge_k_lists(lists):
    heap = [(node.val, i, node) for i, node in enumerate(lists) if node]   # i breaks ties
    heapq.heapify(heap)
    dummy = tail = ListNode()
    while heap:
        _, i, node = heapq.heappop(heap)
        tail.next = tail = node
        if node.next:
            heapq.heappush(heap, (node.next.val, i, node.next))
    return dummy.next
problems.tests:
check(list_values(merge_k_lists([make_list([1, 4, 5]), make_list([1, 3, 4]), make_list([2, 6])])),
      [1, 1, 2, 3, 4, 4, 5, 6])
check(list_values(merge_k_lists([])), [])
check(list_values(merge_k_lists([None, make_list([1])])), [1])

problems.title: Course Schedule (Topological Order)
problems.prompt: prereqs holds pairs [course, needs]. Return an order to take all n courses, or [] if a cycle makes it impossible. Any valid order passes.
problems.solution:
from collections import deque

def find_order(n, prereqs):
    graph = [[] for _ in range(n)]
    indegree = [0] * n
    for course, need in prereqs:
        graph[need].append(course)
        indegree[course] += 1
    q = deque(i for i in range(n) if indegree[i] == 0)   # Kahn's algorithm
    order = []
    while q:
        u = q.popleft()
        order.append(u)
        for v in graph[u]:
            indegree[v] -= 1
            if indegree[v] == 0:
                q.append(v)
    return order if len(order) == n else []

problems.title: Subsets
problems.prompt: Return every subset of a list of distinct numbers. Any order.
problems.solution:
def subsets(nums):
    out, path = [], []
    def go(i):
        if i == len(nums):
            out.append(path[:])
            return
        go(i + 1)                 # skip nums[i]
        path.append(nums[i])      # take nums[i]
        go(i + 1)
        path.pop()
    go(0)
    return out
problems.tests:

problems.title: Meeting Rooms II
problems.prompt: Return the fewest rooms needed to hold every meeting [start, end).
problems.solution:
def min_meeting_rooms(intervals):
    events = []
    for s, e in intervals:
        events += [(s, 1), (e, -1)]
    rooms = best = 0
    for _, delta in sorted(events):     # at equal times the -1 (end) sorts first
        rooms += delta
        best = max(best, rooms)
    return best
problems.tests:

check(min_meeting_rooms([[7, 10], [2, 4]]), 1)
check(min_meeting_rooms([[1, 5], [5, 10]]), 1, "back to back")
check(min_meeting_rooms([]), 0)

problems.title: Insert Interval
problems.prompt: Insert new into sorted, non-overlapping intervals, merging where needed.
problems.solution:
def insert(intervals, new):
    s, e = new
    left = [iv for iv in intervals if iv[1] < s]
    right = [iv for iv in intervals if iv[0] > e]
    overlap = [iv for iv in intervals if not (iv[1] < s or iv[0] > e)]
    if overlap:
        s, e = min(s, overlap[0][0]), max(e, overlap[-1][1])
    return left + [[s, e]] + right

problems.title: Autocomplete Top 3
problems.prompt: After each character typed of query, return up to three products with that prefix, in lexicographic order.
problems.solution:
import bisect

def suggested_products(products, query):
    products = sorted(products)
    out, prefix = [], ""
    for ch in query:
        prefix += ch
        i = bisect.bisect_left(products, prefix)
        out.append([p for p in products[i:i + 3] if p.startswith(prefix)])
    return out
problems.tests:

      [["mobile", "moneypot", "monitor"], ["mobile", "moneypot", "monitor"],
       ["mouse", "mousepad"], ["mouse", "mousepad"], ["mouse", "mousepad"]])
check(suggested_products(["havana"], "tatiana"), [[], [], [], [], [], [], []])

problems.title: Parse Access Logs
problems.prompt: Each line looks like 2026-11-07T10:00:01Z GET /api/items 200 123ms. Skip malformed lines. Return {"requests": n, "errors": count of status >= 500, "p50_ms": …, "by_path": {path: count}}, where p50 is the nearest-rank median (sorted(latencies)[ceil(0.5 * n) - 1]).
problems.solution:
import math
import re
from collections import Counter

LINE = re.compile(r"^\S+ (GET|POST|PUT|DELETE|PATCH) (\S+) (\d{3}) (\d+)ms$")

def summarize_logs(lines):
    latencies, paths, errors = [], Counter(), 0
    for line in lines:
        m = LINE.match(line.strip())
        if not m:
            continue
        _, path, status, ms = m.groups()
        paths[path] += 1
        errors += int(status) >= 500
        latencies.append(int(ms))
    latencies.sort()
    p50 = latencies[math.ceil(0.5 * len(latencies)) - 1] if latencies else None
    return {"requests": len(latencies), "errors": errors, "p50_ms": p50, "by_path": dict(paths)}
problems.tests:
logs = """2026-11-07T10:00:01Z GET /api/items 200 120ms
2026-11-07T10:00:02Z GET /api/items 200 80ms
garbage line
2026-11-07T10:00:03Z POST /api/cart 503 900ms
2026-11-07T10:00:04Z GET /health 200 2ms""".splitlines()
check(summarize_logs(logs), {"requests": 4, "errors": 1, "p50_ms": 80,
                             "by_path": {"/api/items": 2, "/api/cart": 1, "/health": 1}})
check(summarize_logs([])["requests"], 0)

problems.title: Rolling 3-Day Average per Store

import pandas as pd

def rolling_avg(df):
    df = df.sort_values(["store", "day"]).reset_index(drop=True)
    df["avg3"] = df.groupby("store")["sales"].transform(lambda s: s.rolling(3, min_periods=1).mean())
    return df

import numpy as np

def one_hot(y, k):
    y = np.asarray(y, dtype=int)
    out = np.zeros((y.size, k))
    out[np.arange(y.size), y] = 1.0
    return out

problems.title: Moving Average with cumsum
problems.prompt: Return the means of every length-k window of x in O(n) using a cumulative sum.
problems.solution:
import numpy as np

def moving_average(x, k):
    c = np.cumsum(np.concatenate([[0.0], np.asarray(x, float)]))
    return (c[k:] - c[:-k]) / k

problems.title: Tiled Matrix Multiply
problems.prompt: A GPU block computes one tile × tile output tile by looping over the K dimension in tile-wide chunks that it stages in shared memory. Write that loop nest with NumPy tiles (edges may be partial). Return C = A @ B and the number of tile loads from A and B combined.
problems.solution:
import numpy as np

def tiled_matmul(A, B, tile):
    M, K = A.shape
    _, N = B.shape
    C = np.zeros((M, N))
    loads = 0
    for i in range(0, M, tile):              # one "block" per (i, j) output tile
        for j in range(0, N, tile):
            acc = np.zeros((min(tile, M - i), min(tile, N - j)))
            for k in range(0, K, tile):      # stream K through shared memory
                a = A[i:i + tile, k:k + tile]
                b = B[k:k + tile, j:j + tile]
                loads += 2
                acc += a @ b
            C[i:i + tile, j:j + tile] = acc
    return C, loads
problems.tests:

check(C, A @ B, "matches A @ B with ragged edges")
check(loads, 5 * 3 * 3 * 2, "5×3 output tiles × 3 K-steps × (A + B)")

problems.title: Online Softmax (one pass)
problems.prompt: Softmax normally needs three passes (max, sum, normalise). Compute the max m and the normaliser l = Σ exp(x - m) in a single pass over chunks of x, rescaling l whenever the running max grows. Return (m, l).
problems.solution:
import numpy as np

def online_softmax_stats(x, chunk=4):
    m, l = -np.inf, 0.0
    for s in range(0, len(x), chunk):
        block = np.asarray(x[s:s + chunk], float)
        m_new = max(m, block.max())
        l = l * np.exp(m - m_new) + np.exp(block - m_new).sum()   # rescale the old sum
        m = m_new
    return m, l
problems.tests:

m, l = online_softmax_stats(x)
check(m, x.max())
check(l, np.exp(x - x.max()).sum())
check(np.exp(x - m) / l, np.exp(x - x.max()) / np.exp(x - x.max()).sum(), "gives the exact softmax")

problems.title: FlashAttention Forward (tiled)
problems.prompt: Compute softmax(q kᵀ / √d) v for q (Tq, d), k, v (Tk, d) without ever materialising the Tq × Tk score matrix: loop over key/value blocks of size block, keep per-row running max m, normaliser l and output accumulator o, and rescale them as each block arrives.
problems.solution:
import numpy as np

def flash_attention(q, k, v, block=8):
    Tq, d = q.shape
    m = np.full((Tq, 1), -np.inf)
    l = np.zeros((Tq, 1))
    o = np.zeros((Tq, v.shape[1]))
    for s in range(0, k.shape[0], block):
        kb, vb = k[s:s + block], v[s:s + block]
        scores = q @ kb.T / np.sqrt(d)                    # (Tq, block): only one tile in "SRAM"
        m_new = np.maximum(m, scores.max(1, keepdims=True))
        p = np.exp(scores - m_new)
        scale = np.exp(m - m_new)
        l = l * scale + p.sum(1, keepdims=True)
        o = o * scale + p @ vb
        m = m_new
    return o / l
problems.tests:
import numpy as np
rng = np.random.default_rng(3)
q, k, v = rng.normal(size=(10, 16)), rng.normal(size=(29, 16)), rng.normal(size=(29, 16))
s = q @ k.T / 4; p = np.exp(s - s.max(1, keepdims=True)); ref = (p / p.sum(1, keepdims=True)) @ v
check(flash_attention(q, k, v, block=8), ref, "block 8")
check(flash_attention(q, k, v, block=1), ref, "block 1")
check(flash_attention(q, k, v, block=64), ref, "one block")

problems.title: Parallel Reduction Tree
problems.prompt: Simulate a shared-memory tree reduction: at each step, element i adds element i + stride for every i < stride, halving stride from n/2 down to 1. n is a power of two. Return (total, steps); there should be log2(n) steps.
problems.solution:
import numpy as np

def tree_reduce(x):
    buf = np.array(x, dtype=float)
    stride, steps = len(buf) // 2, 0
    while stride >= 1:
        buf[:stride] += buf[stride:2 * stride]     # every "thread" i < stride works in parallel
        stride //= 2
        steps += 1
    return buf[0], steps
problems.tests:

check(tree_reduce(x), (x.sum(), 10))

problems.title: Blelloch Exclusive Scan
problems.prompt: Implement the work-efficient exclusive prefix sum: an up-sweep that builds partial sums in a tree, set the root to 0, then a down-sweep. n is a power of two. Use vectorised slices for each level (that's one parallel step on a GPU).
problems.solution:
import numpy as np

def blelloch_scan(x):
    a = np.array(x, dtype=float)
    n = len(a)
    d = 1
    while d < n:                                   # up-sweep (reduce)
        a[2 * d - 1::2 * d] += a[d - 1::2 * d]
        d *= 2
    a[-1] = 0
    d = n // 2
    while d >= 1:                                  # down-sweep
        left = a[d - 1::2 * d].copy()
        a[d - 1::2 * d] = a[2 * d - 1::2 * d]
        a[2 * d - 1::2 * d] += left
        d //= 2
    return a
problems.tests:

problems.title: Incremental Decoding with a KV Cache
problems.prompt: decode_step(x_t, cache, Wq, Wk, Wv) takes one new token's hidden state x_t (d,), appends its key and value to cache (a dict with lists "k" and "v"), and returns the attention output for that token over all cached positions. Running it token by token must reproduce full causal attention over the sequence.
problems.solution:
import numpy as np

def decode_step(x_t, cache, Wq, Wk, Wv):
    q = x_t @ Wq
    cache["k"].append(x_t @ Wk)          # only the new token's K and V are computed
    cache["v"].append(x_t @ Wv)
    K, V = np.stack(cache["k"]), np.stack(cache["v"])
    s = K @ q / np.sqrt(len(q))
    p = np.exp(s - s.max())
    return (p / p.sum()) @ V
problems.tests:

rng = np.random.default_rng(0)
T, d = 7, 8
X = rng.normal(size=(T, d)); Wq, Wk, Wv = (rng.normal(size=(d, d)) for _ in range(3))
Q, K, V = X @ Wq, X @ Wk, X @ Wv
S = Q @ K.T / np.sqrt(d) + np.triu(np.full((T, T), -np.inf), 1)
P = np.exp(S - S.max(1, keepdims=True)); full = (P / P.sum(1, keepdims=True)) @ V
cache = {"k": [], "v": []}
inc = np.stack([decode_step(X[t], cache, Wq, Wk, Wv) for t in range(T)])
check(inc, full, "token-by-token equals full causal attention")
check(len(cache["k"]), T)

problems.title: Int8 Weight Quantization (per channel)
problems.prompt: Symmetric per-output-channel int8: for each row of W, scale = max|row| / 127 (use 1 for an all-zero row), q = round(W / scale) clipped to [-127, 127] as int8. Return (q, scale) with scale shaped (rows, 1), and write dequantize(q, scale).
problems.solution:
import numpy as np

def quantize_int8(W):
    W = np.asarray(W, float)
    amax = np.abs(W).max(axis=1, keepdims=True)
    scale = np.where(amax > 0, amax / 127, 1.0)
    q = np.clip(np.round(W / scale), -127, 127).astype(np.int8)
    return q, scale

def dequantize(q, scale):
    return q.astype(float) * scale
problems.tests:

problems.title: Cross-Entropy Loss and Its Gradient
problems.prompt: logits (n, k), integer labels (n,). Return (loss, grad): the mean cross-entropy and its gradient with respect to the logits, (softmax - one_hot) / n. Compute log-softmax stably.
problems.solution:
import numpy as np

def cross_entropy(logits, labels):
    logits = np.asarray(logits, float)
    n = logits.shape[0]
    z = logits - logits.max(axis=1, keepdims=True)
    log_p = z - np.log(np.exp(z).sum(axis=1, keepdims=True))
    loss = -log_p[np.arange(n), labels].mean()
    grad = np.exp(log_p)
    grad[np.arange(n), labels] -= 1
    return loss, grad / n
problems.tests:
import numpy as np
loss, grad = cross_entropy([[2.0, 1.0, 0.1]], [0])
check(loss, 0.41702997)
check(grad, [[-0.34099886, 0.24243297, 0.09856589]])
rng = np.random.default_rng(0); L = rng.normal(size=(4, 5)); y = np.array([0, 3, 1, 4])
_, g = cross_entropy(L, y); eps = 1e-6; E = np.zeros_like(L); E[2, 1] = eps
num = (cross_entropy(L + E, y)[0] - cross_entropy(L - E, y)[0]) / (2 * eps)
check(g[2, 1], num, "matches a finite-difference check")

problems.title: Two-Layer MLP Backprop
problems.prompt: forward_backward(X, y, W1, b1, W2, b2) runs h = relu(X @ W1 + b1), out = h @ W2 + b2, loss = mean squared error mean((out - y)²), and returns (loss, {"W1": …, "b1": …, "W2": …, "b2": …}) gradients.
problems.solution:
import numpy as np

def forward_backward(X, y, W1, b1, W2, b2):
    z = X @ W1 + b1
    h = np.maximum(z, 0)
    out = h @ W2 + b2
    diff = out - y
    loss = (diff ** 2).mean()
    d_out = 2 * diff / diff.size
    grads = {"W2": h.T @ d_out, "b2": d_out.sum(0)}
    d_z = (d_out @ W2.T) * (z > 0)
    grads["W1"] = X.T @ d_z
    grads["b1"] = d_z.sum(0)
    return loss, grads
problems.tests:
import numpy as np
rng = np.random.default_rng(0)
X, y = rng.normal(size=(8, 3)), rng.normal(size=(8, 2))
P = {"W1": rng.normal(size=(3, 5)), "b1": rng.normal(size=5), "W2": rng.normal(size=(5, 2)), "b2": rng.normal(size=2)}
loss, g = forward_backward(X, y, **P)
for name in P:
    num = np.zeros_like(P[name]); eps = 1e-6
    for idx in np.ndindex(P[name].shape):
        Pp = {k: v.copy() for k, v in P.items()}; Pp[name][idx] += eps
        Pm = {k: v.copy() for k, v in P.items()}; Pm[name][idx] -= eps
        num[idx] = (forward_backward(X, y, **Pp)[0] - forward_backward(X, y, **Pm)[0]) / (2 * eps)
    check(g[name], num, f"d loss / d {name} matches finite differences", tol=1e-4)

problems.title: Scaled Dot-Product Attention with a Causal Mask
problems.prompt: q, k, v have shape (T, d). Return softmax(q kᵀ / √d + mask) v, where with causal=True position i may only attend to positions ≤ i.
problems.solution:
import numpy as np

def attention(q, k, v, causal=False):
    T, d = q.shape
    s = q @ k.T / np.sqrt(d)
    if causal:
        s = np.where(np.tril(np.ones((T, k.shape[0]), bool)), s, -np.inf)
    s = s - s.max(-1, keepdims=True)
    p = np.exp(s)
    p /= p.sum(-1, keepdims=True)
    return p @ v
problems.tests:

problems.title: Multi-Head Attention
problems.prompt: x (T, d_model), weights Wq, Wk, Wv, Wo (d_model, d_model), n_heads divides d_model. Project, split into heads (n_heads, T, d_head), run causal attention per head, merge back to (T, d_model) and apply Wo. Use batched matmuls, not a Python loop over heads.
problems.solution:
import numpy as np

def mha(x, Wq, Wk, Wv, Wo, n_heads):
    T, D = x.shape
    dh = D // n_heads
    def split(t):                               # (T, D) -> (H, T, dh)
        return t.reshape(T, n_heads, dh).transpose(1, 0, 2)
    q, k, v = split(x @ Wq), split(x @ Wk), split(x @ Wv)
    s = q @ k.transpose(0, 2, 1) / np.sqrt(dh)  # (H, T, T)
    s = np.where(np.tril(np.ones((T, T), bool)), s, -np.inf)
    p = np.exp(s - s.max(-1, keepdims=True))
    p /= p.sum(-1, keepdims=True)
    out = (p @ v).transpose(1, 0, 2).reshape(T, D)
    return out @ Wo
problems.tests:
import numpy as np
rng = np.random.default_rng(1)
T, D, H = 6, 8, 2
x = rng.normal(size=(T, D)); W = [rng.normal(size=(D, D)) / np.sqrt(D) for _ in range(4)]
def ref(x, Wq, Wk, Wv, Wo, H):
    dh = D // H; heads = []
    for h in range(H):
        sl = slice(h * dh, (h + 1) * dh)
        q, k, v = (x @ Wq)[:, sl], (x @ Wk)[:, sl], (x @ Wv)[:, sl]
        s = q @ k.T / np.sqrt(dh) + np.triu(np.full((T, T), -np.inf), 1)
        p = np.exp(s - s.max(1, keepdims=True)); p /= p.sum(1, keepdims=True)
        heads.append(p @ v)
    return np.concatenate(heads, 1) @ Wo
check(mha(x, *W, H), ref(x, *W, H), "matches a per-head loop")
check(mha(x, *W, 1), ref(x, *W, 1), "one head")

problems.title: Top-k and Top-p (Nucleus) Filtering
problems.prompt: Given logits (V,), return a probability vector after filtering. top_k: keep the k largest logits. top_p: keep the smallest set of tokens, taken by descending probability, whose total probability reaches p (always keep at least one). Renormalise; everything else is 0. Apply top_k first when both are set.
problems.solution:
import numpy as np

def filter_probs(logits, top_k=None, top_p=None):
    logits = np.asarray(logits, float).copy()
    if top_k is not None:
        kth = np.sort(logits)[-top_k]
        logits[logits < kth] = -np.inf
    p = np.exp(logits - logits.max())
    p /= p.sum()
    if top_p is not None:
        order = np.argsort(-p, kind="stable")
        cum = np.cumsum(p[order])
        keep = order[: int(np.searchsorted(cum, top_p - 1e-12)) + 1]
        mask = np.zeros_like(p, bool)
        mask[keep] = True
        p = np.where(mask, p, 0)
        p /= p.sum()
    return p
problems.tests:
import numpy as np
lg = np.log([0.5, 0.3, 0.15, 0.05])
check(filter_probs(lg, top_k=2), [0.625, 0.375, 0, 0])
check(filter_probs(lg, top_p=0.8), [0.625, 0.375, 0, 0], "0.5 + 0.3 reaches 0.8")
check(filter_probs(lg, top_p=0.81), [0.5 / 0.95, 0.3 / 0.95, 0.15 / 0.95, 0])
check(filter_probs(lg, top_p=0.1), [1, 0, 0, 0], "keeps at least one token")
check(filter_probs(lg), [0.5, 0.3, 0.15, 0.05])

problems.title: Ring All-Reduce
problems.prompt: Simulate ring all-reduce over n workers, each holding an array split into n chunks. Reduce-scatter: in step s, worker i sends chunk (i − s) mod n to worker i+1, which adds it in. All-gather: in step s, worker i sends chunk (i + 1 − s) mod n to worker i+1, which overwrites. All sends in a step happen at once. Return (arrays, steps) where every worker ends with the elementwise sum and steps == 2(n − 1).
problems.solution:
import numpy as np

def ring_allreduce(arrays):
    n = len(arrays)
    chunks = [np.array_split(np.array(a, dtype=float), n) for a in arrays]
    steps = 0
    for s in range(n - 1):                               # reduce-scatter
        sends = [(i, (i - s) % n, chunks[i][(i - s) % n].copy()) for i in range(n)]
        for i, c, data in sends:
            chunks[(i + 1) % n][c] += data
        steps += 1
    for s in range(n - 1):                               # all-gather
        sends = [(i, (i + 1 - s) % n, chunks[i][(i + 1 - s) % n].copy()) for i in range(n)]
        for i, c, data in sends:
            chunks[(i + 1) % n][c] = data
        steps += 1
    return [np.concatenate(c) for c in chunks], steps
problems.tests:
import numpy as np
rng = np.random.default_rng(1)
arrs = [rng.normal(size=10) for _ in range(4)]
out, steps = ring_allreduce(arrs)
check_true(all(np.allclose(o, sum(arrs)) for o in out), "every worker holds the sum")
check(steps, 6)
out, steps = ring_allreduce([np.ones(3), 2 * np.ones(3)])
check([o.tolist() for o in out], [[3, 3, 3], [3, 3, 3]]); check(steps, 2)
